mcqs.why: A cation is always smaller than its parent atom because the electron cloud contracts when electrons are removed.

mcqs.q: Why does an anion become larger than its parent atom?
options: A new shell is always added
Added electrons increase electron-electron repulsion and expand the cloud
mcqs.why: When electrons are added, increased electron-electron repulsion expands the electron cloud, enlarging the anion.

mcqs.q: Cationic radii down a group follow which sequence in the notes?
mcqs.why: Cationic radii increase down a group as shells are added: Li+ 76, Na+ 102, K+ 138 and Rb+ 152 pm.

mcqs.q: Across a period, cationic radii for Na+, Mg2+, Al3+, Si4+ do what?
mcqs.why: Cationic radii decrease across a period with increased nuclear charge: Na+ 102, Mg2+ 72, Al3+ 54, Si4+ 40 pm.

mcqs.q: The ionic radius of Cl- compared with Br- and I- follows what trend?
options: Cl- 181, Br- 196, I- 220 pm, increasing down the group
mcqs.why: Anionic radii increase down a group with shells: Cl- 181 pm, Br- 196 pm and I- 220 pm in the notes.

mcqs.q: The O2- ion has radius 140 pm while the oxygen atom is 66 pm. This shows what?
options: Anions are much larger than their parent atoms
mcqs.why: O2- at 140 pm versus the O atom at 66 pm shows anions remain much larger than their parent atoms.

mcqs.q: When electrons are removed to form a cation, electron-electron repulsion does what?
options: Decreases, letting the positive charge draw remaining electrons closer
mcqs.why: Loss of electrons decreases repulsion, allowing the positive charge to draw remaining electrons closer to the nucleus.

mcqs.q: F- has radius 133 pm while the F atom is 64 pm. F- is what?
options: Larger, as expected for an anion
mcqs.why: F- at 133 pm is larger than the F atom at 64 pm, consistent with anions being larger than parent atoms.

mcqs.q: Ionic radii generally increase down a group because of what?
mcqs.why: Both cationic and anionic radii increase down a group due to the increase in the number of electronic shells.

mcqs.q: Na atom is 186 pm but Na+ is 102 pm. The contraction is because Na+ has what?
options: Lost an electron, so its cloud contracts
mcqs.why: Sodium loses an electron to form Na+, the cloud contracts from 186 pm to 102 pm as repulsion falls.

lessons.notes_html:
Ionic radii are measurements of the sizes of charged particles called ions, which are formed when atoms gain or lose electrons. The size of an ion is different from that of the neutral atom because of changes in the arrangement of its electrons. Ionic radii are usually measured in nanometres, angstroms or picometres.

Cationic and Anionic Radii

  • Cationic radii: when electrons are removed, the electron cloud contracts. The loss of electrons decreases electron-electron repulsion, allowing the positive charge to draw the remaining electrons closer to the nucleus, so a cation is smaller than its parent atom.
  • Anionic radii: when electrons are added, the electron cloud expands because of increased electron-electron repulsion, so an anion is larger than its parent atom.

Trends in Ionic Radii

Cationic radii generally increase down a group due to the increase in electronic shells: Li+ 76 pm, Na+ 102 pm, K+ 138 pm, Rb+ 152 pm. Cationic radii generally decrease across a period due to increased nuclear charge while the number of shells remains constant:

ElementNaMgAlSi
Atomic radius (pm)186160143118
Ion formedNa+Mg2+Al3+Si4+
Ionic radius (pm)102725440

Anionic radii also increase down a group with the number of shells: Cl- 181 pm, Br- 196 pm, I- 220 pm (compare the atomic radii Cl 99 pm, Br 114 pm, I 133 pm). Along a period, anions remain much larger than their parent atoms, e.g. O2- 140 pm (atom 66 pm) and F- 133 pm (atom 64 pm).

Key Points

  • A cation is always smaller than its parent atom; an anion is always larger.
  • Removing electrons contracts the electron cloud; adding electrons expands it.
  • Ionic radii increase down a group as shells are added.
  • Cationic radii decrease across a period as nuclear charge increases.
lessons.title: Ionic Radii of Elements

mcqs.q: Ionisation energy is defined as the minimum energy required to do what?
options: Add an electron to a gaseous atom
Remove a proton from the nucleus
Remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom or ion
Break all bonds in a molecule
mcqs.why: Ionisation energy is the minimum energy to remove the most loosely bound electron of an isolated gaseous atom or ion.

mcqs.q: The ionisation energy of sodium, Na(g) -> Na+(g) + e-, is given as what?
mcqs.why: The example in the notes gives Na IE = 496 kJ/mol, lower than magnesium's 738 kJ/mol in the same period.

mcqs.q: A greater nuclear charge has what effect on ionisation energy?
options: It raises IE, binding electrons more tightly
mcqs.why: Greater nuclear charge binds electrons more tightly to the nucleus, so the ionisation energy is higher.

mcqs.q: A larger atomic radius leads to what change in IE?
options: Lower IE, because outer electrons are farther and less tightly held
mcqs.why: The larger the atomic radius, the lower the IE, because outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Inner-electron shielding affects IE how?
options: It lowers IE by reducing the effective nuclear charge on outer electrons
mcqs.why: Shielding reduces the effective nuclear charge felt by outer electrons, lowering the ionisation energy.

mcqs.q: Electrons in which orbital are most difficult to remove?
mcqs.why: Electrons in the s orbital are more difficult to remove than those in p, d or f orbitals, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is oxygen easier to ionise than nitrogen?
options: Oxygen has spin-pair repulsion in one 2p orbital; nitrogen's half-filled 2p3 is more stable
mcqs.why: Oxygen (2p4) has paired electrons repelling each other, while nitrogen's half-filled 2p3 has no spin-pair repulsion.

mcqs.q: Across a period, ionisation energy generally does what?
options: Increases, due to rising nuclear charge and decreasing radius
mcqs.why: Across a period IE generally increases due to an increase in nuclear charge and a decrease in atomic radius.

mcqs.q: Down a group, ionisation energy generally does what?
options: Decreases, due to increased atomic size and shielding
mcqs.why: Down a group IE generally decreases due to an increase in atomic size and the shielding effect.

mcqs.q: Half-filled and fully-filled subshells affect IE how?
options: They make IE unpredictable and zero
They give extra stability and higher ionisation energies
mcqs.why: Half-filled and fully-filled orbitals are more stable, so such elements have higher ionisation energies, an exception to trends.

lessons.notes_html:
Ionisation energy (IE) is the minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron of an isolated gaseous atom, positive ion or molecule. It is usually measured in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol) or electron volts (eV). For example: Na(g) → Na+(g) + e-, IE = 496 kJ/mol; Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e-, IE = 738 kJ/mol.

Factors Affecting Ionisation Energy

  • Nuclear charge: the greater the nuclear charge, the higher the ionisation energy, because a larger nuclear charge binds the electrons more tightly to the nucleus.
  • Atomic size (radius): the larger the atomic radius, the lower the ionisation energy, because the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held.
  • Electron shielding (shielding effect): inner electrons shield the outer electrons from part of the nuclear attraction, reducing the effective nuclear charge and lowering the ionisation energy.
  • Subshell and orbital: electrons in higher energy subshells are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are easier to remove; electrons in the s orbital are more difficult to remove than those in p, d or f orbitals.
  • Spin-pair repulsion: two electrons with opposite spins in the same orbital repel each other, which lowers the energy needed to remove one of them. Oxygen (2p4) has paired electrons in one 2p orbital, so oxygen is easier to ionise than nitrogen, whose half-filled 2p3 subshell is more stable and has no spin-pair repulsion.

Trends in Ionisation Energy

  • Across a period: ionisation energy generally increases, due to an increase in nuclear charge and a decrease in atomic radius.
  • Down a group: ionisation energy generally decreases, due to an increase in atomic size and the shielding effect.
  • Exception to trends: half-filled and fully-filled orbitals are more stable than partially-filled ones, so elements with half-filled or fully-filled orbitals have higher ionisation energies.

Key Points

  • Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the most loosely bound electron from a gaseous atom or ion.
  • IE rises with nuclear charge and falls with atomic size and shielding.
  • IE increases across a period and decreases down a group.
  • Half-filled and fully-filled subshells give extra stability and higher IE (e.g. N higher than O).
lessons.title: Ionisation Energy

mcqs.q: Successive ionisation energies are always in which order?
mcqs.why: Successive ionisation energies always increase: IE3 is greater than IE2, which is greater than IE1.

mcqs.q: For magnesium, IE1, IE2 and IE3 are given as what?
mcqs.why: Magnesium's successive values are IE1 = 738, IE2 = 1451 and IE3 = 7730 kJ/mol in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why do successive ionisation energies increase?
options: The ion becomes more positive and smaller, so remaining electrons are held more strongly
mcqs.why: As electrons are removed the ion becomes more positively charged and more compact, increasing attraction for the rest.

mcqs.q: For aluminium, a large jump occurs at which successive IE?
options: The fourth, rising to 11577 kJ/mol after 577, 1817, 2745
mcqs.why: Aluminium values 577, 1817, 2745 then jump to 11577 and 14842, showing the fourth electron is from an inner shell.

mcqs.q: A significant jump in successive IE indicates what?
options: Electrons are in the same outer shell
The next electron is being removed from an inner shell
The element is a noble gas
The atom has gained a shell
mcqs.why: A big jump suggests removal from an inner shell, while small increases mean electrons come from the same outer shell.

mcqs.q: Beryllium's IE3 jumps to 14849 kJ/mol because the third electron comes from where?
mcqs.why: Be IE1 = 899 and IE2 = 1757 remove the 2s electrons; IE3 = 14849 jumps because the third electron is from inner 1s.

mcqs.q: From its successive IEs, beryllium is deduced to be in which group and period?
mcqs.why: The jump after two electrons deduces 1s2 2s2, two valence electrons in shell 2, placing Be in Group 2, Period 2.

mcqs.q: What does the position of the big IE jump reveal about an element?
options: The number of valence electrons, and hence its group
mcqs.why: The position of the jump reveals the number of valence electrons, and hence the group of the element.

mcqs.q: As electrons are removed successively, the ion's size does what?
options: It becomes smaller and more compact
mcqs.why: The ion becomes smaller and more compact as electrons are removed, increasing attraction for remaining electrons.

mcqs.q: Relatively small increases between successive IEs indicate electrons are removed from where?
mcqs.why: A relatively small increase indicates electrons are being removed from the same outer shell, per the notes.

lessons.notes_html:
Successive ionisation energy is the energy required to remove the outermost electron from an atom, followed by the energy required to remove the next electron, and so on, until all electrons have been removed. The energies used to remove the first, second and third electrons are called the first (IE1), second (IE2) and third (IE3) ionisation energies. For magnesium: Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e-, IE1 = 738 kJ/mol; Mg+(g) → Mg2+(g) + e-, IE2 = 1451 kJ/mol; Mg2+(g) → Mg3+(g) + e-, IE3 = 7730 kJ/mol.

Why Successive Ionisation Energies Increase

The order is always IE3 greater than IE2 greater than IE1. As electrons are removed, the atom becomes more positively charged, making it harder to remove another electron; the ion also becomes smaller and more compact, increasing the attraction for the remaining electrons. For aluminium the successive values (kJ/mol) are 577, 1817, 2745, then a large jump to 11577 and 14842, showing that the fourth electron comes from an inner shell.

Prediction of Electronic Configuration and Position of Elements from Ionisation Energies

The electronic configuration and position of an element can be predicted by analysing its successive ionisation energies. A relatively small increase in successive ionisation energies indicates that electrons are being removed from the same outer shell, while a significant jump suggests that the next electron is being removed from an inner shell. For beryllium, IE1 = 899 kJ/mol and IE2 = 1757 kJ/mol are for the two outermost 2s electrons, but IE3 = 14849 kJ/mol jumps sharply because the third electron comes from the inner 1s orbital. This deduces the configuration 1s2 2s2, with two valence electrons in the second shell, placing beryllium in Group 2 and Period 2.

Key Points

  • Successive ionisation energies always increase: each next electron is harder to remove.
  • The ion shrinks and its positive charge grows as electrons are removed.
  • A big jump in successive IE marks the start of removal from an inner shell.
  • The position of the jump reveals the number of valence electrons, and hence the group of the element.
lessons.title: Successive Ionisation Energy

mcqs.q: What are chemical bonds?
options: Forces that hold atoms or ions together in compounds
The motion of electrons inside a nucleus
mcqs.why: The notes define chemical bonds as the forces of attraction that hold atoms or ions together in compounds.

mcqs.q: Why do atoms gain, lose or share electrons when bonding?
options: To complete their valence shell and become stable like noble gases
mcqs.why: Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to complete their valence shell with 2 or 8 electrons, like noble gases, and become stable.

mcqs.q: What is electronegativity?
options: The energy needed to remove an electron
The size of an atom in a molecule
A measure of the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract bonding electrons to itself
The charge on an ion after bonding
mcqs.why: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract bonding (shared) electrons to itself.

mcqs.q: Which element attracts bonding electrons most strongly?
mcqs.why: The notes state that fluorine attracts bonding electrons most strongly, while caesium attracts them very weakly.

mcqs.q: How does atomic radius affect electronegativity?
options: Electronegativity decreases as atomic radius increases
Electronegativity increases as atomic radius increases
Atomic radius has no effect on electronegativity
Electronegativity first rises then falls with radius
mcqs.why: As atomic radius increases the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and attracted weakly, so electronegativity decreases.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of the shielding effect on electronegativity?
options: It lowers electronegativity by shielding outer electrons from the nuclear charge
It has no effect at all
mcqs.why: Electrons in inner shells partly shield the outer electrons from the full effect of the nuclear charge, lowering electronegativity.

mcqs.q: How does electronegativity change along a period from left to right?
options: It increases because nuclear charge increases
It becomes zero for all elements
mcqs.why: Along a period electronegativity increases from left to right because nuclear charge increases; noble gases are taken as zero.

mcqs.q: On Pauling's scale, what are the lowest and highest electronegativity values?
options: 0.00 for noble gases and 3.00 for chlorine
mcqs.why: On Pauling's scale the values range from 0.70 for francium to 3.98 for fluorine, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: A bond has an electronegativity difference (ΔEN) of 1.0. What type of bond is it?
options: Polar covalent, because ΔEN between 0.4 and 1.7 means polar covalent
Ionic, because any difference means ionic
Purely covalent, because ΔEN below 2 is covalent
mcqs.why: Working: ΔEN = 1.0 lies between 0.4 and 1.7. The notes classify 0.4–1.7 as polar covalent, so the bond is polar covalent.

mcqs.q: In HF, ΔEN is about 1.9, near the ionic range. What does the notes say about the HF bond?
options: It is a purely ionic bond
It remains polar covalent rather than ionic
It is a nonpolar covalent bond
mcqs.why: The notes point out that in HF, ΔEN is about 1.9, near the ionic range, yet the bond remains polar covalent rather than ionic.

lessons.notes_html:
The forces of attraction that hold atoms or ions together in compounds are called chemical bonds. Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to complete their valence shell (2 or 8 electrons, like noble gases) and become stable. Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract bonding electrons (shared electrons) to itself. Fluorine attracts bonding electrons most strongly; caesium very weakly.

Factors Affecting Electronegativity

  • Nuclear charge: electronegativity generally increases as nuclear charge (number of protons) increases.
  • Atomic radius: electronegativity decreases as atomic radius increases, because the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and are attracted weakly.
  • Shielding effect: electrons in inner shells partly shield the outer electrons from the full effect of the nuclear charge, lowering electronegativity.

Electronegativity Trends in the Periodic Table

  • Along a period: electronegativity increases from left to right, because nuclear charge increases. Noble gases are taken as zero and do not follow the trend.
  • Down a group: electronegativity decreases from top to bottom, because atomic size and shielding effect increase.
  • Fluorine is the most electronegative atom and caesium the least. Elements at the top right have high values; those at the left have low values.

Pauling's Electronegativity Values to Predict the Formation of Ionic and Covalent Bonds

On Pauling's scale, values range from 0.70 (francium) to 3.98 (fluorine). The greater the difference in electronegativity (ΔEN) between the bonding atoms, the greater the bond polarity and the stronger the bond. ΔEN = larger value − smaller value.

ΔENBond Type
0Purely covalent (100% covalent)
0.4 or lessNonpolar covalent
Between 0.4 and 1.7Polar covalent
Equal to 1.750% covalent and 50% ionic, regarded as ionic
Exceeds 1.7Ionic

Note: in HF, ΔEN is about 1.9, near the ionic range, yet the bond remains polar covalent rather than ionic. Sharing in covalent bonds is rarely equal: in polar covalent H−Cl, one atom pulls electrons more strongly, giving partial charges.

Key Points

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom in a molecule to attract shared electrons to itself.
  • It increases with nuclear charge and decreases with atomic radius and shielding effect.
  • It increases along a period and decreases down a group; F is highest, Cs is lowest.
  • Pauling scale: 0.70 (Fr) to 3.98 (F).
  • ΔEN up to 0.4 = nonpolar covalent; 0.4–1.7 = polar covalent; above 1.7 = ionic.
lessons.title: Electronegativity

mcqs.q: Who formalised the VSEPR theory and in which year?
mcqs.why: Sidgwick and Powell laid the groundwork in 1940, but Gillespie and Nyholm formalised the VSEPR theory in 1957.

mcqs.q: According to VSEPR theory, what does the shape of a molecule depend on?
options: The mass of the central atom only
The number of electron pairs in the outermost shell of the central atom
The melting point of the substance
mcqs.why: VSEPR says shapes depend on the number of electron pairs, both bond pairs and lone pairs, in the outermost shell of the central atom.

mcqs.q: Why do electron pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible?
options: To minimise repulsion between their negative charges
mcqs.why: Electron pairs repel each other because of their negative charges, and this repulsion is minimised at the greatest possible angular distances.

mcqs.q: Which repulsion is the strongest according to VSEPR theory?
mcqs.why: The order of repulsion is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, so lp–lp is strongest.

mcqs.q: How is a multiple bond (double or triple) treated in VSEPR theory?
options: As two or three separate electron pairs
As a single electron pair for structure determination
mcqs.why: The notes state that a multiple bond is treated as a single electron pair for structure determination in VSEPR theory.

mcqs.q: What shape do molecules with only bond pairs have?
mcqs.why: Molecules with only bond pairs have regular shapes, while those with lone pairs exhibit irregular shapes.

mcqs.q: Why does a lone pair occupy more space than a bond pair?
options: Because it has a positive charge
Because it is heavier than a bond pair
mcqs.why: The notes state that a lone pair occupies more space than a bond pair due to strong repulsions.

mcqs.q: What is a limitation of VSEPR theory mentioned in the notes?
options: It does not give a detailed explanation of electron sharing in covalent σ and π bonds
It cannot predict any molecular shape
It only works for ionic compounds
mcqs.why: VSEPR does not give a detailed explanation of electron sharing in covalent sigma and pi bonds, which is essential for understanding bond formation.

mcqs.q: What did Sidgwick and Powell do in 1940?
options: They laid the groundwork for explaining molecular shapes from electron pair arrangement
mcqs.why: In 1940 Sidgwick and Powell laid the groundwork for explaining molecular shapes from the arrangement of electron pairs in the valence shell.

mcqs.q: What happens to bond-pair repulsion when the attached atom is more electronegative?
options: It increases the effect of bond pairs
It has no effect on bond pairs
It reduces the effect of bond pairs
It converts bond pairs into lone pairs
mcqs.why: A higher electronegativity of the central atom increases repulsions, while that of the attached atom reduces the effect of bond pairs.

lessons.notes_html:
In 1940, Sidgwick and Powell laid the groundwork for explaining molecular shapes from the arrangement of electron pairs in the valence shell. In 1957, Gillespie and Nyholm formalised the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory, which explains the shapes and bond angles of molecules and ions through electrostatic repulsion between electron pairs.

Main Features (Postulates) of VSEPR Theory

  • The shapes of molecules depend on the number of electron pairs (both bond pairs and lone pairs) in the outermost shell of the central atom.
  • Electron pairs in the outer shell repel each other because of their negative charges. This repulsion is minimised by placing the electron pairs at the greatest possible angular distances from each other.
  • A lone pair (lp) occupies more space (due to strong repulsions) than a bond pair (bp).
  • The order of repulsion is: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
  • A multiple bond (double or triple) is treated as a single electron pair for structure determination.
  • Molecules with only bond pairs have regular shapes, while those with lone pairs exhibit irregular shapes.

A higher electronegativity of the central atom increases repulsions between bonding pairs, while that of the attached atom reduces the effect of bond pairs. Limitation: VSEPR theory does not give a detailed explanation of electron sharing in covalent (σ and π) bonds, which is essential for understanding bond formation.

Key Points

  • VSEPR theory was formalised by Gillespie and Nyholm in 1957.
  • Molecular shape depends on the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.
  • Electron pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion.
  • Repulsion order: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp.
  • A multiple bond counts as one electron pair.
  • Only bond pairs = regular shape; lone pairs present = irregular shape.
lessons.title: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) Theory: Understanding Molecular Geometry

mcqs.q: In the formula ABmEn for molecular geometry, what does n represent?
options: The atomic number of the central atom
The number of lone pairs on the central atom
mcqs.why: In ABmEn, B is a bonded atom and E is a lone pair; m is the number of bonded atoms and n is the number of lone pairs.

mcqs.q: What is the shape and bond angle of a molecule with 2 electron pairs (AB2)?
mcqs.why: Two electron pairs give a linear AB2 shape with a bond angle of 180°, as in BeCl2, CO2 and HgCl2.

mcqs.q: What is the bond angle in a tetrahedral AB4 molecule such as CH4?
mcqs.why: Four electron pairs in an AB4 arrangement give a tetrahedral shape with a bond angle of 109.5°, as in CH4 and CCl4.

mcqs.q: What is the H–N–H bond angle in NH3 (AB3E)?
mcqs.why: NH3 is AB3E, trigonal pyramidal, with a bond angle of 107.5°, less than 109.5° because the lone pair compresses the bond angles.

mcqs.q: What is the bond angle in H2O (AB2E2)?
mcqs.why: Water is AB2E2, angular or bent, with a bond angle of 104.5°, reduced below 109.5° by its two lone pairs.

mcqs.q: What shape does an AB5 molecule such as PF5 have?
mcqs.why: Five electron pairs give a trigonal (triangular) bipyramidal shape, as in PF5 and PCl5, with 120° equatorial and 90° axial angles.

mcqs.q: In PF5, which bonds are slightly longer and why?
options: Equatorial bonds, because they face less repulsion
All bonds are exactly equal in PF5
Equatorial bonds, because they are double bonds
Axial bonds, because they face more repulsion from the equatorial atoms
mcqs.why: In PF5 the axial fluorine atoms face more repulsion from the equatorial atoms, so axial bonds are slightly longer than equatorial bonds.

mcqs.q: What is the shape and bond angle of an AB6 molecule such as SF6?
mcqs.why: Six electron pairs give an octahedral shape with 90° bond angles, as in SF6 and TeF6, where all six bonds are equivalent.

mcqs.q: What shape does an AB2E molecule such as SO2 have?
options: Distorted triangular / bent, with angle less than 120°
mcqs.why: AB2E molecules such as SO2 and SnCl2 are distorted triangular or bent, with a bond angle of less than 120° due to the lone pair.

mcqs.q: Why does a lone pair compress the angles between bond pairs?
options: Because lone pairs attract bond pairs
Because lone pairs have no charge
Because of lone pair repulsion, which is stronger than bond pair repulsion
Because lone pairs increase the atomic size
mcqs.why: A lone pair compresses the angles between bond pairs because lone pair repulsion is stronger than bond pair–bond pair repulsion.

lessons.notes_html:
The geometry around a central atom A is described by the formula ABmEn, where B is a bonded atom, E is a lone pair, m is the number of bonded atoms and n is the number of lone pairs.

Electron PairsTypeShapeBond AngleExamples
2AB2Linear180°BeCl2, CdCl2, CO2, CS2, HgCl2
3AB3Planar triangular (trigonal planar)120°BCl3, AlCl3, CO3^2-, SO3
3AB2EDistorted triangular / bentLess than 120°SnCl2, SO2
4AB4Tetrahedral109.5°SiH4, CCl4, NH4+, SO4^2-, CH4
4AB3ETrigonal pyramidalLess than 109.5° (107.5° in NH3, H3O+)NH3, NF3, H3O+
4AB2E2Angular / bentLess than 109.5° (104.5° in H2O)H2O, H2S, SCl2, NH2-, SeCl2
5AB5Trigonal (triangular) bipyramidal120° equatorial, 90° axialPF5, PCl5, SbCl5
6AB6Octahedral90°SF6, TeF6

In PF5, the axial fluorine atoms face more repulsion from the equatorial atoms, so axial bonds are slightly longer than equatorial bonds. In an octahedral molecule the terms axial and equatorial are not used, because all six bonds are equivalent. A lone pair compresses the angles between bond pairs because of lone pair repulsion.

Key Points

  • Geometry is written as ABmEn: m = bonded atoms, n = lone pairs on the central atom.
  • 2 pairs = linear, 180°; 3 pairs = trigonal planar, 120°.
  • 4 pairs = tetrahedral, 109.5°; one lone pair gives pyramidal (107.5°), two lone pairs give bent (104.5°).
  • 5 pairs = trigonal bipyramidal, 120° and 90°.
  • 6 pairs = octahedral, 90°, with all bonds equivalent.
  • Lone pairs reduce bond angles below the regular values.
lessons.title: Shapes and Bond Angles in Molecules and Ions

mcqs.q: Who first proposed valence bond theory and in which year?
options: W. Heitler and Fritz London in 1927
mcqs.why: Valence bond theory was first proposed by W. Heitler and Fritz London in 1927 and later developed by Pauling and Slater in 1931.

mcqs.q: According to valence bond theory, how is a covalent bond formed?
options: By the overlapping of half-filled atomic orbitals in the valence shell
By complete transfer of electrons between atoms
By the movement of electrons in a sea of charges
By the repulsion of electron pairs
mcqs.why: VBT states that covalent bonds are formed by the overlapping of half-filled atomic orbitals in the valence shell.

mcqs.q: What happens to electrons when atomic orbitals overlap?
options: They are lost from the molecule
Electrons with opposite spins pair up and become stable by releasing energy
They gain energy and become unstable
mcqs.why: As a result of overlapping, electrons with opposite spins pair up and become stable by releasing energy.

mcqs.q: How does the extent of overlap affect bond strength?
options: Greater overlap gives a weaker bond
Overlap does not affect bond strength
Greater overlap gives a stronger bond
Less overlap gives a stronger bond
mcqs.why: The extent of overlap determines bond strength: the greater the overlapping, the stronger the bond.

mcqs.q: What is the ground state electron configuration of carbon given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The ground state of carbon is 1s2, 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz0: the 2s orbital is filled and only two p-orbitals are half-filled.

mcqs.q: How many bonds should carbon form based only on its ground state configuration?
options: Only two bonds, because only two p-orbitals are half-filled
Four bonds, because it has four valence electrons
Three bonds, because it has three p-orbitals
mcqs.why: In the ground state only two p-orbitals are half-filled, so carbon should form only two bonds, which contradicts the four bonds in methane.

mcqs.q: How is the excited state of carbon obtained?
options: By removing an electron from carbon
By promoting one 2s electron to the empty 2p orbital
By adding an electron to the 1s orbital
By pairing the two p electrons
mcqs.why: Promoting one 2s electron to the empty 2p orbital gives the excited state 1s2, 2s1, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz1 with four unpaired electrons.

mcqs.q: Why can VBT alone not explain the bonding in methane?
options: Because methane has no covalent bonds
Because it predicts three bond angles of 90° with different bond lengths, while all four C–H bonds are identical
Because methane is an ionic compound
mcqs.why: The p-orbitals are perpendicular, so VBT alone predicts 90° angles and different bond lengths, while experiment shows all four C–H bonds of methane are identical.

mcqs.q: What concept was introduced to explain molecules like methane that VBT alone cannot explain?
mcqs.why: VBT alone cannot explain polyatomic molecules like methane; the concept of hybridisation was introduced to explain this.

mcqs.q: What determines the direction of a covalent bond when orbitals other than s-orbitals are involved?
options: The direction of the two overlapping orbitals
mcqs.why: The direction of the bond is determined by the direction of the two overlapping orbitals when orbitals other than s-orbitals are involved.

lessons.notes_html:
Valence bond theory was first proposed by W. Heitler and Fritz London in 1927 and later developed by Linus Pauling and J.C. Slater in 1931. It explains bond formation (sharing of electrons), bond strength and the geometry of molecules.

Main Points

  • Covalent bonds are formed by the overlapping of half-filled atomic orbitals in the valence shell.
  • A single covalent bond is formed by the overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals.
  • A multiple bond (double or triple covalent bond) is formed by the overlap of more than two half-filled atomic orbitals. Overlapping means a common region of two orbitals with high electron density.
  • As a result of overlapping, the electrons with opposite spins pair up and become stable by releasing energy.
  • The extent of overlap determines bond strength: the greater the overlapping, the stronger the bond.
  • The direction of the bond is determined by the direction of the two overlapping orbitals, when orbitals other than s-orbitals are involved.

Bonding in Polyatomic Molecules: Methane as an Example

The ground state configuration of carbon is 1s2, 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz0: the 2s orbital is filled and only two p-orbitals are half-filled, so carbon should form only two bonds. Promoting one 2s electron to the empty 2p orbital gives the excited state 1s2, 2s1, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz1, with four unpaired electrons. But the p-orbitals are perpendicular, so three bond angles would be 90° with different bond lengths, while experiment shows all four C−H bonds of methane are identical. VBT alone cannot explain polyatomic molecules like methane; the concept of hybridisation was introduced to explain this.

Key Points

  • VBT: Heitler and London (1927); developed by Pauling and Slater (1931).
  • A covalent bond forms by overlap of half-filled valence orbitals.
  • Paired electrons with opposite spins release energy and become stable.
  • Greater overlap means a stronger bond.
  • Bond direction follows the direction of the overlapping orbitals.
  • VBT cannot explain the four identical bonds of CH4 without hybridisation.
lessons.title: Valence Bond Theory

mcqs.q: How is a sigma (σ) bond formed?
options: By sidewise overlap of two p-orbitals
By head-to-head (linear) overlap of two atomic orbitals
By transfer of electrons between atoms
By overlap of two filled orbitals only
mcqs.why: A sigma bond is formed by head-to-head (linear) overlap of two atomic orbitals, with electron density maximum around the bond axis.

mcqs.q: Which type of overlap forms the bond in H2?
mcqs.why: In H2 the half-filled 1s orbitals of two H atoms overlap along the bond axis, which is s–s overlap: H + H → H2.

mcqs.q: How is a pi (π) bond formed?
options: By head-on overlap along the bond axis
By sidewise (parallel) overlap of two p-orbitals
mcqs.why: A pi bond is formed by sidewise (parallel) overlap of two p-orbitals and is named after the Greek letter pi.

mcqs.q: Why are pi bonds weaker than sigma bonds?
options: Overlap in pi bonds is less effective than in sigma bonds
Pi bonds are formed only by s-orbitals
Pi bonds have higher electron density on the axis
mcqs.why: Overlap in pi bonds is less effective than in sigma bonds, so pi bonds are weaker than sigma bonds.

mcqs.q: What bonds are present in a double bond?
options: One sigma and one pi bond
mcqs.why: Single bonds are sigma bonds; a double bond has one sigma and one pi bond; a triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds.

mcqs.q: In the O2 molecule, how is the pi bond formed?
mcqs.why: In O2, head-on overlap of 2px orbitals forms the sigma bond and side-to-side overlap of 2py orbitals forms the pi bond (O=O).

mcqs.q: How many sigma and pi bonds are in the N2 molecule?
options: Two sigma and one pi bond
One sigma and two pi bonds
mcqs.why: In N2, linear overlap of 2px gives one sigma bond and parallel overlap of 2py and 2pz gives two pi bonds (N≡N).

mcqs.q: Which overlap forms the bond in HF?
options: s–p overlap: 1s of H with the half-filled 2p of F
p–p overlap of two fluorine atoms
s–s overlap of two hydrogen atoms
mcqs.why: In HF the 1s orbital of H overlaps with the half-filled 2p orbital of F; the filled orbitals of F do not take part, so it is s–p overlap.

mcqs.q: Where is electron density maximum in a pi bond?
options: Above and below the bond axis
mcqs.why: In a pi bond the electron density is maximum above and below the bond axis, unlike a sigma bond where it is on the axis.

mcqs.q: Which molecules are given as examples of p–p overlap?
options: F2, and also Cl2, Br2 and I2
mcqs.why: Half-filled p-orbitals overlapping head-on give F2 by p–p overlap, and the same type applies to Cl2, Br2 and I2.

lessons.notes_html:
On the basis of overlapping of orbitals, covalent bonds are of two types: sigma bond and pi-bond.

Sigma Bond (σ-bond)

A covalent bond formed by head-to-head (linear) overlap of two atomic orbitals, in which electron density is maximum around the bond axis, is a sigma bond.

OverlapExampleHow It Forms
s–sH2Half-filled 1s orbitals of two H atoms overlap along the bond axis: H + H → H2
p–pF2Half-filled p-orbitals of two atoms overlap head-on: F + F → F2 (also Cl2, Br2, I2)
s–pHF1s orbital of H overlaps with the half-filled 2p orbital of F; the filled orbitals of F do not take part

Pi Bond (π-bond)

The bond formed by sidewise (parallel) overlap of two p-orbitals is a pi bond, named after the Greek letter π. Overlap in pi bonds is less effective than in sigma bonds, so pi bonds are weaker. Single bonds are sigma bonds; a double bond has one sigma and one pi bond; a triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds.

  • O2 molecule: each O is 1s2, 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz2, with two half-filled p-orbitals. Head-on overlap of 2px orbitals forms the σ-bond; side-to-side overlap of 2py orbitals forms the π-bond, with electron density maximum above and below the bond axis (O=O).
  • N2 molecule: each N is 1s2, 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz1, with three half-filled p-orbitals. Linear overlap of 2px gives one σ-bond; parallel overlap of 2py and 2pz gives two π-bonds (N≡N).

Key Points

  • Sigma bond: head-to-head overlap; electron density maximum on the bond axis; stronger.
  • s–s overlap gives H2, p–p gives F2, s–p gives HF.
  • Pi bond: sidewise overlap of p-orbitals; density above and below the axis; weaker.
  • Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π; triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π.
  • O2 has one σ and one π bond; N2 has one σ and two π bonds.
lessons.title: Types of Overlapping and Nature of Covalent Bonds

mcqs.q: Who introduced hybridisation and in which year?
mcqs.why: In 1931 Linus Pauling introduced hybridisation to explain the geometric shapes of molecules like CH4, NH3, BeCl2, AlCl3 and H2O.

mcqs.q: What is hybridisation?
options: Atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies combine to form a new set of equivalent hybrid orbitals
Two atoms share a pair of electrons from one atom only
Electrons are transferred completely between atoms
Molecules repel each other in the valence shell
mcqs.why: Hybridisation is the combining of atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies to form a new set of equivalent atomic orbitals called hybrid orbitals.

mcqs.q: How many hybrid orbitals are produced compared with the atomic orbitals combined?
options: Always equal in number to the atomic orbitals combined
mcqs.why: The number of hybrid orbitals produced is always equal to the number of atomic orbitals combined.

mcqs.q: What is true about hybridised orbitals?
options: They are always equivalent in energy and shape
mcqs.why: The hybridised orbitals are always equivalent in energy and shape, and a hybrid orbital is not a pure atomic orbital.

mcqs.q: When does hybridisation occur in an atom?
options: In an isolated atom at rest
Only during a chemical reaction with another element
Within the central atom, after excitation and before bond formation
mcqs.why: Hybridisation occurs within the central atom, after excitation and before bond formation; the concept is not used for isolated atoms.

mcqs.q: How do bonds formed by hybrid orbitals compare with those from pure atomic orbitals?
options: Hybrid orbitals form stronger, more stable bonds
Both form bonds of exactly equal strength
mcqs.why: The notes state that hybrid orbitals form stronger, more stable bonds than pure atomic orbitals.

mcqs.q: Which molecules did Pauling use hybridisation to explain, as listed in the notes?
options: CH4, NH3, BeCl2, AlCl3 and H2O, and multiple bonds in C2H2 and C2H4
mcqs.why: Pauling introduced hybridisation to explain the shapes of CH4, NH3, BeCl2, AlCl3 and H2O and multiple bonds in C2H2 and C2H4.

mcqs.q: What kinds of atomic orbitals are combined in hybridisation?
options: At least two non-equivalent atomic orbitals, such as s and p
mcqs.why: Hybridisation combines at least two non-equivalent atomic orbitals, such as s and p, so a hybrid orbital is not a pure atomic orbital.

mcqs.q: How do the geometries from hybridisation compare with VSEPR predictions?
options: They apply only to ionic solids
They match only for linear molecules
They match precisely those predicted by VSEPR theory
mcqs.why: The notes state that the geometries from hybridisation match precisely those predicted by VSEPR theory.

mcqs.q: How does the shape of a hybrid orbital compare with the original atomic orbitals?
options: The shape of a hybrid orbital differs from that of the original atomic orbitals
It is identical to an s-orbital
It is identical to a p-orbital
Hybrid orbitals have no definite shape
mcqs.why: The notes list as a feature that the shape of a hybrid orbital differs from that of the original atomic orbitals.

lessons.notes_html:
In 1931, Linus Pauling introduced hybridisation to explain the characteristic geometric shapes of polyatomic molecules like CH4, NH3, BeCl2, AlCl3 and H2O, and the formation of multiple bonds in C2H2 and C2H4. According to him, the atomic orbitals of different shapes and energies combine to form a new set of equivalent atomic orbitals called hybrid orbitals; this phenomenon is known as hybridisation.

Important Features

  • The number of hybrid orbitals produced is always equal to the number of atomic orbitals combined.
  • The hybridised orbitals are always equivalent in energy and shape.
  • Hybridisation combines at least two non-equivalent atomic orbitals, such as s and p, so a hybrid orbital is not a pure atomic orbital.
  • The shape of a hybrid orbital differs from that of the original atomic orbitals.
  • The geometries match precisely those predicted by VSEPR theory.
  • Hybridisation occurs within the central atom, after excitation and before bond formation; the concept is not used for isolated atoms.
  • Hybrid orbitals form stronger, more stable bonds than pure atomic orbitals.

Key Points

  • Hybridisation was introduced by Linus Pauling in 1931.
  • Orbitals of different shapes and energies mix to give equivalent hybrid orbitals.
  • Number of hybrid orbitals formed = number of atomic orbitals mixed.
  • All hybrid orbitals are equal in energy and shape.
  • It takes place in the central atom after excitation, before bonding.
  • Hybrid orbitals form stronger bonds than pure atomic orbitals.
lessons.title: Atomic Orbital Hybridisation

mcqs.q: In sp3 hybridisation, which orbitals mix and what is the s character?
options: One s and one p mix; 50% s character
One s and three p-orbitals mix; 25% s and 75% p character
One s and two p-orbitals mix; 33% s character
mcqs.why: Mixing one s and three p-orbitals gives four identical sp3 hybrid orbitals, each with 25% s and 75% p character.

mcqs.q: What bonds are formed in methane (CH4)?
options: Four equivalent sp3–s sigma bonds directed to the corners of a tetrahedron
Two sigma and two pi bonds
mcqs.why: In CH4 the four sp3 orbitals overlap with the 1s orbitals of four H atoms, forming four equivalent sp3–s sigma bonds at 109.5°.

mcqs.q: In ethene (C2H4), what happens to the 2pz orbital of each carbon?
options: It takes part in sp2 hybridisation
It is removed from the atom
It stays unhybridised and forms the pi bond
mcqs.why: In C2H4 one 2s and two 2p orbitals form three sp2 orbitals; the 2pz orbital stays unhybridised and its overlap forms the pi bond.

mcqs.q: What is the s character and bond angle in sp hybridisation?
mcqs.why: Mixing one s and one p-orbital gives two sp hybrid orbitals, each with 50% s and 50% p character, giving a linear shape at 180°.

mcqs.q: How many sigma and pi bonds are there in total in ethyne (C2H2)?
options: Five sigma bonds and no pi bonds
Three sigma bonds and two pi bonds
Two sigma bonds and three pi bonds
Four sigma bonds and one pi bond
mcqs.why: Ethyne is linear at 180° with three sigma bonds (two C–H and one C–C) and two pi bonds formed by the 2py and 2pz orbitals.

mcqs.q: According to the summary table, how many hybrid orbitals, sigma bonds and pi bonds does the sp2 example (ethene) have?
mcqs.why: The table gives sp2: 3 hybrid orbitals, 5 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond for ethene, with trigonal planar shape at 120°.

mcqs.q: What geometry and angle are associated with sp2 hybridisation?
mcqs.why: sp2 hybridisation gives three identical orbitals with trigonal planar geometry and bond angles around 120°, as in ethene.

mcqs.q: What do unhybridised p-orbitals always form?
mcqs.why: The key points state that unhybridised p-orbitals always form pi bonds, as the leftover p in ethene and the two p orbitals in ethyne show.

mcqs.q: In ethene, how is the C–C sigma bond formed?
mcqs.why: In C2H4 the C–H sigma bonds form by sp2–1s overlap, the C–C sigma bond by sp2–sp2 overlap, and the pi bond by unhybridised p overlap.

mcqs.q: What is the arrangement of atoms in ethene?
options: All atoms are in different planes
Only the carbon atoms are coplanar
All six atoms are coplanar, trigonal planar, with angles around 120°
mcqs.why: In ethene all six atoms are coplanar, trigonal planar, with bond angles around 120°, as stated in the notes.

lessons.notes_html:
The common types are sp3, sp2 and sp hybridisation, depending on the number and type of orbitals mixed.

sp3-Hybridisation — Formation of Methane

Mixing one s and three p-orbitals gives four identical sp3 hybrid orbitals, each with 25% s and 75% p character. In CH4, excited carbon (1s2, 2s1, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz1) forms four sp3 orbitals, each with a large lobe in one direction. They overlap with the 1s orbitals of four H atoms, forming four equivalent sp3–s σ bonds directed to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°.

sp2-Hybridisation — Formation of Ethene (Ethylene)

Mixing one s and two p-orbitals gives three identical sp2 hybrid orbitals, each with 33% s and 67% p character. In C2H4, each carbon bonds to three atoms with no lone pair. One 2s and two 2p orbitals form three sp2 orbitals; the 2pz orbital stays unhybridised. C−H σ bonds form by sp2 (carbon)–1s (hydrogen) overlap, the C−C σ bond by sp2–sp2 overlap, and the π bond by overlap of the unhybridised p-orbitals. All six atoms are coplanar, trigonal planar, with bond angles around 120°.

sp-Hybridisation — Formation of Ethyne (Acetylene)

Mixing one s and one p-orbital gives two identical sp hybrid orbitals, each with 50% s and 50% p character. In C2H2, one 2s and one 2p (2px) orbital of carbon hybridise. One sp orbital of each carbon overlaps with a half-filled 1s orbital of hydrogen (C−H σ bond); the other overlaps with the sp orbital of the other carbon (C≡C σ bond). The remaining 2py and 2pz orbitals form two pi bonds by sideways overlap. Ethyne is linear, 180°, with three sigma bonds and two pi bonds in total.

HybridisationAngleShapeHybrid OrbitalsSigma BondsPi BondsExample
sp3109.5°Tetrahedral440Methane
sp2120°Trigonal planar351Ethene
sp180°Linear232Ethyne

Key Points

  • sp3: 1 s + 3 p, 25% s character, tetrahedral, 109.5° — CH4.
  • sp2: 1 s + 2 p, 33% s character, trigonal planar, 120° — C2H4, one p left for the π bond.
  • sp: 1 s + 1 p, 50% s character, linear, 180° — C2H2, two p orbitals left for two π bonds.
  • Unhybridised p-orbitals always form pi bonds.

mcqs.q: Why was molecular orbital theory introduced?
options: To explain bond energies of halogens
To explain the shapes of molecules with lone pairs
Because valence bond theory does not explain why O2 is paramagnetic and N2 is diamagnetic
mcqs.why: VBT does not explain why O2 is paramagnetic and N2 is diamagnetic; around 1932 Hund and Mulliken introduced molecular orbital theory.

mcqs.q: How many molecular orbitals are formed from two combining atomic orbitals, and what are they?
options: Two: one bonding and one antibonding molecular orbital
mcqs.why: The number of MOs formed equals the number of combining atomic orbitals: two atomic orbitals give one bonding MO and one antibonding MO.

mcqs.q: Where is electron density maximum in a bonding molecular orbital?
options: At a node between the nuclei
mcqs.why: Electron density in a bonding orbital is maximum between the nuclei; in an antibonding orbital it is minimum between the nuclei.

mcqs.q: Using Bond Order = (nb − na)/2, what is the bond order when nb = 6 and na = 2?
mcqs.why: Working: Bond Order = (nb − na)/2 = (6 − 2)/2 = 4/2 = 2. A bond order of 2 means a double bond.

mcqs.q: What does a higher bond order indicate?
mcqs.why: Bond order indicates the number of bonds: 1 = single, 2 = double, 3 = triple; higher bond order means stronger and shorter bonds.

mcqs.q: For molecules with Z ≤ 7 such as N2, what is the MO energy order?
options: π2py and π2pz come before σ2px
σ2px comes before π2py and π2pz
mcqs.why: For Z ≤ 7 molecules (H2 to N2), π2py and π2pz come before σ2px; for Z ≥ 8, σ2px comes before the pi orbitals.

mcqs.q: How does an antibonding orbital differ from its parent atomic orbitals in energy?
options: It has exactly the same energy
It is higher in energy than the parent atomic orbitals
It is lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals
mcqs.why: The bonding MO is lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals, while the antibonding orbital (σ*, π*) is higher in energy.

mcqs.q: Which atomic orbitals can combine with a 2px orbital?
options: Only a 2px orbital, because orbitals of the same symmetry only combine
mcqs.why: Atomic orbitals of the same symmetry only combine: a 2px orbital combines with 2px, not with 2py or 2pz.

mcqs.q: How is a pi (π) molecular orbital formed?
options: By parallel (sidewise) overlap, with density above and below the bond axis
mcqs.why: Parallel (sidewise) overlap forms a pi orbital; electron density lies above and below the bond axis, with less attraction in the bonding MO.

mcqs.q: What is special about a molecular orbital compared with an atomic orbital?
options: A molecular orbital extends over all the atoms in the molecule, while an atomic orbital belongs to one atom only
A molecular orbital holds unlimited electrons
A molecular orbital has no definite energy
An atomic orbital extends over the whole molecule
mcqs.why: An atomic orbital belongs to one atom only, whereas a molecular orbital extends over all the atoms in the molecule and holds at most two electrons.

lessons.notes_html:
Valence bond theory does not explain why O2 is paramagnetic and N2 is diamagnetic. Around 1932, Friedrich Hund and Robert Mulliken introduced molecular orbital theory. Like atomic orbitals, molecular orbitals have specific energy and shapes and hold a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins. An atomic orbital belongs to one atom only, whereas a molecular orbital extends over all the atoms in the molecule.

Main Points of MOT

  • The number of molecular orbitals formed equals the number of combining atomic orbitals: two atomic orbitals give one bonding molecular orbital and one antibonding molecular orbital.
  • The overlapped atomic orbitals do not maintain their identity.
  • The molecular orbital of lower energy than the parent atomic orbitals is the bonding orbital (σ, π); the one of higher energy is the antibonding orbital (σ*, π*).
  • Electron density in a bonding orbital is maximum between the nuclei; in an antibonding orbital it is minimum between the nuclei.
  • The bonding orbital is more stable because it is lower in energy than the antibonding orbital.
  • Filling of molecular orbitals follows the same rules as filling of atomic orbitals.
  • Bond order indicates the number of bonds between two atoms: 1 = single, 2 = double, 3 = triple. Higher bond order means stronger and shorter bonds.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Bond Order = (nb − na) / 2nb = electrons in bonding MOs, na = electrons in antibonding MOs

The energy order of MOs is of two types. For molecules with atomic number Z ≤ 7 (H2, He2, Li2, Be2, B2, C2, N2), π2py and π2pz come before σ2px. For Z ≥ 8, σ2px comes before π2py and π2pz; the antibonding order also reverses.

Sigma (σ) and Pi (π) Molecular Orbitals

  • Linear head-on overlap forms a σ orbital; electron density is concentrated around the bond axis, with more attraction in the bonding MO and more repulsion in the antibonding MO (which has a node between the nuclei).
  • Parallel (sidewise) overlap forms a π orbital; electron density lies above and below the bond axis, with less attraction in the bonding MO and less repulsion in the antibonding MO.
  • Atomic orbitals of the same symmetry only combine: a 2px orbital combines with 2px, not with 2py or 2pz.

Key Points

  • MOT (Hund and Mulliken, 1932) explains the paramagnetism of O2, which VBT cannot.
  • MOs formed = atomic orbitals combined; half are bonding, half antibonding.
  • Bonding MO: lower energy, density maximum between nuclei, more stable.
  • Bond order = (nb − na)/2; higher bond order = stronger, shorter bond.
  • Energy order differs for Z ≤ 7 and Z ≥ 8 molecules.
lessons.title: Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)

mcqs.q: What is the bond order of H2 and what does it mean?
options: Bond order 0, so H2 does not exist
Bond order 1, a stable single bond
mcqs.why: Working: H2 has σ(1s)2, so Bond Order = (2 − 0)/2 = 1. A bond order of 1 means a single bond; H2 is stable and exists.

mcqs.q: Why does He2 not exist according to MO theory?
options: Because its bond order is 0, so there is no bond and helium stays monoatomic
mcqs.why: Working: He2 would be σ(1s)2 σ*(1s)2, Bond Order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0. Bond order zero means no bond, so He2 is unstable and helium stays monoatomic.

mcqs.q: What is the bond order of N2?
mcqs.why: Working: For N2, Bond Order = (nb − na)/2 = (8 − 2)/2 = 6/2 = 3. This is a triple bond N≡N: one sigma and two pi bonds.

mcqs.q: Why is O2 paramagnetic?
options: Because it has two unpaired electrons, one each in the π*2py and π*2pz orbitals
Because all its electrons are paired
Because it has a bond order of zero
Because it is repelled by a magnet
mcqs.why: O2 has two unpaired electrons, one each in the π*2py and π*2pz orbitals, so it is paramagnetic and attracted to a magnetic field.

mcqs.q: What is the bond order of O2?
mcqs.why: Working: For O2, Bond Order = (nb − na)/2 = (8 − 4)/2 = 4/2 = 2. A bond order of 2 means a double bond: one sigma and one pi bond.

mcqs.q: When is a molecule diamagnetic?
options: When it has one unpaired electron
When it has two unpaired electrons
When all its electrons are paired in molecular orbitals
When it is attracted to a magnetic field
mcqs.why: Molecules are diamagnetic when all their electrons are paired in molecular orbitals, and paramagnetic if they have one or more unpaired electrons.

mcqs.q: How do paramagnetic and diamagnetic substances behave in a magnetic field?
options: Paramagnetic substances are attracted, while diamagnetic substances are slightly repelled
mcqs.why: Paramagnetic substances are attracted to a magnetic field, while diamagnetic substances are slightly repelled; F2 is diamagnetic and O2 is paramagnetic.

mcqs.q: What happens to the strength of paramagnetism as unpaired electrons increase?
options: The strength of paramagnetism increases with the number of unpaired electrons
It decreases with more unpaired electrons
mcqs.why: The notes state that the strength of paramagnetism increases with the number of unpaired electrons in the molecule.

mcqs.q: What is the MO picture of the H2 molecule?
options: Two 1s orbitals form σ1s and σ*1s; 2 electrons fill σ1s only
mcqs.why: In H2, two 1s orbitals form σ1s and σ*1s and the 2 electrons fill σ1s only, giving the configuration σ(1s)2.

mcqs.q: Is F2 paramagnetic or diamagnetic, and why?
options: Paramagnetic, because it has two unpaired electrons
Paramagnetic, because it has one unpaired electron
Diamagnetic, because it has no unpaired electrons
Diamagnetic, because its bond order is zero
mcqs.why: F2 has no unpaired electrons, so it is diamagnetic, unlike O2 which has two unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic.

lessons.notes_html:
MOT gives the precise electronic configurations of homonuclear diatomic molecules, which explain their properties.

MoleculeMO PictureBond OrderResult
H2Two 1s orbitals form σ1s and σ*1s; 2 electrons fill σ1s only: σ(1s)2(2 − 0)/2 = 1Single bond; stable, exists
He2 (hypothetical)4 electrons: σ(1s)2 σ*(1s)2(2 − 2)/2 = 0No bond; unstable, helium stays monoatomic
N2σ(2s)2 σ*(2s)2 π(2py)2 = π(2pz)2 σ(2px)2(8 − 2)/2 = 3Triple bond N≡N: one σ and two π bonds
O2σ(2s)2 σ*(2s)2 σ(2px)2 π(2py)2 = π(2pz)2 π*(2py)1 = π*(2pz)1(8 − 4)/2 = 2Double bond: one σ and one π bond

Paramagnetism and Diamagnetism in Molecules

Molecules are diamagnetic when all their electrons are paired in molecular orbitals, and paramagnetic if they have one or more unpaired electrons. Paramagnetic substances are attracted to a magnetic field, while diamagnetic substances are slightly repelled. The strength of paramagnetism increases with the number of unpaired electrons. O2 has two unpaired electrons, one each in the π*2py and π*2pz orbitals, so it is paramagnetic. F2 has no unpaired electrons, so it is diamagnetic.

Key Points

  • H2: bond order 1, stable single bond.
  • He2: bond order 0, so it does not exist; helium is monoatomic.
  • N2: bond order 3, a triple bond, diamagnetic.
  • O2: bond order 2, a double bond, with two unpaired electrons.
  • Unpaired electrons = paramagnetic (attracted to a magnet); all paired = diamagnetic (slightly repelled).
  • O2 is paramagnetic and F2 is diamagnetic.
lessons.title: Applications of MO Theory

mcqs.q: What is bond energy?
options: The amount of energy needed to break a bond
The energy released when a bond forms in a gas
The total energy of a molecule
mcqs.why: Bond energy is the amount of energy needed to break a bond; higher bond energy indicates stronger, more stable and less reactive bonds.

mcqs.q: What is bond length?
options: The energy needed to break a bond
The number of bonds between two atoms
The distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms
The size of a whole molecule
mcqs.why: Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms; shorter bond lengths mean stronger bonds and lower reactivity.

mcqs.q: Which halogen molecule has the longest bond length and its value?
mcqs.why: From the table, bond length increases down the halogens: F2 142 pm, Cl2 199 pm, Br2 228 pm and I2 266 pm, so I2 is longest.

mcqs.q: Why is Cl2 more stable than F2?
options: Because Cl2 has a higher bond energy (243 kJ/mol) than F2 (158 kJ/mol), so its bond is harder to break
Because Cl2 has a shorter bond than F2
Because F2 has no covalent bond
Because Cl2 is an ionic compound
mcqs.why: Working: 243 kJ/mol (Cl2) > 158 kJ/mol (F2). Cl2 has the higher bond energy, so the Cl–Cl bond is more difficult to break and Cl2 is more stable.

mcqs.q: Why is the bond energy of fluorine unusually low?
options: Because fluorine atoms are very large
Because of strong electron repulsion between its small, electronegative atoms
Because F2 has a triple bond
Because fluorine has no valence electrons
mcqs.why: The low bond energy of fluorine comes from strong electron repulsion between its small, electronegative atoms, making F2 unusually reactive.

mcqs.q: In general, how do bond energy and bond length relate to reactivity?
options: Higher bond energy and shorter length mean more reactive
Bond energy has no relation to reactivity
Higher bond energy and shorter bond length mean more stable and less reactive
Longer bond length always means less reactive
mcqs.why: Molecules with higher bond energy and shorter bond lengths are more stable and less reactive; lower energy and longer length mean less stable and more reactive.

mcqs.q: What is the bond energy of Br2 from the table?
mcqs.why: The table gives Br2 a bond length of 228 pm and a bond energy of 193 kJ/mol, between Cl2 (243) and I2 (151).

mcqs.q: Why is I2 described as less stable?
options: It has a longer bond length and lower bond energy, making it less stable and more likely to react
It has the shortest bond of all halogens
It has the highest bond energy of all halogens
mcqs.why: I2 has a longer bond length (266 pm) and lower bond energy (151 kJ/mol), making it less stable and more likely to take part in substitution or addition reactions.

mcqs.q: Besides bond energy and bond length, what other factors influence reactivity?
options: Only the colour of the molecule
Functional groups, electronegativity differences and molecular geometry
Only the temperature of the room
mcqs.why: The notes state that functional groups, electronegativity differences and molecular geometry also influence the reactivity of covalent molecules.

mcqs.q: What is the bond length of Cl2?
mcqs.why: The table gives Cl2 a bond length of 199 pm and the highest halogen bond energy in the table, 243 kJ/mol.

lessons.notes_html:
The reactivity of covalent molecules can be compared by looking at their bond energy values and bond lengths.

Bond Energy

Bond energy is the amount of energy needed to break a bond. Higher bond energy indicates stronger and more stable bonds, which make the molecule less reactive.

Bond Length

Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Shorter bond lengths are associated with stronger, higher-energy bonds, giving increased stability and lower reactivity, and vice versa.

Comparing Reactivity

In general, molecules with higher bond energy and shorter bond lengths are more stable and less reactive, while molecules with lower bond energy and longer bond lengths are less stable and more reactive. Other factors, such as functional groups, electronegativity differences and molecular geometry, also influence reactivity.

Example Comparisons of Halogen Molecules

Halogen (X2)Bond Length (pm)Bond Energy (kJ/mol)
F2142158
Cl2199243
Br2228193
I2266151

Cl2 is more stable than F2 because it has a higher bond energy, so the Cl−Cl bond is more difficult to break; F2 is more reactive despite being higher in the group. The low bond energy of fluorine comes from strong electron repulsion between its small, electronegative atoms. I2 has a longer bond length and lower bond energy, making it less stable and more likely to take part in substitution or addition reactions, though its reactivity is limited by its lower bond polarity and oxidising ability compared to Cl2 or Br2.

Key Points

  • Bond energy = energy needed to break a bond; higher = stronger, more stable, less reactive.
  • Bond length = distance between the two nuclei; shorter = stronger bond, lower reactivity.
  • Down the halogens, bond length increases: F2 142 pm to I2 266 pm.
  • Cl2 (243 kJ/mol) is more stable and less reactive than F2 (158 kJ/mol).
  • F2 is unusually reactive because of strong repulsion between its small atoms.
