mcqs.q: What are intramolecular forces?
options: Forces between molecules of a substance
The attractive forces between atoms within each molecule, i.e. the chemical bonds
Forces that decide boiling point only
mcqs.why: Intramolecular forces act within each molecule and are the chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds.

mcqs.q: Which properties depend on intermolecular forces?
options: Boiling point, vapour pressure, surface tension and viscosity
The number of electrons in an atom
mcqs.why: Physical properties such as boiling point, vapour pressure, surface tension, viscosity and heats of vaporisation and fusion depend on intermolecular forces.

mcqs.q: How strong are intramolecular forces compared with intermolecular forces?
options: They are weaker than intermolecular forces
They are exactly equal in strength
Intermolecular forces do not exist in liquids
Intramolecular forces are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces
mcqs.why: Chemical properties, shapes and bond energies depend on intramolecular forces, which are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces.

mcqs.q: How much energy is needed to vaporise water, H2O(l) → H2O(g)?
options: ΔH = +40.67 kJ/mol, breaking only the intermolecular forces
ΔH = +934 kJ/mol, breaking the covalent bonds
mcqs.why: Working: vaporisation of water needs ΔH = +40.67 kJ/mol, which breaks only the intermolecular forces between water molecules.

mcqs.q: What happens to the forces when water decomposes, H2O(g) → 2H(g) + O(g)?
options: Intramolecular forces break, needing ΔH = +934 kJ/mol
mcqs.why: Working: decomposing water needs ΔH = +934 kJ/mol, far more than 40.67 kJ/mol for vaporisation, because intramolecular forces (the bonds) break.

mcqs.q: What type of forces break during evaporation of water?
mcqs.why: Intermolecular forces break during evaporation of water, while intramolecular forces break during its decomposition.

mcqs.q: What happens when intermolecular forces in a substance are stronger?
options: It becomes a gas at room temperature
It is more difficult to separate its molecules
mcqs.why: The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more difficult it is to separate the molecules of a substance.

mcqs.q: Which of the following are intramolecular forces?
mcqs.why: Intramolecular forces are the chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, which are stronger than intermolecular forces.

mcqs.q: Which properties depend on intramolecular forces?
options: Chemical properties, shapes of molecules and bond energies
mcqs.why: The chemical properties, shapes of molecules and bond energies depend on intramolecular forces, while physical properties depend on intermolecular forces.

mcqs.q: Roughly how many times more energy does decomposing water need than vaporising it?
mcqs.why: Working: 934 kJ/mol ÷ 40.67 kJ/mol ≈ 22.97 ≈ 23. Decomposing water needs about 23 times more energy because intramolecular forces are much stronger.

lessons.notes_html:
The attractive forces between atoms within each molecule are called intramolecular forces, while the forces of attraction between molecules of a substance are known as intermolecular forces. Intramolecular forces are the chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds.

  • The physical properties of a substance, such as boiling point, vapour pressure, surface tension, viscosity, heat of vaporisation, heat of fusion and heat of sublimation, depend on intermolecular forces. The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more difficult it is to separate its molecules.
  • The chemical properties, shapes of molecules and bond energies depend on intramolecular forces, which are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces.
  • In general, ionic, covalent and metallic bonding are stronger than intermolecular forces.

For water: H2O(l) → H2O(g) on vaporisation needs ΔH = +40.67 kJ/mol, which breaks only the intermolecular forces. Decomposing H2O(g) → 2H(g) + O(g) needs ΔH = +934 kJ/mol, which breaks the intramolecular forces. Intermolecular forces break during evaporation of water, while intramolecular forces break during its decomposition.

Key Points

  • Intramolecular forces act within a molecule: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds.
  • Intermolecular forces act between molecules and decide physical properties.
  • Intramolecular forces are much stronger than intermolecular forces.
  • Vaporising water needs 40.67 kJ/mol; decomposing it needs 934 kJ/mol.
  • Evaporation breaks intermolecular forces; decomposition breaks intramolecular forces.
lessons.title: Intermolecular Forces

mcqs.q: After whom are intermolecular (van der Waals) forces named?
options: Johannes van der Waals, the Dutch scientist (1837–1923)
mcqs.why: Intermolecular forces are commonly known as van der Waals forces, after the Dutch scientist Johannes van der Waals (1837–1923).

mcqs.q: What are London dispersion forces also called?
mcqs.why: London forces are also called instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces, recognised by Fritz London in 1930.

mcqs.q: How do London dispersion forces arise?
options: Electron motion produces an instantaneous dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, generating a weak attraction
By transfer of electrons between atoms
By hydrogen attached to fluorine only
mcqs.why: Electron motion produces an instantaneous dipole which induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, generating a weak attraction, as described for neon.

mcqs.q: In which substances do London forces exist, as listed in the notes?
options: In halogens, noble gases and non-polar molecules such as H2, N2, CH4 and CO2
mcqs.why: London forces exist in halogens, noble gases and non-polar molecules such as H2, N2, CH4, CO2, SO3, SiH4 and CCl4, letting them condense or solidify.

mcqs.q: How does molecular size affect the strength of London forces?
options: Larger molecules have weaker London forces
Size has no effect on London forces
Larger atoms and molecules polarise more easily, so London forces are stronger and boiling points rise down a group
mcqs.why: Larger atoms and molecules with more electrons polarise more easily; strength is directly proportional to polarisability, so boiling points increase down a group.

mcqs.q: Which pentane isomer has the highest boiling point and what is it?
options: All isomers boil at the same temperature
mcqs.why: C5H12 isomers boil at n-pentane 36°C, iso-pentane 28°C and neo-pentane 9.5°C; n-pentane is highest because its electrons are closer to the surface.

mcqs.q: Why does compact neo-pentane have weaker London forces?
options: Because its valence electrons are farther from the surface than in n-pentane and isopentane
Because it is a polar molecule
Because it has fewer electrons than n-pentane
mcqs.why: In n-pentane and isopentane the valence electrons are closer to the surface, so their London forces are stronger than in compact neo-pentane.

mcqs.q: In which molecules do dipole-dipole forces occur?
mcqs.why: Dipole-dipole (pd-pd) forces are present only in polar molecules, while London forces occur in both polar and non-polar molecules.

mcqs.q: Propane and acetaldehyde both have molar mass 44 g/mol. Why does acetaldehyde boil much higher (20.85°C vs −42.15°C)?
options: Because propane is polar and acetaldehyde is not
Because acetaldehyde has a larger mass
Because polar acetaldehyde has dipole-dipole forces, while non-polar propane has only weak London forces
mcqs.why: Working: 20.85 − (−42.15) = 63°C difference at the same molar mass. Polar acetaldehyde has dipole-dipole forces; non-polar propane does not, so it boils far lower.

mcqs.q: What two types are collectively known as van der Waals forces in the notes?
mcqs.why: The three main types are London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding; London and dipole-dipole forces are collectively called van der Waals forces.

lessons.notes_html:
Intermolecular forces are commonly known as van der Waals forces, after the Dutch scientist Johannes van der Waals (1837–1923). There are three main types: London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding. London forces and dipole-dipole forces are collectively known as van der Waals forces.

London Dispersion Forces

Fritz London (1930) recognised these weak forces between non-polar molecules; they are also called instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (id-id) forces. Electron motion in an atom or molecule produces an instantaneous dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, generating a weak attraction. In neon, when atoms come close, the electron cloud of one atom is disturbed and bends toward one side, forming an instantaneous dipole; this induces a dipole in the next atom. The forces disappear when the electrons become symmetrical again. They exist in halogens, noble gases and non-polar molecules such as H2, N2, CH4, CO2, SO3, SiH4 and CCl4; without them such substances could not condense or solidify.

Strength of London Forces

  • Size: larger atoms and molecules, with more electrons and heavier mass, polarise more easily. Strength is directly proportional to polarisability (the degree to which the electron cloud is distorted). So boiling points of halogens and noble gases increase down a group.
  • Shape: C5H12 isomers boil at different temperatures: n-pentane 36°C, iso-pentane 28°C, neo-pentane 9.5°C. In n-pentane and isopentane the valence electrons are closer to the surface, so their London forces are stronger than in compact neo-pentane.

Dipole-Dipole Forces

These permanent dipole–permanent dipole (pd-pd) forces are present only in polar molecules. In HCl, chlorine is more electronegative, so it gains a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge; the positive end of one HCl attracts the negative end of another. London forces occur in both polar and non-polar molecules, but dipole-dipole forces occur only in polar molecules. Their strength depends on the distance between molecules and the electronegativity difference: greater ΔEN means greater polarity, stronger forces and a higher boiling point. Propane and acetaldehyde both have molar mass 44 g/mol, but polar acetaldehyde boils at 20.85°C while non-polar propane boils at −42.15°C.

Key Points

  • Van der Waals forces: London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding.
  • London forces arise from instantaneous dipole–induced dipole attraction; present in all molecules.
  • London forces grow with size, electron number, polarisability and surface contact.
  • n-Pentane (36°C) > iso-pentane (28°C) > neo-pentane (9.5°C) in boiling point.
  • Dipole-dipole forces act only between polar molecules and grow with polarity.
lessons.title: Types of Intermolecular Forces

mcqs.q: What is hydrogen bonding?
options: A true covalent bond inside a molecule
The attraction between a partially positive hydrogen in one polar molecule and a lone pair of a highly electronegative atom (F, O, N) in another
A bond between hydrogen and a metal
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding is the attraction between a partially positive H in one polar molecule and a lone pair on F, O or N in another polar molecule.

mcqs.q: How strong is hydrogen bonding compared with other dipole-dipole forces?
options: It is weaker than all other forces
It is equal to ordinary dipole-dipole forces
It is about five to ten times stronger than other dipole-dipole forces
It is weaker than London forces
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding is not a true chemical bond but a special, very strong dipole-dipole force, about five to ten times stronger than other dipole-dipole forces.

mcqs.q: To which groups is hydrogen bonding limited?
options: Molecules containing N–H, O–H and H–F groups, e.g. NH3, H2O and HF
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding is limited to molecules containing N–H, O–H and H–F groups, such as NH3, H2O and HF, and is shown as a dotted line.

mcqs.q: Why does ice float on water?
options: Ice has an open hexagonal structure with empty spaces, about 10% more volume and lower density (0.917 g/cm3) than liquid water
Ice is warmer than liquid water
mcqs.why: On cooling, water molecules form a regular hexagonal pattern with empty spaces; ice has about 10% more volume and density 0.917 g/cm3, so it floats.

mcqs.q: What is the specific heat capacity of water given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Water has a high specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/g°C, against iron 0.45 and ethanol 2.46, so it warms and cools slowly.

mcqs.q: What biological structures are held together by hydrogen bonding?
options: Proteins (helical structures) and the DNA double helix
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding holds the structure of proteins and DNA: proteins adopt helical structures through it and it keeps the DNA double helix together.

mcqs.q: Why does the floating ice layer matter for aquatic life?
options: It makes the water warmer underneath
It stops all freezing of lakes
It insulates the water underneath, allowing fish and other aquatic life to survive in winter
mcqs.why: Ice floats and the floating layer insulates the water underneath, allowing fish and other aquatic life to survive in winter.

mcqs.q: Which compounds dissolve in water because of hydrogen bonding, per the notes?
options: Ethanol and acetic acid dissolve; methane and benzene do not
Methane and benzene dissolve; ethanol does not
No compound dissolves because of hydrogen bonding
mcqs.why: Hydrogen-bonded compounds such as ethanol and acetic acid dissolve in water; methane and benzene, which cannot hydrogen-bond with water, do not.

mcqs.q: How does hydrogen bonding help the cleaning action of soaps and detergents?
options: The non-polar ends form hydrogen bonds with water
The polar ends form hydrogen bonds with water, while the non-polar ends attract oil and grease
Soaps break all covalent bonds in grease
Detergents remove hydrogen bonds from water
mcqs.why: The polar ends of soaps and detergents form hydrogen bonds with water, while the non-polar ends attract oil and grease, giving the cleaning action.

mcqs.q: What happens to hydrogen bonds in liquid water?
options: They constantly break and reform, so molecules are connected irregularly
mcqs.why: In liquid water hydrogen bonds constantly break and reform, so molecules are connected irregularly; on cooling they form the regular hexagonal pattern of ice.

lessons.notes_html:
The attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom in one polar molecule and a lone pair of a highly electronegative atom (F, O, N) in another polar molecule is called hydrogen bonding. It is not a true chemical bond; it is a special, very strong type of dipole-dipole force, about five to ten times stronger than other dipole-dipole forces. It is limited to molecules containing N−H, O−H and H−F groups, e.g. NH3, H2O and HF, and is shown as a dotted line between molecules.

Anomalous Properties of Water

In liquid water, hydrogen bonds constantly break and reform, so molecules are connected irregularly. On cooling, the molecules arrange into a regular hexagonal pattern with stable hydrogen bonds, creating empty spaces in the structure of ice, which causes it to expand. Ice occupies about 10% more volume, so its density falls: liquid water at 4°C is about 1.00 g/cm3, while ice at 0°C is about 0.917 g/cm3. Ice therefore floats on water; the floating layer insulates the water underneath, allowing fish and other aquatic life to survive in winter.

Significance of Hydrogen Bonding

  • Thermodynamic properties: hydrogen-bonded molecules show higher heats of vaporisation, melting points and boiling points, e.g. NH3, H2O and HF.
  • Biological significance: it holds the structure of proteins and DNA; proteins adopt helical structures through hydrogen bonding between amino acids, and hydrogen bonds keep the DNA double helix together.
  • High specific heat capacity: water (4.18 J/g°C, against iron 0.45 and ethanol 2.46) warms and cools slowly, stabilising temperatures on Earth's surface.
  • Solubility: hydrogen-bonded compounds such as ethanol and acetic acid dissolve in water; methane and benzene do not.
  • Cleaning action: the polar ends of soaps and detergents form hydrogen bonds with water, while the non-polar ends attract oil and grease.
  • Materials: it gives properties to food materials (carbohydrates), adhesives in paints and dyes, and the stickiness of honey and glycerin; water also shows high heat of vaporisation, surface tension and viscosity.

Key Points

  • Hydrogen bond: H attached to F, O or N attracted to a lone pair on F, O or N of another molecule.
  • It is a very strong dipole-dipole force, 5–10 times stronger than ordinary dipole-dipole forces.
  • Ice has an open hexagonal structure, about 10% more volume and lower density (0.917 g/cm3), so it floats.
  • It raises boiling points, melting points and specific heat, and helps solubility and cleaning action.
  • It is essential for protein folding and the DNA double helix.
lessons.title: Hydrogen Bonding

mcqs.q: What is an expanded octet?
options: Fewer than eight electrons around the central atom
Exactly eight electrons around every atom
More than eight electrons around the central atom in a molecular or polyatomic ion
Eight electrons shared between two atoms
mcqs.why: An expanded octet means a central atom appears to have more than eight electrons around it, common from the third period onwards.

mcqs.q: From which period onwards is an expanded octet common, and why?
options: First period, because s-orbitals are available
Second period, because p-orbitals are available
Fourth period only, because f-orbitals appear
Third period onwards, where d-orbitals are available for bonding
mcqs.why: Expanded octets are common in elements from the third period onwards, where d-orbitals are available for bonding.

mcqs.q: In the nitrate ion NO3−, why are all three N–O bonds equivalent?
options: Because the negative charge is delocalised, causing resonance among the three N–O bonds
Because all three bonds are double bonds
Because oxygen atoms are identical in mass only
mcqs.why: In NO3− the negative charge is delocalised, causing resonance among the three N–O bonds, so all three N–O bonds are equivalent.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are around nitrogen in NO3−?
options: Exactly eight electrons; nitrogen satisfies the octet rule
mcqs.why: Nitrogen is in the second period with no vacant d-orbitals, so it cannot expand its octet and has exactly eight electrons in NO3−.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are around sulphur in the sulphate ion SO4^2−?
options: 12 electrons, from two single and two double bonds
mcqs.why: Working: 2 single bonds give 2×2 = 4 electrons and 2 double bonds give 2×4 = 8 electrons; total = 4 + 8 = 12 electrons around sulphur.

mcqs.q: Why can sulphur expand its octet but nitrogen cannot?
options: Sulphur is a larger atom in mass only
Nitrogen has d-orbitals but sulphur does not
Both can expand their octets equally
Sulphur is in the third period so its d-orbitals are available; nitrogen is in the second period with no vacant d-orbitals
mcqs.why: Sulphur is in the third period, so its available d-orbitals allow an expanded octet; second-period nitrogen has no vacant d-orbitals.

mcqs.q: In NO3−, what are the formal charges described in the Lewis structure?
options: The two single-bonded oxygens carry a negative charge each and nitrogen carries a positive charge, giving the overall 1− charge
Nitrogen carries a negative charge and oxygens are neutral
Each oxygen carries a positive charge
mcqs.why: Nitrogen forms one double and two single bonds; the two single-bonded oxygens carry a negative charge each and nitrogen a positive charge, giving overall 1−.

mcqs.q: How is the sulphate ion's bonding described?
options: Four single bonds to four oxygens
Two single bonds with two oxygens and two double bonds with the other two oxygens
Four double bonds to four oxygens
One triple bond and one single bond
mcqs.why: In SO4^2− sulphur forms two single bonds with two oxygen atoms and two double bonds with the other two oxygen atoms, totalling 12 electrons.

mcqs.q: Where are the π-electrons in the nitrate ion?
options: Delocalised over the three N–O bonds
mcqs.why: Nitrogen satisfies the octet rule with exactly eight electrons, and the pi-electrons are delocalised over the three N–O bonds in NO3−.

mcqs.q: Which central atom in these ions shows an expanded octet?
mcqs.why: Only sulphur in SO4^2− exceeds the octet with 12 electrons; nitrogen in NO3− keeps exactly 8 electrons and cannot expand its octet.

lessons.notes_html:
Molecular ions or polyatomic ions can sometimes appear to have more than eight electrons around the central atom. This is called an expanded octet. It is common in elements from the third period onwards, where d-orbitals are available for bonding.

Expanded Octets in Nitrate Ions

The nitrate ion (NO3-) has three oxygen atoms attached to a central nitrogen atom. In its Lewis structure, nitrogen forms one double bond with one oxygen and two single bonds with the other two oxygens; the two single-bonded oxygens carry a negative charge each and nitrogen carries a positive charge, giving the overall 1− charge. The negative charge is delocalised, causing resonance among the three N−O bonds, so all three N−O bonds are equivalent. Nitrogen belongs to the second period and has no vacant d-orbitals, so it cannot expand its octet: it satisfies the octet rule with exactly eight electrons around it, and the π-electrons are delocalised over the three N−O bonds.

Expanded Octets in Sulphate Ions

The sulphate ion (SO4^2-) has four oxygen atoms bonded to the central sulphur atom. Sulphur forms two single bonds with two oxygen atoms and two double bonds with the other two oxygen atoms. This gives a total of 12 electrons around the sulphur atom, exceeding the octet. Sulphur is in the third period, so its available d-orbitals allow this expanded octet.

Key Points

  • An expanded octet means more than 8 electrons around the central atom.
  • It is possible only from the third period onwards, where d-orbitals are available.
  • NO3-: nitrogen keeps exactly 8 electrons; resonance makes all three N−O bonds equivalent.
  • SO4^2-: sulphur has 12 electrons around it (two single and two double bonds).
  • Second-period elements like nitrogen cannot expand their octet.
lessons.title: Expanded Octets in Molecular Ions

mcqs.q: What is a dative (coordinate covalent) bond?
options: A bond where each atom gives one electron
A bond where two atoms share a pair of electrons, with both electrons originating from one of the atoms
A bond formed by complete electron transfer
mcqs.why: A dative bond occurs when two atoms share a pair of electrons, with both electrons originating from one of the atoms involved.

mcqs.q: What bonds make up the triple bond in carbon monoxide (CO)?
options: Two covalent bonds and one dative bond from oxygen to carbon
One covalent and two dative bonds
mcqs.why: CO contains a triple bond made up of two covalent bonds and one dative bond: oxygen donates a lone pair into carbon's empty orbital.

mcqs.q: In the formation of ozone (O3), how is the dative bond formed?
options: A hydrogen ion donates electrons to oxygen
Carbon donates a lone pair to oxygen
Nitrogen donates a lone pair to oxygen
One atom in the oxygen molecule donates a lone pair to the third oxygen atom (nascent oxygen)
mcqs.why: In O3 formation, one atom in O2 donates a lone pair to the third oxygen atom, which has six electrons, forming a dative bond to complete its octet.

mcqs.q: How is the hydronium ion H3O+ formed?
options: The oxygen atom in water donates a lone pair to the hydrogen ion H+, which has a vacant orbital: H+ + H2O → [H3O]+
Two water molecules share hydrogen atoms
A hydrogen atom loses its electron to oxygen permanently
Water gains an extra oxygen atom
mcqs.why: The oxygen in water donates a lone pair to H+, which has a vacant orbital, forming a dative bond: H+ + H2O → [H3O]+.

mcqs.q: In H3O+, what does the oxygen atom look like in the product?
options: It is bonded to two hydrogens with no lone pair
It is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and still carries a lone pair, inside brackets with a + charge
It has an expanded octet of 12 electrons
mcqs.why: In [H3O]+ oxygen is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and still carries a lone pair, written inside brackets with a + charge.

mcqs.q: What must the donor and acceptor have for a dative bond to form?
options: The donor must have a lone pair; the acceptor must have a vacant orbital
mcqs.why: The key points state: the donor must have a lone pair and the acceptor must have a vacant orbital for a dative bond to form.

mcqs.q: In CO, which atom donates the lone pair for the dative bond?
options: Oxygen donates a lone pair into carbon's empty orbital
mcqs.why: In CO, carbon first forms a double bond with oxygen and has an empty orbital; oxygen donates a lone pair into it, written :C≡O:.

mcqs.q: What is another name for a dative bond?
mcqs.why: A dative bond is also known as a coordinate covalent bond, because both shared electrons come from one atom only.

mcqs.q: In ozone formation, how many electrons does the third (nascent) oxygen atom have before bonding?
mcqs.why: The third oxygen atom (nascent oxygen) has six electrons; the donated lone pair forms a dative bond to complete its octet: :O=O: + :O: → O3.

mcqs.q: In CO formation, what does carbon have after forming the double bond with oxygen?
options: A full octet with no empty orbital
An empty orbital, into which oxygen donates a lone pair
mcqs.why: Carbon, with four valence electrons, first forms a double bond with oxygen; carbon then has an empty orbital that accepts oxygen's lone pair.

lessons.notes_html:
A dative bond, also known as a coordinate covalent bond, occurs when two atoms share a pair of electrons, with both electrons originating from one of the atoms involved.

Formation of Dative Bond in Carbon Monoxide

Carbon, with four valence electrons, first forms a double bond with oxygen. Carbon then has an empty orbital. Oxygen donates a lone pair into this orbital, forming a dative (coordinate covalent) bond. As a result, CO contains a triple bond made up of two covalent bonds and one dative bond: in the Lewis picture, carbon carries a lone pair and oxygen donates its lone pair toward carbon, written :C≡O:.

Formation of Dative Bond in Ozone

An ozone molecule forms when an oxygen molecule reacts with an oxygen atom. One atom in the oxygen molecule donates a lone pair of electrons to the third oxygen atom (nascent oxygen), which has six electrons, forming a dative bond to complete its octet: :O=O: + :O: → O3.

Formation of Dative Bond in Hydronium Ion

The hydronium ion is created when water reacts with a hydrogen ion. The oxygen atom in the water molecule donates a lone pair of electrons to the hydrogen ion, which has a vacant orbital, forming a dative bond: H+ + H2O → [H3O]+. In the product, oxygen is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and still carries a lone pair, inside brackets with a + charge.

Key Points

  • A dative (coordinate covalent) bond: both shared electrons come from one atom only.
  • CO has a triple bond: two covalent bonds plus one dative bond from oxygen to carbon.
  • In O3, an oxygen of O2 donates a lone pair to a third oxygen atom.
  • In H3O+, oxygen of water donates a lone pair to H+, which has a vacant orbital.
  • The donor must have a lone pair; the acceptor must have a vacant orbital.
lessons.title: The Formation of Dative Bond in CO, O3, and H3O+

mcqs.q: What does dipole moment measure?
options: The polarity of a bond in a covalently bonded molecule
mcqs.why: Dipole moment measures the polarity of a bond in a covalently bonded molecule; the greater the dipole moment, the greater the polarity.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for dipole moment?
options: μ = q × d, charge at each end multiplied by the distance between the charges
mcqs.why: Dipole moment μ = q × d, where q is the charge at each end of a polar bond and d is the distance between the charges.

mcqs.q: How is 1 Debye (D) expressed in SI units?
mcqs.why: Working: the conversion given is 1 D = 3.34 × 10^−30 C.m, used to convert Debye values into coulomb metres.

mcqs.q: Convert the dipole moment of water, 1.85 D, into C.m.
mcqs.why: Working: μ = 1.85 D × 3.34 × 10^−30 C.m/D = 6.179 × 10^−30 ≈ 6.18 × 10^−30 C.m. Water (1.85 D) is more polar than ammonia (1.47 D).

mcqs.q: Dipole moment is a vector quantity. In which direction is it directed?
mcqs.why: Dipole moment is a vector directed from positive to negative, shown by an arrow with the head toward δ− and a cross toward δ+.

mcqs.q: Which molecule is more polar, water or ammonia?
options: Water, 1.85 D, is more polar than ammonia, 1.47 D
mcqs.why: Working: 1.85 D (H2O) > 1.47 D (NH3), and greater dipole moment means greater polarity, so water is more polar.

mcqs.q: Why is CO2 non-polar despite having polar bonds?
options: Because it has no polar bonds
Because it is linear and the bond dipoles cancel
Because it is an ionic compound
mcqs.why: In polyatomic molecules both bond polarity and geometry decide the dipole moment; CO2 is linear and non-polar because the bond dipoles cancel.

mcqs.q: Which molecules have polar bonds but zero net dipole moment due to symmetry?
mcqs.why: SO3 and CCl4 have polar bonds but no dipole moment due to their symmetrical structures; CO2 is the linear example of the same effect.

mcqs.q: What does a zero dipole moment tell us about a molecule?
mcqs.why: The greater the dipole moment the greater the polarity; a molecule with zero dipole moment is non-polar, like H2 and O2.

mcqs.q: In HCl, which partial charges are present?
options: Chlorine is δ+ and hydrogen is δ−
Chlorine pulls electrons toward itself, gaining δ−, while hydrogen gains δ+
Hydrogen gains δ− because it is more electronegative
mcqs.why: In HCl chlorine pulls electrons toward itself, gaining a partial negative charge (δ−) while hydrogen gains a partial positive charge (δ+).

lessons.notes_html:
Dipole moment measures the polarity of a bond in a covalently bonded molecule. The greater the dipole moment, the greater the polarity; a molecule with zero dipole moment is non-polar. Polar covalent bonds form between atoms with different electronegativities: in HCl, chlorine pulls electrons toward itself, gaining a partial negative charge (δ-) while hydrogen gains a partial positive charge (δ+). Such a molecule with a net charge separation is polar and has a dipole moment.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
μ = q × dDipole moment = charge at each end of a polar bond × distance between the charges
1 D = 3.34 × 10^-30 C.mConverting Debye (D) to SI units of coulomb metres (C.m)

Dipole moment (μ) is a vector quantity directed from positive to negative. It is shown by an arrow with the arrowhead pointing toward the negative side (δ-) and a cross toward the positive side (δ+). Water has a dipole moment of 1.85 D and ammonia 1.47 D, so water is more polar. In a diatomic molecule like HF or HCl, the charge q is equal to δ+ and δ-.

  • Diatomic molecules of different atoms (HF, HCl, CO) are polar and have dipole moments; those of the same atoms (H2, O2) are non-polar.
  • In polyatomic molecules, both bond polarity and molecular geometry decide the overall dipole moment. CO2 is linear and non-polar despite having polar bonds, because the bond dipoles cancel.
  • SO3 and CCl4 have polar bonds but no dipole moment, due to their symmetrical structures. Shapes of molecules can also be determined from dipole moment.

Key Points

  • Dipole moment measures bond/molecular polarity; zero means non-polar.
  • μ = q × d, measured in Debye (D) or C.m; 1 D = 3.34 × 10^-30 C.m.
  • It is a vector, directed from positive to negative.
  • H2O (1.85 D) is more polar than NH3 (1.47 D).
  • Symmetrical molecules like CO2, SO3 and CCl4 have polar bonds but zero net dipole moment.
lessons.title: Dipole Moment

mcqs.q: What is matter?
options: Anything that has mass and occupies space
Only things that can be seen
mcqs.why: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space; it is classified by physical states: solids, liquids, gases and plasma.

mcqs.q: How are the molecules packed in a liquid compared with solids and gases?
options: Closely packed compared to gases, but not as tightly as in solids
Exactly like gases with huge gaps
Liquids have no molecules close together
mcqs.why: In liquids the particles are closely packed compared to gases, but not as tightly as in solids, with gaps larger than solids but smaller than gases.

mcqs.q: Why are liquids almost incompressible?
options: Because their molecules are far apart
Because they have no intermolecular forces
Because their molecules are tightly packed, so volume reduces only slightly when pressure rises
mcqs.why: Liquids are almost incompressible because their molecules are tightly packed; when pressure rises their volume reduces only slightly, unlike gases.

mcqs.q: How do intermolecular forces in liquids compare with solids and gases?
options: Stronger than in gases but weaker than in solids
mcqs.why: The intermolecular forces in liquids are stronger than in gases but weaker than in solids; the greater these forces, the higher the boiling point.

mcqs.q: Why do liquids flow and take the shape of their container?
options: Because liquid molecules slip and slide over one another
Because liquid molecules are fixed in place
Because liquids have no definite volume
Because liquids are gases in disguise
mcqs.why: Liquid molecules slip and slide over one another, so liquids flow and take the shape of their container; they have no definite shape but a definite volume.

mcqs.q: How does the kinetic energy of liquid molecules change with temperature?
options: It increases with temperature and decreases on cooling
It is higher than that of gases
mcqs.why: The kinetic energy of liquid molecules is higher than solids and lower than gases; it increases with temperature and decreases on cooling.

mcqs.q: Why is diffusion in liquids slow?
options: Because liquid molecules do not move at all
Because molecules move gradually past each other in continuous movement
mcqs.why: Liquids diffuse slowly into miscible liquids due to the continuous movement of their molecules, which move gradually past each other.

mcqs.q: What happens to the volume of a liquid on heating?
options: It increases greatly like a gas
It doubles with a small temperature rise
It shows no appreciable increase in volume on heating
mcqs.why: The notes state that liquids show no appreciable increase in volume on heating, unlike gases which expand greatly.

mcqs.q: Which statement about liquids is correct?
options: Liquids have a definite volume but no definite shape
Liquids have a definite shape but no definite volume
Liquids have neither definite shape nor volume
Liquids have both definite shape and volume
mcqs.why: Because their molecules slip and slide, liquids flow and take the container's shape: definite volume but no definite shape.

mcqs.q: What is the relation between intermolecular forces and boiling point in liquids?
options: Stronger forces give a lower boiling point
The greater the intermolecular forces, the higher the boiling point
Forces do not affect boiling point
Weaker forces give a higher boiling point
mcqs.why: The notes state that the intermolecular forces in liquids lie between gases and solids, and the greater these forces, the higher the boiling point.

lessons.notes_html:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It is classified by its physical states: solids, liquids, gases and plasma. In liquids, the particles are closely packed compared to gases, but not as tightly as in solids.

Composition and Spaces Between Molecules

Liquids consist of atoms or molecules. The molecules are so close together that there is very little empty space between them; the gaps are larger than those in solids but smaller than those in gases.

Compression and Expansion

Liquids are almost incompressible because their molecules are tightly packed; when pressure rises, their volume reduces only slightly, unlike gases. Liquids also show no appreciable increase in volume on heating.

Intermolecular Forces and Kinetic Energy

The intermolecular forces in liquids are stronger than in gases but weaker than in solids; the greater these forces, the higher the boiling point. The kinetic energy of liquid molecules is higher than that of solids and lower than that of gases; it increases with temperature and decreases on cooling.

Motion of Molecules and Diffusion

Liquid molecules slip and slide over one another, so liquids flow and take the shape of their container; they have no definite shape but a definite volume. Liquids diffuse slowly into other liquids with which they are miscible, due to the continuous movement of their molecules.

Key Points

  • Liquid particles are closely packed, with little empty space between them.
  • Liquids are almost incompressible and expand very little on heating.
  • Intermolecular forces in liquids lie between those of gases and solids.
  • Liquid molecules slip and slide over each other, so liquids flow.
  • Liquids have a definite volume but no definite shape.
  • Diffusion in liquids is slow because molecules move gradually past each other.
lessons.title: Simple Properties of Liquids Based on Kinetic Molecular Theory

mcqs.q: What is evaporation?
options: The spontaneous conversion of liquid molecules into vapours from the surface of a non-boiling liquid in an open container
The return of vapours into liquid
mcqs.why: Evaporation is the spontaneous conversion of liquid molecules into vapours from the surface of a non-boiling liquid in an open container at a given temperature.

mcqs.q: Why does evaporation occur at a given temperature?
options: All molecules have exactly the same kinetic energy
A fast-moving molecule reaching the surface may overcome the attractions of its neighbours and escape
mcqs.why: Not all molecules have the same kinetic energy; a fast-moving molecule reaching the surface may overcome neighbours' attractions and escape into the vapour state.

mcqs.q: Why does evaporation cool the remaining liquid?
options: Because cold air enters the liquid
Because the liquid absorbs cold from outside
Because it is endothermic: escaping molecules carry away energy, cooling the remaining liquid
mcqs.why: Evaporation is endothermic because energy is needed to overcome intermolecular forces; escaping molecules carry away energy, so the remaining liquid cools, like sweat cooling skin.

mcqs.q: How does temperature affect the rate of evaporation?
options: The rate increases with rising temperature, because molecular kinetic energy rises
The rate decreases with rising temperature
Temperature has no effect on evaporation
mcqs.why: Evaporation occurs at all temperatures and its rate increases with rising temperature because the kinetic energy of the molecules rises.

mcqs.q: Why does a larger surface area increase evaporation?
options: Because evaporation happens in the bulk of the liquid
Because evaporation is a surface phenomenon; a larger surface area gives greater evaporation
Because surface area lowers the temperature
Because surface area weakens all bonds
mcqs.why: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon, so the larger the surface area, the greater the evaporation from the liquid.

mcqs.q: Why does petrol evaporate faster than water?
options: Because petrol is hotter than water
Because water has no molecules at its surface
Because petrol's intermolecular forces are weaker than water's
Because petrol has a smaller surface area
mcqs.why: The stronger the intermolecular forces, the lower the rate of evaporation; petrol evaporates faster than water because its intermolecular forces are weaker.

mcqs.q: Evaporation is a type of which process?
options: Vaporisation, the process by which a liquid or solid changes into a gas
mcqs.why: Evaporation is a type of vaporisation, the process by which a liquid or solid changes into a gas.

mcqs.q: At which temperatures does evaporation take place?
mcqs.why: The key points state that evaporation takes place at all temperatures and is an endothermic, cooling process.

mcqs.q: How does sweating cool the body?
options: Sweat evaporating from the skin carries away energy and cools the body
mcqs.why: Sweat evaporating from the skin cools the body in the same way that evaporation cools the remaining liquid, by carrying away energy.

mcqs.q: Which molecules escape during evaporation?
options: Molecules from the bottom of the liquid
High-energy (fast-moving) molecules from the surface of the liquid
Only molecules with no kinetic energy
mcqs.why: Evaporation is the escape of high-energy molecules from the surface of a liquid; they overcome the attractions of their neighbours.

lessons.notes_html:
Evaporation is the spontaneous conversion of liquid molecules into vapours from the surface of a non-boiling liquid in an open container at a given temperature. It is a type of vaporisation, the process by which a liquid or solid changes into a gas.

Why Evaporation Occurs

At a given temperature, not all liquid molecules have the same kinetic energy. A fast-moving molecule reaching the surface may overcome the attractions of its neighbours and escape into the vapour state. Evaporation is an endothermic process, because energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces; the escaping molecules carry away energy, so evaporation cools the remaining liquid. Sweat evaporating from the skin cools the body in the same way.

Factors Affecting Evaporation

  • Temperature: evaporation occurs at all temperatures; its rate increases with rising temperature, because the kinetic energy of the molecules rises.
  • Surface area: evaporation is a surface phenomenon; the larger the surface area, the greater the evaporation.
  • Intermolecular forces: the stronger the intermolecular forces, the lower the rate of evaporation; petrol evaporates faster than water because its intermolecular forces are weaker.

Key Points

  • Evaporation is the escape of high-energy molecules from the surface of a liquid.
  • It takes place at all temperatures and is an endothermic, cooling process.
  • Rate of evaporation increases with temperature and surface area.
  • Rate of evaporation decreases as intermolecular forces become stronger.
lessons.title: Evaporation

mcqs.q: What is vapour pressure?
options: The pressure of air above a liquid
The pressure exerted by liquid vapours in equilibrium with their pure liquid at a given temperature
The pressure needed to freeze a liquid
The atmospheric pressure at sea level
mcqs.why: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by liquid vapours in equilibrium with their pure liquid at a given temperature.

mcqs.q: What is condensation?
options: The escape of molecules from a liquid surface
The return of vapours into liquid when vapour molecules striking the surface are captured again
The freezing of vapours directly to solid
mcqs.why: Some vapour molecules striking the surface are captured again by the liquid; this return of vapours into liquid is condensation.

mcqs.q: What is dynamic equilibrium in a sealed container of liquid?
options: The number of molecules leaving the liquid equals the number returning, so evaporation and condensation rates are equal
mcqs.why: At dynamic equilibrium the rates of evaporation and condensation become equal: Liquid ⇌ Vapours, with evaporation forward and condensation back.

mcqs.q: At 25°C, why does water (24 mmHg) have a lower vapour pressure than chloroform (200 mmHg)?
options: Because water has strong hydrogen bonds while chloroform has only weak London forces
Because chloroform is colder than water
Because water has more liquid in the container
Because chloroform has stronger hydrogen bonds
mcqs.why: Working: 200 mmHg (chloroform) > 24 mmHg (water). Vapour pressure is inversely related to intermolecular attractions; water's strong hydrogen bonds hold its molecules back.

mcqs.q: How does vapour pressure change with temperature for water?
options: It falls from 760 mmHg to 24 mmHg
It rises from 24 mmHg at 25°C to 760 mmHg at 100°C
It stays at 24 mmHg at all temperatures
mcqs.why: Working: vapour pressure increases with temperature; for water it rises from 24 mmHg at 25°C to 760 mmHg at 100°C, an increase of 736 mmHg.

mcqs.q: Does vapour pressure depend on the amount of liquid or its surface area?
options: It depends only on the amount of liquid
It does not depend on the amount of liquid or on its surface area
It depends only on surface area
mcqs.why: Vapour pressure does not depend on the amount of liquid or surface area, because at equilibrium a change of surface area affects evaporation and condensation equally.

mcqs.q: In a sealed evacuated container, how do evaporation and condensation change at first?
options: Condensation is faster from the start
Both rates are equal from the start
At first evaporation is faster than condensation, but eventually the two rates become equal
mcqs.why: Vapours accumulate above the liquid; at first evaporation is faster than condensation, but eventually the two rates become equal at dynamic equilibrium.

mcqs.q: What is the relation between intermolecular forces and vapour pressure?
options: Weaker intermolecular forces give a higher vapour pressure
Stronger forces give a higher vapour pressure
Forces do not affect vapour pressure
Vapour pressure depends only on surface area
mcqs.why: Vapour pressure is inversely related to intermolecular attractions: weaker forces let more molecules escape, giving a higher vapour pressure.

mcqs.q: When is vapour pressure measured?
options: When evaporation and condensation rates are equal
Only at the boiling point of every liquid
When the container is open to the air
mcqs.why: The key points state that vapour pressure is measured when evaporation and condensation rates are equal, i.e. at dynamic equilibrium.

mcqs.q: Chloroform's vapour pressure at 25°C is how many times water's (approx.)?
mcqs.why: Working: 200 mmHg ÷ 24 mmHg ≈ 8.33, so chloroform's vapour pressure at 25°C is about 8 times water's because its forces are much weaker.

lessons.notes_html:
Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by liquid vapours in equilibrium with their pure liquid at a given temperature.

Dynamic Equilibrium

In a sealed, evacuated container, vapours formed by evaporation accumulate above the liquid. Some vapour molecules striking the surface are captured again by the liquid; this return of vapours into liquid is condensation. At first evaporation is faster than condensation, but eventually the two rates become equal. This state, in which the number of molecules leaving the liquid equals the number returning, is dynamic equilibrium: Liquid ⇌ Vapours (evaporation forward, condensation back).

Factors Affecting Vapour Pressure

  • Intermolecular forces: vapour pressure is inversely related to intermolecular attractions. At 25°C, water (24 mmHg) has a lower vapour pressure than chloroform (200 mmHg), because water has strong hydrogen bonds while chloroform has only weak London forces.
  • Temperature: vapour pressure increases with temperature; for water it rises from 24 mmHg at 25°C to 760 mmHg at 100°C.

Vapour pressure does not depend on the amount of liquid or on its surface area, because at equilibrium a change of surface area affects evaporation and condensation equally.

Key Points

  • Vapour pressure is measured when evaporation and condensation rates are equal.
  • Weaker intermolecular forces give a higher vapour pressure.
  • Vapour pressure rises with temperature.
  • It does not depend on the amount of liquid or its surface area.
lessons.title: Vapour Pressure

mcqs.q: What is the boiling point of a liquid?
options: The temperature at which a liquid freezes
The temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the atmospheric or external pressure
The temperature at which evaporation stops
The highest temperature a liquid can reach in a sealed vessel
mcqs.why: The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the atmospheric or external pressure.

mcqs.q: Why does the temperature remain constant during boiling?
options: Because no heat is supplied during boiling
Because the vapour escapes too quickly
Because the heat supplied is used only to break the intermolecular forces and convert the liquid into vapour
mcqs.why: During boiling the temperature stays constant because the heat supplied is used only to break intermolecular forces and convert liquid into vapour.

mcqs.q: What is the boiling point of acetone at 1 atm?
mcqs.why: The table of boiling points at 1 atm gives acetone 56.0°C, ethyl alcohol 78.3°C, acetic acid 118.5°C and ethylene glycol 197°C.

mcqs.q: Why does water (100°C) boil higher than ethyl alcohol (78.26°C)?
options: Because of stronger intermolecular forces; without hydrogen bonding water would boil at about −75°C
Because water is heavier in the container
Because alcohol has hydrogen bonding and water does not
Because water has a larger surface area
mcqs.why: Stronger intermolecular forces give a higher boiling point; water's hydrogen bonding raises it to 100°C, and without it water would boil at about −75°C.

mcqs.q: How does external pressure affect the boiling point?
options: Boiling point falls as pressure rises
The boiling point rises with external pressure and falls when pressure falls
Pressure has no effect on boiling point
Boiling point depends only on the amount of liquid
mcqs.why: Water boils at 100°C at 760 mmHg, about 98°C at Murree (700 mmHg), about 71°C on Everest (240 mmHg) and 110°C at 1074.6 mmHg.

mcqs.q: At what temperature does water boil on Mount Everest (240 mmHg)?
mcqs.why: Working: at the low pressure of 240 mmHg on Mount Everest, water boils at about 71°C, well below its 100°C value at 760 mmHg.

mcqs.q: How does a pressure cooker cook food faster?
options: It removes steam from the cooker
Trapped steam raises the pressure, the boiling point of water rises (a commercial cooker reaches 140°C), and food cooks faster
mcqs.why: In a pressure cooker trapped steam raises the pressure so the boiling point of water rises, up to 140°C in a commercial cooker, and food cooks faster.

mcqs.q: Why is vacuum distillation used for glycerin?
options: Glycerin decomposes at 290°C at 760 torr but boils safely at 210°C at 50 torr, so low-pressure distillation purifies it
Glycerin cannot be heated at all
mcqs.why: Working: lowering pressure from 760 torr to 50 torr lowers glycerin's boiling point from 290°C (where it decomposes) to a safe 210°C.

mcqs.q: What forms throughout the liquid when it boils?
options: Bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface
mcqs.why: On heating, vapour pressure rises until bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface; this is boiling.

mcqs.q: Does the boiling point depend on the amount of liquid?
options: Yes, more liquid always boils higher
No, boiling point does not depend on the amount of liquid
It depends only on the size of the container
mcqs.why: The key points state that boiling point does not depend on the amount of liquid; it depends on intermolecular forces and external pressure.

lessons.notes_html:
The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the atmospheric or external pressure. On heating, the average kinetic energy and the vapour pressure rise until bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface. The temperature remains constant during boiling, because the heat supplied is used only to break the intermolecular forces and convert the liquid into vapour.

Boiling Points of Some Liquids (at 1 atm)

LiquidBoiling Point (°C)LiquidBoiling Point (°C)
Acetic acid118.5Carbon tetrachloride76.5
Acetone56.0Ethyl alcohol78.3
Ammonia-33.3Ethylene glycol197

Factors Affecting the Boiling Point

  • Intermolecular forces: the stronger the forces, the higher the boiling point; water (100°C) boils higher than ethyl alcohol (78.26°C). Without hydrogen bonding, water would boil at about -75°C.
  • External pressure: the boiling point rises with external pressure and falls when pressure falls. Water boils at 100°C at 760 mmHg, at about 98°C at Murree (700 mmHg), at about 71°C on Mount Everest (240 mmHg), and at 110°C at 1074.6 mmHg.

Applications

In a pressure cooker, trapped steam raises the pressure, the boiling point of water rises (a commercial cooker reaches 140°C), and food cooks faster. In vacuum distillation, distillation is done at low pressure so that liquids which decompose at their boiling points can be purified; glycerin decomposes at 290°C at 760 torr but boils safely at 210°C at 50 torr.

Key Points

  • At the boiling point, vapour pressure equals external pressure.
  • Temperature stays constant while a liquid boils.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces give a higher boiling point.
  • Higher external pressure raises the boiling point; lower pressure lowers it.
  • Boiling point does not depend on the amount of liquid.
lessons.title: Boiling Point

mcqs.q: What is viscosity?
options: The energy of a liquid surface
The internal resistance to the flow of a liquid, denoted by eta (η)
The pressure exerted by a vapour
The temperature at which a liquid boils
mcqs.why: Viscosity is the internal resistance to the flow of a liquid, denoted by eta (η); the greater the viscosity, the slower a liquid flows.

mcqs.q: Which liquids flow slowly and which flow quickly, per the notes?
options: Gasoline and water flow slowly; honey flows quickly
All liquids flow at the same rate
Honey and glycerin flow slowly, while gasoline and water flow quickly
Water is the slowest of all liquids
mcqs.why: The greater the viscosity the slower the flow: honey and glycerin flow slowly, while gasoline and water flow quickly.

mcqs.q: Why does a liquid flow slowest near the walls and fastest in the centre?
options: Because of gravity at the centre
Because there are no molecules near the walls
Because each layer resists the flow of the others due to internal friction from cohesive forces
mcqs.why: A liquid flows in layers; each layer resists the others because of internal friction from cohesive forces, so flow is slowest near walls and fastest in the centre.

mcqs.q: What are the units of viscosity?
options: The poise (1 poise = 100 centipoise); SI unit Nsm^−2, and 1 poise = 10^−1 kgm^−1s^−1
mcqs.why: Working: 1 poise = 100 centipoise = 10^−1 kgm^−1s^−1; the SI unit of viscosity is newton-second per metre square, Nsm^−2.

mcqs.q: How do intermolecular forces affect viscosity?
options: Stronger forces make a liquid less viscous
Stronger forces make a liquid more viscous, because molecules resist sliding past one another
Forces have no effect on viscosity
mcqs.why: Stronger intermolecular forces make a liquid more viscous; hydrogen-bonded liquids have high viscosity and small non-polar molecules like benzene have low viscosity.

mcqs.q: Which liquid has the highest viscosity among those compared in the notes?
options: Glycerin, with more hydrogen bonding sites
mcqs.why: Water is more viscous than methyl alcohol, and glycerin, with more hydrogen bonding sites, has the highest viscosity of the three.

mcqs.q: How does temperature affect viscosity?
options: Viscosity decreases as temperature increases, because molecules gain kinetic energy and overcome attractions more easily
mcqs.why: Viscosity decreases with rising temperature; honey and cooking oil flow faster when warm because molecules overcome attractive forces more easily.

mcqs.q: Besides intermolecular forces and temperature, what else affects viscosity?
options: The size and shape of the molecules
The shape of the container only
mcqs.why: The notes state that viscosity also depends on the size and shape of the molecules, as well as on intermolecular forces and temperature.

mcqs.q: What causes viscosity inside a liquid?
options: Internal friction between the layers of a liquid
mcqs.why: Viscosity is caused by internal friction between the layers of a liquid, arising from cohesive forces between the molecules.

mcqs.q: What is the symbol for viscosity?
mcqs.why: Viscosity is denoted by eta (η); gamma (γ) is the symbol used for surface tension in the next lesson.

lessons.notes_html:
The internal resistance to the flow of a liquid is called viscosity, denoted by eta (η). The greater the viscosity, the slower a liquid flows; honey and glycerin flow slowly, while gasoline and water flow quickly. A liquid flows in layers; each layer resists the flow of the others because of internal friction arising from cohesive forces between the molecules, so the flow is slowest near the walls and fastest in the centre.

Units

The unit of viscosity is the poise (1 poise = 100 centipoise). Its SI unit is newton-second per metre square, Nsm^-2; 1 poise = 10^-1 kgm^-1s^-1.

Factors Affecting Viscosity

  • Intermolecular forces: stronger forces make a liquid more viscous, because the molecules resist sliding past one another. Small, non-polar molecules like benzene have low viscosity; hydrogen-bonded liquids have high viscosity. Water is more viscous than methyl alcohol, and glycerin, with more hydrogen bonding sites, has the highest viscosity.
  • Temperature: viscosity decreases as temperature increases, because the molecules gain kinetic energy and overcome the attractive forces more easily; honey and cooking oil flow faster when warm.
  • Molecular size and shape: viscosity also depends on the size and shape of the molecules.

Key Points

  • Viscosity is the internal resistance of a liquid to flow, symbol η.
  • It is caused by internal friction between the layers of a liquid.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces and hydrogen bonding increase viscosity.
  • Viscosity decreases with an increase in temperature.
  • SI unit of viscosity is Nsm^-2; the common unit is the poise.
lessons.title: Viscosity

mcqs.q: What is surface tension?
options: The pressure inside a liquid droplet
The energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid by one unit
The resistance of a liquid to flow
The temperature at which a surface boils
mcqs.why: Surface tension is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid by one unit, represented by the Greek letter γ (gamma).

mcqs.q: What is the formula for surface tension?
options: γ = Force / Length, force per unit length acting on the liquid surface
mcqs.why: Working: Surface tension γ = Force / Length. It is also defined as the force along the surface at right angles to any line of unit length on the surface.

mcqs.q: What are the units of surface tension?
options: Dyne/cm in CGS or N/m in SI units (energy form: erg/cm^2)
mcqs.why: The unit of surface tension is dyne/cm in CGS or N/m in SI units; in energy form it is erg/cm^2.

mcqs.q: What causes surface tension?
options: Surface molecules are pulled only downwards and sideways by inner molecules, with no upward pull, so the surface contracts
Surface molecules are pulled equally in all directions
Air pressure pushes the surface outward
mcqs.why: Molecules inside are pulled equally in all directions, but surface molecules are pulled only downwards and sideways, so the inward pull makes the surface contract.

mcqs.q: What everyday observations show surface tension, per the notes?
options: A water strider insect can walk on water and a carefully placed razor blade can float on it
mcqs.why: The surface behaves like a stretched piece of rubber, so a water strider can walk on water and a carefully placed razor blade can float on it.

mcqs.q: How does the liquid surface behave because of surface tension?
options: Like a stretched elastic skin / stretched piece of rubber
mcqs.why: The key points state that the liquid surface behaves like a stretched elastic skin because of the unbalanced inward pull on surface molecules.

mcqs.q: On what does the magnitude of surface tension depend?
options: Only on the amount of liquid
On the intermolecular forces and on temperature
mcqs.why: The notes state that the magnitude of surface tension depends on the intermolecular forces and on temperature.

mcqs.q: How are molecules inside the liquid pulled?
options: Molecules inside the liquid are pulled equally in all directions
They are not pulled at all
They are pulled only toward the surface
mcqs.why: Molecules inside the liquid are pulled equally in all directions, unlike surface molecules which experience an unbalanced inward pull.

mcqs.q: Surface tension can also be defined as which quantity?
options: The force acting along the surface at right angles to any line of unit length drawn on the surface
mcqs.why: Surface tension is also defined as the force acting along the surface of a liquid at right angles to any line of unit length drawn on the surface.

mcqs.q: What symbol represents surface tension?
mcqs.why: Surface tension is represented by the Greek letter γ (gamma), while η (eta) is the symbol for viscosity.

lessons.notes_html:
Surface tension is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid by one unit. It is represented by the Greek letter γ (gamma). It can also be defined as the force acting along the surface of a liquid at right angles to any line of unit length drawn on the surface.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Surface tension (γ) = Force / LengthForce per unit length acting on the liquid surface

Its unit is dyne/cm in CGS or N/m in SI units (energy form: erg/cm^2).

Cause of Surface Tension

Molecules inside the liquid are pulled equally in all directions, but molecules at the surface are pulled only downwards and sideways by the inner molecules, with no upward pull. This inward pull makes the surface contract and behave like a stretched piece of rubber, so a water strider insect can walk on water and a carefully placed razor blade can float on it. The magnitude of surface tension depends on the intermolecular forces and on temperature.

Key Points

  • Surface tension is the energy needed to increase surface area by one unit.
  • γ = Force / Length; SI unit is N/m.
  • It arises from the unbalanced inward pull on surface molecules.
  • The liquid surface behaves like a stretched elastic skin.
  • It depends on intermolecular forces and temperature.
lessons.title: Surface tension

mcqs.q: Why does water have a high boiling point of 100°C?
options: Because water molecules are very heavy
Because much energy is needed to break the strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules
Because water has a low vapour pressure only
mcqs.why: Much energy is needed to break the strong hydrogen bonds, so water boils at 100°C; without hydrogen bonding it would boil at about −75°C.

mcqs.q: What is cohesion in water?
options: Attraction between water and other substances
The attraction between molecules of the same substance, caused by hydrogen bonding
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding causes cohesion, the attraction between molecules of the same substance, which gives water a high surface tension.

mcqs.q: Why does water have a low vapour pressure?
options: Because its molecules escape very easily
Because it has no intermolecular forces
Because the hydrogen bonds hold the molecules tightly, so few molecules escape into the gas phase
Because its surface area is small
mcqs.why: The hydrogen bonds hold water molecules tightly, so few molecules escape into the gas phase; water therefore has a low vapour pressure.

mcqs.q: What is the specific heat capacity of water and its effect?
options: 4.18 J/g°C; it absorbs heat by day and releases it at night, moderating the climate
mcqs.why: Working: water's specific heat capacity is 4.18 J/g°C. It absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, moderating climate, especially in coastal areas.

mcqs.q: Why does water have a high heat of vaporisation?
options: Strong hydrogen bonds need much energy to be overcome during evaporation
Because evaporation is exothermic for water
Because water vapour is very heavy
Because water has weak intermolecular forces
mcqs.why: Strong hydrogen bonds need much energy to be overcome during evaporation, so water has a high heat of vaporisation, making sweating an effective cooling method.

mcqs.q: Without hydrogen bonding, at about what temperature would water boil?
options: At about −75°C, and it would not exist as a liquid at ordinary temperatures
mcqs.why: Without hydrogen bonding water would boil at about −75°C and would not exist as a liquid at ordinary temperatures.

mcqs.q: What does water's high surface tension allow?
options: Water to boil at lower temperatures
It lets water form droplets and allows small insects to walk on its surface
mcqs.why: Cohesion from hydrogen bonding gives water a high surface tension, which lets it form droplets and allows small insects to walk on its surface.

mcqs.q: How does water's high heat of vaporisation help organisms?
options: It makes sweating an effective way of cooling organisms and prevents rapid temperature changes
mcqs.why: The high heat of vaporisation makes sweating an effective way of cooling organisms and prevents rapid temperature changes in the environment.

mcqs.q: Which properties of water are influenced by hydrogen bonding, per the notes?
options: High boiling and melting points, high surface tension, low vapour pressure, high specific heat and high heat of vaporisation
Only its ability to dissolve salts
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding gives water unusually high boiling/melting points, high surface tension, low vapour pressure, high specific heat capacity and high heat of vaporisation.

mcqs.q: Why is water's melting point described as unusual?
options: It is lower than expected for its size
It is higher than expected for a molecule of its size, because of hydrogen bonding
mcqs.why: Much energy is needed to break strong hydrogen bonds, so water has a melting point higher than expected for a molecule of its size.

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrogen bonding between water molecules gives water its unusual properties. The key properties influenced by hydrogen bonding are:

High Boiling and Melting Points

Much energy is needed to break the strong hydrogen bonds, so water has a boiling point of 100°C and a melting point higher than expected for a molecule of its size. Without hydrogen bonding, water would boil at about -75°C and would not exist as a liquid at ordinary temperatures.

Cohesion and Surface Tension

Hydrogen bonding causes cohesion, the attraction between molecules of the same substance. This gives water a high surface tension, which lets it form droplets and allows small insects to walk on its surface.

Low Vapour Pressure of Water

The hydrogen bonds hold the molecules tightly, so few molecules escape into the gas phase; water therefore has a low vapour pressure.

High Specific Heat Capacity

Water has a high specific heat capacity (4.18 J/g°C). It absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, moderating the climate, especially in coastal areas.

High Heat of Vaporisation

Strong hydrogen bonds need much energy to be overcome during evaporation, so water has a high heat of vaporisation. This makes sweating an effective way of cooling organisms and prevents rapid temperature changes in the environment.

Key Points

  • Hydrogen bonding is responsible for the special properties of water.
  • Water has unusually high boiling and melting points for its size.
  • Cohesion from hydrogen bonding gives water high surface tension.
  • Water has a low vapour pressure and a high specific heat capacity.
  • Its high heat of vaporisation makes evaporation a strong cooling process.
lessons.title: The Role of Hydrogen Bonding in the Properties of Water

mcqs.q: What is a phase change?
options: A chemical reaction forming new substances
The transformation of a substance from one physical state to another; it is a physical change
The breaking of covalent bonds only
A change in the atomic number
mcqs.why: A phase change (state change) is the transformation of a substance from one physical state to another; it is a physical change with enthalpy change ΔH.

mcqs.q: Which phase changes are endothermic (ΔH positive)?
mcqs.why: ΔH is positive when energy is absorbed (endothermic: melting, sublimation, evaporation) and negative when heat is released (exothermic processes).

mcqs.q: What is the molar heat of fusion of ice?
mcqs.why: Working: ΔHfus of ice is 6.02 kJ/mol for H2O(s) → H2O(l); freezing is the reverse and releases the same amount, ΔH = −6.02 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: What is the molar heat of vaporisation of water?
mcqs.why: Working: ΔHvap of water is 40.67 kJ/mol for H2O(l) → H2O(g); condensation releases the same amount with ΔHvap = −40.67 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: What is sublimation? Give the example from the notes.
options: Solid → gas, e.g. iodine → iodine vapours
mcqs.why: Sublimation is solid → gas, with the example iodine → iodine vapours; its reverse, gas → solid, is deposition.

mcqs.q: What is deposition?
options: Gas → solid, e.g. iodine vapours → iodine
mcqs.why: Deposition is the change gas → solid, exemplified by iodine vapours → iodine; it is exothermic with ΔH negative.

mcqs.q: How much heat is needed to melt 1 mole of ice and then vaporise the water completely?
mcqs.why: Working: total ΔH = ΔHfus + ΔHvap = 6.02 kJ/mol + 40.67 kJ/mol = 46.69 kJ/mol for H2O(s) → H2O(g) in two steps.

mcqs.q: What is the ΔH for condensation of steam, H2O(g) → H2O(l)?
options: −40.67 kJ/mol, the same magnitude as vaporisation with opposite sign
mcqs.why: Working: condensation is the reverse of vaporisation, so ΔH = −40.67 kJ/mol; the reverse process has the same magnitude of ΔH with the opposite sign.

mcqs.q: At what pressure is the enthalpy change ΔH for a phase transformation defined in the notes?
options: At any pressure, it never matters
mcqs.why: The energy change during a transformation at 1 atmosphere pressure is the enthalpy change, ΔH, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the molar heat of fusion?
options: Heat to vaporise 1 mole of liquid
The amount of heat required to convert one mole of a solid into its liquid state at the melting point
Heat released when 1 mole freezes at any temperature
mcqs.why: The molar heat of fusion (ΔHfus) is the heat required to convert one mole of a solid into liquid at the melting point; for ice it is 6.02 kJ/mol.

lessons.notes_html:
A phase change (state change) is the transformation of a substance from one physical state to another; it is a physical change. The energy change during a transformation at 1 atmosphere pressure is the enthalpy change, ΔH. ΔH is positive when energy is absorbed (endothermic: melting, sublimation, evaporation) and negative when heat is released (exothermic: freezing, condensation, deposition).

The Six Phase Changes

Change of StateProcessExample
Solid → LiquidMelting or fusionIce → Water
Solid → GasSublimationIodine → Iodine vapours
Liquid → SolidFreezingWater → Ice
Liquid → GasVaporisationWater → Steam
Gas → LiquidCondensationSteam → Water
Gas → SolidDepositionIodine vapours → Iodine

Molar Heat of Fusion

The amount of heat required to convert one mole of a solid into its liquid state at the melting point is the molar heat of fusion (molar enthalpy of fusion), ΔHfus. For ice it is 6.02 kJ/mol: H2O(s) → H2O(l). Freezing is the reverse process; it releases the same amount of heat, so ΔHfus for freezing is -6.02 kJ/mol.

Molar Heat of Vaporisation

The amount of heat required to convert one mole of a liquid into vapours at its boiling point is the molar heat of vaporisation, ΔHvap. For water it is 40.67 kJ/mol: H2O(l) → H2O(g). Condensation releases the same amount, with ΔHvap = -40.67 kJ/mol.

Key Formulae

ProcessΔH (kJ/mol)
H2O(s) → H2O(l) (fusion of ice)+6.02
H2O(l) → H2O(g) (vaporisation of water)+40.67
H2O(g) → H2O(l) (condensation of steam)-40.67

Key Points

  • Phase changes are physical changes with an enthalpy change ΔH.
  • Melting, sublimation and evaporation are endothermic (ΔH positive).
  • Freezing, condensation and deposition are exothermic (ΔH negative).
  • ΔHfus of ice is 6.02 kJ/mol; ΔHvap of water is 40.67 kJ/mol.
  • The reverse process has the same magnitude of ΔH with the opposite sign.
lessons.title: Energetics of Phase Changes

mcqs.q: What is molar heat capacity (Cm)?
options: The heat needed to melt one mole of a solid
The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by one degree Celsius or one kelvin
The heat released by one mole on freezing
The total heat contained in one mole
mcqs.why: Molar heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by 1°C or 1 K, symbol Cm, in J/mol.K.

mcqs.q: What is the molar heat capacity of water?
mcqs.why: Working: water has a high molar heat capacity of about 75.3 J/mol.K, so it absorbs a large amount of heat with only a small temperature change.

mcqs.q: How much heat is needed to raise 2 moles of water by 10 K? (Cm = 75.3 J/mol.K)
mcqs.why: Working: Q = Cm × n × ΔT = 75.3 J/mol.K × 2 mol × 10 K = 1506 J. Water's high Cm keeps coastal cities like Karachi and Gwadar stable.

mcqs.q: What do the heats of fusion and vaporisation indicate?
options: They indicate the strengths of the intermolecular forces; they increase as the forces grow stronger
They indicate the atomic mass only
They indicate the colour of the substance
They are always equal for a substance
mcqs.why: The heats of fusion and vaporisation indicate the strengths of intermolecular forces; more energy is needed to change state when forces are stronger.

mcqs.q: Which liquids have high heats of vaporisation, per the notes?
options: Liquids showing hydrogen bonding, such as water, ethylene glycol and ethyl alcohol
mcqs.why: Liquids showing hydrogen bonding, such as water, ethylene glycol and ethyl alcohol, have high heats of vaporisation.

mcqs.q: Why is ΔHvap generally much greater than ΔHfus?
options: Fusion breaks all intermolecular forces completely
Fusion only loosens particles with a small change in distances, while vaporisation must completely break the intermolecular forces
The two values are measured in different units only
mcqs.why: Fusion only loosens particles so they can move, with small distance changes, while vaporisation must completely break intermolecular forces to separate molecules.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of molar heat capacity?
mcqs.why: Molar heat capacity Cm is expressed in J/mol.K (or J/mol.°C); for water Cm is about 75.3 J/mol.K.

mcqs.q: What happens to substances with a high molar heat capacity?
options: They need more energy to change their temperature and resist temperature change
mcqs.why: Substances with a high molar heat capacity need more energy to change their temperature, so high heat capacity substances resist temperature change.

mcqs.q: Why do coastal cities like Karachi and Gwadar have stable temperatures?
options: Because water has a high molar heat capacity and absorbs much heat with a small temperature change
Because they are far from the equator only
Because sand has a high heat capacity
mcqs.why: Water's high molar heat capacity (about 75.3 J/mol.K) lets it absorb a large amount of heat with a small temperature change, stabilising coastal temperatures.

mcqs.q: As intermolecular forces grow stronger, what happens to heats of fusion and vaporisation?
options: These heats increase, because more energy is needed to change the physical state
mcqs.why: The notes state these heats increase as intermolecular forces grow stronger, because more energy is needed to change the physical state.

lessons.notes_html:
Molar heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a substance by one degree Celsius or one kelvin. It is represented by the symbol Cm and expressed in J/mol.K (or J/mol.°C). Substances with a high molar heat capacity need more energy to change their temperature. Water has a high molar heat capacity of about 75.3 J/mol.K, so it absorbs a large amount of heat with only a small temperature change; this keeps temperatures stable in coastal cities like Karachi and Gwadar.

Energy Change and Intermolecular Forces

The heats of fusion and vaporisation indicate the strengths of the intermolecular forces. These heats increase as the intermolecular forces grow stronger, because more energy is needed to change the physical state. Liquids showing hydrogen bonding, such as water, ethylene glycol and ethyl alcohol, have high heats of vaporisation. Heats of vaporisation are generally much higher than heats of fusion: fusion only loosens the particles so they can move around, with a small change in intermolecular distances, while vaporisation must completely break the intermolecular forces to separate the molecules.

Key Points

  • Molar heat capacity Cm is the heat needed to raise 1 mole by 1°C or 1 K.
  • Its unit is J/mol.K; for water Cm is about 75.3 J/mol.K.
  • High heat capacity substances resist temperature change.
  • Heats of fusion and vaporisation measure intermolecular force strength.
  • ΔHvap is much greater than ΔHfus for the same substance.
lessons.title: Molar Heat Capacity

mcqs.q: Why is the heat of fusion important for glaciers and ice sheets?
options: It is the energy needed to turn ice into water without changing its temperature, governing ice formation, movement and melting
It determines the colour of glaciers
It only affects liquid water in oceans
It has no role in climate
mcqs.why: The heat of fusion is the energy needed to turn ice into water without changing temperature, playing an essential role in ice formation, movement and melting.

mcqs.q: What does the heat of fusion help with in glacier formation?

It removes ice from the poles
mcqs.why: The heat of fusion helps in the formation of glaciers from snow and tells us the energy required to convert ice back into water during melting.

mcqs.q: Why are glaciers and ice sheets indicators of climate change?
options: Because they change colour with temperature
Because they move faster in summer only
Changes linked to the heat of fusion help predict temperature variations in the ice, crucial for understanding climate change
mcqs.why: Glaciers are climate change indicators; changes linked to the heat of fusion help predict temperature variations in ice for understanding climate change.

mcqs.q: Why do polar glaciers resist small increases in temperature?
options: Because ice has a low heat of fusion
Because polar regions receive no sunlight
Because glaciers are too heavy to move
Because ice has a high heat of fusion, so a lot of energy is needed to melt it, keeping ice sheets intact and stabilising climate
