mcqs.q: How is the heat of fusion linked to sea level rise?
options: It determines the amount of water released when ice melts; melted ice entering the oceans causes sea levels to rise
It lowers sea levels by freezing ocean water
It has no connection with oceans
mcqs.why: The heat of fusion determines the amount of water released when ice melts; melted ice entering oceans causes sea levels to rise.

mcqs.q: What is glacial dynamics helped by the heat of fusion?
options: Predicting glacier behaviour and modelling glacier dynamics
mcqs.why: The heat of fusion also helps in predicting glacier behaviour and modelling glacier dynamics, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: When ice melts using its heat of fusion, what happens to its temperature during melting?
options: It stays unchanged: the energy turns ice into water without changing its temperature
mcqs.why: The heat of fusion is the energy needed to turn ice into water without changing its temperature, absorbed mainly as heat of fusion during melting.

mcqs.q: Where is the heat of fusion especially crucial, per the notes?
options: In studying glaciers and ice sheets, especially the polar ice caps
mcqs.why: The heat of fusion is crucial in studying glaciers and ice sheets, especially the polar ice caps, for formation, movement and melting.

mcqs.q: What energy is mainly absorbed when glacier ice melts?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the heat absorbed during melting is mainly the heat of fusion, which determines how much water is released.

options: They help stabilise the Earth's climate by resisting small temperature increases
They have no effect on climate
They cause sea levels to fall quickly
mcqs.why: Because of the high heat of fusion, polar glaciers and ice sheets resist small warming, stay intact and help stabilise the Earth's climate.

lessons.notes_html:
The heat of fusion is crucial in studying glaciers and ice sheets, especially the polar ice caps. It is the energy needed to turn ice into water without changing its temperature, and it plays a hidden yet essential role in ice formation, movement and melting.

Ice Formation and Melting

The heat of fusion helps in the formation of glaciers from snow and tells us the energy required to convert ice back into water during melting.

Climate Change Indicators

Glaciers and ice sheets are indicators of climate change. Changes linked to the heat of fusion help in predicting temperature variations in the ice, which is crucial for understanding climate change.

Glacial Dynamics

Ice has a high heat of fusion, so a lot of energy is needed to melt it. Polar glaciers and ice sheets therefore resist small increases in temperature, stay intact and help stabilise the Earth's climate. The heat of fusion also helps in predicting glacier behaviour and modelling glacier dynamics.

Sea Level Rise

The heat of fusion determines the amount of water released when ice melts. Melted ice entering the oceans causes sea levels to rise; the heat absorbed during melting is mainly the heat of fusion.

Key Points

  • Heat of fusion is the energy that melts ice at constant temperature.
  • It governs glacier formation from snow and glacier melting.
  • Glaciers act as indicators of climate change.
  • The high heat of fusion of ice protects polar ice from small warming.
  • Melting ice, driven by the heat of fusion, raises sea levels.
lessons.title: Importance of Heat of Fusion

mcqs.q: Why are gases highly compressible?
options: Because gas molecules are tightly packed
Because most of the volume of a gas is empty space (about 99.9%), so pressure pushes molecules closer together
Because gases have strong intermolecular forces
Because gases have a fixed volume
mcqs.why: Gas molecules are widely spaced; about 99.9% of a gas's volume is empty space, so pressure pushes molecules closer and volume falls greatly, e.g. LPG in cylinders.

mcqs.q: What is expandability of gases?
options: The ability to decrease volume under pressure
The ability to liquefy on cooling
The property of a gas to increase in volume and fill all the space available
The ability to keep a fixed shape
mcqs.why: Expandability is the property of a gas to increase in volume and fill all available space; with high kinetic energy a gas occupies its whole container, like perfume spreading.

mcqs.q: What causes gas pressure?
options: The force exerted by gas molecules when they collide with the walls of their container, per unit area
The temperature of the room alone
mcqs.why: Gas pressure is the force exerted by gas molecules colliding with container walls, measured as force per unit area, e.g. air pressure in car and bicycle tyres.

mcqs.q: State the Ideal Gas Law and what R stands for.
options: PV = nRT, where R is the gas constant
PV = n/R T, where R is resistance
P/V = nRT, where R is radius
PT = nRV, where R is reactivity
mcqs.why: Working: the Ideal Gas Law is PV = nRT: P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = gas constant, T = temperature in kelvin.

mcqs.q: Convert 2 atm into mmHg and pascals.
mcqs.why: Working: 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101,325 Pa. So 2 atm = 2 × 760 = 1520 mmHg and 2 × 101,325 = 202,650 Pa.

mcqs.q: Using PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K, what volume does 1 mole of gas occupy at 1 atm and 273 K?
options: About 22.4 L, because V = nRT/P = 1 × 0.0821 × 273 / 1 ≈ 22.4 L
mcqs.why: Working: V = nRT/P = (1 mol × 0.0821 × 273 K) / 1 atm = 22.41 ≈ 22.4 L, the molar volume from the Ideal Gas Law.

mcqs.q: What shape and volume do gases have?
options: Fixed shape but no fixed volume
Fixed volume but no fixed shape
No fixed shape and no fixed volume
mcqs.why: With high kinetic energy and no significant intermolecular forces, a gas expands to occupy its whole container; gases have no fixed shape or volume.

mcqs.q: Give the example of gas compressibility from the notes.
options: Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is stored in compressed form in steel cylinders
mcqs.why: Compressibility is shown by LPG stored in compressed form in steel cylinders; perfume spreading shows expandability instead.

mcqs.q: What units of pressure are listed in the notes?
options: Atmosphere (atm), pascal (Pa), mmHg or Torr, and bar
mcqs.why: Units of pressure include atmosphere (atm), pascal (Pa), mmHg or Torr, and bar; 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101,325 Pa.

mcqs.q: Why does perfume spread quickly through a room when the bottle is opened?
options: Because perfume is a liquid under pressure
Because the bottle creates a vacuum
Because gas particles expand to fill all the space available, with high kinetic energy and no significant intermolecular forces
Because air stops moving in the room
mcqs.why: Expandability: a gas expands to occupy its whole container or space; perfume particles spread quickly through the room for this reason.

lessons.notes_html:
Gases differ from solids and liquids because of their particles and the large gaps between them. The kinetic molecular theory explains their compressibility, expandability and the pressure they exert.

Compressibility of Gases

Compressibility is the ability of a gas to decrease in volume when external pressure is applied. Gas molecules are widely spaced and move randomly; most of the volume of a gas is empty space (about 99.9%), so pressure pushes the molecules closer together and the volume falls greatly. For example, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is stored in compressed form in steel cylinders.

Expandability of Gases

Expandability is the property of a gas to increase in volume and fill all the space available. With high kinetic energy and no significant intermolecular forces, a gas expands to occupy its whole container; gases have no fixed shape or volume. When a perfume bottle is opened, its particles spread quickly through the room.

Pressure Exerted by Gases

Gas pressure is the force exerted by gas molecules when they collide with the walls of their container, measured as force per unit area. The total of these molecular impacts per unit area creates the pressure, for example the air pressure that keeps car and bicycle tyres in shape. Units of pressure include atmosphere (atm), pascal (Pa), mmHg or Torr, and bar.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
PV = nRTIdeal Gas Law: P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = gas constant, T = temperature in kelvin
1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101,325 PaConversion of pressure units

Key Points

  • Gases are highly compressible because of the large empty space between molecules.
  • Gases expand to fill the whole volume of their container.
  • Gas pressure is caused by molecular collisions with the container walls.
  • Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume.
  • The Ideal Gas Law, PV = nRT, relates pressure, volume, moles and temperature.
lessons.title: Physical Properties of Gases

mcqs.q: What are liquid crystals?
options: A type of pure solid with no motion
The intermediate state between solids and liquids, with particle arrangement like solids but freedom of motion like liquids
Gases cooled to very low temperatures
Liquids with no particle order at all
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are the intermediate state: Solid ⇌ Liquid Crystals ⇌ Liquid, with arrangement like solids but freedom of motion like liquids.

mcqs.q: Who discovered liquid crystals and in which year?
options: Austrian botanist and chemist Frederick Reinitzer in 1888
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals were discovered by the Austrian botanist and chemist Frederick Reinitzer in 1888, while studying cholesteryl benzoate.

mcqs.q: What happens to cholesteryl benzoate at 145.5°C and 178.5°C?
options: It melts at 145.5°C into a viscous, milky liquid and becomes a clear liquid at 178.5°C
mcqs.why: Working: cholesteryl benzoate melts at 145.5°C into a viscous, milky (liquid crystalline) liquid and becomes a clear liquid at 178.5°C; on cooling the changes reverse.

mcqs.q: Which properties do liquid crystals share with solids and liquids?
options: Properties of solids such as optical activity, and of liquids such as fluidity, viscosity and surface tension
Only the fixed shape of solids
mcqs.why: These turbid liquids possess properties of both solids, such as optical activity, and liquids, such as fluidity, viscosity and surface tension.

mcqs.q: What is the most common use of liquid crystals?
options: In liquid crystal displays (LCDs) of watches, televisions, computers, laptops, cell phones and pH meters
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are used in LCDs of digital wristwatches, clocks, flat-panel televisions, computers, laptop screens, cell phones and pH meters.

mcqs.q: Which medical uses of liquid crystals are listed in the notes?
options: To detect blockages in veins and arteries and infected areas like tumours, by mapping skin temperatures
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals detect blockages in veins and arteries and infected areas like tumours by mapping skin temperatures, and serve in infant thermometers.

mcqs.q: Why are some liquid crystals used in hydraulic brakes?
mcqs.why: The notes state that some liquid crystals are used in hydraulic brakes because of their high viscosity.

mcqs.q: What did Reinitzer conclude from his observations?
options: That cholesteryl benzoate is a gas
That the liquid crystalline state lies between the crystalline solid and liquid states
mcqs.why: From the two melting behaviours (145.5°C and 178.5°C) he concluded the liquid crystalline state lies between the crystalline solid and liquid states.

mcqs.q: Which use involves detecting faulty connections?
options: As temperature sensors to detect faulty connections in microelectronic circuit boards
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals are used as temperature sensors to detect faulty connections in microelectronic circuit boards, and as a solvent in chromatographic separations.

mcqs.q: What happens to cholesteryl benzoate on cooling from the clear liquid?
options: It stays a clear liquid forever
The changes reverse: clear liquid returns through the milky liquid crystalline state to the solid
mcqs.why: Working: on cooling, the changes reverse — the clear liquid (above 178.5°C) passes back through the milky liquid crystal state to the crystalline solid below 145.5°C.

lessons.notes_html:
Liquid crystals are the intermediate state between solids and liquids: substances have an arrangement of particles like solids but freedom of motion like liquids: Solid ⇌ Liquid Crystals ⇌ Liquid.

Discovery

Liquid crystals were discovered by the Austrian botanist and chemist Frederick Reinitzer in 1888, while studying cholesteryl benzoate. This compound melts at 145.5°C into a viscous, milky liquid and becomes a clear liquid at 178.5°C; on cooling, the changes reverse. He concluded that the liquid crystalline state lies between the crystalline solid and liquid states.

Properties

These turbid liquids possess properties of both solids, such as optical activity, and liquids, such as fluidity, viscosity and surface tension. Liquid crystals show some molecular order and are anisotropic (see the comparison in the next lesson).

Applications (Uses) of Liquid Crystals

  • As temperature sensors to detect faulty connections in microelectronic circuit boards.
  • In thermometers to measure the body temperature of infants.
  • To detect blockages in veins and arteries and infected areas like tumours, by mapping skin temperatures.
  • As a solvent in chromatographic separations.
  • In liquid crystal displays (LCDs) of digital wristwatches, clocks, flat-panel televisions, computers, laptop screens, cell phones and pH meters.
  • Some liquid crystals are used in hydraulic brakes because of their high viscosity.

Key Points

  • Liquid crystals form an intermediate state between solids and liquids.
  • They have particle order like solids and flow like liquids.
  • Cholesteryl benzoate shows two melting points: 145.5°C and 178.5°C.
  • Their most common use is in LCD screens and displays.
  • They are also used as temperature sensors and medical detectors.
lessons.title: Liquid Crystals

mcqs.q: Which states show fluidity (can flow)?
options: Pure liquids and liquid crystals; crystalline solids do not flow
mcqs.why: From the comparison table: fluidity is Yes for pure liquids and liquid crystals, and No for crystalline solids.

mcqs.q: Which of the three states has a definite shape?
options: Only crystalline solids have a definite shape
mcqs.why: Definite shape: No for pure liquids, No for liquid crystals, Yes for crystalline solids, which maintain a fixed shape.

mcqs.q: Which states show anisotropic behaviour?
options: Liquid crystals and crystalline solids; pure liquids do not
mcqs.why: Anisotropic behaviour: No for pure liquids, Yes for liquid crystals and Yes for crystalline solids, per the comparison table.

mcqs.q: How does particle order compare in the three states?
options: Pure liquids: no orderly arrangement; liquid crystals: partial order; crystalline solids: orderly (full) arrangement
Liquid crystals have no order at all
mcqs.why: Orderly arrangement: pure liquids No, liquid crystals Partial, crystalline solids Yes, which is why liquid crystals stand between the other two.

mcqs.q: Which states have definite melting points?
options: Only crystalline solids have definite melting points
mcqs.why: Definite melting points: No for pure liquids, No for liquid crystals, Yes for crystalline solids, per the comparison table.

mcqs.q: Why are liquid crystals used in LCD screens?
options: Because they are isotropic like liquids
Because they have a fixed shape like solids
Because they flow like liquids but show molecular alignment giving unique optical properties (optical anisotropy)
Because they have definite melting points
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals flow like liquids but show molecular alignment, giving unique optical properties (optical anisotropy) used in LCD screens; they are anisotropic.

mcqs.q: Pure liquids are described as what in terms of optical behaviour?
options: Isotropic, with no orderly arrangement of particles
mcqs.why: Pure liquids are isotropic, with no orderly arrangement of particles, and lack long-range order, flowing freely to take the container's shape.

mcqs.q: How do liquid crystals respond, as mentioned in the notes?
options: They are anisotropic and respond to temperature changes
They are isotropic and respond to light only
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals stand between liquids and solids: they flow but show molecular alignment, are anisotropic and respond to temperature changes.

mcqs.q: Which state lacks long-range order and flows freely to take the shape of its container?
mcqs.why: Pure liquids lack long-range order and flow freely to take the shape of their container, unlike crystalline solids with a highly ordered structure.

mcqs.q: Which property is shared by liquid crystals and crystalline solids but not pure liquids?
mcqs.why: Optical properties: pure liquids No, while both liquid crystals and crystalline solids show optical anisotropy, per the comparison table.

lessons.notes_html:
Liquid crystals, pure liquids and crystalline solids are three distinct states of matter. Pure liquids lack long-range order and flow freely to take the shape of their container. Crystalline solids have a highly ordered structure and maintain a fixed shape. Liquid crystals stand between them: they flow like liquids but show some degree of molecular alignment, which gives them unique optical properties used in LCD screens; they are anisotropic and respond to temperature changes.

Comparison Table

PropertyPure LiquidsLiquid CrystalsCrystalline Solids
FluidityYesYesNo
Definite ShapeNoNoYes
Definite Melting PointsNoNoYes
Anisotropic BehaviourNoYesYes
Optical PropertiesNoOptical AnisotropyOptical Anisotropy
Orderly Arrangement of ParticlesNoPartialYes

Key Points

  • Pure liquids are isotropic, with no orderly arrangement of particles.
  • Liquid crystals have partial particle order and show optical anisotropy.
  • Crystalline solids have a fixed, repeating arrangement and definite melting points.
  • Only crystalline solids have a definite shape; the other two flow.
lessons.title: Difference between Crystalline Solids, Liquid Crystals, and Pure Liquids

mcqs.q: How compressible are solids compared with liquids?
options: Solids are more compressible than liquids
Solids are generally less compressible than liquids and are considered incompressible
mcqs.why: Solids are generally less compressible than liquids and are considered incompressible; foam and cork only appear compressible because air in their spaces is compressed.

mcqs.q: Why do foam, wood and cork only appear compressible?
options: Because their solid matter compresses easily
Because the air in their spaces is compressed; the solid matter itself remains unaffected
mcqs.why: Foam, wood and cork only appear compressible because the air in their spaces is compressed; the solid matter itself remains unaffected.

mcqs.q: What motion do solid particles have?
options: They slip and slide over one another
They move freely through the whole solid
They have no motion at all, even on heating
Only vibrational motion about their fixed positions, growing stronger on heating until the lattice melts
mcqs.why: Solid particles are locked in place with only vibrational motion about fixed positions; vibration grows on heating until the lattice melts.

mcqs.q: How do interparticle spaces compare in solids?
options: The spaces between solid particles are the smallest of all three states, with particles tightly packed and most ordered
Solid spaces are larger than in gases
Solid spaces equal those in liquids exactly
Solids have no particles close together
mcqs.why: Particles in solids are very close and tightly packed, more ordered than liquids and gases; the spaces between them are the smallest of all three states.

mcqs.q: Why do solids have higher melting and boiling points?
options: Because their kinetic energy is highest
Because the intermolecular forces in solids are much more effective than in liquids and gases
mcqs.why: The intermolecular forces in solids are much more effective than in liquids and gases, so solids have higher melting and boiling points.

mcqs.q: How does the kinetic energy of solid particles compare?
options: It is higher than in gases
It is equal to that of liquids
Solid particles have lower kinetic energy than liquids and gases, directly proportional to temperature
It does not depend on temperature
mcqs.why: Solid particles have lower kinetic energy than liquids and gases; kinetic energy is directly proportional to temperature.

mcqs.q: What happens if a substance is cooled sufficiently?
options: All substances are converted into solids
mcqs.why: The key points state that sufficient cooling converts every substance into a solid, because kinetic energy falls with temperature.

mcqs.q: How much do temperature or pressure changes affect the volume of solids?
options: Changes of temperature or pressure have very little influence on the volume of solids
Solids double in volume on heating
Pressure halves the volume of solids
mcqs.why: Expansion: changes of temperature or pressure have very little influence on the volume of solids, unlike gases.

mcqs.q: Why can solids not flow?
options: Because they have too much kinetic energy
Because their particles are locked in place and cannot slip or slide over one another, so solids are rigid
Because they have no intermolecular forces
Because they take the shape of a vessel
mcqs.why: Solid particles cannot slip or slide, so solids cannot flow, are rigid, and retain their shape and volume without a vessel.

mcqs.q: On heating a solid, what happens to particle vibration?
options: Vibration grows stronger on heating until the lattice melts
mcqs.why: The particles have only vibrational motion about fixed positions; this vibration grows stronger on heating until the lattice melts.

lessons.notes_html:
The kinetic molecular theory explains the behaviour of solids through the arrangement and motion of their particles.

Compression

Solids are generally less compressible than liquids and are considered incompressible. Foam, wood and cork only appear compressible because the air in their spaces is compressed; the solid matter itself remains unaffected.

Expansion

Changes of temperature or pressure have very little influence on the volume of solids.

Motion of Molecules

Solid particles are locked in place and cannot slip or slide over one another, so solids cannot flow, are rigid, and retain their shape and volume without a vessel. The particles have only vibrational motion about their fixed positions; this vibration grows stronger on heating until the lattice melts.

Interparticle Space

The particles in solids are very close to each other, tightly packed and more ordered than in liquids and gases; the spaces between them are the smallest of all three states.

Intermolecular Forces

The intermolecular forces in solids are much more effective than in liquids and gases, so solids have higher melting and boiling points.

Kinetic Energy

Solid particles have lower kinetic energy than liquids and gases. Kinetic energy is directly proportional to temperature; if cooled sufficiently, all substances are converted into solids.

Key Points

  • Solids are incompressible and expand very little.
  • Solid particles only vibrate about fixed positions, so solids are rigid.
  • Interparticle spaces are smallest and forces strongest in solids.
  • Solids have the lowest kinetic energy of the three states.
  • Sufficient cooling converts every substance into a solid.
lessons.title: Simple Properties of Solids Based on Kinetic Molecular Theory

mcqs.q: What are crystalline solids?
options: Solids with no arrangement of particles
Solids that have a repetitive three-dimensional arrangement of particles, also called true solids
Solids formed only by sudden cooling
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have a repetitive three-dimensional arrangement of particles and are called true solids, with flat faces at specific angles.

mcqs.q: What are amorphous solids also called?
options: Pseudo solids (and supercooled liquids), from a Greek word meaning shapeless
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids are called pseudo solids; amorphous comes from a Greek word meaning shapeless, and they are sometimes called supercooled liquids.

mcqs.q: How do crystalline and amorphous solids differ in melting point?
options: Crystalline solids have sharp and distinct melting points; amorphous solids have no sharp melting points
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have sharp, distinct melting points, while amorphous solids have no sharp melting points, per the difference table.

mcqs.q: Which solids are anisotropic and which are isotropic?
options: Crystalline solids are anisotropic (properties differ in different directions); amorphous solids are isotropic (same properties in all directions)
Amorphous solids are anisotropic; crystalline are isotropic
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids are anisotropic because of their ordered arrangement; amorphous solids are isotropic with the same properties in all directions.

mcqs.q: How are crystalline and amorphous solids formed from a liquid?
options: Crystalline solids by slow cooling of the liquid; amorphous solids by sudden cooling of the liquid
Crystalline by sudden cooling; amorphous by slow cooling
mcqs.why: The difference table states crystalline solids are formed by slow cooling of the liquid and amorphous solids by sudden cooling of the liquid.

mcqs.q: Which are examples of amorphous solids?
options: Glass, rubber, plastic, cement, ceramics and concrete
mcqs.why: Examples of amorphous solids include glass, rubber, plastic, cement, ceramics and concrete; diamond, quartz and table salt are crystalline.

mcqs.q: Into which groups are crystalline solids further classified?
options: Ionic, covalent, molecular and metallic solids
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids are further grouped as ionic, covalent, molecular and metallic solids, in addition to the crystalline/amorphous division.

mcqs.q: Why are amorphous solids called supercooled liquids / intermediates?
options: Their structures resemble those of liquids, but their particles lack the freedom of motion of liquids; they are intermediates between liquid and solid states
Because they flow rapidly like liquids
Because they are colder than all solids
Because they have sharp melting points
mcqs.why: Amorphous structures resemble liquids but particles lack liquid-like freedom of motion; they are intermediates between the liquid and solid states.

mcqs.q: Which are examples of crystalline solids from the notes?
options: Diamond, quartz (SiO2), sucrose, table salt, alum, urea, KNO3 and CuSO4
mcqs.why: Crystalline examples include diamond, quartz (SiO2), sucrose, table salt, alum, urea, KNO3 and CuSO4, each particle in a fixed position.

mcqs.q: What geometric difference exists between the two types of solids?
options: Crystalline solids have definite geometric shapes; amorphous solids have no definite geometric shapes
Amorphous solids have more regular shapes
mcqs.why: The difference table gives crystalline solids definite geometric shapes, while amorphous solids have no definite geometric shapes.

lessons.notes_html:
There are two types of solids based on the arrangement of particles: (i) crystalline solids and (ii) amorphous solids. Crystalline solids are further grouped as ionic, covalent, molecular and metallic solids.

Crystalline Solids

The solids that have a repetitive three-dimensional arrangement of particles are called crystalline solids, or true solids. Each particle occupies a fixed position, so they typically have flat faces that form specific angles with one another. Examples: diamond, quartz (SiO2), sucrose, table salt, alum, urea, KNO3 and CuSO4.

Amorphous or Non-Crystalline Solids

Solids with a non-repetitive three-dimensional arrangement of particles are called amorphous solids or pseudo solids; amorphous comes from a Greek word meaning shapeless. Their structures resemble those of liquids, but their particles lack the freedom of motion of liquids. They are intermediates between the liquid and solid states and are sometimes called supercooled liquids. Examples: glass, rubber, plastic, cement, ceramics and concrete.

Difference Between the Two Types

Crystalline SolidsAmorphous Solids
Definite geometric shapesNo definite geometric shapes
Sharp and distinct melting pointsNo sharp melting points
Anisotropic: properties differ in different directionsIsotropic: same properties in all directions
Formed by slow cooling of the liquidFormed by sudden cooling of the liquid
Examples: NaCl, CuSO4, sugar, diamondExamples: glass, plastic, rubber, coke

Key Points

  • Crystalline solids have a regular, repeating 3D arrangement of particles.
  • Amorphous solids have no regular arrangement and are called pseudo solids.
  • Amorphous solids are also known as supercooled liquids.
  • Crystalline solids are anisotropic; amorphous solids are isotropic.
  • Crystalline solids have sharp melting points; amorphous solids do not.
lessons.title: Types of Solids or Classification of Solid States

mcqs.q: Why do crystalline solids have definite geometrical shapes?
options: Because of the orderly arrangement of their atoms, ions or molecules, held by strong attractive forces
Because they are formed by sudden cooling
Because they have no internal arrangement
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have definite geometrical shapes due to the orderly arrangement of particles; interfacial angles and distances stay the same regardless of preparation.

mcqs.q: What happens at the melting point of a crystalline solid?
options: Particles gain enough kinetic energy to overcome attractive forces and free themselves from fixed positions; solids and liquid particles have the same average kinetic energies
mcqs.why: At the sharp melting point the kinetic energy becomes sufficient to overcome attractive forces and free particles from fixed positions, so crystals can be identified by sharp melting points.

mcqs.q: What is a cleavage plane?
options: The usual shape in which a crystal grows
The specific planes along which a crystal fractures when broken into smaller, identical crystals by pressure
The angle between two crystal faces
The surface of a liquid crystal
mcqs.why: Cleavage is breaking larger crystals into smaller identical ones by pressure; the specific planes along which a crystal fractures are its cleavage planes.

mcqs.q: Why does a mica crystal separate easily parallel to its layers?
options: Because mica has no attractive forces
Because mica is an amorphous solid
Because mica consists of infinite layers of sheets with weak attractive forces between them
Because mica melts at room temperature
mcqs.why: A mica crystal consists of infinite layers of sheets with weak attractive forces, which separate easily parallel to the layers along cleavage planes.

mcqs.q: What is the habit of a crystal? Give NaCl's habit.
options: The melting point of the crystal; NaCl is 801°C
The cleavage plane; NaCl is layered
The temperature of growth; NaCl grows at 100°C
The shape in which a crystal usually grows; NaCl has a cubic habit
mcqs.why: The habit is the shape in which a crystal usually grows: NaCl has a cubic habit, white tin a tetragonal habit and graphite a hexagonal habit.

mcqs.q: How are crystals grown, per the notes?
options: By slowly cooling a liquid or a saturated solution
By sudden cooling of a vapour
By heating an amorphous solid rapidly
mcqs.why: Crystals are grown by slowly cooling a liquid or a saturated solution; impurities or changed conditions can change the habit.

mcqs.q: What happens to NaCl's habit in the presence of 10% urea?
options: It stays cubic in all conditions
NaCl is cubic when pure but octahedral in the presence of 10% urea, though interfacial angles always remain the same
mcqs.why: Working: impurities can change the habit — NaCl is cubic when pure but octahedral with 10% urea — a change of habit, though interfacial angles remain the same.

mcqs.q: What remains the same in a crystal even when its habit changes?
options: The interfacial angles always remain the same
mcqs.why: Impurities can change the habit but not the interfacial angles; the interfacial angles and distances are the same regardless of preparation conditions.

mcqs.q: What is the habit of graphite and of white tin?
options: Graphite is tetragonal and white tin is hexagonal
Graphite has a hexagonal habit and white tin a tetragonal habit
mcqs.why: The notes give: NaCl cubic habit, white tin tetragonal habit and graphite hexagonal habit, as the usual growth shapes of these crystals.

mcqs.q: Why can crystalline solids be identified by their melting points?
options: Because they have sharp melting points at a definite temperature
Because they have no melting points
Because all crystals melt at the same temperature
Because they melt over a wide range
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have sharp melting points: at this temperature particles escape their fixed positions, so crystalline solids can be identified by their sharp melting points.

lessons.notes_html:
Crystalline solids show characteristic properties that arise from their orderly internal arrangement of particles.

Geometric Shape

Crystalline solids have definite geometrical shapes due to the orderly arrangement of their atoms, ions or molecules, held by strong attractive forces. Their interfacial angles and distances are the same regardless of the method or conditions of preparation; even the fragments of finely divided crystalline solids have definite geometric shapes.

Melting Point

The temperature at which the change from solid to liquid occurs is the melting point of a solid. At the melting point, the particles of the solid and liquid have the same average kinetic energies. Crystalline solids have sharp melting points: at this temperature the kinetic energy becomes sufficient to overcome the attractive forces and free the particles from their fixed positions, so crystalline solids can be identified by their sharp melting points.

Cleavage Plane

The process of breaking larger crystals into smaller, identical ones by applying pressure is called cleavage, and the specific planes along which a crystal fractures are its cleavage planes. A crystal breaks easily in one direction but not in others; a mica crystal consists of infinite layers of sheets with weak attractive forces, which separate easily parallel to the layers.

Habit of Crystal and Crystal Growth

The shape in which a crystal usually grows is called the habit of the crystal: NaCl has a cubic habit, white tin a tetragonal habit and graphite a hexagonal habit. Crystals are grown by slowly cooling a liquid or a saturated solution. Impurities or changed conditions can change the habit; NaCl is cubic when pure but octahedral in the presence of 10% urea, a change of habit, though the interfacial angles always remain the same.

Key Points

  • Crystalline solids have definite geometric shapes and fixed interfacial angles.
  • They melt sharply at a definite melting point.
  • They break along definite cleavage planes, as in mica.
  • The usual growth shape of a crystal is its habit, e.g. cubic for NaCl.
  • Impurities can change the habit but not the interfacial angles.
lessons.title: Properties of Crystalline Solids or Crystals

mcqs.q: What does thermochemistry deal with?
options: Heat changes during a chemical reaction
mcqs.why: The notes define thermochemistry as the branch of chemistry that deals with heat changes during a chemical reaction.

From the system to the surroundings
Neither into nor out of the system

mcqs.why: Heat released is shown by a negative ΔH. The notes give C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g) with ΔH = -393.51 kJ.

mcqs.why: Melting, evaporation and sublimation are endothermic processes, while freezing, condensation and deposition are exothermic.

mcqs.q: For CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → 2H2O + CO2(g), the notes give ΔH as:
mcqs.why: The notes state CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → 2H2O + CO2(g) with ΔH = -890.4 kJ, showing burning is exothermic.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis in plants is given as an example of:
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the notes list it as an endothermic reaction example.

mcqs.q: For N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180.51 kJ. This reaction is:
options: Endothermic because heat is absorbed and ΔH is positive
mcqs.why: Heat absorbed is shown by a positive ΔH, so +180.51 kJ means the reaction is endothermic as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the heat of reaction?
options: Heat needed to start any reaction
Heat evolved or absorbed when reactants are converted into products
mcqs.why: The notes define heat of reaction as the amount of heat evolved or absorbed when reactants are converted into products.

mcqs.q: If evaporation is endothermic in the forward direction, condensation in the reverse direction is:
mcqs.why: A process endothermic in the forward direction is exothermic in reverse; evaporation and condensation are the given pair.

mcqs.q: An equation that shows the amount of heat evolved or absorbed is called a:
mcqs.why: The notes state that an equation showing the amount of heat is a thermochemical equation, also linked to heat of reaction.

lessons.notes_html:
Thermochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with heat changes during a chemical reaction. Chemical energetics is a subfield of thermodynamics: it studies the energy stored in chemical bonds, the absorption or release of heat, and the overall energy balance of a reaction. Chemical reactions are either exothermic or endothermic.

Exothermic Reactions

Reactions that evolve heat from the system to the surroundings are exothermic (Greek: exo = outside; heat flows out). Examples: burning of gasoline, coal and wood; freezing, condensation and deposition are exothermic processes.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → 2H2O + CO2(g), ΔH = -890.4 kJ
C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = -393.51 kJ

Heat released is shown by a negative ΔH, because heat flows from the system to its surroundings. Most reactions at ordinary temperatures are exothermic.

Endothermic Reactions

Reactions in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings by the system are endothermic (Greek: endon = within; heat flows in). Examples: photosynthesis in plants; melting, evaporation and sublimation are endothermic processes.

C(s) + H2O(g) → CO(g) + H2(g), ΔH = +131.4 kJ
N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180.51 kJ

Heat absorbed is shown by a positive ΔH. A process that is endothermic in the forward direction is exothermic in the reverse direction, e.g. evaporation (endothermic) and condensation (exothermic).

Heat of Reaction

The amount of heat evolved or absorbed when reactants are converted into products is called the heat of reaction (also called chemical energy). An equation that shows this amount of heat is a thermochemical equation.

Key Points

  • Thermochemistry deals with heat changes during chemical reactions.
  • Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative.
  • Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive.
  • Burning of fuels is exothermic; photosynthesis, melting and evaporation are endothermic.
  • A forward exothermic process is endothermic in the reverse direction, and vice versa.
  • The heat of reaction is the heat evolved or absorbed when reactants change into products.
lessons.title: Energy Change During Chemical Reaction

mcqs.q: Activation energy (Ea) is best defined as:
options: The minimum extra energy, besides average energy, needed for a reactant to take part in a reaction
The average energy of all reactant molecules
The energy released when products form
The difference between reactants and products only
mcqs.why: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy besides the average energy required for a reactant to take part in a reaction.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of activation energy given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state the unit of activation energy Ea is kJ/mol, the same unit used for molar energy changes.

mcqs.q: On an energy pathway diagram, Ea is measured from:
options: The products up to the reactants
The products down to zero energy
The reactants up to the peak of the barrier (activated complex)
mcqs.why: Ea is the energy difference between the reactants and the activated complex at the peak of the barrier on the diagram.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reaction, the potential energy of reactants compared with products is:
options: Lower than that of the products
Exactly equal to that of the products
Higher than that of the products
mcqs.why: In an exothermic reaction reactants have higher potential energy than products and the difference is released as negative ΔH.

mcqs.q: For an endothermic reaction, forward Ea compared with reverse Ea is:
mcqs.why: The table in the notes states for endothermic reactions forward Ea is greater than reverse Ea, opposite to exothermic reactions.

mcqs.q: If more energy is released in forming bonds than is needed to break bonds, then ΔH is:
options: Positive and the reaction is endothermic
Negative and the reaction is exothermic
Positive and the reaction is exothermic
mcqs.why: When bond formation releases more energy than bond breaking requires, the excess is released so ΔH is negative and exothermic.

mcqs.q: Breaking bonds during a reaction:
mcqs.why: The notes state breaking bonds requires energy while forming bonds releases energy; their balance decides the sign of ΔH.

mcqs.q: The activated complex is formed when reactant molecules:
options: Absorb energy to reach the peak of the barrier
mcqs.why: Reactants absorb energy to form the activated complex, which then decomposes into products, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic pathway diagram, ΔH is:
options: The height of the barrier peak
The energy of the activated complex only
The difference between reactants and products, and it is negative
Always larger than Ea in magnitude with positive sign
mcqs.why: ΔH is the difference between reactants and products; for exothermic reactions products lie lower so ΔH is negative.

mcqs.q: If energy required to break bonds is greater than energy released forming bonds, the reaction is:
mcqs.why: When bond breaking needs more energy than bond making releases, extra heat is absorbed so ΔH is positive and endothermic.

lessons.notes_html:
Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum amount of energy, besides the average energy, required for a reactant to take part in a chemical reaction. It is the energy needed for molecules to form an activated complex, or to weaken the existing bonds enough that they can be broken through collision. Its unit is kJ/mol. Reactants absorb energy to form the activated complex, which then decomposes into products.

The Energy Pathway Diagrams for Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions

In an exothermic reaction, the potential energy of the reactants is higher than that of the products; the difference is shown by ΔH (negative). In an endothermic reaction, the potential energy of the reactants is lower than that of the products, and ΔH is positive. In both diagrams, Ea is the energy difference between the reactants and the activated complex at the peak of the barrier, and ΔH is the difference between reactants and products.

Forward and Reverse Activation Energies

FeatureExothermicEndothermic
Energy of reactants vs productsReactants higherReactants lower
Sign of ΔHNegativePositive
Ea of forward vs reverse reactionForward Ea is less than reverse EaForward Ea is greater than reverse Ea

Enthalpy Change and Bond Energies

Energy transfer occurs because bonds are broken and formed. Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases energy. If the energy required to break bonds is greater than the energy released in forming bonds, ΔH is positive and the reaction is endothermic. If more energy is released in bond formation than is needed for bond breaking, ΔH is negative and the reaction is exothermic.

Key Points

  • Activation energy is the minimum extra energy needed to form an activated complex; unit kJ/mol.
  • On a pathway diagram, Ea is measured from the reactants up to the peak of the barrier.
  • Exothermic: products lie lower than reactants, ΔH negative, forward Ea smaller than reverse Ea.
  • Endothermic: products lie higher than reactants, ΔH positive, forward Ea larger than reverse Ea.
  • ΔH is decided by the balance between energy used in breaking bonds and energy released in making bonds.
lessons.title: Activation Energies and Energy Pathway Diagrams in Chemical Reactions

mcqs.q: Enthalpy H is defined by which relation?
mcqs.why: The notes define enthalpy as internal energy E plus the product of pressure and volume: H = E + PV at constant pressure.

mcqs.q: The standard state of a substance is its most stable state at:
options: 298 K and 1 M only for gases
mcqs.why: The physical state at 25°C and one atmosphere, its most stable state, is the standard state according to the notes.

mcqs.q: Burning 2 mol of carbon: 2C(s) + 2O2(g) → 2CO2(g). If 1 mol gives -393.51 kJ, ΔH°rxn is:
mcqs.why: Working: ΔH is proportional to amount, so 2 × (-393.51 kJ) = -787.02 kJ, exactly the value given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Standard enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change when:
options: One mole of a compound forms from its elements
One mole of a substance burns completely
One mole of water forms from H+ and OH-
One mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state
mcqs.why: Atomisation forms one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state, e.g. 1/2 H2(g) → H(g).

mcqs.q: For 1/2 H2(g) → H(g), ΔH°at given in the notes is:
mcqs.why: The notes give 1/2 H2(g) → H(g) with ΔH°at = +218 kJ mol-1; atomisation is always endothermic.

mcqs.q: Standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when:
options: One mole of gaseous atoms forms
One mole of a substance burns in oxygen
One mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states
One mole of ions forms a lattice
mcqs.why: Formation forms one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states, symbolised ΔH°f in the notes.

mcqs.q: If N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 has ΔH° = -46.11 kJ mol-1 as written in the notes, the reverse reaction 2NH3 → N2 + 3H2 has ΔH°:
mcqs.why: Reversing a reaction keeps the magnitude but reverses the sign, so -46.11 kJ mol-1 becomes +46.11 kJ mol-1.

mcqs.q: A highly negative ΔH°f for a compound means the compound is:
options: An element in its standard state
mcqs.why: The notes state a highly negative ΔH°f means a very stable compound, while a positive value means an unstable compound.

mcqs.q: The symbol ° in ΔH° indicates:
mcqs.why: In ΔH° the superscript ° indicates that all substances are in their standard states, as explained in the notes.

mcqs.q: For 1/2 N2 + 1/2 O2 → NO, the notes give ΔH°f as:
mcqs.why: The notes list 1/2 N2 + 1/2 O2 → NO with ΔH°f = +90.37 kJ mol-1, a positive formation enthalpy example.

lessons.notes_html:
The total heat content of a system at constant pressure is called enthalpy: the internal energy E plus the product of pressure (P) and volume (V), H = E + PV. The physical state of a substance at 25°C and one atmosphere, its most stable state, is its standard state. In ΔH°, ° indicates standard states. Units are kJ mol-1.

Standard Enthalpy of Reaction

The heat released or absorbed during a reaction when all reactants and products are in their standard states is the standard enthalpy of reaction, ΔH°rxn (heat of reaction). Example: C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH°rxn = -393.51 kJ mol-1. ΔH is directly proportional to the quantity of reactants consumed: burning 2 mol of carbon releases twice as much heat, 2C(s) + 2O2(g) → 2CO2(g), ΔH°rxn = -787.02 kJ.

Standard Enthalpy of Atomisation (ΔH°at)

The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state: 1/2 H2(g) → H(g), ΔH°at = +218 kJ mol-1; 1/2 Cl2(g) → Cl(g), ΔH°at = +121 kJ mol-1.

Standard Enthalpy of Formation (ΔH°f)

The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. Examples: C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH°f = -393.51 kJ mol-1; 1/2 N2 + 1/2 O2 → NO, ΔH°f = +90.37 kJ mol-1. A reaction exothermic in the forward direction is endothermic in reverse with the same magnitude: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, ΔH° = -46.11 kJ mol-1; 2NH3 → N2 + 3H2, ΔH° = +46.11 kJ mol-1. A highly negative ΔH°f means a very stable compound; a positive value means an unstable compound.

Key Formulae

QuantitySymbolMeaning
EnthalpyH = E + PVHeat content at constant pressure
Standard enthalpy of reactionΔH°rxnHeat change, all substances in standard states
Standard enthalpy of atomisationΔH°atElement → 1 mol gaseous atoms
Standard enthalpy of formationΔH°fElements → 1 mol of compound

Key Points

  • Enthalpy H = E + PV; standard state is 25°C, 1 atm, most stable state.
  • ΔH°rxn is proportional to the amounts in the equation.
  • Atomisation forms one mole of gaseous atoms from the element; always endothermic.
  • Formation forms one mole of a compound from its elements.
  • Reversing a reaction keeps |ΔH| but reverses its sign.
  • Highly negative ΔH°f = very stable compound.
lessons.title: Standard States and Standard Enthalpy Changes

mcqs.q: Standard enthalpy of combustion ΔH°c is the enthalpy change when:
options: One mole of a substance is completely burnt in excess oxygen at standard states
One mole of a substance is formed from elements
One mole of gaseous atoms is formed
One mole of water forms from H+ and OH-
mcqs.why: Combustion is complete burning of one mole of a substance in excess oxygen at standard states, symbol ΔH°c in kJ mol-1.

mcqs.q: Why are ΔH°c values always negative?
options: Because one mole is always used
mcqs.why: The notes state combustion is always exothermic, so standard enthalpies of combustion are always negative values.

mcqs.q: From the table, ΔH°c of octane C8H18(l) is:
mcqs.why: The combustion table gives octane C8H18(l) as -5474 kJ/mol, the largest magnitude listed and a good fuel value.

mcqs.q: From the table, ΔH°c of butane C4H10(l) is:
mcqs.why: The table in the notes lists butane C4H10(l) with ΔH°c = -2880 kJ/mol, showing it releases a large amount of heat.

mcqs.q: Standard enthalpy of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when one mole of H+ reacts with one mole of OH- to form:
options: One mole of water at standard states
One mole of a salt only
mcqs.why: Neutralisation forms one mole of water from H+(aq) and OH-(aq) at standard states, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: For any strong acid with a strong base, ΔH°n is about:
mcqs.why: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l) gives ΔH°n = -57.4 kJ mol-1 for every strong acid-strong base pair in the notes.

mcqs.q: In acid-base mixing, Na+ and Cl- ions that remain unchanged are called:
mcqs.why: The notes call Na+ and Cl- spectator ions because they remain unchanged and take no part in the neutralisation change.

mcqs.q: For C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g), the notes give ΔH°c as:
mcqs.why: The notes list C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g) with ΔH°c = -283 kJ mol-1, also the value for CO(g) in the table.

mcqs.q: The heat of neutralisation is used in the application mentioned in the notes:
options: Self-heating food packs for soldiers and hikers
mcqs.why: The notes state this heat is used in self-heating food packs for soldiers and hikers, an application of neutralisation enthalpy.

mcqs.q: From the table, ΔH°c of hydrogen H2(g) is:
mcqs.why: The combustion table gives hydrogen H2(g) ΔH°c = -285 kJ/mol, distinct from methane -890 and ethylene -1412 kJ/mol.

lessons.notes_html:
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burnt in excess oxygen at standard states is the standard enthalpy of combustion, ΔH°c, in kJ mol-1. Combustion is always exothermic, so ΔH°c values are negative. Examples: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), ΔH°c = -890 kJ mol-1; C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH°c = -393.51 kJ mol-1; C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g), ΔH°c = -283 kJ mol-1.

Standard Enthalpies of Combustion at 25°C

SubstanceFormulaΔH°c (kJ/mol)
HydrogenH2(g)-285
MethaneCH4(g)-890
ButaneC4H10(l)-2880
OctaneC8H18(l)-5474
EthyleneC2H4(g)-1412
AcetyleneC2H2(g)-1300
BenzeneC6H6(l)-3270
Carbon monoxideCO(g)-283

Standard Enthalpy of Neutralisation (ΔH°n)

The enthalpy change when one mole of hydrogen ions from an acid reacts with one mole of hydroxide ions from a base to form one mole of water at standard states is the standard enthalpy of neutralisation. In acid-base mixing the Na+ and Cl- ions remain unchanged (spectator ions); the only reaction is:

H+(aq) + OH-(aq) ⇌ H2O(l), ΔH°n = -57.4 kJ mol-1

The heat of neutralisation of any strong acid with a strong base is about -57.4 kJ/mol, because it involves only H+ and OH- ions. This heat is used in self-heating food packs for soldiers and hikers.

Key Points

  • ΔH°c: complete burning of one mole of a substance in excess oxygen; always negative.
  • Octane (-5474 kJ/mol) and butane (-2880 kJ/mol) release large amounts of heat, so they are good fuels.
  • ΔH°n: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l); -57.4 kJ/mol for every strong acid-strong base pair.
  • Spectator ions take no part in the neutralisation enthalpy change.
lessons.title: Standard Enthalpy of Combustion

mcqs.q: Bond energy is defined as the energy required to:
options: Break one mole of identical bonds in a substance
Form one mole of a compound from elements
Burn one mole of a substance
mcqs.why: Bond energy is the amount of energy required to break one mole of identical bonds in a substance and is always positive.

mcqs.q: In the bond-energy formula, product bond energies are entered with a negative sign because:
options: Bond formation releases the same amount of energy
mcqs.why: Bond formation releases the same amount that breaking absorbs, so product terms are negative in ΔH = ΣBE(reactants) + ΣBE(products).

mcqs.q: For H2 + F2 → 2HF: break H-H 436 and F-F 159 kJ/mol; form 2 × H-F 565 kJ/mol. ΔH is:
mcqs.why: Working: break = 436 + 159 = 595 kJ; form = 2 × 565 = 1130 kJ released; ΔH = +595 + (-1130) = -535 kJ, exothermic.

mcqs.q: Bond breaking is described in the notes as:
mcqs.why: Bond breaking is endothermic and positive, while bond making is exothermic and negative, as summarised in the key points.

mcqs.q: Using the worked example numbers only, total energy to break bonds in H2 + F2 is:
mcqs.why: Working: H-H 436 kJ/mol + F-F 159 kJ/mol = 595 kJ total energy required to break the reactant bonds.

mcqs.q: Using the worked example, energy released forming 2 mol of H-F bonds is:
mcqs.why: Working: one H-F bond is 565 kJ/mol, so 2 mol release 2 × 565 = 1130 kJ when the product bonds form.

mcqs.q: A second bond calculation: break bonds totalling 800 kJ, form bonds releasing 800 kJ. ΔH is:
mcqs.why: Working: ΔH = (energy to break) - (energy released making) = 800 - 800 = 0 kJ, so the two terms exactly balance.

mcqs.q: A bond calculation: break 500 kJ, form releases 700 kJ. ΔH and type are:
mcqs.why: Working: ΔH = 500 - 700 = -200 kJ; negative ΔH means more energy was released forming bonds, so exothermic.

mcqs.q: Why must every bond be counted multiplied by moles in the balanced equation?
options: Because bond energies are in kcal only
Because the notes require counting every bond broken and formed with its coefficient
mcqs.why: The key points require counting every bond broken and formed, multiplied by the moles in the balanced equation, e.g. 2 × H-F.

mcqs.q: The reaction H2 + F2 → 2HF with ΔH = -535 kJ is classified as:
mcqs.why: The worked example concludes ΔH = -535 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic because the sign is negative.

lessons.notes_html:
The enthalpy change of a reaction is the sum of the energies required to break old bonds in the reactants plus the energies released when new bonds form in the products. Bond energy is the amount of energy required to break one mole of identical bonds in a substance; it is always positive. Bond formation releases the same amount, so product bond energies are entered with a negative sign:

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔH = ΣBE(reactants) + ΣBE(products)Enthalpy change from bond energies; product terms are negative (energy released on forming bonds)
ΔH = (energy to break bonds) - (energy released in making bonds)Same relation in words

Worked Example: H2(g) + F2(g) → 2HF(g)

  • Step 1: energy to break bonds: H-H = 436 kJ/mol and F-F = 159 kJ/mol; total = 436 + 159 = 595 kJ.
  • Step 2: energy released forming bonds: one H-F bond = 565 kJ/mol, so 2 mol of H-F bonds release 2 x 565 = 1130 kJ.
  • Step 3: ΔH = (+595 kJ) + (-1130 kJ) = -535 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

Key Points

  • Bond breaking is endothermic (positive); bond making is exothermic (negative).
  • ΔH = Σ bond energies of reactants - Σ bond energies of products in magnitude terms.
  • Count every bond broken and formed, multiplied by the moles in the balanced equation.
  • For H2 + F2 → 2HF, ΔH = 595 - 1130 = -535 kJ.
lessons.title: Calculation of Bond Energies for the Enthalpy Change of Reaction

mcqs.q: Exact bond energies are found in which type of molecule?
options: Diatomic molecules such as H2 and O2 with only one bond
mcqs.why: Exact bond energies are found in diatomic molecules such as H2 and O2 where only one bond is present and measured precisely.

options: Because diatomic molecules have no bonds
Because the same bond changes strength with molecular environment and geometry
Because bond energies are always exact
mcqs.why: In complex molecules the environment and geometry change the strength of the same bond, so average approximate values are used.

mcqs.q: The C-C single bond value quoted in the notes is approximately:
mcqs.why: The notes quote the C-C single bond as approximately 80 kcal/mol, an average energy based on models and many experiments.

mcqs.q: The C=C double bond value quoted in the notes is approximately:
mcqs.why: The notes quote the C=C double bond as approximately 145 kcal/mol, an approximate average bond energy value.

mcqs.q: Approximate bond energies are described as:
options: Average values taken from similar compounds or theoretical calculations
Exact values for one specific molecule only
Values with no experimental basis at all
Values used only for ionic compounds
mcqs.why: Chemists use average approximate bond energies taken from similar compounds or theoretical calculations when measurement is difficult.

mcqs.q: Enthalpy changes calculated from average bond energies are:
mcqs.why: The key points state enthalpy changes from average bond energies are estimates, not exact, because the values are averages.

mcqs.q: How are exact bond energies determined?
mcqs.why: Exact bond energies are determined precisely through controlled experimental measurements on diatomic molecules like H2 and O2.

mcqs.q: The same bond in different compounds has:
options: Slightly different strengths in different molecular environments
mcqs.why: The notes state the same bond has slightly different strengths in different molecular environments, hence average values are needed.

mcqs.q: Approximate values are commonly used when:
mcqs.why: Approximate values are commonly used when experimental measurement is difficult and they give reasonable predictions of energy changes.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches bond type to its approximate value from the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give C-C ≈ 80 kcal/mol and C=C ≈ 145 kcal/mol, both approximate average energies, not exact values.

lessons.notes_html:
Bond energies are categorised as exact or approximate values.

Exact Bond Energies

Exact bond energies are found in diatomic molecules such as H2 and O2, where only one bond is present. They are determined precisely through controlled experimental measurements.

Approximate Bond Energies

In complex molecules, finding an exact bond energy is challenging because the molecular environment and geometry change the strength of the same bond in different compounds. Chemists therefore use average (approximate) bond energies taken from similar compounds or theoretical calculations. Approximate values are commonly used when experimental measurement is difficult, and they give reasonable predictions of energy changes in reactions. Examples: the C-C single bond is quoted as approximately 80 kcal/mol and the C=C double bond as approximately 145 kcal/mol; these are average energies needed to break these bonds, based on theoretical models and data from numerous experiments.

Key Points

  • Exact bond energies apply to diatomic molecules like H2 and O2 and are measured precisely.
  • Approximate bond energies are average values from similar compounds.
  • The same bond has slightly different strengths in different molecular environments.
  • C-C ≈ 80 kcal/mol and C=C ≈ 145 kcal/mol are approximate (average) values.
  • Enthalpy changes calculated from average bond energies are estimates, not exact.
lessons.title: Exact and Approximate Bond Energies

mcqs.q: Heat capacity c is given by which formula?
options: c = q / mΔT only for gases
q = mcΔT rearranged as c = m / q
mcqs.why: Heat capacity is heat required to raise temperature by one degree: c = q/ΔT, where q is heat and ΔT is temperature change.

mcqs.q: The heat transferred to a solution is calculated by:
mcqs.why: Specific heat c = q/mΔT rearranges to q = mcΔT, the central calorimetry formula used throughout the notes.

mcqs.q: Given m = 150 g, c = 4.18 J/g°C, ΔT = 25°C, q is:
mcqs.why: Working: q = mcΔT = 150 × 4.18 × 25 = 15675 J, exactly the calculation shown in the notes for this data.

mcqs.q: With q = 15675 J and n = 0.75 mol, ΔH = -q/n is:
mcqs.why: Working: ΔH = -15675 / 0.75 = -20900 J/mol = -20.9 kJ/mol; negative sign shows the reaction is exothermic.

mcqs.q: Why is there a negative sign in ΔH = -mcΔT/n?
options: Because heat gained by the solution is heat lost by the reaction
Because n is less than one
mcqs.why: Heat gained by the solution is heat lost by the reaction, so a positive ΔT for the solution gives a negative ΔH.

mcqs.q: If the solution temperature rises during a reaction, the reaction is:
mcqs.why: A temperature rise means the solution gained heat from the reaction, so ΔH is negative and the reaction is exothermic.

mcqs.q: Calculate q for m = 100 g, c = 4.18 J/g°C, ΔT = 10°C:
mcqs.why: Working: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.18 × 10 = 4180 J absorbed by the water or solution in the calorimeter.

mcqs.q: Calculate q for m = 200 g, c = 4.18 J/g°C, ΔT = 5°C, then ΔH if n = 1 mol and solution gained heat:
mcqs.why: Working: q = 200 × 4.18 × 5 = 4180 J; ΔH = -q/n = -4180/1 = -4180 J/mol = -4.18 kJ/mol, exothermic.

mcqs.q: Specific heat is the heat required to raise the temperature of:
options: 1 mol of a substance by one degree
1 g of a substance by one degree
1 g of water only by 25 degrees
mcqs.why: Specific heat is the heat required to raise 1 g of a substance by one degree (1°C or 1 K): c = q/mΔT.

mcqs.q: For water in these calculations, c is taken as:
mcqs.why: The notes use c = 4.18 J/g°C for water when calculating q = mcΔT from experimental calorimetry results.

lessons.notes_html:
Enthalpy changes are measured experimentally, usually in calorimetry, from the temperature change of a known mass of water or solution.

Heat Capacity

Heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a substance by one degree: c = q/ΔT, where q is heat and ΔT is the temperature change.

Specific Heat

Specific heat is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by one degree (1°C or 1 K): c = q/mΔT. Rearranged, the heat transferred is q = mcΔT.

Enthalpy Change per Mole

The enthalpy change for one mole of substance is ΔH = -q/n, i.e. ΔH = -mcΔT/n, where m is usually the mass of water or solution in the calorimeter and n is the amount of reactant. The negative sign is needed because the heat gained by the solution is the heat lost by the reaction: if the solution gains heat (ΔT positive), ΔH is negative (exothermic); if the solution loses heat (ΔT negative), ΔH is positive (endothermic).

Calculation of q and ΔH from Experimental Data

  • Given: mass of reaction mixture m = 150 g, specific heat capacity of water c = 4.18 J/g°C, ΔT = 25°C, moles reacted n = 0.75 mol.
  • q = mcΔT = 150 g x 4.18 J/g°C x 25°C = 15675 J.
  • ΔH = -mcΔT/n = -15675 J / 0.75 mol = -20900 J/mol = -20.9 kJ/mol (exothermic).

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
c = q/ΔTHeat capacity of a substance
c = q/mΔTSpecific heat (per gram)
q = mcΔTHeat absorbed or released by the solution
ΔH = -mcΔT/nEnthalpy change per mole of reactant

Key Points

  • q = mcΔT gives the heat change of the water or solution in a calorimeter.
  • Divide by the moles reacted and change the sign to get ΔH per mole.
  • Temperature rise of the solution means the reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative).
  • Temperature fall of the solution means the reaction is endothermic (ΔH positive).
  • For water, c = 4.18 J/g°C is used in these calculations.
lessons.title: Calculation of Enthalpy Changes from Experimental Results

mcqs.q: Electron affinity is the energy released when:
options: An electron is added to the lowest energy state of a gaseous atom, forming an anion
An electron is removed from a gaseous atom
A gaseous atom forms a cation
mcqs.why: Electron affinity is energy released when an electron is added to the lowest energy state of a gaseous atom, forming an anion.

mcqs.q: For Cl(g) + 1e- → Cl-(g), ΔH given in the notes is:
mcqs.why: The notes give Cl(g) + 1e- → Cl-(g) with ΔH = -349 kJ/mol, showing a strongly exothermic first electron affinity.

mcqs.q: The second electron affinity of oxygen, O-(g) + 1e- → O2-(g), is +844 kJ/mol because:
options: The nucleus attracts the electron more strongly
Oxygen has a small atomic radius
The incoming electron is repelled by the negative ion, so energy is absorbed
The first electron affinity was endothermic
mcqs.why: A second electron is repelled by the negative ion, so energy is absorbed and the second electron affinity is endothermic.

mcqs.q: As atomic radius increases, electron affinity:
options: Decreases - the greater the radius, the smaller the electron affinity
mcqs.why: The notes state the greater the atomic radius, the smaller the electron affinity, one of three listed factors.

mcqs.q: Electron affinity across a period from left to right generally:
options: Increases because nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases
mcqs.why: Across a period nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases, so electron affinity increases from left to right.

mcqs.q: Down a group, electron affinity decreases because:
options: Atomic size increases with more shells and shielding increases
mcqs.why: Down a group atomic size increases (more shells) and shielding increases, so electron affinity decreases as stated.

mcqs.q: For H(g) + 1e- → H-(g), ΔH given in the notes is:
mcqs.why: The notes give H(g) + 1e- → H-(g) with ΔH = -73 kJ/mol as an example of exothermic electron affinity.

mcqs.q: Greater shielding effect leads to:
options: A positive first electron affinity always
mcqs.why: The notes state the greater the shielding effect, the smaller the electron affinity, alongside radius and nuclear charge effects.

mcqs.q: Which group is noted for high electron affinities, with chlorine used to kill micro-organisms in drinking water?
mcqs.why: Halogens have high electron affinities; chlorine's strong electron affinity lets it oxidise and kill micro-organisms in water.

mcqs.q: The first electron affinity of oxygen O(g) + 1e- → O-(g) is given as:
mcqs.why: The notes give the first E.A. of oxygen as -141 kJ/mol (exothermic), contrasting with the second E.A. of +844 kJ/mol.

lessons.notes_html:
Electron affinity is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to the lowest energy state of a gaseous atom, forming an anion. Examples: H(g) + 1e- → H-(g), ΔH = -73 kJ/mol; Cl(g) + 1e- → Cl-(g), ΔH = -349 kJ/mol. Its units are kJ/mol, kcal/mol and electron volt. Electron affinity measures the attraction between the nucleus and the extra incoming electron.

When a second electron is added to a univalent negative ion, the incoming electron is repelled by the negative ion, so energy is absorbed and the second electron affinity is endothermic: O(g) + 1e- → O-(g), ΔH = -141 kJ/mol (1st E.A.); O-(g) + 1e- → O2-(g), ΔH = +844 kJ/mol (2nd E.A.).

Factors Affecting Electron Affinity

  • Atomic radius: the greater the atomic radius, the smaller the electron affinity.
  • Nuclear charge: the greater the nuclear charge, the greater the electron affinity.
  • Shielding effect: the greater the shielding effect, the smaller the electron affinity.

Trends in the Periodic Table

  • Electron affinity decreases down a group, because atomic size increases (more shells) and shielding increases.
  • Electron affinity increases across a period from left to right, because nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases.
  • Halogens have high electron affinities; chlorine's strong electron affinity lets it oxidise and kill micro-organisms in drinking water.

Key Points

  • First electron affinity is usually exothermic (energy released, negative ΔH).
  • Second electron affinity is always endothermic because the electron is repelled by the negative ion.
  • Electron affinity falls with larger atomic radius and stronger shielding.
  • Electron affinity rises with greater nuclear charge.
  • Down a group electron affinity decreases; across a period it increases.
lessons.title: Electron Affinity

mcqs.q: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change for a reaction is:
options: The same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in a series of steps
mcqs.why: Hess's law: ΔH is the same in one step or a series of steps, ΔH = ΔH1 + ΔH2 + ΔH3, depending only on initial and final states.

mcqs.q: Hess's law was formulated in 1840 by:
mcqs.why: The notes state Hess's law was formulated in 1840 by the Swiss chemist Germain Henri Hess.

mcqs.q: Via CO: ΔH1 = -110.5 and ΔH2 = -283.0 kJ mol-1. The total for C + O2 → CO2 is:
mcqs.why: Working: sum of steps = -110.5 + (-283.0) = -393.5 kJ mol-1, the same as the single-step value -393.51 kJ mol-1.

mcqs.q: Why is Hess's law needed for the enthalpy of formation of CO?
options: Because ΔH°f of elements is not zero
Because CO formed from C and O2 reacts further with O2 to give CO2, so it is found indirectly
mcqs.why: CO reacts further to CO2, so its formation enthalpy cannot be measured directly and is found indirectly via Hess's law.

mcqs.q: The formula for reaction enthalpy from formation enthalpies is:
mcqs.why: The notes give ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f (Products) - Σ ΔH°f (Reactants) for indirect calculations using Hess's law.

mcqs.q: In the methane calculation, ΔH°f(CH4) works out to -74.8 kJ/mol. The combustion ΔH°rxn used was:
mcqs.why: Working uses CH4 combustion ΔH°rxn = -890.3 kJ/mol with CO2 -393.5 and H2O -285.8 to obtain ΔH°f(CH4) = -74.8 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Verify the methane result: products sum = -393.5 + 2(-285.8) = -965.1; then ΔH°f(CH4) = -965.1 - (-890.3) with sign as in notes gives:
mcqs.why: Working: -890.3 = -965.1 - ΔH°f(CH4), so ΔH°f(CH4) = -965.1 + 890.3 = -74.8 kJ/mol as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: Elements in their standard states, such as O2 in the methane calculation, have ΔH°f:
mcqs.why: Elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0; the notes use O2 = 0 in the methane formation calculation.

mcqs.q: Total enthalpy change depends only on:
options: The initial and final states, not on the route
mcqs.why: A key point of Hess's law is that total enthalpy change depends only on initial and final states, not on the route.

mcqs.q: Which substances are listed as having formation enthalpies found indirectly by Hess's law?
options: Methane, ethyne, CO, benzene and ethyl alcohol
mcqs.why: The notes list methane, ethyne, CO, benzene, ethyl alcohol etc. as compounds whose ΔH°f is determined indirectly using Hess's law.

lessons.notes_html:
Hess's law states that the enthalpy change during a chemical reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in a series of steps: ΔH = ΔH1 + ΔH2 + ΔH3. It was formulated in 1840 by the Swiss chemist Germain Henri Hess. It is needed when a ΔH cannot be measured directly: for example, carbon monoxide formed from carbon and oxygen reacts further with oxygen to give CO2, so the enthalpy of formation of CO is found indirectly.

Determination of Standard Enthalpy Change for Carbon Dioxide

  • Single step: C(graphite) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = -393.51 kJ mol-1.
  • Multi-steps: C(graphite) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g), ΔH1 = -110.5 kJ mol-1; then CO(g) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH2 = -283.0 kJ mol-1.
  • Sum of steps: -110.5 + (-283.0) = -393.5 kJ mol-1, the same as the single step.

Applications of Hess's Law

The enthalpies of formation of methane, ethyne, CO, benzene, ethyl alcohol, etc., cannot be calculated directly; they are determined indirectly using Hess's law and the formula ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f (Products) - Σ ΔH°f (Reactants).

Determination of the Standard Enthalpy of Formation of Methane

  • Combustion: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l), ΔH°rxn = -890.3 kJ/mol; ΔH°f: CO2 = -393.5, H2O(l) = -285.8, O2 = 0 (element in standard state).
  • -890.3 = [-393.5 + 2(-285.8)] - [ΔH°f(CH4) + 2(0)].
  • ΔH°f(CH4) = -965.1 + 890.3 = -74.8 kJ/mol.

Key Points

  • Total enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the route.
  • ΔH for a multi-step route is the sum of the step values.
  • Hess's law finds enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly, such as ΔH°f of methane and CO.
  • ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f(products) - Σ ΔH°f(reactants).
  • Elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0.
lessons.title: Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation

mcqs.q: The two definitions of lattice energy have:
mcqs.why: The key points state the two definitions have equal magnitude and opposite sign, e.g. +715 and -715 kJ/mol for KCl.

mcqs.q: Smaller ions and higher charges give lattice energy that is:
options: Larger in magnitude due to stronger attractions
mcqs.why: Magnitude depends on ionic size, charge and arrangement; smaller ions and higher charges give stronger attractions and larger lattice energy.

mcqs.q: Lattice energy is calculated indirectly with:
options: The Born-Haber cycle, an application of Hess's law
mcqs.why: Lattice energy cannot be measured directly; it is calculated indirectly with the Born-Haber cycle, an application of Hess's law.

mcqs.q: Lattice energy is expressed in units of:
mcqs.why: The notes state lattice energy is expressed in kJ/mol, e.g. ±715 kJ/mol for potassium chloride KCl.

mcqs.q: Which factor is NOT listed as affecting the magnitude of lattice energy?
options: Arrangement of ions in the solid
mcqs.why: Magnitude depends on ionic size, ionic charge and arrangement of ions in the solid; colour is not listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Breaking an ionic crystal into gaseous ions:
options: Needs heat, ΔH positive in the breaking definition
mcqs.why: As a breaking process lattice energy is the heat needed to break one mole of crystal into gaseous ions, so it is positive.

mcqs.q: Forming one mole of crystalline ionic compound from gaseous ions:
mcqs.why: As a forming process, gaseous ions of opposite charges combine and release energy, giving a negative lattice energy value.

mcqs.q: Why can lattice energy not be measured directly in an experiment?
options: Because the notes state it cannot be measured directly and must be found indirectly
Because ionic compounds are always gases
Because calorimeters cannot be used at all
mcqs.why: The notes explicitly state lattice energy cannot be measured directly in an experiment; the Born-Haber cycle is used instead.

lessons.notes_html:
Lattice energy can be defined in two opposite ways. As a breaking process: the amount of heat needed to break one mole of an ionic crystal into its gaseous ions; this value is positive. Example: KCl(s) → K+(g) + Cl-(g), ΔH° = +715 kJ/mol. As a forming process: the amount of energy released when gaseous ions of opposite charges combine to form one mole of a crystalline ionic compound; this value is negative. Example: K+(g) + Cl-(g) → KCl(s), ΔH° = -715 kJ/mol. Lattice energy is expressed in kJ/mol.

The magnitude of lattice energy depends on the ionic size, the ionic charge and the arrangement of ions in the solid: smaller ions and higher charges give stronger attractions and a larger lattice energy. Lattice energy cannot be measured directly in an experiment; it is calculated indirectly with the Born-Haber cycle (an application of Hess's law).

Key Points

  • Breaking a crystal into gaseous ions needs energy: lattice energy positive (+715 kJ/mol for KCl).
  • Forming a crystal from gaseous ions releases energy: lattice energy negative (-715 kJ/mol for KCl).
  • The two definitions have equal magnitude and opposite sign.
  • Magnitude depends on ionic size, ionic charge and ion arrangement.
  • Lattice energy is found indirectly, never by direct measurement.
lessons.title: Lattice Energy

mcqs.q: The Born-Haber cycle was developed by:
mcqs.why: The cycle was developed by German physicist Max Born and German chemist Fritz Haber to calculate lattice energies of ionic compounds.

mcqs.q: The Born-Haber cycle is a special application of:
mcqs.why: The notes state the Born-Haber cycle is a special application of Hess's law, where the sum of enthalpy changes in a cycle equals zero.

mcqs.q: For NaCl, the direct route ΔH°f is:

mcqs.why: Step 1 sublimation of solid sodium is +107.7 kJ/mol, an endothermic step in the five-step indirect route.

mcqs.q: Ionisation of sodium Na(g) → Na+(g) + 1e- in the cycle is:
mcqs.why: Step 3 ionisation of sodium is +496.0 kJ/mol; sublimation, atomisation and ionisation are all endothermic steps.

mcqs.q: Applying Hess's law to NaCl: -411 = 376.4 + ΔH°latt, so ΔH°latt is:
Electron affinity of chlorine in the NaCl cycle is:
mcqs.why: Step 4 Cl(g) + 1e- → Cl-(g) is -349.0 kJ/mol; first electron affinity and lattice formation are the exothermic steps.
