mcqs.why: Step 2 atomisation of chlorine is +121.7 kJ/mol, consistent with ΔH°at for chlorine given earlier as about +121 kJ mol-1.

mcqs.q: The same Born-Haber method gives lattice energy of KBr as:
mcqs.why: The notes state the same method gives the lattice energy of KBr as -688.2 kJ/mol using the formation definition.

mcqs.q: The five indirect steps for NaCl formation are:
options: Sublimation, atomisation, ionisation, electron affinity, lattice formation
Bond breaking only and bond forming only
mcqs.why: The indirect route splits formation into sublimation, atomisation, ionisation, electron affinity and lattice formation steps.

lessons.notes_html:
The Born-Haber cycle was developed by the German physicist Max Born and the German chemist Fritz Haber to calculate the lattice energies of binary ionic compounds such as NaCl. The cycle states that the sum of all the enthalpy changes in a cyclic process always equals zero; it is a special application of Hess's law. Lattice energy cannot be determined directly, so the formation of the ionic solid is split into steps.

Calculation of the Lattice Energy of NaCl

Direct route: Na(s) + 1/2 Cl2(g) → NaCl(s), ΔH°f = -411 kJ mol-1. The indirect route has five steps:

StepProcessΔH° (kJ/mol)
1Sublimation of solid sodium: Na(s) → Na(g)+107.7
2Atomisation of chlorine: 1/2 Cl2(g) → Cl(g)+121.7
3Ionisation of sodium: Na(g) → Na+(g) + 1e-+496.0
4Electron affinity of chlorine: Cl(g) + 1e- → Cl-(g)-349.0
5Lattice formation: Na+(g) + Cl-(g) → NaCl(s)ΔH°latt = ?

Applying Hess's law: ΔH°f = ΔH°sub + ΔH°IE + ΔH°at + ΔH°EA + ΔH°latt, so -411 = 107.7 + 496.0 + 121.7 + (-349.0) + ΔH°latt = 376.4 + ΔH°latt, giving ΔH°latt = -787.4 kJ/mol. The same method gives, for example, the lattice energy of KBr as -688.2 kJ/mol.

Key Points

  • The Born-Haber cycle is Hess's law applied to the formation of an ionic solid.
  • Steps: sublimation, atomisation, ionisation, electron affinity, lattice formation.
  • Sublimation, atomisation and ionisation are endothermic; electron affinity (first) and lattice formation are exothermic.
  • ΔH°f = sum of all step enthalpy changes, so the unknown lattice energy is found by rearrangement.
  • Lattice energy of NaCl = -787.4 kJ/mol (formation definition).
lessons.title: Born-Haber Cycle

mcqs.q: Heat of solution ΔHsoln is the enthalpy change when:
options: One mole of a solute dissolves in a specified amount of solvent at constant pressure to infinite dilution
One mole of ions is hydrated

One mole of a crystal breaks into ions
mcqs.why: Heat of solution is for one mole of solute dissolving at constant pressure resulting in infinite dilution, per the notes.

mcqs.q: When KNO3 dissolves, temperature decreases and ΔH = +35.7 kJ mol-1, so the process is:
mcqs.why: KNO3 dissolving is endothermic (+35.7 kJ mol-1); the solution becomes colder because heat is absorbed on dissolving.

mcqs.q: When LiCl dissolves, ΔH = -37 kJ mol-1 and temperature increases, so the process is:
mcqs.why: LiCl dissolving is exothermic (-37 kJ mol-1); the solution becomes warmer because heat is released on dissolving.

mcqs.q: Solutes with negative heats of solution, like LiCl, become more soluble when temperature:
mcqs.why: The notes state solubility of solutes with negative ΔHsoln increases when temperature falls and decreases when it rises.

mcqs.q: Cold packs contain which substances that absorb heat on dissolving?
mcqs.why: Cold packs contain NH4NO3 or NH4Cl which absorb heat on dissolving; hot packs contain CaCl2 or MgSO4 which release heat.

mcqs.q: Hot packs contain which substances that release heat on dissolving?
mcqs.why: Hot packs contain CaCl2 or MgSO4, which release heat on dissolving in the exothermic instant-pack application.

mcqs.q: The heat of solution measures attraction between:
options: Ions in a dry crystal only
mcqs.why: ΔHsoln measures the intermolecular attraction between solute and solvent molecules, as defined at the start of the lesson.

mcqs.q: Temperature change of the solution on dissolving reveals:
options: The sign of the heat of solution
mcqs.why: A temperature fall shows endothermic dissolving (positive ΔH) and a rise shows exothermic dissolving (negative ΔH).

mcqs.q: KNO3(s) + H2O(l) ⇌ K+(aq) + NO3-(aq) has ΔH:
mcqs.why: The notes give KNO3 dissolving with ΔH = +35.7 kJ mol-1, distinct from LiCl at -37 kJ mol-1.

mcqs.q: LiCl(s) + H2O(l) ⇌ Li+(aq) + Cl-(aq) has ΔH:
mcqs.why: The notes give LiCl dissolving with ΔH = -37 kJ mol-1, an exothermic heat of solution example.

lessons.notes_html:
The heat of solution (enthalpy of solution, ΔHsoln) is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute dissolves in a specified amount of solvent at constant pressure, resulting in infinite dilution. It measures the intermolecular attraction between solute and solvent molecules. The heat of solution is negative for an exothermic process and positive for an endothermic process.

Examples

When KNO3 is added to water, the temperature of the solution decreases, showing an endothermic process: KNO3(s) + H2O(l) ⇌ K+(aq) + NO3-(aq), ΔH = +35.7 kJ mol-1. When LiCl is added to water, the temperature increases, showing an exothermic process: LiCl(s) + H2O(l) ⇌ Li+(aq) + Cl-(aq), ΔH = -37 kJ mol-1.

Solubility follows the sign: the solubility of solutes with negative heats of solution (like LiCl) increases when the temperature falls and decreases when it rises. The same principle is used in instant packs: cold packs contain NH4NO3 or NH4Cl, which absorb heat on dissolving; hot packs contain CaCl2 or MgSO4, which release heat on dissolving.

Key Points

  • ΔHsoln is for one mole of solute dissolving to infinite dilution at constant pressure.
  • KNO3 dissolving is endothermic (+35.7 kJ/mol); the solution becomes colder.
  • LiCl dissolving is exothermic (-37 kJ/mol); the solution becomes warmer.
  • Temperature change of the solution reveals the sign of the heat of solution.
  • Cold packs use endothermic dissolving (NH4NO3, NH4Cl); hot packs use exothermic dissolving (CaCl2, MgSO4).
lessons.title: Heat of Solution

options: ΔHhyd = ΔHsoln + ΔHlattice always with lattice forming sign
mcqs.why: The formula table gives Heat of hydration = ΔHsoln - ΔHlattice, linking hydration, solution and lattice energies.

mcqs.why: Dissolving needs energy to break the lattice and releases energy on hydration: ΔHsoln = ΔHlattice (breaking) + ΔHhyd.

mcqs.q: If heat of hydration is greater in magnitude than lattice energy (breaking), ΔHsoln is:
mcqs.why: If hydration releases more than lattice breaking absorbs, the heat of solution is negative and dissolving is exothermic, and vice versa.

mcqs.q: Breaking the lattice apart during dissolving:
mcqs.why: Energy is needed to break the lattice apart, while energy is released when the ions are hydrated - the two terms in dissolving.

mcqs.q: Hydration of ions during dissolving:
mcqs.why: When ions are hydrated, water surrounds them and releases energy in the form of heat, the heat of hydration.

mcqs.why: Working: ΔHsoln = ΔHlattice (breaking) + ΔHhyd = 700 + (-750) = -50 kJ/mol, so dissolving is exothermic.

options: -750 kJ/mol when lattice breaking term is +700 in the balance equation

mcqs.q: Heat of hydration is a specific type of dissolution energy in which the solvent is:
mcqs.why: Hydration is a specific type of dissolution energy in which water is the solvent, usually measured in kJ/mol.

lessons.notes_html:
The heat of hydration (ΔHhyd) measures the energy released or absorbed when one mole of ions undergoes complete hydration. It is a specific type of dissolution energy in which water is the solvent, and it is usually measured in kJ/mol. The process is associated with salts and other compounds that can form hydrated crystals.

When an ionic compound dissolves in water, the positive and negative ions are attracted to the polar water molecules. This attraction creates ion-dipole interactions: water molecules surround the ions and release energy in the form of heat, which is the heat of hydration. Dissolving involves two energy terms: energy is needed to break the lattice apart, and energy is released when the ions are hydrated.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Heat of hydration = ΔHsoln - ΔHlatticeLinks hydration enthalpy with the heat of solution and the lattice energy
ΔHsoln = ΔHlattice (breaking) + ΔHhydHeat of solution as the balance of lattice breaking and hydration

If the heat of hydration is greater than the lattice energy, the heat of solution is negative (exothermic), and vice versa.

Key Points

  • Heat of hydration is the energy change when one mole of ions is completely hydrated.
  • It comes from ion-dipole attractions between ions and polar water molecules.
  • Hydration of ions releases energy; breaking the lattice absorbs energy.
  • The sign of ΔHsoln depends on which of hydration and lattice energy is larger.
  • Heat of hydration = ΔHsoln - ΔHlattice.
lessons.title: Heat of Hydration

mcqs.why: Down the alkali metals radius grows from Li+ to Cs+ and hydration enthalpy becomes less negative: -519 to -263 kJ/mol.

options: More negative due to stronger attraction to water

mcqs.why: The notes conclude hydration enthalpy is directly proportional to ionic charge and inversely proportional to ionic radius.

lessons.notes_html:
The magnitude of the enthalpy change of hydration depends mainly on the ionic charge and the radius of the ion. Hydration enthalpy becomes more exothermic as the ionic charge increases or the ionic radius decreases. Both factors act through charge density, which determines the strength of attraction between the ion and the polar water molecules.

Effect of Ionic Radius

The smaller the ionic radius, the higher the charge density and the stronger the electrostatic attraction to water molecules, so hydration enthalpy becomes more negative. For monovalent alkali metal ions:

IonIonic Radius (pm)Hydration Enthalpy (kJ/mol)
Li+76-519
Na+102-406
K+138-322
Cs+167-263

Effect of Ionic Charge

The higher the ionic charge, the stronger the attraction to surrounding water molecules and the more negative the hydration enthalpy:

IonIonic ChargeIonic Radius (pm)Hydration Enthalpy (kJ/mol)
Na++1102-406
Mg2++272-1922
Al3++353-4665

Li+ (76 pm) and Mg2+ (72 pm) have similar radii, yet the hydration enthalpy of Mg2+ is about four times more negative, because the doubled charge increases the product of charges between the cation and the water dipoles. Hence, the enthalpy of hydration is directly proportional to the ionic charge and inversely proportional to the ionic radius.

Key Points

  • Smaller ion → higher charge density → stronger attraction to water → more negative ΔHhyd.
  • Higher ionic charge → much more negative ΔHhyd (Na+ -406, Mg2+ -1922, Al3+ -4665 kJ/mol).
  • Down the alkali metals, radius grows and hydration enthalpy becomes less negative.
  • Charge has a stronger effect than radius when the two are compared at similar size.
lessons.title: Effect of Ionic Charge and Ionic Radius on the Enthalpy Change of Hydration

mcqs.why: Freezing and condensation make molecules lose freedom and become more ordered, e.g. water to ice, so ΔS° is negative.

options: Positive due to greater freedom and movement of gas molecules
mcqs.why: More gas molecules means greater freedom and movement, e.g. combustion of methane, so entropy change is positive.

mcqs.q: Heating a metal rod has entropy change:
options: Positive, molecules gain energy and move faster
mcqs.why: Heating increases particle energy and faster movement, so the table lists heating with a positive entropy change.

Observable macroscopic properties such as temperature, pressure and volume
mcqs.why: Macrostates are observable macroscopic properties such as temperature, pressure and volume, distinct from microstates or arrangements.

lessons.notes_html:
Entropy, symbolised as S, measures the level of disorder or randomness in a system: the number of possible microscopic arrangements of particles and their energy in a given macroscopic state. When the constituents of a system become more spread out, or a gas expands at constant temperature, the number of available microscopic arrangements (microstates) increases along with entropy. Macrostates are the observable macroscopic properties, such as temperature, pressure and volume. Entropy is related to heat and temperature by S = q/T and ΔS = Δq/T.

Standard Entropy

The standard entropy change, ΔS°, is the measure of disorder of a system during a reaction under standard conditions, found from the standard molar entropies S° of reactants and products. Standard conditions here are 298.15 K (25°C), 1 atm and 1 M concentration. The SI unit of entropy is J/K.mol.

Predicting the Sign of Entropy Changes in States, Temperatures, and Gas Reactions

Three main factors affect the entropy change: change in state, temperature change, and the change in the number of gaseous molecules.

ProcessEntropy Change (ΔS°)ExplanationExample
Melting / vaporisation+Molecules move more freely and become less orderedIce melting to water
Freezing / condensation-Molecules lose freedom and become more orderedWater turning to ice
Heating+Molecules gain energy and move fasterHeating a metal rod
Cooling-Molecules lose energy and move more slowlyCooling a metal rod
More gas molecules produced+Greater freedom and movement of gas moleculesCombustion of methane
Fewer gas molecules produced-Reduced freedom and movement of gas moleculesNaOH and HCl reaction

Key Points

  • Entropy S measures disorder; more microstates means higher entropy.
  • ΔS = Δq/T; the unit of entropy is J/K.mol.
  • Positive ΔS° means more disorder; negative ΔS° means less disorder.
  • Melting, vaporisation, heating and producing more gas molecules increase entropy.
  • Freezing, condensation, cooling and producing fewer gas molecules decrease entropy.
lessons.title: Entropy

mcqs.q: Standard entropy change of a reaction is calculated by:

mcqs.q: For 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O(g) with S° H2 130.6, O2 205, H2O 188.7 J/K.mol, ΔS° is:

mcqs.q: The reactants sum in the worked example, 2(130.6) + 205, equals:
mcqs.why: Working: 2 × 130.6 = 261.2, plus 205 = 466.2 J/K.mol for the reactants in the entropy calculation.

mcqs.q: The notes warn that exothermic reactions are:
options: Spontaneous only if ΔS is negative
Not always spontaneous; spontaneity needs both ΔH and ΔS
mcqs.why: Heat release alone does not decide spontaneity; both enthalpy and entropy changes are essential, e.g. wood needs a spark.

mcqs.why: Positive ΔS° means more disorder; negative ΔS° means less disorder, as established in the entropy lessons.

mcqs.why: The note uses wood combustion to show exothermic reactions are not always spontaneous in practice and need both ΔH and ΔS considered.

lessons.notes_html:
The standard entropy change of a reaction (ΔS°) is the change in entropy when reactants are converted to products under standard conditions (1 atm pressure and 298 K temperature). It shows the change in disorder or randomness within the system during the reaction.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔS° = ΣS°(products) - ΣS°(reactants)Standard entropy change of a reaction from standard molar entropies

Worked Example: 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g)

  • Standard entropies used: S°(H2) = 130.6 J/K.mol, S°(O2) = 205 J/K.mol, S°(H2O) = 188.7 J/K.mol.
  • ΔS° = [2(188.7)] - [2(130.6) + (205)] = 377.4 - 466.2 J/K.mol.
  • ΔS° = -88.8 J/K.mol: entropy decreases, as expected when 3 mol of gas form 2 mol of gas.

Note: exothermic reactions are not always spontaneous. Heat release alone does not decide spontaneity; both enthalpy and entropy changes are essential. Combustion of wood is exothermic, yet it still needs a spark to start it.

Key Points

  • ΔS° = ΣS°(products) - ΣS°(reactants), using standard molar entropies.
  • Multiply each S° value by the coefficient in the balanced equation.
  • A decrease in the number of gas molecules usually gives a negative ΔS°.
  • Spontaneity depends on both ΔH and ΔS, not on heat release alone.
lessons.title: Standard Entropy Change of a Reaction

mcqs.q: Heat is best described as:
options: Energy transferred between objects or systems due to a temperature difference
The average kinetic energy of particles

mcqs.why: Energy changes form, e.g. chemical potential energy into heat, but overall energy stays the same before and after the reaction.

Slower with less energetic collisions and lower average kinetic energy
mcqs.why: Lower temperature means lower average kinetic energy, slower movement and less energetic collisions, the direct correlation stated.

mcqs.q: Heat comes from random movement of particles creating kinetic energy transferred when particles:
mcqs.why: Random movement creates kinetic energy which is transferred between particles when they collide, as described in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Total energy of the system including reactants and products throughout a reaction:
mcqs.why: Conservation: total energy of the system including reactants and products remains constant throughout a reaction.

lessons.notes_html:
Heat as a Form of Energy

Heat is a type of energy defined by the movement of thermal energy between objects or systems due to a temperature difference. It comes from the random movement of particles at a very small level; this movement creates kinetic energy, which is transferred between particles when they collide. Heat and temperature are different but related ideas: temperature shows the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance, while heat is the transfer of energy between substances because of a temperature difference. Heat typically moves from objects at higher temperature to those at lower temperature until they reach thermal equilibrium, where the temperatures are the same.

Relationship between Temperature and Kinetic Energy of Particles

According to the kinetic theory of matter, all particles of matter are constantly moving and have kinetic energy. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. When the temperature of a substance increases, the average kinetic energy of its particles also increases, leading to faster movement and more energetic collisions. When temperature decreases, the average kinetic energy decreases, with slower movement and less energetic collisions. There is a direct correlation between temperature and the kinetic energy of particles.

Conservation of Total Energy in Chemical Reactions

The total energy of the system, including the reactants and the products, remains constant throughout a reaction. Energy can change forms during a chemical reaction, such as chemical potential energy transforming into heat, but the overall energy stays the same before and after the reaction. This is the first law of thermodynamics: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.

Key Points

  • Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature measures average particle kinetic energy.
  • Heat flows from hotter to colder bodies until thermal equilibrium is reached.
  • Higher temperature means faster particles and more energetic collisions.
  • Total energy is conserved in chemical reactions (first law of thermodynamics).
  • Energy changes form in reactions but is never created or destroyed.
lessons.title: Principles of Energy Transfer and Conservation

mcqs.q: Gibbs free energy G is related to H, S and T by:
mcqs.why: Gibbs free energy is related by G = H - TS, where H is enthalpy, S is entropy and T is temperature.

mcqs.q: The free energy change formula is:
mcqs.why: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS combines enthalpy and entropy effects at temperature T in Kelvin to measure spontaneity and useful energy.

mcqs.q: If ΔG° is negative, the process:
mcqs.why: Negative ΔG° means spontaneous; positive means non-spontaneous needing energy input; zero means equilibrium.

mcqs.q: If ΔG° = 0, the system is:
mcqs.why: The notes state if ΔG° = 0 the system is at equilibrium, distinct from negative (spontaneous) and positive (non-spontaneous).

mcqs.q: A reaction with ΔH negative and ΔS positive has ΔG that is:
mcqs.why: Exothermic with entropy increase is always spontaneous: ΔH negative and ΔS positive gives negative ΔG at all temperatures.

mcqs.q: A reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative is:
options: Non-spontaneous at all temperatures with positive ΔG
mcqs.why: Endothermic with entropy decrease gives positive ΔG and is non-spontaneous at all temperatures, per the spontaneity table.

mcqs.q: Calculate ΔG: ΔH = -100 kJ, ΔS = +0.20 kJ/K, T = 298 K. ΔG is:
mcqs.why: Working: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = -100 - 298(0.20) = -100 - 59.6 = -159.6 kJ, negative so spontaneous.

mcqs.q: Calculate ΔG: ΔH = +50 kJ, ΔS = +0.20 kJ/K, T = 298 K. ΔG is:
mcqs.why: Working: ΔG = 50 - 298(0.20) = 50 - 59.6 = -9.6 kJ; with same-sign ΔH and ΔS, high enough T makes it spontaneous.

mcqs.q: For ΔH positive and ΔS positive, e.g. 2HgO(s) → 2Hg(l) + O2(g), spontaneity occurs:
options: When TΔS° is greater than ΔH°, i.e. at high T
mcqs.why: When both are positive, ΔG is negative when TΔS° exceeds ΔH°, so the process is spontaneous at high temperature.

mcqs.q: Gibbs free energy is also known as:
options: Free enthalpy, Gibbs function, or available energy
mcqs.why: G is also known as free enthalpy, Gibbs function, or available energy, used to determine spontaneity without external energy.

lessons.notes_html:
Gibbs free energy is a thermodynamic function used to determine the spontaneity of a process. It indicates whether a reaction or physical change can proceed on its own, without requiring external energy. It is denoted by G and is also known as free enthalpy, Gibbs function, or available energy. Gibbs free energy is related to enthalpy (H), entropy (S) and temperature (T) by G = H - TS.

Free Energy Change and Reaction Spontaneity

The free energy change ΔG measures the spontaneity of a process and the useful energy available from it: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. Under standard conditions: ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°, where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin. If ΔG° is negative, the process happens spontaneously; if positive, it will not happen spontaneously and needs an input of energy; if ΔG° = 0, the system is at equilibrium.

Spontaneity and the Sign of ΔG°

ΔH°ΔS°ΔG°Spontaneity
NegativePositiveNegativeSpontaneous at all temperatures
PositiveNegativePositiveNon-spontaneous at all temperatures
PositivePositiveNegative when TΔS° greater than ΔH°Spontaneous at high T (e.g. 2HgO(s) → 2Hg(l) + O2(g))
NegativeNegativeNegative when TΔS° less than ΔH°Spontaneous at low T (e.g. H2O(l) → H2O(s))

Key Points

  • Gibbs free energy G = H - TS decides whether a process is spontaneous.
  • ΔG = ΔH - TΔS combines the enthalpy and entropy effects at temperature T (in Kelvin).
  • ΔG negative = spontaneous; ΔG positive = non-spontaneous; ΔG = 0 = equilibrium.
  • Exothermic with entropy increase is always spontaneous; endothermic with entropy decrease is never spontaneous.
  • When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, temperature decides spontaneity.
lessons.title: Gibbs Free Energy

mcqs.q: Standard free energy of formation ΔG°f is the free energy change when:
options: One mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states

mcqs.why: ΔG°f is for one mole of a compound forming from its elements in standard states; it predicts spontaneity at 25°C and 1 atm.

mcqs.q: The formula for standard free energy change of a reaction is:
mcqs.why: ΔG°rxn = Σ n.ΔG°f(products) - Σ n.ΔG°f(reactants), where n is the stoichiometric coefficient for each substance.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 with ΔG°f(NH3) = -16.4 kJ/mol and elements 0, ΔG°rxn is:
mcqs.why: Working: ΔG°rxn = [2 × (-16.4)] - [0 + 3(0)] = -32.8 - 0 = -32.8 kJ/mol, spontaneous under standard conditions.

mcqs.q: Elements in their standard states have ΔG°f:
mcqs.why: For elements ΔG°f = 0; the worked example uses N2 = 0.0 and H2 = 0.0 kJ/mol as elements in standard states.

mcqs.q: Standard states listed for ΔG°f include solution at:
mcqs.why: Standard states: gas 1 atm, solid pure solid, liquid pure liquid, solution 1 M, and elements have ΔG°f = 0.

mcqs.q: A negative ΔG°rxn in the ammonia example shows the reaction is:
mcqs.why: ΔG°rxn = -32.8 kJ/mol is negative, which shows the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

mcqs.q: Each ΔG°f in the ΔG°rxn calculation must be multiplied by:
options: Its coefficient in the balanced equation
mcqs.why: Each ΔG°f is multiplied by its coefficient, e.g. 2 × ΔG°f(NH3) in the ammonia worked example.

mcqs.q: The alternative formula linking free energy, enthalpy and entropy is:
mcqs.why: The formula table gives ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS° for free energy change from enthalpy and entropy changes.

mcqs.q: Gibbs free energy also predicts everyday changes such as:
options: Whether iron will rust in moist air
mcqs.why: The key points state Gibbs free energy also predicts everyday changes, such as whether iron will rust in moist air.

mcqs.q: The products term in the ammonia example, 2 × (-16.4), equals:
mcqs.why: Working: 2 × (-16.4) = -32.8 kJ/mol for products; subtracting reactants (0) leaves ΔG°rxn = -32.8 kJ/mol.

lessons.notes_html:
The standard free energy of formation (ΔG°f) is the free energy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states; it predicts reaction spontaneity at 25°C and 1 atm. Standard states: gas = 1 atm, solid = pure solid, liquid = pure liquid, solution = 1 M, and for elements ΔG°f = 0.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔG°rxn = Σ n.ΔG°f(products) - Σ n.ΔG°f(reactants)Standard free energy change of a reaction; n is the stoichiometric coefficient
ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°Free energy change from enthalpy and entropy changes

Worked Example: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g)

  • Given ΔG°f values: NH3(g) = -16.4 kJ/mol; N2(g) = 0.0 kJ/mol and H2(g) = 0.0 kJ/mol (elements in their standard states).
  • ΔG°rxn = [2 x ΔG°f(NH3)] - [ΔG°f(N2) + 3 x ΔG°f(H2)] = [2 x (-16.4)] - [0 + 0].
  • ΔG°rxn = -32.8 kJ/mol. The negative value shows the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

Key Points

  • ΔG°rxn is calculated from standard free energies of formation of products minus reactants.
  • Each ΔG°f is multiplied by its coefficient in the balanced equation.
  • Elements in their standard states have ΔG°f = 0.
  • A negative ΔG°rxn means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
  • Gibbs free energy also predicts everyday changes, such as whether iron will rust in moist air.
lessons.title: Calculation of Gibbs Free Energy (ΔG°)

mcqs.q: Reaction kinetics studies:
options: Reaction rates, mechanisms and factors affecting rates
mcqs.why: Definition: reaction kinetics is the branch that studies reaction rates, reaction mechanisms, and the factors that affect these rates.

mcqs.q: Which is given as a slow reaction?

mcqs.q: Unit of rate given in the notes is:
mcqs.why: The notes state the unit of rate is mol/L·s; time may be measured in seconds, minutes or hours.

mcqs.q: As reaction proceeds, reactant concentrations:
mcqs.why: The notes state reactant concentrations decrease while product concentrations increase with time during a reaction.

mcqs.q: For aA + bB -> cC + dD, the rate expression divides by:
mcqs.why: Rate = -(1/a)d[A]/dt = -(1/b)d[B]/dt = (1/c)d[C]/dt = (1/d)d[D]/dt, dividing each change by its coefficient so all give one rate.

mcqs.q: The negative sign in the rate expression shows:
mcqs.why: The notes explain the negative sign shows a reactant's concentration decreases (consumption); positive sign shows product formation.

mcqs.q: For 2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2, rate in terms of N2O5 is:
mcqs.why: Example: for 2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2, Rate = -(1/2) d[N2O5]/dt, dividing by coefficient 2.

mcqs.why: Working: Rate = -(1/2) x (-1.28/8) = -(1/2) x (-0.16) = 0.08 mol/L·h, as calculated from the book's data.

mcqs.q: Which is given as a fast reaction?
mcqs.why: Fast examples given: combustion of petrol, explosion of gunpowder and neutralisation of HCl by NaOH are fast reactions.

lessons.notes_html:
Reaction kinetics is the branch of chemistry that studies reaction rates, reaction mechanisms, and the factors that affect these rates. Reactions occur at very different rates: rusting of iron, setting of cement and decay of plants into coal are slow, while combustion of petrol, explosion of gunpowder and neutralisation of HCl by NaOH are fast.

The rate of reaction is defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product over a unit of time. Reactant concentrations decrease while product concentrations increase with time. The unit of rate is mol/L·s; time may be measured in seconds, minutes or hours.

Rate Expression for a General Reaction

For aA + bB → cC + dD, where a, b, c and d are the coefficients:

FormulaUse
Rate of Reaction = Change in Concentration / Change in TimeBasic definition of rate
Rate = −(1/a) Δ[A]/Δt = −(1/b) Δ[B]/Δt = (1/c) Δ[C]/Δt = (1/d) Δ[D]/ΔtOne equal rate from any reactant or product

The negative sign shows a reactant's concentration decreases (consumption); the positive sign shows a product's concentration increases (formation). Example: for 2N2O5 → 4NO2 + O2, Rate = −(1/2) Δ[N2O5]/Δt. From the book's data ([N2O5] falls from 1.4 to 0.12 mol/L in 8 h), Rate = −(1/2) x (−1.28 / 8) = 0.08 mol/L·h.

Key Points

  • Rate = change in concentration per unit time; unit mol/L·s.
  • Divide each Δ[ ]/Δt by the substance's coefficient so all give the same rate.
  • Minus sign for reactants (decreasing), plus sign for products (increasing).
  • Kinetics studies rates, mechanisms and the factors affecting them.
lessons.title: Rate of Reaction

mcqs.q: The rate law states rate is proportional to:
options: Product of reactant concentrations each raised to some power
mcqs.why: Rate law: rate is directly proportional to the product of concentrations of reactants, each raised to some power: Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n.

mcqs.q: In Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, k is called:
options: Rate constant or specific rate constant
mcqs.why: k is the proportionality constant called the rate constant or specific rate constant in the rate law.

mcqs.q: The value of k depends on:
options: Nature of reaction, reaction order and temperature
mcqs.why: The notes state k depends on nature of reaction, reaction order and temperature, and remains fixed at constant temperature.

mcqs.q: k increases with:

mcqs.q: The rate law is determined:

lessons.notes_html:
The rate law (rate equation) states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants, each raised to some power. For aA + bB → cC + dD, by the law of mass action:

FormulaUse
Rate of reaction = k [A]^m [B]^nRate law; k is the rate constant, m and n are the orders with respect to A and B

Here k is the proportionality constant, called the rate constant or specific rate constant. Its value depends on the nature of the reaction, reaction order and temperature. It increases with temperature and with catalysts, and remains fixed for a specific reaction at constant temperature, unaffected by reactant or product concentrations or by time.

Important Features

  • The rate law shows how the rate relates to reactant concentrations.
  • It is determined experimentally, not predicted from the balanced equation.
  • The exponents in the rate law may or may not equal the coefficients in the balanced equation.
  • The exponents indicate the order of reaction with respect to each reactant.

Key Points

  • Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where k is the rate constant.
  • k depends on the reaction, its order and temperature — not on concentrations or time.
  • k increases with temperature and in the presence of a catalyst.
  • The rate law is found by experiment; exponents need not match equation coefficients.
lessons.title: The Rate Law

mcqs.q: A single step in a multi-step mechanism is called:
mcqs.why: Definition: a single step in the mechanism is called an elementary reaction or elementary step.

mcqs.q: The mechanism of a reaction is:
options: Step-by-step sequence of elementary steps behind the overall reaction
mcqs.why: Mechanism is the series of steps (reaction pathway) through which most reactions proceed, made of elementary steps.

mcqs.q: Experimental rate law for NO2 + CO overall reaction is:
mcqs.why: Experimentally Rate = k[NO2]^2 — rate depends only on NO2, not CO, and reaction is second-order overall.

mcqs.q: Step 1 of the NO2 + CO mechanism is:
options: Slow, rate-determining step: NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO
mcqs.why: Proposed Step 1 (slow, rate-determining): NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO; Step 2 is the fast step with CO.

mcqs.q: NO3 in the mechanism is:
mcqs.why: NO3 is a reaction intermediate — short-lived species formed in one step and consumed in another; it does not appear overall.

mcqs.q: An intermediate is:
options: Formed in one step and used up in another; cancels from overall equation
mcqs.why: Definition: an intermediate is formed in one step and consumed in another; it does not appear in the overall equation and is unstable.

mcqs.q: The slowest step in a multi-step reaction is called:
mcqs.why: The slowest step controls overall rate and is called the rate-determining step or rate-limiting step.

mcqs.q: Rate law is written for:
mcqs.why: The notes state the rate law is written for the rate-determining step only: Rate = k[NO2]^2 for the example.

mcqs.q: Adding the two steps of NO2 + CO mechanism gives:
options: The overall reaction NO2 + CO -> NO + CO2
mcqs.why: Adding Step 1 and Step 2 gives the overall reaction NO2(g) + CO(g) -> NO(g) + CO2(g), with NO3 cancelling.

mcqs.q: If NO2 + CO occurred in one step, rate law would be:
mcqs.why: The notes state if it occurred in one step, rate law would be Rate = k[NO2][CO], but experiment shows otherwise.

lessons.notes_html:
Some reactions occur in a single step, but most proceed through a series of steps. The steps in a multi-step reaction are called the mechanism (reaction pathway) of the reaction. A single step in the mechanism is called an elementary reaction or elementary step.

Example: NO2 + CO Reaction

Overall reaction: NO2(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO2(g). If it occurred in one step, the rate law would be Rate = k[NO2][CO]. Experimentally the rate law is Rate = k[NO2]^2 — the rate depends only on NO2, not on CO, and the reaction is second-order overall. The proposed mechanism is:

  • Step 1 (slow, rate-determining step): NO2(g) + NO2(g) → NO3(g) + NO(g)
  • Step 2 (fast step): NO3(g) + CO(g) → NO2(g) + CO2(g)

Adding the two steps gives the overall reaction. The rate law is written for the rate-determining step only: Rate = k[NO2]^2. Here NO3 is a reaction intermediate — a short-lived species formed in one step and consumed in another; it does not appear in the overall equation and is unstable.

In a multi-step reaction the steps do not all happen at the same speed. The slowest step controls the overall rate and is called the rate-determining step or rate-limiting step.

Key Points

  • Mechanism = step-by-step sequence of elementary steps behind the overall reaction.
  • The experimental rate law comes from the slowest, rate-determining step.
  • An intermediate is formed in one step and used up in another; it cancels from the overall equation.
  • Example: NO2 + CO has Rate = k[NO2]^2, with NO3 as the intermediate.
lessons.title: Elementary and Overall Reactions

mcqs.q: Order of reaction is:
options: Sum of all exponents in the rate equation
mcqs.why: Definition: order is sum of all exponents of concentration terms in rate equation; for Rate = k[A]^a[B]^b, order = a+b.

mcqs.q: Doubling concentration in first order makes rate:

mcqs.q: Doubling concentration in second order makes rate:
mcqs.why: Working: second order rate proportional to concentration squared: 2^2 = 4, so rate quadruples (x4) on doubling.

mcqs.q: Unit of k for first order is:
mcqs.why: Table gives unit of k for first order as s-1; second order L mol-1 s-1, third order L2 mol-2 s-1.

mcqs.q: Book example of first order is:
mcqs.why: Table lists N2O5 decomposition as first order with Rate = k[N2O5] and unit s-1 for k.

mcqs.q: H2 + I2 -> 2HI with Rate = k[H2][I2] is:
mcqs.why: Table lists H2 + I2 -> 2HI as second order because exponents sum to 1+1 = 2, with k unit L mol-1 s-1.

mcqs.q: 2NO + O2 -> 2NO2 with Rate = k[NO]^2[O2] is:
mcqs.why: Working: order = 2 + 1 = 3, so third order; doubling gives x8 effect as in the table.

mcqs.q: Order with respect to one reactant is:
options: Its own exponent in the rate law
mcqs.why: Key points state order with respect to one reactant is its own exponent in the rate law, while overall order is the sum.

mcqs.q: Unit of k for third order is:
mcqs.why: Table gives third order unit of k as L2 mol-2 s-1, distinct from first (s-1) and second (L mol-1 s-1).

lessons.notes_html:
The order of reaction is the sum of all the exponents of the concentration terms in the rate equation. For Rate = k[A]^a[B]^b, order of reaction = a + b. The order is determined experimentally; it cannot be predicted from a balanced equation, because the exponents may differ from the coefficients.

OrderRate lawEffect of doubling concentrationUnit of kBook example
First orderRate = k[A]^1Rate doubless-1N2O5(g) → 2NO2(g) + 1/2 O2(g); Rate = k[N2O5]
Second orderRate = k[A][B] or k[A]^2Rate quadruples (x4)L mol-1 s-1H2 + I2 → 2HI; Rate = k[H2][I2]. Also 2O3(g) → 3O2(g); Rate = k[O3]^2
Third orderRate = k[A][B][C] or k[A]^2[B]Rate octuples (x8)L^2 mol-2 s-12NO + O2 → 2NO2; Rate = k[NO]^2[O2]. Also 2NO + 2H2 → N2 + 2H2O; Rate = k[NO]^2[H2]

Definitions

  • First order: rate directly proportional to the first power of the concentration of one reacting substance.
  • Second order: rate proportional to the square of one concentration, or to the product of two concentrations.
  • Third order: rate proportional to the product of three concentrations, or to the first power of one substance and the square of another.

Key Points

  • Order = sum of exponents in the rate law; always found experimentally.
  • Doubling concentration: first order x2, second order x4, third order x8.
  • Units of k change with order: s-1, L mol-1 s-1, L^2 mol-2 s-1.
  • Order with respect to one reactant is its own exponent in the rate law.
lessons.title: Order of Reaction

mcqs.q: A zeroth order reaction has rate that:
options: Does not depend on concentration of any reactant
mcqs.why: Definition: zeroth order rate does not depend on concentration: Rate = k[A]^0 = k.

mcqs.q: Rate equation for zero order is:
mcqs.why: The notes give zeroth order as Rate = k[A]^0 = k, independent of concentration.

mcqs.q: Unit of k for zero order is:
mcqs.why: The notes state for zero order the unit of k is mol L-1 s-1, since rate itself equals k.

mcqs.q: Example of zero order given is:
options: 2NH3 -> N2 + 3H2 over tungsten with Rate = k[NH3]^0
mcqs.why: Book example: 2NH3(g) over tungsten -> N2 + 3H2 with Rate = k[NH3]^0 is zero order; photosynthesis also given.

mcqs.q: In Experiments 1 and 2, [B] doubled and rate went 0.0048 to 0.0192. Order in B is:
mcqs.why: Working: rate ratio = 0.0192/0.0048 = 4 = 2^2, so Rate proportional to [B]^2 — second order in B.

mcqs.q: In Experiments 1 and 3, [A] doubled and rate doubled. Order in A is:
mcqs.why: Working: rate ratio = 0.0096/0.0048 = 2 = 2^1, so Rate proportional to [A]^1 — first order in A.

mcqs.q: Overall order for A + 2B example is:
mcqs.why: Working: overall order = 1 (in A) + 2 (in B) = 3, with Rate = k[A]^1[B]^2 as determined.

mcqs.q: To find an order by initial rates you:
options: Change one concentration at a time and compare rates
mcqs.why: Key points: to find order, change one concentration at a time and compare rates; x2 = first, x4 = second in that reactant.

mcqs.q: Rate x4 on doubling concentration means:
mcqs.why: Key points state rate x2 on doubling = first order; rate x4 on doubling = second order in that reactant.

mcqs.q: Zero order reactions may include:
mcqs.why: The notes state enzyme-catalysed reactions and thermal decomposition reactions may be zero order.

lessons.notes_html:
A reaction whose rate does not depend on the concentration of any reactant is called a zeroth order reaction: Rate of reaction = k[A]^0 = k. Enzyme-catalysed reactions and thermal decomposition reactions may be zero order. The unit of k is mol L-1 s-1. Examples given in the book: photosynthesis (photochemical reactions), and 2NH3(g) →(Tungsten) N2(g) + 3H2(g), with Rate = k[NH3]^0.

Experimental Determination of the Order of Reaction (Initial Rates)

Order is calculated from measured rates of reaction, generally by physical and chemical methods. The book's example studies A + 2B → Product with k = 1.20 mol-2 dm6 s-1:

Experiment[A] (mol/dm3)[B] (mol/dm3)Initial rate (mol/dm3·s)
10.200.020.0048
20.200.040.0192
30.400.020.0096
  • Experiments 1 and 2: [A] constant, [B] doubled → rate quadruples (0.0048 → 0.0192), so Rate ∝ [B]^2 — second order in B.
  • Experiments 1 and 3: [B] constant, [A] doubled → rate doubles (0.0048 → 0.0096), so Rate ∝ [A]^1 — first order in A.
  • Rate = k[A]^1[B]^2; overall order = 1 + 2 = 3.

Key Points

  • Zero order: rate = k, independent of concentration; unit of k is mol L-1 s-1.
  • To find an order, change one concentration at a time and compare the rates.
  • Rate x2 on doubling = first order; rate x4 on doubling = second order in that reactant.
  • Overall order = sum of the individual orders.
lessons.title: Zeroth Order Reaction and Experimental Determination of the Order of Reaction

mcqs.q: Rate constant k by initial rates is found from:
mcqs.why: Formula: k = Rate / ([A]^m [B]^n), rearranging Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n in terms of k.

mcqs.q: First step to calculate k is to:

mcqs.why: Key points: first find orders from initial-rate data, then write rate equation, rearrange for k and substitute one experiment.

mcqs.why: Doubling [A] doubles rate each time (0.6->1.2->2.4), so first order in A with Rate = k[A].

mcqs.q: k for 2A -> B example (Rate 0.6 at [A] 0.01) is:
mcqs.why: Working: k = Rate/[A] = 0.6 / 0.01 = 60 s-1 for the first-order reaction, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: For a first-order single reactant, k formula simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Key formulae give k = Rate / [A] for the first-order case with a single reactant.

mcqs.q: Which experiment's values are substituted for k?
options: Only the last experiment must be used
Any one experiment's rate and concentrations
mcqs.why: Steps state substitute values from one experiment after rearranging; any one experiment gives the same k.

mcqs.q: Unit of k depends on:
mcqs.why: Key points state the unit of k depends on the overall order of the reaction, e.g. s-1 for first order.

mcqs.q: The two methods to determine k mentioned are:
options: Initial rates method and half-life method
mcqs.why: The lesson states k can be determined by initial rates method and by half-life method; this lesson covers initial rates.

mcqs.q: Rearranging Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n for k gives division by:
mcqs.why: Step ii is rearrange equation in terms of k: k = Rate divided by the concentration terms [A]^m[B]^n.

mcqs.q: Example result k = 60 s-1 is for a:
mcqs.why: The worked example result k = 60 s-1 is for a first-order reaction 2A -> B, consistent with unit s-1.

lessons.notes_html:
The rate constant k can be determined by the initial rates method and by the half-life method. This lesson covers the initial rates method for aA + bB → Product.

Steps

  • i) Write out the rate equation: Rate of reaction = k [A]^m [B]^n.
  • ii) Rearrange the equation in terms of k.
  • iii) Substitute the values from one experiment.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
k = Rate / ([A]^m [B]^n)Rate constant from initial rate and concentrations
k = Rate / [A]First-order case (single reactant)

Worked Example

For 2A → B, the initial rates are 0.6, 1.2 and 2.4 mol/dm3·s at [A] = 0.01, 0.02 and 0.04 mol/dm3 — the reaction is first order in A, so Rate = k[A] and k = 0.6 / 0.01 = 60 s-1.

Key Points

  • First find the orders from the initial-rate data, then write the rate equation.
  • Rearrange for k and substitute any one experiment's rate and concentrations.
  • The unit of k depends on the overall order of the reaction.
  • Example result: k = 60 s-1 for a first-order reaction.
lessons.title: Calculation of Rate Constant by Initial Rates Method

mcqs.q: Half-life t1/2 is the time required to:
options: Convert half of initial reactant concentration into products
mcqs.why: Definition: half-life is time required to convert half of initial reactant concentration [A] into products, denoted t1/2.

mcqs.q: Half-life of N2O5 decomposition at 45C given is:
mcqs.why: Example given: decomposition of N2O5 at 45°C has a half-life of 24 minutes, depending on nature and conditions.

mcqs.q: For first-order reaction, t1/2 formula is:
mcqs.why: Formula: t1/2 = ln2 / k for a first-order reaction, so k = ln2 / half-life = 0.693 / half-life.

mcqs.q: k from half-life is calculated as:
mcqs.why: Formula given: Rate constant k = ln2 / half-life = 0.693 / half-life for a first-order reaction.

mcqs.q: k for half-life 1.5 min in worked example is:
mcqs.why: Working: 1.5 min = 1.5x60 = 90 s; k = 0.693/90 = 7.7x10^-3 s-1, as in the worked example for 2A -> B.

mcqs.q: Shorter half-life means:
mcqs.why: The notes state for first order half-life is inversely proportional to k: shorter half-life means larger k and faster reaction.

mcqs.q: Greater half-life means:
options: Longer overall time needed to complete the reaction
mcqs.why: The notes state greater half-life means longer overall time needed to complete the reaction; half-life depends on nature and conditions.

mcqs.q: Before calculating k in s-1, half-life must be:
mcqs.why: Key points stress convert half-life to seconds before calculating k in s-1, e.g. 1.5 min to 90 s.

mcqs.q: Half-life depends on:
options: Nature of reactants and conditions of reaction
mcqs.why: The notes state half-life depends on nature of reactants and conditions of reaction.

mcqs.q: For first order, half-life is ___ to rate constant:
mcqs.why: The notes state for first-order reaction half-life is inversely proportional to rate constant k.

lessons.notes_html:
The time required to convert half of the initial reactant concentration, [A]°, into products is called the half-life period, denoted by t1/2. For example, the decomposition of N2O5 at 45°C has a half-life of 24 minutes. The half-life depends on the nature of the reactants and the conditions of the reaction: the greater the half-life, the longer the overall time needed to complete the reaction.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life is inversely proportional to the rate constant. A fast reaction with a shorter half-life has a larger rate constant; a slow reaction with a longer half-life has a smaller rate constant.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
t1/2 = ln 2 / kHalf-life of a first-order reaction
Rate constant (k) = ln 2 / half-life = 0.693 / half-lifek from a measured half-life

Worked Example

For 2A → B with half-life 1.5 min: convert to seconds (1.5 x 60 = 90 s), then k = 0.693 / 90 = 7.7 x 10^-3 s-1.

Key Points

  • Half-life t1/2 = time for half the initial reactant to be converted to products.
  • For first order: t1/2 = ln2 / k, so k = 0.693 / t1/2.
  • Shorter half-life means larger k and a faster reaction.
  • Convert the half-life to seconds before calculating k in s-1.
lessons.title: Half-life Method

mcqs.q: Activation energy Ea is:
options: Minimum energy required to form an activated complex
mcqs.why: Definition: minimum amount of energy required for molecules to form an activated complex is activation energy, represented by Ea.

mcqs.q: Units of Ea are:
options: J or kJ per mole (kJ mol-1)
mcqs.why: The notes state Ea units are joules or kilojoules per mole (kJ mol-1).

mcqs.q: Reactants form products by first forming:
options: An activated complex which then decomposes into products
mcqs.why: The notes state reactants first gain energy to form an activated complex, which then decomposes into products.

mcqs.q: Activation energy acts as:
options: An energy barrier (energy hill) between reactants and products
mcqs.why: Ea is an energy barrier between reactants and products; molecules must cross this barrier before they can form products.

mcqs.q: Peak of the energy diagram curve is:
mcqs.why: Reading the diagram: peak of curve is activated complex; Ea is energy difference between reactants and activated complex.

mcqs.q: Ea on the diagram is energy difference between:
mcqs.why: The notes state Ea is energy difference between reactants and activated complex (height from reactants to peak).

mcqs.q: Difference between reactants and products is:
mcqs.why: The notes state difference between reactants and products is heat of reaction dH, distinct from Ea.

mcqs.q: For exothermic reaction, dH is:
options: Negative, products lie lower than reactants
mcqs.why: For exothermic reaction products lie lower than reactants and dH is negative; endothermic has products higher and dH positive.

mcqs.q: For endothermic reaction, dH is:
options: Positive, products lie higher than reactants
mcqs.why: For endothermic reaction products lie higher than reactants and dH is positive, as described for the energy diagram.

mcqs.q: If activation energy is not provided:
options: Reaction will not start and reactants not converted
mcqs.why: The notes state if activation energy is not provided, reaction will not start and reactants will not be converted into products.

lessons.notes_html:
The minimum amount of energy required for the molecules to form an activated complex is called activation energy. It is represented by Ea, and its units are joules or kilojoules per mole (kJ mol-1).

Reactants are not directly converted into products. They first gain energy to form an activated complex, which then decomposes into products. Activation energy is therefore an energy barrier (energy hill) between reactants and products: reactant molecules must cross this barrier before they can form products. It is like carrying a ball to the top of a hill and rolling it down the other side — if the ball does not reach the top, it rolls back. Similarly, if activation energy is not provided, the reaction will not start and the reactants will not be converted into products.

Reading the Energy Diagram

  • The peak of the curve is the activated complex; Ea is the energy difference between the reactants and the activated complex.
  • The difference between reactants and products is the heat of reaction, ΔH.
  • For an exothermic reaction the products lie lower than the reactants and ΔH is negative.
  • For an endothermic reaction the products lie higher than the reactants and ΔH is positive.

Key Points

  • Activation energy Ea = minimum energy needed to form the activated complex.
  • Units of Ea: J/mol or kJ mol-1.
  • Ea is the height of the energy barrier from reactants to the peak of the diagram.
  • Without enough energy to cross the barrier, no reaction takes place.
  • ΔH (products minus reactants) is negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.
lessons.title: Activation Energy

mcqs.q: Boltzmann distribution curve plots:
options: Number of particles (y-axis) against energy level (x-axis)
mcqs.why: The notes state curve plots number of particles (y-axis) against energy level (x-axis) for molecular speeds/energies.

mcqs.q: Boltzmann defined distribution of:
options: Molecular speeds (energies) in a gas at a specific temperature
mcqs.why: Ludwig Boltzmann defined distribution of molecular speeds (energies) in a gas at a specific temperature, shown by the curve.

mcqs.q: As temperature increases, the curve:
options: Spreads out more, peak shifts right and becomes lower
mcqs.why: The notes state as temperature increases curve spreads out more and peak (most probable speed) shifts to higher speeds, to right and lower.

mcqs.q: Area under curve to right of Ea line represents:
options: Fraction of molecules with necessary energy to react on collision
mcqs.why: The notes state area to right of activation energy line represents fraction of molecules with necessary energy to react upon collision.

mcqs.q: For a successful collision, molecules must have kinetic energy:
options: Equal to or greater than activation energy
mcqs.why: The notes state for collision to be successful, colliding molecules must have kinetic energy equal to or greater than activation energy.

mcqs.q: Curve shape depends on:
options: Temperature and type of particles in the system
mcqs.why: The notes state shape depends on temperature and type of particles in system, explaining distribution of energy among particles.

mcqs.q: Raising temperature makes reaction faster because:
options: More molecules exceed Ea as curve flattens and spreads
mcqs.why: Key points: raising temperature flattens and spreads curve, so more molecules exceed Ea — why heating makes reaction faster.

mcqs.q: Peak of Boltzmann curve represents:
mcqs.why: The notes state peak is the most probable speed, which shifts to higher speeds as temperature increases.

mcqs.q: Only molecules that can react on collision are those with:
options: Energy >= Ea (to right of Ea line)
mcqs.why: Key points state only molecules with energy >= Ea (area to right of Ea line) can react on collision.

mcqs.q: Boltzmann curve explains:
options: Distribution of energy among particles in a gas or liquid
mcqs.why: The notes state curve explains distribution of energy among particles in a gas or liquid at a given temperature.

lessons.notes_html:
Ludwig Boltzmann defined the distribution of molecular speeds (energies) in a gas at a specific temperature, shown by the Boltzmann distribution curve. The curve plots the number of particles (y-axis) against the energy level (x-axis). Its shape depends on the temperature and the type of particles in the system, and it explains the distribution of energy among particles in a gas or liquid.

What the Curve Shows

  • The curve helps determine the number of molecules with sufficient energy to initiate a reaction.
  • As temperature increases, the curve spreads out more and its peak — the most probable speed — shifts to higher speeds (to the right, and the peak becomes lower).
  • The area under the curve to the right of the activation energy line represents the fraction of molecules that have the necessary energy to react upon collision.
  • For a collision to be successful, the colliding molecules must have kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.

Key Points

  • The Boltzmann curve shows how molecular energies are distributed at a given temperature.
  • Only molecules with energy ≥ Ea (area to the right of the Ea line) can react on collision.
  • Raising the temperature flattens and spreads the curve, so more molecules exceed Ea.
  • This is why heating a reaction makes it faster.
lessons.title: Boltzmann Distribution Curve

mcqs.q: A catalyst is a substance that:
options: Changes rate without being consumed during reaction
mcqs.why: Definition: substance not consumed during reaction but changes rate is a catalyst; usually increases rate, sometimes decreases it.

mcqs.q: A catalyst that speeds up reaction is:
mcqs.why: The notes state catalyst that speeds up is positive catalyst; one that slows down is negative catalyst or inhibitor.

mcqs.q: A catalyst works by:
options: Decreasing activation energy via new pathway with lower barrier
mcqs.why: How it works: primary function is increase rate by decreasing activation energy, providing new pathway with lower energy barrier.

mcqs.q: With lower barrier, result is:
options: Greater number of molecules can cross it, so rate increases
mcqs.why: The notes state with lower barrier greater number of reactant molecules can cross it, so rate increases at lower temperature.

mcqs.q: A catalyst does NOT:
options: Increase amount of product; only makes product form faster
mcqs.why: The notes state it does not increase amount of product; only makes product form in shorter time and dH remains same.

mcqs.q: Example of catalyst use given is:
options: Water as catalyst in Haber only
mcqs.why: Example given: in laboratory MnO2 speeds up 2KClO3(s) -> 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g); Haber catalyst also mentioned.

mcqs.q: Poisoning of a catalyst is:
options: Deactivation by very small amount of impurity
mcqs.why: Poisoning is deactivation by very small amount of impurity (poison), e.g. As2O3 poisons V2O5 in Contact process.

mcqs.q: A promoter is a substance that:
mcqs.why: The notes define promoter (activator) as substance that increases a catalyst's activity, opposite of a poison.

mcqs.q: Catalysts are most effective when:
options: Finely divided (powder) due to high surface activity
mcqs.why: The notes state catalysts most effective when finely divided (powder) because of high surface activity, e.g. Raney nickel.

mcqs.q: In the body, enzyme pepsin:
options: Accelerates protein digestion in the stomach
mcqs.why: Example given: in the body, enzyme pepsin accelerates protein digestion in the stomach, illustrating biological catalysis.

lessons.notes_html:
A substance that is not consumed during a reaction but changes the rate of a chemical reaction is called a catalyst. Usually a catalyst increases the rate, but in some cases it can decrease it. A catalyst that speeds up a reaction is a positive catalyst; one that slows a reaction down is a negative catalyst or inhibitor. The process of increasing the reaction rate by adding a catalyst is called catalysis.

How a Catalyst Works

  • Its primary function is to increase the rate by decreasing the activation energy: it alters the path or mechanism, providing a new pathway with a lower energy barrier.
  • With the lower barrier, a greater number of reactant molecules can cross it, so the rate increases — at a higher rate and a lower temperature.
  • It does not increase the amount of product; it only makes the product form in a shorter time. ΔH remains the same.
  • Example: in the Haber process, a catalyst makes ammonia production more economical; in the laboratory, MnO2 speeds up 2KClO3(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g).

Poisoning and Promoters

A catalyst can be deactivated by a very small amount of impurity — this is poisoning, and the impurity is a poison (e.g. As2O3 poisons the V2O5 catalyst in the Contact process for H2SO4). A substance that increases a catalyst's activity is a promoter (activator). Catalysts are most effective when finely divided (powder form) because of their high surface activity, e.g. Raney nickel in the hydrogenation of vegetable oil to ghee. In the body, the enzyme pepsin accelerates protein digestion in the stomach.

Key Points

  • A catalyst changes the rate without being consumed; positive catalysts speed up, negative catalysts (inhibitors) slow down.
  • It works by providing a new pathway of lower activation energy; ΔH is unchanged.
  • It does not change the amount of product, only the time taken to form it.
  • Poisons deactivate catalysts; promoters increase their activity.
  • Finely divided catalysts work best because of their large surface area.
lessons.title: Catalysis

mcqs.q: Gibbs free energy formula is:
mcqs.why: Formula: dG° = dH° - T dS° relates Gibbs change to enthalpy change, temperature and entropy change at constant T and P.

mcqs.q: dG° measures:
options: Maximum practical work from reaction at constant T and P
mcqs.why: Definition: dG° measures maximum practical work from reaction at constant temperature and pressure and relates to feasibility.

mcqs.q: If dG° is negative, reaction is:
mcqs.why: Sign rule: dG° negative (<0) means spontaneous, proceeds forward (exergonic), releases energy toward lower energy state.

mcqs.q: If dG° is positive, reaction is:
mcqs.why: Sign rule: dG° positive means non-spontaneous (endergonic), requires energy input, unfavourable under standard conditions.

mcqs.q: If dG° = 0, system is:
options: At equilibrium, neither forward nor reverse at measurable rate
mcqs.why: dG° = 0 means system at equilibrium — dynamic equilibrium between reactants and products, neither direction measurable.

mcqs.q: Exergonic reaction is one with:
mcqs.why: The notes pair exergonic with dG° negative spontaneous forward reaction that releases energy.

mcqs.q: Endergonic reaction is one with:
mcqs.why: The notes pair endergonic with dG° positive non-spontaneous reaction requiring energy input to proceed forward.

mcqs.q: Application of dG° given is:
mcqs.why: Application stated: dG° essential in designing rechargeable batteries — spontaneous during discharge, needs energy during charging.

mcqs.q: dG° relates to:
mcqs.why: The lesson states dG° relates to reaction feasibility — whether reaction is spontaneous (feasible) or non-spontaneous under given conditions.

mcqs.q: Positive dG° reaction under standard conditions occurs only:
options: At higher temperature with energy input
mcqs.why: The notes state positive dG° reaction is unfavourable under standard conditions and occurs only at higher temperature (with input).

lessons.notes_html:
Gibbs free energy change (ΔG°) measures the maximum practical work from a reaction at constant temperature and pressure. It relates to reaction feasibility — whether a reaction is spontaneous (feasible) or non-spontaneous (infeasible) under given conditions.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°Gibbs free energy change from enthalpy change, temperature and entropy change

Sign of ΔG° and Feasibility

  • ΔG° negative (less than 0): the reaction is spontaneous and proceeds in the forward direction (exergonic); it releases energy and the system moves toward a state of lower energy.
  • ΔG° positive: the reaction is non-spontaneous (endergonic) and requires energy input to proceed forward; it is unfavourable under standard conditions and occurs only at higher temperature.
  • ΔG° = 0: the system is at equilibrium — the process neither proceeds forward nor reverses at a measurable rate; this is a dynamic equilibrium between reactants and products.

Application: ΔG° is essential in designing rechargeable batteries — reactions inside the battery must be spontaneous during discharge but need energy during charging.

Key Points

  • ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, at constant temperature and pressure.
  • ΔG° less than 0: spontaneous (feasible), exergonic.
  • ΔG° greater than 0: non-spontaneous (infeasible), endergonic, needs energy input.
  • ΔG° = 0: equilibrium between reactants and products.
lessons.title: Gibbs Free Energy Change and the Feasibility of Reaction

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy of particles is ___ to temperature:
mcqs.why: The notes state kinetic energy of particles is directly proportional to temperature; increasing temperature increases kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: Increasing temperature increases:
options: Rate constant and rate of reaction
mcqs.why: The notes state increasing temperature increases kinetic energy, which increases rate constant and rate — for both endo- and exothermic.

mcqs.q: If rate constant increases at constant concentration, rate:
mcqs.why: The notes state if rate constant increases, reaction rate also increases assuming reactant concentrations remain constant.

mcqs.q: Rate constant generally ___ as temperature rises:
mcqs.why: Key points state rate constant generally increases as temperature rises, leading to faster reaction at constant concentration.

mcqs.q: Rule of thumb near room temperature: rates ___ per 10C rise:
mcqs.why: The notes state usually at room temperature reaction rates double with every 10°C increase in temperature.

mcqs.q: Temperature effect applies to:
mcqs.why: The notes explicitly state effect applies to both endothermic and exothermic reactions when temperature increases.

mcqs.q: Boltzmann explanation for faster rate at higher T is:
options: More molecules have energy >= Ea, so more successful collisions
mcqs.why: The notes agree with Boltzmann: at higher T more molecules have energy >= Ea, so more collisions are successful.

mcqs.q: Higher temperature -> larger k -> at constant concentration:
mcqs.why: Key points chain: higher temperature -> larger rate constant k -> faster reaction at constant concentration.

mcqs.q: Particle kinetic energy increases when:
mcqs.why: By direct proportionality, increasing temperature increases kinetic energy of substance particles, raising rate.

mcqs.q: Assuming concentrations constant, rate follows:
mcqs.why: The notes state rate also increases if k increases assuming reactant concentrations remain constant.

lessons.notes_html:
The kinetic energy of the particles in a substance is directly proportional to its temperature. By increasing the temperature, the kinetic energy of the substance increases, which in turn increases the rate constant and the rate of reaction — for both endothermic and exothermic reactions.

  • If the rate constant increases, the reaction rate also increases, assuming the reactant concentrations remain constant.
  • The rate constant generally increases as the temperature rises.
  • Usually, at room temperature, reaction rates double with every 10°C increase in temperature.

This agrees with the Boltzmann distribution: at a higher temperature more molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

Key Points

  • Particle kinetic energy is directly proportional to temperature.
  • Higher temperature → larger rate constant k → faster reaction, at constant concentration.
  • The effect applies to both endothermic and exothermic reactions.
  • Rule of thumb: the rate roughly doubles for every 10°C rise near room temperature.
lessons.title: The Effect of Temperature Change on the Rate Constant and Rate of a Reaction

mcqs.q: Arrhenius equation is:
mcqs.why: Formula: k = A·e^(-Ea/RT) explains how rate constant changes with temperature T and activation energy Ea.

mcqs.q: In Arrhenius equation, A is:
mcqs.why: Symbols: A = Arrhenius constant or frequency factor; Ea is activation energy, R gas constant, T absolute temperature.

mcqs.q: Value of R given is:
mcqs.why: Symbols list R = universal gas constant = 8.314 J/mol·K, to be used with Kelvin temperatures in the equation.

mcqs.q: T in Arrhenius equation must be in:
mcqs.why: The notes state T = absolute temperature in Kelvin (K); use Kelvin temperatures in the equation.

mcqs.q: Logarithmic form is:
mcqs.why: Formula given: ln k = ln A - (Ea/R)·(1/T) is logarithmic form of Arrhenius equation.

mcqs.q: Two-temperature form ln(k2/k1) is used to:
options: Find k2 at T2 when k1 at T1 is known
mcqs.why: The ln(k2/k1) form finds k2 at T2 when k1 at T1 is known, obtained by subtracting ln k equations at two temperatures.

mcqs.q: Larger Ea makes k:
mcqs.why: Key points state larger Ea makes k smaller and rate more temperature-sensitive in k = A·e^(-Ea/RT).

mcqs.q: As temperature increases, k in Arrhenius equation:
mcqs.why: Key points state k = A·e^(-Ea/RT): k rises quickly as temperature increases, explaining temperature effect on rate.

mcqs.q: Ea units in Arrhenius equation are:
mcqs.why: Symbols list Ea = activation energy (J/mol), consistent with R in J/mol·K and T in Kelvin.

mcqs.q: Two-temperature formula is obtained by:
options: Writing ln k at T1 and T2 and subtracting one from other
mcqs.why: The notes state two-temperature form obtained by writing ln k at T1 and T2 and subtracting one equation from the other.

lessons.notes_html:
The Arrhenius equation explains how the rate constant (k) changes with temperature (T) and activation energy (Ea).

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
k = A·e^(−Ea/RT)Arrhenius equation: rate constant at temperature T
ln k = ln A − (Ea/R)·(1/T)Logarithmic form of the Arrhenius equation
ln (k2/k1) = (Ea/R) x ((T2 − T1)/(T2·T1))Finds k2 at T2 when k1 at T1 is known

Symbols

  • k = rate constant for the reaction.
  • A = Arrhenius constant, or frequency factor.
  • Ea = activation energy (J/mol).
  • R = universal gas constant = 8.314 J/mol·K.
  • T = absolute temperature in Kelvin (K).

The two-temperature form is obtained by writing ln k at T1 and at T2 and subtracting one equation from the other; it is used to determine the rate constant k2 at temperature T2 when k1 is known at T1.

Key Points

  • k = A·e^(−Ea/RT): k rises quickly as temperature increases.
  • A larger Ea makes k smaller and the rate more temperature-sensitive.
  • Use Kelvin temperatures and R = 8.314 J/mol·K in the equation.
  • The ln(k2/k1) form compares the rate constant at two temperatures.
lessons.title: Arrhenius Equation

chapters.title: Unit 7: Acid, Base and Chemical Equilibrium

mcqs.q: Vinegar contains which acid?
mcqs.why: The notes state that vinegar contains acetic acid, CH3COOH, as an everyday example of an acid.

mcqs.q: Citrus fruits contain citric acid and which other acid?
mcqs.why: The notes state that citrus fruits contain citric acid and ascorbic acid, which is Vitamin C.

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is used in making:
mcqs.why: The notes give sodium hydroxide as the substance used in soap making; ammonia is the one used in household cleaners.

mcqs.q: Ammonia (NH3) is commonly used in:
mcqs.why: The notes state that ammonia, NH3, is used in household cleaners, while NaOH is used in soap making.

mcqs.q: An irreversible reaction is one that:
options: Runs forward and backward at the same time
Takes place in only one direction and converts reactants completely into products
Always needs a catalyst to start
mcqs.why: By definition an irreversible reaction proceeds in only one direction to completion, completely converting reactants into products.

mcqs.q: An irreversible reaction is shown by which symbol?
mcqs.why: Irreversible reactions use a single arrow (→), whereas reversible reactions use two half-arrows (⇌).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is given as an irreversible reaction?
mcqs.why: The precipitation of AgCl from AgNO3 and NaCl is listed with a single arrow as an irreversible reaction that goes to completion.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a reversible reaction?
options: Burning of a fuel to completion
mcqs.why: H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI is listed as reversible, shown by ⇌; the other listed reactions use a single arrow and go to completion.

mcqs.q: In the body, haemoglobin carries oxygen by the reversible reaction:
mcqs.why: The notes give Hb + O2 ⇌ HbO2 as the reversible reaction by which haemoglobin carries oxygen in the body.

mcqs.q: Reversible reactions are generally:
options: Incomplete and do not go to full completion
mcqs.why: The key points state that reversible reactions do not go to full completion because products convert back into reactants at the same time.

lessons.notes_html:
Acids, bases and salts are used daily: vinegar contains acetic acid (CH3COOH), citrus fruits contain citric acid and ascorbic acid (Vitamin C), sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is used in soap making and ammonia (NH3) in household cleaners. Chemical equilibrium explains how such reactions balance in nature and industry.

Irreversible Reactions

An irreversible reaction takes place in only one direction and completely converts reactants into products; it is said to proceed to completion and is shown by a single arrow (→). Examples: 2H2O(g) → 2H2(g) + O2(g) (electric discharge); AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq).

Reversible Reactions

A reversible reaction can go in both forward and reverse directions at the same time: reactants form products and products convert back into reactants. Such reactions are generally incomplete and are shown by two half-arrows (⇌). Examples: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g); N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g); 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g). In the body, haemoglobin carries oxygen by a reversible reaction: Hb + O2 ⇌ HbO2.

Key Points

  • Irreversible reactions go to completion in one direction only and use a single arrow (→).
  • Reversible reactions run forward and backward together and use ⇌.
  • Reversible reactions do not go to full completion.
  • Examples of reversible reactions: formation of HI, NH3 and SO3.
lessons.title: Reversible and Irreversible Reactions

mcqs.q: Chemical equilibrium is the state in which:
options: The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal
mcqs.why: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations of reactants and products stay constant over time.

mcqs.q: Equilibrium is called dynamic because:
options: Both reactions keep occurring at the same rate, with no overall macroscopic change
The concentrations keep rising and falling visibly
The system is open to the surroundings
mcqs.why: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at the molecular level at the same rate, so there is no overall change at the macroscopic level.

mcqs.q: In the N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 system, N2O4 is colourless while NO2 is:
mcqs.why: The notes describe colourless N2O4 forming dark brown NO2, so the colour of the mixture deepens as NO2 forms.

mcqs.q: As N2O4 is used up in the forward reaction, the forward rate:
options: Decreases as the N2O4 concentration falls
mcqs.why: The notes state that as the N2O4 concentration falls, the rate of the forward reaction decreases towards the reverse rate.

mcqs.q: As NO2 builds up in the flask, the reverse rate:
options: Increases until it equals the forward rate
mcqs.why: As NO2 builds up, the reverse rate increases; when the two rates become equal, equilibrium is reached and concentrations become constant.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products:
options: Remain constant, though not necessarily equal
Must be exactly equal to each other
mcqs.why: A key point states that at equilibrium concentrations remain constant, but they are not necessarily equal to each other.

mcqs.q: Once equilibrium is established, it lasts forever if:
mcqs.why: The notes state that once established, equilibrium lasts forever if the conditions of the system are not changed.

mcqs.q: The N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 system shows that equilibrium has been reached by:
mcqs.why: When the rates become equal the NO2 concentration stops changing, so the brown colour of the mixture stays steady.

mcqs.q: Which statement about equilibrium is correct?
options: Reactions stop at the molecular level
Reactions continue at the molecular level with no net change
mcqs.why: Equilibrium is dynamic: reactions continue at the molecular level, but equal forward and reverse rates give no net macroscopic change.

mcqs.q: In N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g), one mole of N2O4 produces how many moles of NO2?
mcqs.why: The balanced equation N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g) shows the coefficient of NO2 is 2, so one mole of N2O4 gives two moles of NO2.

lessons.notes_html:
Chemical equilibrium is the state of balance where the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant over time. It is a dynamic condition because both reactions keep occurring at the same rate, so there is no overall change at the macroscopic level.

Example: N2O4 and NO2

N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g). Colourless N2O4 placed in a flask forms dark brown NO2, so the colour deepens. As N2O4 concentration falls, the forward rate decreases; as NO2 builds up, the reverse rate increases. When the two rates become equal, equilibrium is reached and concentrations become constant. Once established, equilibrium lasts forever if conditions are not changed.

Key Points

  • At equilibrium, rate of forward reaction = rate of reverse reaction.
  • Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, not necessarily equal.
  • Equilibrium is dynamic: reactions continue at the molecular level.
  • The N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 system shows equilibrium by a steady brown colour.
lessons.title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

mcqs.q: A necessary condition for equilibrium is that the reaction takes place in:
options: A sealed (closed) system so nothing escapes
mcqs.why: Equilibrium requires a closed system so that no reactant or product escapes and both reactions can balance each other.

mcqs.q: Which condition must remain constant for equilibrium, especially for gases, along with temperature?
mcqs.why: The necessary conditions list constant temperature and constant pressure, with pressure being especially important for gaseous systems.

mcqs.q: Equilibrium is recognised when concentrations of reactants and products:
mcqs.why: Constant concentrations over time, together with stable measurable properties, are the signs by which equilibrium is recognised.

mcqs.q: Which measurable properties become stable at equilibrium?
options: Only the mass of the flask
Only the shape of the container
mcqs.why: The notes list pressure, colour and density as measurable properties that become stable once equilibrium is reached.

mcqs.q: A catalyst at equilibrium:
options: Does not affect the equilibrium concentrations
mcqs.why: The notes state that catalysts do not affect equilibrium concentrations; equilibrium is dynamic and can be approached from either side.

mcqs.q: A homogeneous equilibrium is one in which:
options: Reactants and products are in different physical states
Reactants and products are in the same physical state
mcqs.why: In homogeneous equilibrium all species are in the same state, for example N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) where everything is gaseous.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a homogeneous equilibrium?
mcqs.why: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 has all species in the gaseous state, so it is homogeneous; the others mix solids with gases or aqueous species.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a heterogeneous equilibrium?
mcqs.why: CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g) involves solids and a gas in different physical states, which makes the equilibrium heterogeneous.

mcqs.q: Equilibrium can be approached:
mcqs.why: One characteristic of equilibrium is that it can be approached from either side, starting with reactants or with products.

mcqs.q: Besides a closed system and constant temperature and pressure, equilibrium also requires:
mcqs.why: The necessary conditions include giving sufficient time for the forward and reverse rates to become equal and equilibrium to be reached.

lessons.notes_html:
Equilibrium needs fixed conditions, clear signs by which it can be recognised, and it is of two types.

Necessary Conditions for Equilibrium

  • The reaction must take place in a sealed (closed) system so nothing escapes.
  • Temperature must remain constant.
  • Pressure should stay constant, especially for gases.
  • Both forward and reverse reactions must be possible and occur simultaneously.
  • Sufficient time must be given to reach equilibrium.

Recognition of Equilibrium

  • Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant over time.
  • Measurable properties such as pressure, colour or density become stable.
  • Rate of forward reaction exactly equals rate of reverse reaction.
  • No net macroscopic change is observed, although molecular changes continue.

Other characteristics: equilibrium is dynamic, is achieved in a closed system, can be approached from either side, and catalysts do not affect equilibrium concentrations.

Types of Chemical Equilibria

TypeMeaning and Example
HomogeneousReactants and products in the same physical state: N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g); N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)
HeterogeneousReactants and products in different physical states: CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g); 2Fe(s) + 3H2O(g) ⇌ Fe2O3(s) + 3H2(g)

Key Points

  • Equilibrium requires a closed system, constant temperature and pressure, and enough time.
  • It is recognised by constant concentrations and stable colour, pressure or density.
  • Homogeneous equilibrium: all species in the same state.
  • Heterogeneous equilibrium: species in different states.
  • A catalyst does not change equilibrium concentrations.
lessons.title: Conditions for Equilibrium and Its Recognition

mcqs.q: Microscopic events in a reaction are processes that occur at:
options: The atomic or molecular level and cannot be seen with the naked eye
The level of the whole laboratory
The level of grams and litres only
