mcqs.why: Microscopic events are atomic or molecular processes such as bond breaking and forming, invisible to the naked eye.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a microscopic event?
options: A colour change in a beaker
Breaking and forming of chemical bonds
A temperature change read on a thermometer
mcqs.why: Breaking and forming of bonds, rearranging atoms and molecular collisions are microscopic events; bubbles and colour changes are macroscopic.

mcqs.q: Microscopic events are studied with instruments such as:
mcqs.why: The notes state that microscopic events are studied with electron microscopes and spectrometers and described in nm, pm or atomic mass units.

mcqs.q: Macroscopic events are:
options: Visible, measurable results of many microscopic interactions
Changes in molecular energy states only
mcqs.why: Macroscopic events are the visible bulk results, such as bubbles, colour change and temperature change, arising from many microscopic interactions.

mcqs.q: Macroscopic quantities are measured in units such as:
mcqs.why: The notes give grams, litres, degrees Celsius and atmospheres as the units used for macroscopic measurements with balances, thermometers and gauges.

mcqs.q: Heating the system N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 causes the mixture to turn deeper brown because:
options: N2O4 molecules become brown when heated
More NO2 molecules form as bond breaking in N2O4 increases
mcqs.why: Heating increases molecular vibrations and bond breaking in N2O4 (microscopic), forming more brown NO2, so the colour deepens (macroscopic).

mcqs.q: When an equilibrium is disturbed, the visible macroscopic changes are caused by:
options: Continuous microscopic events altering collision frequency and energy and the relative forward and reverse rates
mcqs.why: Changes in concentration, temperature or pressure alter the frequency and energy of molecular collisions, adjusting the relative rates until a new equilibrium is reached.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a macroscopic event?
options: Pressure shifts in a closed system
mcqs.why: Pressure shifts, along with bubbles, colour and temperature changes and mass or volume variation, are listed as macroscopic events.

mcqs.q: Molecular collisions with energy transfer belong to which category?
mcqs.why: Molecular collisions with energy transfer happen at the molecular level and cannot be seen, so they are microscopic events.

mcqs.q: A change in colour, pressure or concentration seen when equilibrium shifts is a change at the:
options: Macroscopic level, caused by microscopic events
mcqs.why: The key points state that macroscopic shifts in equilibrium are visible bulk changes caused by underlying microscopic events.

lessons.notes_html:
Events in a reaction can be viewed at two levels: the invisible molecular level and the visible bulk level.

Microscopic Events

Microscopic events are processes at the atomic or molecular level that cannot be seen with the naked eye: breaking and forming of chemical bonds, rearranging of atoms, molecular collisions with energy transfer, and changes in molecular energy states. They are studied with instruments like electron microscopes and spectrometers and described in nanometres, picometres or atomic mass units.

Macroscopic Events

Macroscopic events are the visible, measurable results of many microscopic interactions: formation of gas bubbles, colour change, temperature change, mass or volume variation and pressure shifts in a closed system. They are measured with balances, thermometers and pressure gauges in grams, litres, °C and atmospheres.

Microscopic Events and Macroscopic Shifts in Equilibrium

When conditions of a system at equilibrium are disturbed, macroscopic properties such as colour, pressure or concentration change until a new equilibrium is reached. These visible changes are caused by continuous microscopic events: changes in concentration, temperature or pressure alter the frequency and energy of molecular collisions and adjust the relative rates of forward and reverse reactions. Example: heating N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 increases molecular vibrations and bond breaking in N2O4, forming more NO2 molecules (microscopic), so the gas mixture turns deeper brown (macroscopic).

Key Points

  • Microscopic events happen at atomic/molecular level and are invisible.
  • Macroscopic events are visible and measurable bulk changes.
  • Macroscopic shifts in equilibrium are caused by microscopic events.
  • Heating N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 deepens the brown colour as more NO2 forms.
lessons.title: Microscopic and Macroscopic Events in a Reaction

mcqs.q: The law of mass action was given by Guldberg and Waage in:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the law of mass action was given by Guldberg and Waage in 1864.

mcqs.q: The law of mass action states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to:
options: The product of the active masses of the reactants
The sum of the masses of the products
mcqs.why: By the law of mass action, rate is proportional to the product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants.

mcqs.q: Active mass means the molar concentration, expressed in:
mcqs.why: The notes define active mass as molar concentration in mol/dm3, used in expressions such as Rf = Kf[A][B].

mcqs.q: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant Kc is:
mcqs.why: Kc is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium, Kc is obtained from the forward and reverse rate constants as:
mcqs.why: At equilibrium Rf = Rr, so Kf[A][B] = Kr[C][D], giving Kc = Kf/Kr = [C][D]/[A][B].

mcqs.q: The value of Kc depends on:
mcqs.why: Kc is independent of initial concentrations and is constant at a fixed temperature; its value changes only when temperature changes.

mcqs.q: A higher value of Kc means that at equilibrium there are:
mcqs.why: The characteristics state that a higher Kc value means more products than reactants at equilibrium, and vice versa for a lower value.

mcqs.q: Which species do NOT appear in the Kc expression?
options: Pure solids, pure liquids and solvents
mcqs.why: Concentrations of pure solids, pure liquids and solvents stay constant and are left out of the equilibrium constant expression.

mcqs.q: For CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2, Kc has no unit because:
options: The moles of reactants and products are equal
mcqs.why: The notes state that when the moles of reactants and products are equal, Kc has no unit, as in CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, the unit of Kc given in the notes is:
mcqs.why: With unequal moles (4 reactant moles, 2 product moles), Kc has units, and the notes give mol^-2 dm^+6 for ammonia synthesis.

lessons.notes_html:
The law of mass action was given by Guldberg and Waage in 1864. It states: the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of the active masses of the reactants. Active mass means molar concentration, in mol/dm3. For A + B ⇌ C + D: Rf = Kf[A][B] and Rr = Kr[C][D]. At equilibrium Rf = Rr, so Kf/Kr = [C][D]/[A][B] = Kc, the equilibrium constant: the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium. For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.

Characteristics of the Equilibrium Constant

  • It is independent of the initial concentrations at a given temperature.
  • Its value changes with temperature and is constant at fixed temperature.
  • A higher value means more products than reactants at equilibrium, and vice versa.
  • Concentrations of pure solids, pure liquids and solvents do not appear in the expression.
  • Units: if moles of reactants and products are equal, Kc has no unit (e.g. CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2). If unequal, Kc has units; for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc unit is mol^-2 dm^+6.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^bEquilibrium constant in terms of concentration
Kp = (PC)^c(PD)^d / (PA)^a(PB)^bIn terms of partial pressures (gases)
Kx = (XC)^c(XD)^d / (XA)^a(XB)^bIn terms of mole fractions
Kn = (nC)^c(nD)^d / (nA)^a(nB)^bIn terms of number of moles

Key Points

  • Law of mass action: rate ∝ product of active masses of reactants.
  • Kc = Kf/Kr = products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
  • Kc depends only on temperature, not on initial concentrations.
  • Pure solids and liquids are left out of the Kc expression.
  • For gases, Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations.
lessons.title: Law of Mass Action and Expression for Equilibrium Constant

mcqs.q: The relation between Kp and Kc is:
mcqs.why: Substituting P = CRT into the Kp expression gives Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is gaseous product moles minus gaseous reactant moles.

mcqs.q: In the relation Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, Δn is defined as:
options: Moles of liquids minus moles of solids
Sum of moles of gaseous products minus sum of moles of gaseous reactants
Moles of reactants minus moles of products of all kinds
mcqs.why: Δn counts only gaseous moles: (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants), as used in both book examples.

mcqs.q: When Δn = 0, the relation between Kp and Kc is:
mcqs.why: When Δn = 0, (RT)^0 = 1, so Kp = Kc(RT)^0 = Kc, meaning the two constants are equal.

mcqs.q: For N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g), Δn is:
mcqs.why: Working: Δn = gaseous product moles − gaseous reactant moles = 2 − 1 = 1, so Kp = Kc(RT)^1 = Kc(RT), as in Book Example 7.1(a).

mcqs.q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), Δn is:
mcqs.why: Working: Δn = 2 (NH3) − [1 (N2) + 3 (H2)] = 2 − 4 = −2, so Kp = Kc(RT)^-2, as in Book Example 7.1(b).

mcqs.q: When Δn is negative, Kp compared with Kc is:
mcqs.why: The notes state that a negative Δn gives Kp less than Kc, while a positive Δn gives Kp greater than Kc.

mcqs.q: The partial pressure of a gas in terms of its concentration is given by:
mcqs.why: From PV = nRT, P = (n/V)RT = CRT, so each partial pressure equals its molar concentration multiplied by RT.

mcqs.q: For N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g), the Kc expression is:
mcqs.why: Book Example 7.1(a) gives Kc = [NO2]^2/[N2O4]: products over reactants, with NO2 raised to its coefficient 2.

mcqs.q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), the Kc expression is:
mcqs.why: Book Example 7.1(b) gives Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3), each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient.

mcqs.q: In counting Δn for Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, which moles are counted?
mcqs.why: A key point states that only gaseous moles are counted in Δn, because the relation comes from partial pressures of gases.

lessons.notes_html:
The same equilibrium can be expressed through concentration (Kc), partial pressure (Kp), mole fraction (Kx) or number of moles (Kn); all are interconnected at the same temperature.

Relationship between Kc and Kp

From PV = nRT, P = (n/V)RT = CRT, so each partial pressure equals concentration × RT. Substituting in the Kp expression gives Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = (sum of moles of gaseous products) − (sum of moles of gaseous reactants).

  • When Δn = 0: (RT)^0 = 1, so Kp = Kc.
  • When Δn is greater than 0: Kp is greater than Kc.
  • When Δn is less than 0: Kp is less than Kc.

Book Example 7.1: (a) N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g): Kc = [NO2]^2/[N2O4], Δn = 1, so Kp = Kc(RT). (b) N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g): Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3), Δn = 2 − 4 = −2, so Kp = Kc(RT)^-2.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Kp = Kc(RT)^ΔnRelates Kp and Kc; Δn = gaseous product moles − gaseous reactant moles
P = CRTPartial pressure from concentration

Key Points

  • Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where R is the gas constant and T is absolute temperature.
  • Δn = 0 gives Kp = Kc.
  • Positive Δn gives Kp greater than Kc; negative Δn gives Kp less than Kc.
  • Only gaseous moles are counted in Δn.
lessons.title: Relationship Between Different Equilibrium Constants (Kc, Kp, Kx, and Kn)

mcqs.q: According to Dalton's law, the partial pressure of a gas is:
options: Its mole fraction divided by the total pressure
Its mole fraction times the total pressure, Pi = Xi x PT
Its number of moles times the total volume
Always equal to the total pressure
mcqs.why: Dalton's law as given in the notes: Pi = Xi × PT, the partial pressure equals the mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.

mcqs.q: The mole fraction of a gas is calculated as:
mcqs.why: The notes define the mole fraction as Xi = ni/nT, the moles of that gas divided by the total number of moles.

mcqs.q: The relation between Kp and Kx is:
mcqs.why: Substituting PA = XA.PT and so on into the Kp expression gives Kp = Kx(PT)^Δn, as listed in the key formulae.

mcqs.q: The relation between Kp and Kn is:
mcqs.why: Substituting Xi = ni/nT in the partial pressures gives Kp = Kn(PT/nT)^Δn, the formula given in the notes for Kp and Kn.

mcqs.q: When Δn = 0, the four equilibrium constants are related as:
options: Kc is the largest of them
Only Kp and Kc are equal
mcqs.why: When the moles of reactants and products are equal (Δn = 0), every ( )^Δn factor becomes 1, so Kc = Kp = Kx = Kn.

mcqs.q: For one mole of gas, PT = RT/V, so Kp can also be written in terms of Kx as:
mcqs.why: The notes give Kp = Kx(RT/V)^Δn for one mole of gas, obtained by putting PT = RT/V into Kp = Kx(PT)^Δn.

mcqs.q: Kc, Kp, Kx and Kn all describe:
options: The same equilibrium at the same temperature
mcqs.why: A key point states that all four constants describe the same equilibrium at the same temperature, expressed in different quantities.

mcqs.q: If a gas has ni = 2 mol in a mixture with nT = 10 mol, its mole fraction Xi is:
mcqs.why: Working: Xi = ni/nT = 2 mol / 10 mol = 0.2. Mole fraction is a ratio of moles, so it has no unit.

mcqs.q: A gas with mole fraction 0.25 in a mixture at total pressure 4 atm has a partial pressure of:
mcqs.why: Working: Pi = Xi × PT = 0.25 × 4 atm = 1 atm, using Dalton's law as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Kx is the equilibrium constant expressed in terms of:
mcqs.why: The notes define Kx through mole fractions: Kx = (XC)^c(XD)^d / (XA)^a(XB)^b for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD.

lessons.notes_html:
By Dalton's law, the partial pressure of a gas equals its mole fraction times the total pressure: Pi = Xi × PT, and the mole fraction is Xi = ni/nT.

Relationship between Kp and Kx

Substituting PA = XA.PT etc. into the Kp expression gives Kp = Kx(PT)^Δn. For one mole of gas, PT = RT/V, so Kp = Kx(RT/V)^Δn.

Relationship between Kp and Kn

Substituting Xi = ni/nT in the partial pressures gives Kp = Kn(PT/nT)^Δn, and also Kp = Kx(RT/(V.nT))^Δn in the book's combined form. When the number of moles of reactants and products are equal (Δn = 0), all the equilibrium constants have the same value: Kc = Kp = Kx = Kn.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Pi = Xi × PTPartial pressure from mole fraction (Dalton's law)
Xi = ni/nTMole fraction of a gas
Kp = Kx(PT)^ΔnRelates Kp and Kx
Kp = Kn(PT/nT)^ΔnRelates Kp and Kn

Key Points

  • Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
  • Kp = Kx(PT)^Δn and Kp = Kn(PT/nT)^Δn.
  • When Δn = 0, Kc = Kp = Kx = Kn.
  • All four constants describe the same equilibrium at the same temperature.
lessons.title: Relationship between Kp and Kx, and Kp and Kn

mcqs.q: A high value of Kc indicates that:
options: Products are favoured and the reaction proceeds far
mcqs.why: Under extent of reaction, the notes state that a high Kc means products are favoured at equilibrium, while a low Kc shows reactants dominate.

mcqs.q: Predicting the direction of a reaction is done by comparing:
options: The reaction quotient Q with Kc
mcqs.why: The applications state that comparing the reaction quotient Q with Kc tells whether the reaction will move forward or reverse until equilibrium is achieved.

mcqs.q: Once Kc is known, it can be used to calculate:
options: Unknown equilibrium concentrations using algebraic relations
The boiling point of the mixture
mcqs.why: The notes list calculating equilibrium concentrations as an application: with Kc known, unknown equilibrium concentrations are found algebraically.

mcqs.q: In industry, Kc guides the choice of conditions to increase product output in:
mcqs.why: Industrial optimisation with Kc is applied in the Haber and Contact processes to choose temperature, pressure and concentration for more product.

mcqs.q: A higher Kc means the products are:
options: More stable, while a lower Kc means reactants are more stable
mcqs.why: Under relative stability, a higher Kc means products are more stable and a lower Kc means reactants are more stable under the given conditions.

mcqs.q: Equilibrium constants help explain which biological and environmental phenomena?
options: Buffer action, solubility equilibria and how common ions affect pH and solubility
mcqs.why: The notes state that equilibrium constants explain buffer action, solubility equilibria and the effect of common ions on pH and solubility.

mcqs.q: A low Kc shows that at equilibrium:
mcqs.why: For extent of reaction, a low Kc shows reactants dominate at equilibrium, the opposite of a high Kc favouring products.

mcqs.q: Comparing Q with Kc tells us the reaction will move:
options: Forward or reverse until equilibrium is achieved
mcqs.why: The direction application states that the Q-versus-Kc comparison predicts whether the reaction moves forward or in reverse until equilibrium is achieved.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT an application of the equilibrium constant listed in the notes?
options: Choosing a suitable catalyst for a reaction
mcqs.why: The listed applications are extent, direction, equilibrium concentrations, industrial optimisation, stability and biological systems; choosing a catalyst is not among them.

mcqs.q: The equilibrium constant is described in the lesson as useful in controlling reactions in:
options: The laboratory, industry, biology and the environment
mcqs.why: The lesson introduction states that Kc is used to judge and control reactions in the laboratory, industry, biology and the environment.

lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant is far more than a number; it is used to judge and control reactions in the laboratory, industry, biology and the environment.

  • Extent of reaction: Kc indicates how far a reaction proceeds. A high Kc means products are favoured at equilibrium; a low Kc shows reactants dominate.
  • Predicting direction: comparing the reaction quotient (Q) with Kc tells whether the reaction will move forward or reverse until equilibrium is achieved.
  • Calculating equilibrium concentrations: once Kc is known, unknown equilibrium concentrations can be found using algebraic relations.
  • Industrial optimisation: in the Haber and Contact processes, Kc guides the choice of temperature, pressure and concentration to increase product output.
  • Relative stability: a higher Kc means products are more stable; a lower Kc means reactants are more stable under the given conditions.
  • Biological and environmental systems: equilibrium constants explain buffer action, solubility equilibria and how common ions affect pH and solubility.

Key Points

  • Large Kc = products favoured; small Kc = reactants favoured.
  • Comparing Q with Kc predicts the direction of reaction.
  • Kc is used to calculate unknown equilibrium concentrations.
  • Industry uses Kc to optimise yields in the Haber and Contact processes.
lessons.title: Applications of the Equilibrium Constant

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 at 500°C with [N2] = 0.030M, [H2] = 0.037M and [NH3] = 0.016M, Kc is:
The first step in any Kc calculation is to:
options: Write the Kc expression first, then substitute equilibrium values
mcqs.why: A key point states: write the Kc expression first, then substitute the equilibrium values; initial concentrations are never used in Kc.

mcqs.q: To find an unknown equilibrium concentration from Kc, you should:
options: Add Kc to the known concentrations
Rearrange the Kc expression and solve for the unknown
mcqs.why: The key points state that an unknown concentration is found by rearranging the Kc expression, e.g. [SO3]^2 = Kc[SO2]^2[O2], and then solving.

mcqs.q: For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), the Kc expression is:
mcqs.why: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient: Kc = [SO3]^2/([SO2]^2[O2]), the expression used in Book Example 7.3.

mcqs.q: In Kc calculations, the concentrations substituted must be:
mcqs.why: A key point stresses: always use equilibrium, not initial, concentrations in Kc, because Kc is defined at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: For the reaction in Book Example 7.2, the equilibrium concentration of NH3 used was:
mcqs.why: Book Example 7.2 uses [NH3] = 0.016M, [N2] = 0.030M and [H2] = 0.037M at 500°C to obtain Kc = 1.68 x 10^2.

mcqs.q: If Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3) and all concentrations are doubled in the expression, the power applied to [H2] is:
mcqs.why: Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation; H2 has coefficient 3 in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.

mcqs.q: Rearranging Kc = [SO3]^2/([SO2]^2[O2]) to find [SO3] gives:
mcqs.why: Working: multiply both sides by [SO2]^2[O2] to get [SO3]^2 = Kc[SO2]^2[O2], then take the square root: [SO3] = √(Kc[SO2]^2[O2]).

mcqs.q: The equilibrium constant can be calculated from equilibrium values of concentration or of:
mcqs.why: The lesson states Kc is calculated from concentration values at equilibrium, and Kp likewise from partial pressure values at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: In Book Example 7.2, the temperature at which the ammonia equilibrium concentrations were measured was:
mcqs.why: Book Example 7.2 gives the concentrations [N2] = 0.030M, [H2] = 0.037M, [NH3] = 0.016M at 500°C, yielding Kc = 168.46.

lessons.notes_html:
The equilibrium constant is calculated from the concentration or partial pressure values at equilibrium. When Kc is known, an unknown equilibrium concentration or partial pressure can be determined from it.

Book Example 7.2: Finding Kc

For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) at 500°C, equilibrium concentrations are [N2] = 0.030M, [H2] = 0.037M and [NH3] = 0.016M. Step 1: write Kc = [NH3]^2/([N2][H2]^3). Step 2: substitute values: Kc = (0.016)^2/((0.030)(0.037)^3) = 168.46 = 1.68 x 10^2.

Book Example 7.3: Finding an Unknown Concentration

For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), [SO2] = 0.59M, [O2] = 0.45M and Kc = 4.32. Step 1: Kc = [SO3]^2/([SO2]^2[O2]), so [SO3]^2 = Kc[SO2]^2[O2]. Step 2: [SO3]^2 = (4.32)(0.59)^2(0.45) = 0.0677. Step 3: [SO3] = √0.0677 = 0.26M.

Key Points

  • Write the Kc expression first, then substitute equilibrium values.
  • To find Kc, use the known equilibrium concentrations directly.
  • To find an unknown concentration, rearrange the Kc expression and solve.
  • Always use equilibrium, not initial, concentrations in Kc.
lessons.title: Calculation or Determination of Equilibrium Constant

mcqs.q: Le Chatelier's principle states that if a system in equilibrium is disturbed, it will:
mcqs.why: Le Chatelier's principle: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to oppose the applied change; it applies to all dynamic equilibria, physical and chemical.

mcqs.q: Le Chatelier lived from:
mcqs.why: The notes give Henri Louis Le Chatelier's dates as 1850–1936, the scientist after whom the principle is named.

mcqs.q: For A + B ⇌ C + D, increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts the equilibrium:
options: To the left, forming more reactants
To the right, forming more products
mcqs.why: Increasing a reactant shifts equilibrium to the right (more products); increasing a product shifts it left, as stated for A + B ⇌ C + D.

mcqs.q: In N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, removing N2 or H2 from the system causes:
options: NH3 to decompose as equilibrium shifts left
mcqs.why: Decreasing a reactant shifts equilibrium to the left, so ammonia decomposes to replace the removed N2 or H2.

mcqs.q: Changing the concentration of a reactant or product changes the value of Kc:
options: False, concentration changes do not change Kc
Only if a catalyst is present
mcqs.why: A key point states that concentration changes shift the position but do not change the value of Kc, which depends only on temperature.

mcqs.q: Increasing the pressure (decreasing the volume) at constant temperature shifts equilibrium towards:
options: The side with more moles of gas
The side with fewer moles of gas
The solid side in all cases
mcqs.why: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles; lower pressure favours the side with more gas moles, at constant temperature.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, increasing the pressure:
options: Shifts equilibrium left and NH3 decreases
Has no effect on the position
Shifts equilibrium right and NH3 increases, with Kc unchanged
mcqs.why: Reactants have 4 gas moles and products 2, so increased pressure shifts right, NH3 increases, and Kc stays unchanged.

mcqs.q: For PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium:
options: To the left, because products have more gas moles
mcqs.why: Here n(reactants) is less than n(products) (1 against 2 gas moles), so increased pressure shifts the equilibrium to the left.

mcqs.q: For N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO, a change in pressure has what effect?
options: No effect on the position or on Kc, because gas moles are equal on both sides
It changes Kc but not the position
mcqs.why: With 2 gas moles on each side, the notes state pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium or on Kc.

mcqs.q: In CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), only which species responds to a pressure change?
options: The gas CO2, because solids are almost incompressible
mcqs.why: Solids and liquids are almost incompressible, so in this equilibrium only the gaseous CO2 responds to a change in pressure.

lessons.notes_html:
Le Chatelier's principle (Henri Louis Le Chatelier, 1850–1936) states: if a system in equilibrium is disturbed by a change, it will shift to counteract (oppose) that effect. It applies to all dynamic equilibria, physical and chemical. Note: strength and concentration are different — a dilute HCl solution is still a strong acid, while a concentrated acetic acid solution is still weak.

The Effect of Concentration Change

For A + B ⇌ C + D: increasing a reactant shifts equilibrium to the right (more products); increasing a product shifts it to the left; decreasing a reactant shifts it to the left; decreasing a product shifts it to the right. Example: in N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, adding N2 or H2 produces more NH3, while removing them decomposes NH3. Concentration changes do not change the value of Kc.

Effect of Pressure or Volume Change

Increasing pressure (decreasing volume) at constant temperature shifts the reaction towards the side with fewer moles of gas; decreasing pressure shifts it towards more moles of gas. If n(reactants) is greater than n(products), e.g. N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, increased pressure shifts right and NH3 increases, Kc unchanged. If n(reactants) is less than n(products), e.g. PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2, increased pressure shifts left. If moles are equal on both sides, e.g. N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO, pressure has no effect on position or Kc. Solids and liquids are almost incompressible, so in CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g) only the gas CO2 responds to pressure change.

Key Points

  • Le Chatelier: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.
  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts equilibrium forward.
  • Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles.
  • Equal gas moles on both sides: pressure change has no effect.
  • Concentration and pressure changes do not change Kc.
lessons.title: Le Chatelier's Principle

mcqs.q: The equilibrium constant Kc changes only when which factor changes?
mcqs.why: The lesson states that concentration, pressure and volume alter only the position, while Kc itself changes only with temperature.

mcqs.q: Raising the temperature favours which direction of a reaction?
mcqs.why: A key point states that raising temperature favours the endothermic direction and lowering temperature favours the exothermic direction.

mcqs.q: For N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), ΔH = +90.25 kJ/mol, raising the temperature:
options: Favours NO formation, the endothermic forward reaction
mcqs.why: The forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH positive), so raising temperature favours NO formation; a temperature above 3000°C is used.

mcqs.q: For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH = −46.11 kJ/mol, ammonia formation is favoured by:
mcqs.why: Ammonia synthesis is exothermic in the forward direction, so lowering temperature favours NH3; raising temperature shifts equilibrium left and decomposes NH3.

mcqs.q: A reaction that is exothermic in the forward direction is, in the reverse direction:
mcqs.why: The notes state that a reaction exothermic in the forward direction is endothermic in the reverse direction, and vice versa.

mcqs.q: A catalyst is a substance that:
options: Is not consumed but changes the rate of reaction
mcqs.why: By definition a catalyst is not consumed in the reaction but changes its rate; the reaction in its presence is called catalysis.

mcqs.q: A catalyst affects the equilibrium position and Kc by:
options: Changing neither the position nor Kc, only speeding up both reactions equally
mcqs.why: A catalyst lowers the activation energy and speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner with position and Kc unchanged.

mcqs.q: In ammonia manufacture, the catalyst mentioned is:
mcqs.why: The example states that iron mixed with aluminium oxide as catalyst in ammonia manufacture gives more NH3 in a shorter time.

mcqs.q: The temperature above which NO formation from N2 and O2 is carried out is:
mcqs.why: For the endothermic formation of NO (ΔH = +90.25 kJ/mol), the notes state a temperature above 3000°C is used to favour NO.

mcqs.q: Lowering the temperature favours:
options: The exothermic direction, e.g. NH3 synthesis
mcqs.why: A key point gives lowering temperature favouring the exothermic direction, with ammonia synthesis as the example.

lessons.notes_html:
Concentration, pressure and volume changes alter only the equilibrium position. The equilibrium constant itself changes only when temperature changes.

Effect of Temperature Change

Exothermic reactions are less favoured by an increase in temperature, while endothermic reactions are more favoured. Example 1 (endothermic forward): N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), ΔH = +90.25 kJ.mol^-1 — raising temperature favours NO formation (a temperature above 3000°C is used), lowering temperature favours the reverse reaction. Example 2 (exothermic forward): N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −46.11 kJ.mol^-1 — ammonia formation is favoured by a decrease in temperature; raising temperature shifts equilibrium left and decomposes NH3. A reaction exothermic in the forward direction is endothermic in the reverse direction.

The Effect of Catalyst

A catalyst is a substance that is not consumed in a reaction but changes its rate; the reaction in its presence is called catalysis. A catalyst does not affect the equilibrium position or the value of Kc. It lowers the activation energy and speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner. Example: iron mixed with aluminium oxide as catalyst in ammonia manufacture gives more NH3 in a shorter time.

Key Points

  • Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of Kc.
  • Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction.
  • Lowering temperature favours the exothermic direction, e.g. NH3 synthesis.
  • A catalyst changes neither equilibrium position nor Kc.
  • A catalyst shortens the time needed to reach equilibrium.
lessons.title: Effect of Temperature and Catalyst on Equilibrium

mcqs.q: The Contact Process is the large-scale manufacture of:
mcqs.why: The Contact Process manufactures sulphuric acid by the catalytic oxidation of sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide.

mcqs.q: The key reaction of the Contact Process is:
mcqs.why: The key step is 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g) with ΔH = −196 kJ/mol, a reversible exothermic reaction.

mcqs.q: The conditions used in the Contact Process are:
mcqs.why: The notes give about 400–450°C, 1–2 atm (typically 1.5–1.7 atm) and vanadium(V) oxide, V2O5, as the catalyst.

mcqs.q: The catalyst used in the Contact Process is:
mcqs.why: V2O5 speeds up the oxidation of SO2 so that equilibrium is achieved quickly in the Contact Process.

mcqs.q: The temperature 400–450°C in the Contact Process is a compromise because:
options: Low temperature favours yield but slows the rate, since the reaction is exothermic
High temperature favours both yield and rate
mcqs.why: The reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours SO3 yield but makes the rate slow; 400–450°C balances rate and yield at reasonable cost.

mcqs.q: In the Contact Process, increasing the pressure is kept low (1–2 atm) because:
options: Pressure has no effect at all on this reaction
The gain from higher pressure is small, since 3 moles of gas form 2 moles of product
The catalyst fails at high pressure
mcqs.why: Higher pressure does shift the equilibrium right (3 gas moles → 2), but the gain is small, so the pressure stays low at 1–2 atm.

mcqs.q: SO3 is removed from the Contact Process by absorbing it in concentrated H2SO4 to form:
mcqs.why: SO3(g) + H2SO4(l) → H2S2O7(l), oleum; removing SO3 shifts the equilibrium right and increases the yield.

mcqs.q: Increasing the concentration of SO2 or O2 in the Contact Process:
mcqs.why: By Le Chatelier's principle, more SO2 or O2 shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing the amount of SO3 formed.

mcqs.q: The enthalpy change of the key Contact Process reaction is:
mcqs.why: The notes give ΔH = −196 kJ/mol for 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, so the forward reaction is exothermic.

mcqs.q: The Contact Process conditions are chosen, using Le Chatelier's principle, to maximise:
options: Rate and yield at reasonable cost
mcqs.why: Because the reaction is reversible and slow at room temperature, conditions are a compromise to maximise rate and yield at reasonable cost.

lessons.notes_html:
The Contact Process is the large-scale manufacture of sulphuric acid by the catalytic oxidation of sulphur dioxide: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g), ΔH = −196 kJ/mol. The reaction is reversible and slow at room temperature, so conditions are chosen by Le Chatelier's principle to maximise rate and yield at reasonable cost: about 400–450°C, pressure 1–2 atmospheres (typically 1.5–1.7 atm) and vanadium(V) oxide (V2O5) catalyst.

  • Increasing concentration: more SO2 or O2 shifts equilibrium right, increasing SO3.
  • Temperature: the reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours yield but slows the rate; 400–450°C is the compromise.
  • Increasing pressure: 3 moles of gaseous reactants form 2 moles of product, so higher pressure shifts right; the gain is small, so pressure stays low.
  • Catalyst: V2O5 speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is achieved quickly.
  • Removing the product: SO3 is absorbed in concentrated H2SO4 to form oleum: SO3(g) + H2SO4(l) → H2S2O7(l). Removing SO3 shifts equilibrium right and increases yield.

Key Points

  • Key step: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, ΔH = −196 kJ/mol (exothermic).
  • Conditions: 400–450°C, 1–2 atm, V2O5 catalyst.
  • SO3 is removed as oleum, H2S2O7, pulling the equilibrium forward.
  • Conditions are a compromise between yield, rate and cost.
lessons.title: Contact Process (Production of Sulphuric Acid)

mcqs.q: Haber's Process is the industrial synthesis of ammonia from:
mcqs.why: Haber's Process synthesises ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: The conditions used in Haber's Process are:
mcqs.why: The notes give 450–500°C and 200–300 atmospheres with an iron catalyst for the synthesis of ammonia.

mcqs.q: High pressure favours ammonia formation because the reaction goes from:
options: 4 moles of reactants to 2 moles of product
mcqs.why: N2 + 3H2 gives 4 reactant moles forming 2 moles of NH3, so high pressure (200–300 atm) shifts equilibrium right and raises the yield.

mcqs.q: The catalyst in Haber's Process is iron (Fe3O4) combined with:
mcqs.why: The notes state the catalyst is iron (Fe3O4) combined with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3, and it loses effectiveness below 400°C.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is removed from the Haber mixture by:
options: Liquefying it by cooling below its boiling point of −33°C
mcqs.why: NH3(g) → NH3(l) by cooling below −33°C; removing NH3 shifts the equilibrium right and increases the yield.

mcqs.q: The temperature 450–500°C in Haber's Process is used because:
options: Low temperature favours NH3 but slows the reaction, so this temperature balances rate and yield
High temperature favours NH3 formation directly
mcqs.why: The synthesis is exothermic, so low temperature favours NH3 but slows the rate; 450–500°C is the compromise balancing rate and yield.

mcqs.q: Increasing the concentration of N2 or H2 in Haber's Process:
options: Shifts equilibrium right, increasing NH3 production
mcqs.why: By Le Chatelier's principle, more N2 or H2 shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing ammonia production.

mcqs.q: The enthalpy change for ammonia synthesis in Haber's Process is:
mcqs.why: The process data in the notes give ΔH = −92 kJ/mol for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, so the forward reaction is exothermic.

mcqs.q: The iron catalyst in Haber's Process loses effectiveness below:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the iron catalyst (Fe3O4 with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3) loses effectiveness below 400°C.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, the Haber process revolutionised agriculture because:
options: Without it, nearly half the world's population would not have enough food
It replaced all natural fertilizers instantly
It produced ammonia without any energy input
mcqs.why: The notes state that without the Haber process, nearly half the world's population would not have enough food, showing its importance for fertilizers.

lessons.notes_html:
Haber's Process is the industrial synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. Conditions: 450–500°C and 200–300 atmospheres with an iron catalyst.

  • Increasing concentration: more N2 or H2 shifts equilibrium right, increasing NH3 production.
  • Temperature: the synthesis is exothermic, so low temperature favours NH3 but slows the reaction; 450–500°C balances rate and yield.
  • Increasing pressure: 4 moles of reactants form 2 moles of product, so high pressure (200–300 atm) shifts equilibrium right and raises the yield.
  • Catalyst: iron (Fe3O4) combined with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3; it loses effectiveness below 400°C.
  • Removing the product: ammonia is liquefied by cooling below its boiling point (−33°C): NH3(g) → NH3(l). Removing NH3 shifts equilibrium right and increases yield.

The Haber process revolutionised agriculture: without it, nearly half the world's population would not have enough food.

Key Points

  • Reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol (exothermic).
  • Conditions: 450–500°C, 200–300 atm, iron catalyst.
  • High pressure favours NH3 because moles decrease (4 → 2).
  • NH3 is removed by liquefaction, shifting equilibrium forward.
lessons.title: Haber's Process (Synthesis of Ammonia)

mcqs.q: According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a substance that:
options: Donates a proton (H+) to another substance
mcqs.why: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor, so acid–base reactions are proton-transfer reactions.

mcqs.q: In HCl(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq), water acts as:
options: The base, accepting a proton from HCl
mcqs.why: HCl donates a proton and is the acid; water accepts the proton and is therefore the base in this reaction.

mcqs.q: In the gas-phase reaction HCl(g) + NH3(g) → NH4Cl(s), NH3 acts as a base because it:
options: Accepts a proton from HCl, with no solvent required
Donates an electron pair to water
mcqs.why: NH3 accepts a proton from HCl to form NH4Cl; the Brønsted–Lowry theory needs no solvent and no OH- ions for a base.

mcqs.q: Soluble bases are called:
mcqs.why: The notes state that soluble bases are called alkalis; all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.

mcqs.q: A conjugate acid–base pair consists of an acid and a base that differ only by:
mcqs.why: Conjugate pairs differ by only one proton: an acid forms its conjugate base by losing H+, and a base forms its conjugate acid by gaining H+.

mcqs.q: In HCl + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + Cl-, the conjugate acid is:
mcqs.why: H3O+ is formed when the base H2O gains a proton, so H3O+ is the conjugate acid and Cl- is the conjugate base of HCl.

mcqs.q: In the general reaction HA + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + A-, the two conjugate pairs are:
mcqs.why: HA loses a proton to become A-, and H2O gains a proton to become H3O+, giving the conjugate pairs HA/A- and H3O+/H2O.

mcqs.q: Every acid has a conjugate base, which is formed by:
mcqs.why: The key points state: acid → conjugate base by losing H+; base → conjugate acid by gaining H+.

mcqs.q: NH3 is a Brønsted–Lowry base even though:
mcqs.why: A key point notes that NH3 is a base even though it contains no OH- ions, because it accepts a proton.

mcqs.q: Acid–base reactions in the Brønsted–Lowry theory are therefore:
mcqs.why: Since acids donate protons and bases accept them, Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reactions are proton-transfer reactions.

lessons.notes_html:
According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a substance that donates a proton (H+) to another substance, and a base is a substance that accepts a proton from another substance. Acid–base reactions are therefore proton-transfer reactions. Example: HCl(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + Cl-(aq) — HCl is the acid (proton donor) and water is the base (proton acceptor). In the gas phase, HCl(g) + NH3(g) → NH4Cl(s): HCl donates a proton and NH3 accepts it, with no solvent required. Soluble bases are called alkalis; all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.

Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs

An acid and a base that differ only by a single proton form a conjugate acid–base pair. Every acid has a conjugate base, formed by loss of a proton; every base has a conjugate acid, formed by gaining a proton. General reaction: HA(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + A-(aq), where HA/A- and H3O+/H2O are the two conjugate pairs. For HCl in water: HCl is the acid, H2O the base, H3O+ the conjugate acid and Cl- the conjugate base.

Key Points

  • Brønsted–Lowry acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor.
  • Acid–base reactions are proton-transfer reactions.
  • Conjugate pairs differ by only one proton (H+).
  • Acid → conjugate base by losing H+; base → conjugate acid by gaining H+.
  • NH3 is a base even though it contains no OH- ions.
lessons.title: Brønsted-Lowry Definitions of Acids and Bases

mcqs.why: pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = −log[H+], a scale introduced by Sørensen in 1909.

mcqs.q: A solution with pH less than 7 is:

mcqs.q: Carrot juice with [H+] = 5.5 x 10^-6 M has a pH of:
mcqs.why: Working: pH = −log[H+] = −log(5.5 x 10^-6) = 6 − log 5.5 = 6 − 0.74 = 5.26, as in Book Example 7.4.

mcqs.why: Working: [H+] = 10^-pH = 10^-5.0 = 1.0 x 10^-5 M, as in Book Example 7.5 for a banana of pH 5.0.

mcqs.q: Human blood of pH 7.4 has [H+] equal to:
mcqs.why: Working: [H+] = 10^-pH = 10^-7.4 = 3.98 x 10^-8 M, the value given in Book Example 7.5 for human blood.

mcqs.q: For human blood of pH 7.4, using [H+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14, [OH-] is:
At 25°C, pH and pOH are related by:
mcqs.why: pKw = −log(1.0 x 10^-14) = 14, and pKw = pH + pOH = 7 + 7 = 14 for pure water at 25°C.

mcqs.q: Which substance has a pH in the range 7.3–7.5?
mcqs.why: The pH table gives human blood as 7.3–7.5, while gastric juice is 1.0–3.0, lemon juice 1.8–2.4 and sea water 8.0–8.5.

mcqs.q: The pH of apple juice and of milk, as given in the lesson examples, are:
mcqs.why: The examples give pure water pH 7, apple juice 3.1, egg 7.8 and milk 6.5, showing acidic, neutral and basic examples.

mcqs.q: A greater pH value means:
options: A larger [H+] and a stronger acid
A smaller [H+] and a weaker acid
mcqs.why: A key point states that greater pH means smaller [H+] and a weaker acid, since pH = −log[H+] works in the opposite direction.

lessons.notes_html:
The pH and pOH scales were introduced by Sørensen in 1909. pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration: pH = −log[H+]. pOH is the negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration: pOH = −log[OH-]. pH values range from 0 to 14: pH less than 7 is acidic, pH = 7 is neutral and pH greater than 7 is basic. Examples: pure water pH 7, apple juice 3.1, egg 7.8, milk 6.5. The pOH scale is essentially the reverse of the pH scale. pKw is the negative logarithm of Kw: pKw = −log Kw = −log(1.0 x 10^-14) = 14, and pKw = pH + pOH = 7 + 7 = 14.

pH of Some Common Substances

SubstancepHSubstancepH
Gastric juice1.0–3.0Pure water7.0
Lemon juice1.8–2.4Human blood7.3–7.5
Vinegar2.4–3.4Sea water8.0–8.5
Orange juice3.5–4.0Rain water6.2

Book Example 7.4: carrot juice with [H+] = 5.5 x 10^-6 M has pH = −log(5.5 x 10^-6) = 5.26. Book Example 7.5: banana of pH 5.0 has [H+] = 10^-5 M; human blood of pH 7.4 has [H+] = 3.98 x 10^-8 M and, using [H+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14, [OH-] = 2.51 x 10^-7 M.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
pH = −log[H+]pH from hydrogen ion concentration
pOH = −log[OH-]pOH from hydroxide ion concentration
[H+] = 10^-pHHydrogen ion concentration from pH
pH + pOH = pKw = 14Relation at 25°C; Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14

Key Points

  • pH = −log[H+]; pOH = −log[OH-].
  • pH less than 7 acidic, equal to 7 neutral, greater than 7 basic.
  • Greater pH means smaller [H+] and a weaker acid.
  • pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C.
  • Human blood pH is held near 7.4 by buffers.
lessons.title: pH, Ka, pKa, and pKw

mcqs.q: The acid ionisation constant Ka for HA + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + A- is:
mcqs.why: In dilute solution [H2O] is nearly constant, so Kc x [H2O] = [H3O+][A-]/[HA] = Ka, the acid ionisation constant.

mcqs.q: The greater the value of Ka, the:
options: Stronger the acid and the higher the H+ concentration at equilibrium
mcqs.why: The notes state acid strength is proportional to Ka: the greater Ka, the stronger the acid and the higher the equilibrium H+ concentration.

mcqs.q: Weak acids are those with Ka:
mcqs.why: The classification given is: weak acids have Ka less than 10^-3, moderately weak acids Ka from 1 to 10^-3, and strong acids Ka greater than 1.

mcqs.q: pKa is defined as:
mcqs.why: pKa = −log Ka, so the greater the Ka, the smaller the pKa and the stronger the acid.

mcqs.q: A difference of two pKa units between two acids means one acid is stronger than the other by:
mcqs.why: The notes state one pKa unit means 10 times stronger, two units 100 times and three units 1000 times, because pKa is a logarithmic scale.

mcqs.q: The pH of a 0.05M weak acid with Ka = 2.5 x 10^-5 is:
For a weak acid with [HA] = 2.5 x 10^-1 M and [H3O+] = [A-] = 4.2 x 10^-2 M, Ka is:
In calculating the pH of a weak acid, x is neglected in (C − x) because:
options: Ionisation of a weak acid is very small, so C − x ≈ C
mcqs.why: A key point states that for a weak acid x is neglected in (C − x) because the ionisation is very small compared with the concentration C.

mcqs.q: For a weak acid of concentration C, [H+] can be approximated by:
mcqs.why: From Ka ≈ x^2/C, x = √(Ka x C), so [H+] ≈ √(Ka·C); this is the approximation used in Book Example 7.6.

mcqs.q: Strong acids have Ka:
mcqs.why: The notes classify strong acids as having Ka greater than 1, moderately weak acids from 1 to 10^-3, and weak acids below 10^-3.

lessons.notes_html:
For the ionisation of an acid HA in water, HA + H2O ⇌ H3O+ + A-, the law of mass action gives Kc = [H3O+][A-]/([HA][H2O]). In dilute solution the concentration of water stays nearly constant, so Kc x [H2O] = [H3O+][A-]/[HA] = Ka, the acid ionisation constant. The greater the Ka, the stronger the acid and the higher the H+ concentration at equilibrium. Acid strength ∝ Ka: weak acids have Ka less than 10^-3, moderately weak acids have Ka from 1 to 10^-3, and strong acids have Ka greater than 1. pKa = −log Ka: the greater the Ka, the smaller the pKa and the stronger the acid. A difference of one pKa unit means one acid is 10 times stronger; two units, 100 times; three units, 1000 times.

Book Example 7.6: pH of 0.05M weak acid with Ka = 2.5 x 10^-5. With HA ⇌ H+ + A-, Ka = x^2/(0.05 − x) ≈ x^2/0.05, so x^2 = 1.25 x 10^-6, x = [H+] = 1.12 x 10^-3 M and pH = −log(1.12 x 10^-3) = 2.95. Book Example 7.7: with [HA] = 2.5 x 10^-1 M and [H3O+] = [A-] = 4.2 x 10^-2 M, Ka = (4.2 x 10^-2)(4.2 x 10^-2)/(2.5 x 10^-1) = 7.06 x 10^-3.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Ka = [H3O+][A-]/[HA]Acid ionisation constant
pKa = −log KaAcid strength on the pKa scale
[H+] ≈ √(Ka x C)H+ concentration of a weak acid of concentration C (x neglected)

Key Points

  • Ka measures acid strength: larger Ka = stronger acid.
  • pKa = −log Ka: smaller pKa = stronger acid.
  • Weak acids: Ka less than 10^-3; strong acids: Ka greater than 1.
  • For a weak acid, x is neglected in (C − x) because ionisation is very small.
  • Knowing Ka and concentration gives pH, and vice versa.
lessons.title: Acid Ionisation constant, Ka and pKa

mcqs.q: The Lewis concept of acids and bases, proposed in 1923 by Gilbert N. Lewis, is based on:
mcqs.why: Lewis proposed a broader concept based on electron pairs, not limited to any element or solvent, unlike the proton-based Brønsted–Lowry concept.

mcqs.q: A Lewis acid is a substance that can:
options: Accept an electron pair to form a coordinate covalent bond
mcqs.why: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor, the product forming through a coordinate covalent bond.

mcqs.q: Which of the following acts as a Lewis acid?
options: BF3, an electron-deficient molecule with an incomplete octet
mcqs.why: Electron-deficient molecules with an incomplete octet, such as BeCl2, AlCl3 and BF3, act as Lewis acids; NH3, H2O and Cl- are Lewis bases.

mcqs.q: Which of the following acts as a Lewis base?
options: NH3, a molecule with a lone pair
mcqs.why: Molecules with lone pairs, such as H2O and NH3, act as Lewis bases because they can donate an electron pair.

mcqs.q: All simple cations, such as H+, Sn2+ and Sn4+, act as:
mcqs.why: The notes state that all simple cations act as Lewis acids, and smaller cations like H+ and Be2+ are stronger Lewis acids.

mcqs.q: All anions, such as Cl-, O2- and OH-, act as Lewis bases because they:
mcqs.why: Anions act as Lewis bases because they donate electron pairs to form coordinate covalent bonds with Lewis acids.

mcqs.q: In the reaction Cl- + AlCl3 → AlCl4-, the Lewis acid is:
mcqs.why: Cl- (the base) donates an electron pair to AlCl3 (the acid), forming AlCl4- through a coordinate covalent bond.

mcqs.q: The Brønsted–Lowry concept cannot explain the acidic behaviour of:
options: AlCl3 and FeCl3, which contain no hydrogen ions
mcqs.why: The lesson states Brønsted–Lowry cannot explain acids and bases with no hydrogen ions, such as AlCl3 and FeCl3, or reactions in non-protonic solvents.

mcqs.q: Smaller cations such as H+ and Be2+ are, as Lewis acids:
mcqs.why: The notes state that smaller cations like H+ and Be2+ are stronger Lewis acids than larger cations.

mcqs.q: The product of a Lewis acid–base reaction is formed through a:
mcqs.why: A key point states that the Lewis acid accepts and the base donates an electron pair, so the product is formed through a coordinate covalent bond.

lessons.notes_html:
The Brønsted–Lowry concept cannot explain acids and bases that contain no hydrogen ions, such as AlCl3 and FeCl3, or reactions in non-protonic solvents. In 1923 Gilbert N. Lewis proposed a broader concept based on electron pairs, not limited to any element or solvent: a Lewis acid is a substance (atom, molecule or ion) that can accept an electron pair to form a coordinate covalent bond, and a Lewis base is a substance that can donate an electron pair to form a coordinate covalent bond. Acids are electron-pair acceptors; bases are electron-pair donors.

  • All simple cations, such as H+, Sn2+ and Sn4+, act as Lewis acids; smaller cations like H+ and Be2+ are stronger Lewis acids.
  • Electron-deficient molecules with an incomplete octet, such as BeCl2, AlCl3 and BF3, act as Lewis acids.
  • All anions, such as Cl-, O2-, OH- and halide ions, act as Lewis bases because they donate electron pairs.
  • Molecules with lone pairs, such as H2O and NH3, act as Lewis bases.

Example of a Lewis acid–base reaction: Cl- (base) + AlCl3 (acid) → AlCl4-, where the base donates an electron pair and a coordinate covalent bond forms.

Key Points

  • Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base = electron-pair donor.
  • The product is formed through a coordinate covalent bond.
  • Cations and electron-deficient molecules (BF3, AlCl3) are Lewis acids.
  • Anions and lone-pair molecules (NH3, H2O) are Lewis bases.
  • The Lewis concept covers reactions with no protons and no solvent.
lessons.title: Lewis Acid-Base Concept

mcqs.q: A buffer solution is a solution that:
options: Changes pH rapidly on adding acid
Resists any change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added
mcqs.why: By definition a buffer resists pH change on adding small amounts of acid or base; buffer tablets, for example, stabilise stomach pH.

mcqs.q: An acidic buffer consists of:
options: A strong acid and its salt
A weak base and its salt with a strong acid
A weak acid and its salt with a strong base, e.g. CH3COOH and CH3COONa
mcqs.why: The composition given is a weak acid plus its salt with a strong base, exemplified by CH3COOH and CH3COONa (sodium acetate).

mcqs.q: A basic buffer consists of:
options: A weak base and its salt with a strong acid, e.g. NH4OH and NH4Cl
A weak acid and its salt
mcqs.why: The notes give a weak base plus its salt with a strong acid as a basic buffer, exemplified by NH4OH and NH4Cl.

mcqs.q: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for the pH of an acidic buffer is:
mcqs.why: The key formula is pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), where [A-] is the conjugate base concentration and [HA] the weak acid concentration.

mcqs.q: For a buffer of 1M acetic acid and 1M acetate with pKa = 4.74, the pH is:
mcqs.why: Working: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 4.74 + log(1/1) = 4.74 + 0 = 4.74, as in Book Example 7.8.

mcqs.q: When [A-] = [HA] in a buffer, the pH is equal to:
mcqs.why: When the concentrations are equal, log([A-]/[HA]) = log 1 = 0, so a key point states pH = pKa for the buffer.

mcqs.q: For a buffer with pKa = 4.74 and [A-]/[HA] = 2, the pH is:
mcqs.why: Working: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 4.74 + log 2 = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04, using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

mcqs.q: Before substituting into the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, you must first find:
options: Only the colour of the buffer
The volume of the container only
mcqs.why: The calculation steps state: first find pKa, [A-] and [HA], then substitute them into pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

mcqs.q: Buffers are important in the body because they keep:
mcqs.why: A key point states that buffers keep blood pH near 7.4, and the pH lesson notes human blood is held near 7.4 by buffers.

mcqs.q: Buffer tablets are used to:
options: Stabilise stomach pH in acidity problems
mcqs.why: The lesson introduction gives buffer tablets as an example: they stabilise stomach pH in acidity problems.

lessons.notes_html:
A buffer solution is a solution that resists any change in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added to it. Buffer tablets, for example, stabilise stomach pH in acidity problems.

Composition of Buffer Solution

  • A weak acid and its salt with a strong base, e.g. CH3COOH and CH3COONa.
  • A weak base and its salt with a strong acid, e.g. NH4OH and NH4Cl.

Calculation of pH in a Buffer Solution

The pH is calculated with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), where [A-] is the conjugate base concentration and [HA] is the weak acid concentration. First find pKa, [A-] and [HA], then substitute. Book Example 7.8: for a buffer of 1M acetic acid and 1M acetate with pKa = 4.74, pH = 4.74 + log(1/1) = 4.74 + 0 = 4.74.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA])pH of an acidic buffer (Henderson–Hasselbalch)

Key Points

  • A buffer resists pH change on adding small amounts of acid or base.
  • Acidic buffer: weak acid + its salt with a strong base.
  • Basic buffer: weak base + its salt with a strong acid.
  • When [A-] = [HA], pH = pKa.
  • Buffers keep blood pH near 7.4.
lessons.title: Buffer Solution

mcqs.q: The solubility product, Ksp, describes the dissolution of:
options: A sparingly soluble ionic compound in water
mcqs.why: Ksp is the equilibrium constant for a sparingly soluble ionic compound dissolving in water, defined at a specific temperature.

mcqs.q: For AB(s) ⇌ A+(aq) + B-(aq), the solubility product is:
mcqs.why: Ksp is the product of the molar concentrations of the ions, each raised to its coefficient; for a 1:1 salt this is Ksp = [A+][B-].

mcqs.q: A smaller value of Ksp means:
options: No solubility at all in any case
The salt is a strong acid
mcqs.why: The notes state that a smaller Ksp means lower solubility and a larger Ksp means higher solubility of the salt.

mcqs.q: For BaSO4(s) ⇌ Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq), the Ksp expression is:
mcqs.why: The solid's concentration stays constant and does not appear, so Ksp = [Ba2+][SO4^2-] for barium sulphate.

mcqs.q: Precipitation occurs when:
options: Ksp is greater than the ionic product
Ksp is less than the ionic product, so the solution is supersaturated
mcqs.why: If Ksp is less than the ionic product the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs until the ionic product equals Ksp.

mcqs.q: If Ksp is greater than the ionic product, the solution is:
options: Unsaturated, no precipitation occurs and more solid dissolves
mcqs.why: The applications state that Ksp greater than the ionic product means an unsaturated solution: no precipitation, and more solid can dissolve.

mcqs.q: The solubility of ZnS, whose Ksp = 3.0 x 10^-23, is:
mcqs.why: Working: Ksp = s x s = s^2, so s = √Ksp = √(3.0 x 10^-23) = 5.477 x 10^-12 M, as in Book Example 7.9.

mcqs.q: BaSO4 with a solubility of 1.03 x 10^-5 M has Ksp equal to:
For a 1:1 salt, the solubility s is obtained from Ksp by:
mcqs.why: The key formulae give s = √Ksp for a 1:1 salt, because Ksp = s^2 when the two ion concentrations are both equal to s.

mcqs.q: The low Ksp of BaSO4 makes it safe for:
mcqs.why: A key point states that the low Ksp of BaSO4 makes it safe for medical X-ray use, since very little of it dissolves.

lessons.notes_html:
The solubility product (Ksp) is the equilibrium constant that describes the dissolution of a sparingly soluble ionic compound in water. It is the maximum product of the molar concentrations of the ions produced, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient, at a specific temperature. For AB(s) ⇌ A+(aq) + B-(aq), Ksp = [A+][B-]. A smaller Ksp means lower solubility; a larger Ksp means higher solubility. Ksp is temperature-dependent. For BaSO4(s) ⇌ Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq), the solid's concentration stays constant, so Ksp = [Ba2+][SO4^2-].

Applications of Solubility Product: Prediction of Precipitation

  • If Ksp is greater than the ionic product: solution is unsaturated, no precipitation; more solid dissolves.
  • If Ksp is less than the ionic product: solution is supersaturated, precipitation occurs until ionic product = Ksp.
  • If Ksp = ionic product: solution is saturated and at equilibrium; no precipitation.

Book Example 7.9: ZnS with Ksp = 3.0 x 10^-23: Ksp = s x s = s^2, so solubility s = √(3.0 x 10^-23) = 5.477 x 10^-12 M. Book Example 7.10: BaSO4 with solubility 1.03 x 10^-5 M: Ksp = (1.03 x 10^-5)(1.03 x 10^-5) = 1.06 x 10^-10 M^2.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Ksp = [A+][B-]Solubility product of a 1:1 salt AB
s = √KspSolubility of a 1:1 salt from Ksp

Key Points

  • Ksp applies to sparingly soluble salts in saturated solution.
  • The solid salt does not appear in the Ksp expression.
  • Precipitation occurs only when ionic product exceeds Ksp.
  • Ksp changes with temperature.
  • Low Ksp of BaSO4 makes it safe for medical X-ray use.
lessons.title: Solubility Product and Precipitation Reactions

mcqs.q: The common ion effect is the process by which:
options: The ionisation of a weak electrolyte increases on adding a strong electrolyte
The degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte decreases due to a strong electrolyte having a common ion
Ksp increases on adding a common ion
A salt becomes more soluble on adding a common ion
mcqs.why: By definition, adding a strong electrolyte with a common ion decreases the degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte.

mcqs.q: The common ion effect follows which principle?
options: The law of mass action only
mcqs.why: The lesson states the common ion effect follows Le Chatelier's principle: adding a product ion shifts the equilibrium towards the solid side.

mcqs.q: Adding CaCl2 to a saturated solution of CaCO3 causes CaCO3 to precipitate because:
options: The added Ca2+ increases [Ca2+], shifting CaCO3(s) ⇌ Ca2+ + CO3^2- to the left
CaCl2 is less soluble than CaCO3
mcqs.why: CaCl2 is more soluble and raises [Ca2+], the common ion, so the equilibrium shifts right to left and CaCO3 precipitates.

mcqs.q: For KClO4(s) ⇌ K+(aq) + ClO4-(aq), adding the more soluble KCl:
options: Raises [K+], shifting equilibrium left so KClO4 precipitates
mcqs.why: KCl raises the K+ (common ion) concentration, shifting the equilibrium left and causing KClO4 to precipitate.

mcqs.q: In water treatment, hard water is softened by adding lime, Ca(OH)2, to:
options: Increase the Ca2+ in solution permanently
mcqs.why: The notes state lime is added to hard water to precipitate calcium carbonate, softening the water for domestic and industrial use.

mcqs.q: Adding a common ion to a slightly soluble salt:
options: Suppresses its ionisation and reduces its solubility
mcqs.why: A key point states that adding a common ion suppresses ionisation and solubility, shifting equilibrium towards the undissolved solid.

mcqs.q: When a common ion is added, Ksp itself:
options: Does not change; only the ion concentrations adjust
mcqs.why: A key point states Ksp itself does not change; only the ion concentrations adjust to keep the product equal to Ksp.

mcqs.q: The equilibrium in the common ion effect shifts towards:
mcqs.why: The key points state the equilibrium shifts towards the solid (undissolved) side when a common ion is added.

mcqs.q: The common ion effect is used in:
options: Water softening and controlling salt solubility
mcqs.why: The key points list water softening and controlling salt solubility as uses of the common ion effect.

mcqs.q: In the CaCO3 example, the common ion supplied by CaCl2 is:
mcqs.why: CaCl2 shares the Ca2+ ion with CaCO3, so Ca2+ is the common ion whose increase shifts the equilibrium left.

lessons.notes_html:
The common ion effect is the process by which the degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte decreases due to the addition of a strong electrolyte that has a common ion. It is used to reduce the solubility of slightly soluble salts by adding a more soluble electrolyte sharing a common ion, and it follows Le Chatelier's principle.

Example 1: CaCO3 and CaCl2

CaCO3(s) ⇌ Ca2+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq), with Ksp = [Ca2+][CO3^2-]. Adding CaCl2, a more soluble salt, increases the Ca2+ concentration, so the equilibrium shifts from right to left and CaCO3 precipitates out of the solution.

Example 2: KClO4 and KCl

KClO4(s) ⇌ K+(aq) + ClO4-(aq), with Ksp = [K+][ClO4-]. Adding the more soluble KCl raises the K+ (common ion) concentration, shifting the equilibrium left and causing KClO4 to precipitate. In water treatment, lime [Ca(OH)2] is added to hard water to precipitate calcium carbonate, softening the water for domestic and industrial use.

Key Points

  • Adding a common ion suppresses ionisation and solubility.
  • The equilibrium shifts towards the solid (undissolved) side.
  • The effect is an application of Le Chatelier's principle.
  • Used in water softening and in controlling salt solubility.
  • Ksp itself does not change; only the ion concentrations adjust.
lessons.title: Common Ion Effect

mcqs.q: Salt hydrolysis is the reaction of a salt's cations, anions, or both with:
options: Water, to form acidic, basic or neutral solutions
mcqs.why: Hydrolysis is defined as the reaction of cations, anions, or both with water, and it usually affects the pH of the solution.

mcqs.q: A salt of a weak acid and a strong base, such as CH3COONa, gives a solution that is:
mcqs.why: CH3COO- + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH- produces hydroxide ions, so the solution of a weak acid–strong base salt is basic.

mcqs.q: A salt of a strong acid and a weak base, such as NH4Cl, gives a solution that is:
mcqs.why: NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH4OH + H+ produces hydrogen ions, so the solution of a strong acid–weak base salt is acidic.

mcqs.q: A salt of a strong acid and a strong base, such as NaCl, in water:
options: Is hydrolysed to an acidic solution
Is hydrolysed to a basic solution
Is not hydrolysed and the solution is neutral, pH = 7
mcqs.why: The table states NaCl is not hydrolysed; Na+ and Cl- are both very weak in Brønsted terms, so neither affects the pH.

mcqs.q: For a salt of a weak acid and a weak base, the nature of the solution depends on:
options: The relative strengths of the weak acid and weak base, comparing Ka and Kb
mcqs.why: For weak–weak salts, compare the Ka of the cation with the Kb of the anion: greater Ka gives acidic, greater Kb gives basic, nearly equal gives neutral.

mcqs.q: If, for a weak acid–weak base salt, Ka is greater than Kb, the solution is:
mcqs.why: The rule given is: Ka greater than Kb → acidic; Ka less than Kb → basic; Ka almost equal to Kb → neutral or nearly neutral.

mcqs.q: In NaCl solution, neither ion affects the pH because:
options: NaCl does not dissolve in water
Na+ is a very weak Brønsted base and Cl- a very weak Brønsted acid
Water cannot react with any salt
mcqs.why: The notes explain that Na+ is a very weak Brønsted base and Cl- a very weak Brønsted acid, so neither hydrolyses appreciably.

mcqs.q: The hydrolysis equation for sodium acetate in water is:
mcqs.why: The acetate ion hydrolyses as CH3COO- + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH-, and the OH- formed makes the solution basic.

mcqs.q: The hydrolysis equation for ammonium chloride in water is:
mcqs.why: The ammonium ion hydrolyses as NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH4OH + H+, and the H+ formed makes the solution acidic, pH less than 7.

mcqs.q: How many types of salts are discussed for hydrolysis in this lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson states there are four types of salts: weak acid–strong base, strong acid–weak base, strong acid–strong base, and weak acid–weak base.

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis is the reaction of cations, anions, or both with water to form acidic, basic or neutral solutions. Salt hydrolysis usually affects the pH of a solution. There are four types of salts.

Salt TypeExample and Result
Weak acid + strong baseCH3COONa: CH3COO- + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH-; solution is basic, pH greater than 7
Strong acid + weak baseNH4Cl: NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH4OH + H+; solution is acidic, pH less than 7
Strong acid + strong baseNaCl: not hydrolysed; solution is neutral, pH = 7
Weak acid + weak baseDepends on relative strengths of the weak acid and weak base

For a salt of a weak acid and a weak base, compare the Ka of the cation with the Kb of the anion: if Ka is greater than Kb the solution is acidic (pH less than 7); if Ka is less than Kb the solution is basic (pH greater than 7); if Ka is almost equal to Kb the solution is neutral or nearly neutral (pH almost equal to 7). In NaCl solution, Na+ is a very weak Brønsted base and Cl- a very weak Brønsted acid, so neither affects the pH.

Key Points

  • Hydrolysis = reaction of a salt's ions with water.
  • Salt of weak acid + strong base gives a basic solution.
  • Salt of strong acid + weak base gives an acidic solution.
  • Salt of strong acid + strong base stays neutral (no hydrolysis).
  • Weak–weak salts: nature depends on Ka versus Kb.

mcqs.q: Acid–base titration is an analytical technique used to determine:
options: The concentration (molarity) of an acidic or basic solution
The molar mass of an acid directly
mcqs.why: The lesson defines titration as a technique to determine the concentration (molarity) of an acidic or basic solution from a known titrant.

mcqs.q: The titration relation between two solutions is:
mcqs.why: The key formula is M1V1/n1 = M2V2/n2, where n1 and n2 are the stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation.

mcqs.q: For H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O, the mole ratio of acid to base is:
mcqs.why: The balanced equation shows 1 mole of H2SO4 reacting with 2 moles of NaOH, so the ratio is 1:2, not always 1:1.

mcqs.q: If n1 = n2 in a titration, the unknown molarity is given by:
mcqs.why: When the coefficients are equal, M1V1/n1 = M2V2/n2 reduces to M1V1 = M2V2, so M2 = M1V1/V2.

mcqs.q: 25.0 mL of 0.500 mol/L HCl neutralises 35.0 mL of NaOH. The molarity of the NaOH is:
mcqs.why: Working: moles HCl = 0.500 x 0.0250 = 0.0125 mol; ratio HCl:NaOH is 1:1, so moles NaOH = 0.0125 mol; molarity = 0.0125/0.0350 = 0.357 mol/L (Book Example 7.11).

mcqs.q: The strength in g/L of the NaOH solution in Book Example 7.11 (molarity 0.357 mol/L, molar mass 40.00 g/mol) is:
mcqs.why: Working: Strength (g/L) = Molarity x Molar mass = 0.357 mol/L x 40.00 g/mol = 14.28 g/L, as calculated in Book Example 7.11.

mcqs.q: Before calculating moles from molarity and volume, volumes must be converted to:
mcqs.why: A key point states to convert volumes to litres before calculating moles, since Moles = M x V with V in litres.

mcqs.q: The number of moles in a solution is calculated as:
options: Moles = M x V, with V in litres
mcqs.why: The key formulae give Moles = M x V; in Example 7.11, 0.500 mol/L x 0.0250 L = 0.0125 mol of HCl.

mcqs.q: The strength of a solution in g/L is found by:
mcqs.why: The key formula is Strength (g/L) = Molarity x Molar mass (g/mol), used in Example 7.11 to get 14.28 g/L for NaOH.

mcqs.q: An everyday example of neutralisation mentioned in the lesson is:
mcqs.why: A key point gives antacid action in the stomach as an everyday neutralisation example, where a base neutralises excess acid.

lessons.notes_html:
Acid–base titration is an analytical technique used to determine the concentration (molarity) of an acidic or basic solution. The moles of titrant and analyte are related by M1V1/n1 = M2V2/n2, where n1 and n2 are the stoichiometric coefficients and the mole ratio comes from the balanced equation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O has ratio 1:1, while H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O has ratio 1:2. If n1 = n2, then M2 = M1V1/V2. The strength of the analyte is found by multiplying its molarity by its molar mass: Strength (g/L) = M2 x Molar mass (g/mol).

Book Example 7.11

25.0 mL of 0.500 mol/L HCl neutralises 35.0 mL of NaOH. Step 1: moles of HCl = 0.500 x 0.0250 = 0.0125 mol. Step 2: ratio 1:1, so moles of NaOH = 0.0125 mol. Step 3: molarity of NaOH = 0.0125/0.0350 = 0.357 mol/L. Step 4: strength = 0.357 x 40.00 = 14.28 g/L.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
M1V1/n1 = M2V2/n2Titration relation between two solutions
Moles = M x VMoles from molarity and volume (in litres)
Strength (g/L) = Molarity x Molar massStrength of a solution

Key Points

  • Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, not always 1:1.
  • Convert volumes to litres before calculating moles.
  • Molarity = moles/volume; strength = molarity x molar mass.
  • Antacid action in the stomach is an everyday neutralisation example.
lessons.title: Calculation of Molarity and Strength in Acid-Base Titration

mcqs.q: Indicators in acid–base titrations are used to show:
options: The exact molarity of the acid
When the acid has completely reacted with the base, by a colour change at the endpoint
mcqs.why: Indicators are special chemicals that change colour at the endpoint, indicating completion of the reaction between acid and base.

mcqs.q: The right indicator for a titration is the one whose pH range:
options: Falls within the sharp pH change at the equivalence point
Does not overlap the equivalence point at all
mcqs.why: The lesson states the right indicator is the one whose pH range falls within the sharp pH change at the equivalence point.

mcqs.q: For a strong acid–strong base titration, the equivalence point is at about pH 7 with a sharp change between:
mcqs.why: The table gives a sharp change between pH 4 and 10 for strong acid–strong base, so methyl orange, bromothymol blue or phenolphthalein all work.

mcqs.q: For a strong acid–weak base titration, suitable indicators are:
options: No indicator can ever be used
mcqs.why: The solution is slightly acidic with equivalence point between pH 3 and 6, so methyl orange or methyl red, whose ranges fall in this region, are suitable.

mcqs.q: For a weak acid–strong base titration, the most suitable indicator is:
options: Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0), colourless in acid and pink in base
mcqs.why: The solution is slightly basic with equivalence point between pH 8 and 10, so phenolphthalein, colourless in acid and pink in base, is most suitable.

mcqs.q: For a weak acid–weak base titration, indicators are unreliable because:
options: The pH changes gradually with no sharp equivalence point, so a pH meter is used
The equivalence point is exactly pH 14
mcqs.why: The table states that for weak acid–weak base the pH changes gradually with no sharp equivalence point, so a pH meter is used instead of an indicator.

mcqs.q: The pH range of methyl orange given in the lesson is:
mcqs.why: The table gives methyl orange's range as 3.1–4.4; methyl red is 4.4–6.2, bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6 and phenolphthalein 8.2–10.0.

mcqs.q: In a strong acid–weak base titration, methyl orange changes colour:
options: From red to yellow as acidity decreases
mcqs.why: The table notes that methyl orange changes red to yellow as acidity decreases in the strong acid–weak base titration.

mcqs.q: Bromothymol blue, with pH range 6.0–7.6, is suitable for which titration?
mcqs.why: Bromothymol blue is listed for strong acid–strong base titrations, whose sharp pH change between 4 and 10 covers its 6.0–7.6 range.

mcqs.q: Farmers use simple indicator kits to test soil pH in order to:
options: Decide suitable crops and whether lime (a base) is needed to neutralise acidic soil
Find the Ksp of soil salts
mcqs.why: The lesson states farmers test soil pH with indicator kits to decide suitable crops and whether lime is needed to neutralise acidic soil.

lessons.notes_html:
Indicators are special chemicals used in acid–base titrations to show when the acid has completely reacted with the base. The indicator changes colour at the endpoint, indicating completion of the reaction. The right indicator is the one whose pH range falls within the sharp pH change at the equivalence point.

Titration TypeEquivalence Point and Suitable Indicators
Strong acid + strong basepH about 7; sharp change between pH 4 and 10. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4), bromothymol blue (6.0–7.6) or phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0)
Strong acid + weak baseSolution slightly acidic; equivalence point between pH 3 and 6. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4) or methyl red (4.4–6.2); methyl orange changes red to yellow as acidity decreases
Weak acid + strong baseSolution slightly basic; equivalence point between pH 8 and 10. Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) is most suitable: colourless in acid, pink in base
Weak acid + weak basepH changes gradually with no sharp equivalence point; indicators are unreliable, so a pH meter is used

Farmers use simple indicator kits to test soil pH, decide suitable crops and whether lime (a base) is needed to neutralise acidic soil.

Key Points

  • An indicator signals the endpoint by a colour change.
  • Strong acid–strong base: methyl orange, bromothymol blue or phenolphthalein all work.
  • Strong acid–weak base: methyl orange or methyl red.
  • Weak acid–strong base: phenolphthalein is best.
  • Weak acid–weak base: no suitable indicator; use a pH meter.

mcqs.q: How many elements are currently known and arranged in the periodic table?
mcqs.why: The notes state that there are currently 118 known elements arranged in a specific format in the periodic table for studying their properties systematically.

mcqs.q: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing:
mcqs.why: The modern periodic table is arranged by increasing atomic number, not atomic mass; atomic number is the number of protons and serves as the identification number of an element.

mcqs.q: Whose work in 1913 corrected the anomalies in Mendeleev's table?
mcqs.why: Mendeleev's early table used atomic mass and contained anomalies that were corrected by Moseley's discovery of atomic number in 1913, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why do the properties of elements repeat periodically as atomic number increases?
options: Because of the repeating arrangement of electrons
Because all elements have the same density pattern
mcqs.why: Periodicity arises from the arrangement of an element's electrons, influenced by the number of protons in its nucleus, so properties repeat in a periodic manner.

mcqs.q: The periodic table is sometimes called:
mcqs.why: The notes call the periodic table the 'chemist's map' because it is essential for predicting element properties, understanding interactions and developing new materials.

mcqs.q: In the periodic table, elements with similar properties are grouped in:
mcqs.why: Elements with similar properties are grouped in columns, and these columns are organised to reveal the relationships between the elements, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: What does the atomic number of an element indicate?
options: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
The number of protons in the nucleus

mcqs.why: The notes list size, mass, melting point, density, electronegativity and metallic character as repeating periodically; the printed colour of a name is not a chemical property mentioned.

mcqs.q: Mendeleev's early periodic table was arranged by:
