lessons.notes_html:
As more elements and their compounds were discovered, chemists recognised the need to classify them. This classification enables us to understand the properties of elements systematically. Currently, there are 118 known elements arranged in a specific format for studying their properties. Elements with similar properties are grouped in columns, and these columns are organised to reveal the relationships between them. This arrangement of elements in groups and periods is known as the periodic table, and it has significantly simplified the study of elements and their compounds.

Arrangement by Atomic Number

The elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number (proton number) in the periodic table. The atomic number indicates the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, so the atomic number serves as the identification number of an element. The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number, not by atomic mass: Mendeleev's early table used atomic mass, but it contained anomalies that were corrected by Moseley's discovery of atomic number in 1913.

This arrangement is not random. The properties of elements (such as size, mass, melting point, density, electronegativity and metallic character) repeat in a periodic manner as the atomic number increases. This periodicity arises from the arrangement of an element's electrons, influenced by the number of protons in its nucleus. The table is essential for predicting element properties, understanding element interactions and developing new materials; it is sometimes called the "chemist's map".

Key Points

  • There are 118 known elements arranged in the periodic table.
  • Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number (proton number), not atomic mass.
  • Atomic number is the identification number of an element.
  • Properties repeat periodically because of the repeating arrangement of electrons.
  • Moseley's work (1913) removed the anomalies of Mendeleev's atomic-mass table.
lessons.title: The Arrangement of Elements in the Periodic Table

mcqs.q: The classification of elements into s, p, d and f blocks is based on:
options: The subshell into which the last electron enters
The atomic mass of the element
The melting point of the element
mcqs.why: Block classification is based on the valence orbital involved in bond formation, that is, the subshell into which the last electron enters, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: How many s-block elements are there in each period, and why?
options: 6, because the s-subshell holds six electrons
2, because the s-subshell holds a maximum of two electrons
10, because the s-subshell holds ten electrons
14, because the s-subshell holds fourteen electrons
mcqs.why: There are two s-block elements in each period because the s-subshell can hold a maximum of two electrons; likewise p holds six, d holds ten and f holds fourteen.

mcqs.q: The general electronic configuration of the p-block is:
mcqs.why: The table in the notes gives the p-block general configuration as ns2 np^1-6, for elements in Groups 13 to 18 excluding helium, with the last electron entering a p-subshell.

mcqs.q: The d-block elements are also known as:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the d-block elements, in Groups 3 to 12 with the last electron entering a d-subshell, are also known as transition elements.

mcqs.q: For f-block elements, the f-subshell being filled is:
options: (n-2), two less than the period number
(n-1), one less than the period number
n, equal to the period number
(n+1), one more than the period number
mcqs.why: For f-block elements the f-subshell being filled is (n-2), two less than the period number, and these elements are usually placed below the main table to save space.

mcqs.q: Which block contains Groups 1 and 2, and period 1 elements?
mcqs.why: The s-block contains Groups 1 and 2 and period 1, with general configuration ns^1-2 and the last electron entering an s-subshell, per the notes table.

mcqs.q: How many d-block elements occur in each period?
mcqs.why: There are ten d-block elements in each period because the d-subshell holds a maximum of ten electrons; the block sizes are s = 2, p = 6, d = 10 and f = 14.

mcqs.q: The lanthanides and actinides belong to which block?
mcqs.why: The notes place the lanthanides and actinides in the f-block, with general configuration (n-2)f^1-14 (n-1)d^0-1 ns^1-2 and fourteen elements per period.

mcqs.q: In the p-block, the last electron enters which subshell?
mcqs.why: In the p-block (Groups 13 to 18, excluding helium) the last electron enters the p-subshell, which can hold at most six electrons, giving six elements per period.

mcqs.q: Why are f-block elements placed below the main periodic table in most tables?
options: Because they were discovered last week
mcqs.why: The notes state that in most periodic tables the f-block elements are placed below the main table to save space, since the f-subshell holds fourteen elements per period.

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table can be divided into four blocks: s, p, d and f-blocks. The classification of elements into these blocks is based on the valence orbital of the element involved in bond formation, that is, the subshell into which the last electron enters.

BlockGroupsLast Electron EntersElements in Each PeriodGeneral Electronic Configuration
s-blockGroups 1 and 2, and period 1s-subshell2ns^1-2
p-blockGroups 13 to 18 (excluding helium)p-subshell6ns2 np^1-6
d-blockGroups 3 to 12d-subshell10(n-1)d^1-10 ns^1-2
f-blockLanthanides and actinidesf-subshell14(n-2)f^1-14 (n-1)d^0-1 ns^1-2
  • There are two s-block elements in each period because the s-subshell can hold a maximum of two electrons; six p-block elements because the p-subshell holds at most six; ten d-block elements because the d-subshell holds ten; and fourteen f-block elements because the f-subshell holds fourteen.
  • The d-block elements are also known as transition elements.
  • For f-block elements, the f-subshell being filled is (n - 2), two less than the period number; in most periodic tables the f-block elements are placed below the main table to save space.

Key Points

  • Blocks are decided by the subshell that receives the last electron.
  • s-block: ns^1-2; p-block: ns2 np^1-6; d-block: (n-1)d^1-10 ns^1-2; f-block: (n-2)f^1-14 (n-1)d^0-1 ns^1-2.
  • Block sizes per period: s = 2, p = 6, d = 10, f = 14 elements.
  • d-block elements are the transition elements; f-block elements are shown below the main table.
lessons.title: Blocks of Elements

mcqs.q: How many groups are there in the modern periodic table according to the latest IUPAC system?
mcqs.why: According to the latest IUPAC system, the modern periodic table has 18 groups, which are the vertical columns of elements in the periodic table grid.

mcqs.q: Elements in the same group show similar properties because they have:

mcqs.why: The horizontal rows of elements are called periods, and the modern periodic table has seven periods, with lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32 elements.

mcqs.why: The 1st period is the shortest period with only 2 elements, hydrogen and helium, while the 6th and 7th periods are the longest with 32 elements each.

mcqs.q: Using the period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, what is the total number of elements?
mcqs.why: Working: total = 2 + 8 + 8 + 18 + 18 + 32 + 32 = 118 elements. This matches the 118 known elements stated in the notes for the periodic table.

mcqs.q: The 4th and 5th periods are described as long periods because each contains:
mcqs.why: The notes describe the 4th and 5th periods as long periods with 18 elements each, while the 2nd and 3rd are short periods with 8 elements each.

mcqs.q: Groups in the periodic table are the:
mcqs.why: Groups are the vertical columns of elements in the periodic table; there are eighteen groups, and periods are the horizontal rows, of which there are seven.

mcqs.q: The 6th and 7th periods each contain how many elements?
mcqs.why: The 6th and 7th periods are the longest periods with 32 elements each, according to the period table given in the notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: The 2nd and 3rd periods are called short periods because each contains:
mcqs.why: The notes call the 2nd and 3rd periods short periods because each contains 8 elements, compared with 18 in the long 4th and 5th periods.

mcqs.q: There are two systems for numbering groups; the 18-group system belongs to:
mcqs.why: The notes say there are two systems for numbering groups, the older system and the newer IUPAC system; according to the latest IUPAC system the table has 18 groups.

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table is a grid of vertical columns called groups and horizontal rows called periods.

Groups of Elements

The vertical columns of elements in the periodic table are called groups. There are eighteen groups in the periodic table. There are two systems for numbering the groups: the older system and the newer IUPAC system; according to the latest IUPAC system, the modern periodic table has 18 groups. Elements in the same group of the periodic table show similar properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.

Periods of Elements

The horizontal rows of elements in the periodic table are called periods. The modern periodic table has seven periods.

PeriodNumber of ElementsDescription
1st2 (hydrogen and helium)Shortest period
2nd and 3rd8 eachShort periods
4th and 5th18 eachLong periods
6th and 7th32 eachLongest periods

Key Points

  • Groups are vertical columns; there are 18 groups (IUPAC system).
  • Same group means the same number of valence electrons and similar properties.
  • Periods are horizontal rows; there are 7 periods.
  • Period lengths: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 elements.
lessons.title: Periods and Groups of Elements

mcqs.q: The period number (n) of an element indicates:
options: The highest energy level that contains electrons
The atomic mass of the element
The group number of the element
mcqs.why: The period number indicates the highest energy level that contains electrons within that atom; all elements in the same period have outermost electrons in the same energy level.

mcqs.q: Lithium is in Period 2. This means its outermost electrons are in:
mcqs.why: The notes' example: lithium is in Period 2, so its electrons are arranged in two energy levels, with the outermost electrons in the second energy level (n = 2).

mcqs.q: All elements in the same period have their outermost electrons in:
options: Different energy levels in every case
mcqs.why: All elements in the same period have their outermost electrons in the same energy level, which is exactly what the period number tells us about an element.

mcqs.q: As we move down the periodic table, the period number increases, so:
mcqs.why: Moving down the table the period number increases, meaning more energy levels are occupied by electrons in the atoms of successive periods.

mcqs.q: Reading an element's period number helps us predict its:
mcqs.why: Knowing the period number tells how many energy levels are occupied and which shell holds the valence electrons, allowing us to predict an element's chemical behaviour.

mcqs.q: An element in Period 3 has electrons arranged in how many energy levels?
mcqs.why: The period number equals the number of occupied energy levels, so a Period 3 element has electrons in three energy levels, with outermost electrons in the third shell.

mcqs.q: Which shell holds the valence electrons of a Period 4 element?
mcqs.why: For a Period 4 element the highest occupied energy level is the fourth shell, so its valence electrons reside in the fourth energy level (n = 4).

mcqs.q: The period number is also described as the number of:
mcqs.why: The notes state the period number of an element indicates how many principal energy levels, or shells, contain electrons within that atom.

mcqs.q: Which statement about periods is correct?
options: Period number gives the number of valence electrons
Period number decreases down the table
Elements in one period share the same outermost shell
mcqs.why: Elements in one period have outermost electrons in the same shell; the period number increases down the table and gives occupied shells, not valence electron count.

mcqs.q: If an atom's outermost electrons are in the second energy level, the element is in:
mcqs.why: The period number equals the highest occupied energy level, so outermost electrons in the second energy level (n = 2) place the element in Period 2, like lithium.

lessons.notes_html:
The period number (n) of an element indicates the highest energy level that contains electrons within that atom. In other words, all elements in the same period have their outermost electrons in the same energy level.

Example

Lithium is in Period 2, which means its electrons are arranged in two energy levels, with the outermost electrons in the second energy level (n = 2).

This arrangement helps us understand an element's energy levels and allows us to predict its chemical behaviour from its position in the table: read the period number and you know how many energy levels are occupied and which shell holds the valence electrons.

Key Points

  • Period number = the highest occupied energy level (shell) of the atom.
  • All elements in one period have outermost electrons in the same shell.
  • Moving down the table, the period number increases, so more energy levels are occupied.
  • Position in a period helps predict chemical behaviour.
lessons.title: Period Number and Electron Energy Levels

mcqs.q: Elements in Period 2, such as lithium and oxygen, have electrons in:
options: Two energy levels: 1s followed by 2s and 2p
mcqs.why: The notes state Period 2 elements have electrons in two energy levels: the first (1s2), followed by the second (2s and 2p), e.g. lithium and oxygen.

mcqs.q: For main group elements (Groups IA to VIIIA), the group number gives:
mcqs.why: From the group position we can determine the number of valence electrons for main group elements in Groups IA to VIIIA; these electrons decide how an element reacts chemically.

mcqs.q: Oxygen is in Group VIA. How many valence electrons does it have, and what is its configuration?
mcqs.why: Oxygen in Group VIA has six valence electrons with configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4, as given in the notes; the group number VIA corresponds to six valence electrons.

mcqs.q: Potassium is in Period 4 and Group I. Its electron configuration ends with:
mcqs.why: Potassium has four energy levels and one valence electron in the fourth shell: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1, exactly as shown in the notes' trend example.

mcqs.q: Sodium, in Period 3 and Group IA, has its one valence electron in:
mcqs.why: In Period 3, sodium (Group IA) has one valence electron in the third shell, while chlorine in Group VIIA has seven valence electrons, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Chlorine is in Group VIIA. How many valence electrons does it have?
mcqs.why: Chlorine in Group VIIA has seven valence electrons; for main group elements the group number (VIIA = 7) gives the number of valence electrons in the outermost shell.

mcqs.q: Lithium in Group IA has the electronic configuration:
mcqs.why: The notes give lithium in Group IA one valence electron with electronic configuration 1s2 2s1, consistent with Period 2 and one electron in the 2s subshell.

mcqs.q: Valence electrons are important because they:
options: Play a significant role in determining how an element reacts chemically
mcqs.why: Valence electrons, the electrons in the outermost shell, play a significant role in determining how an element reacts chemically, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: Across the main groups, the number of valence electrons:
options: Increases from one in Group I across the groups
Stays at one for all groups
mcqs.why: Group I elements have one valence electron, and the count increases across the main groups, e.g. Group IA has 1, VIA has 6 and VIIA has 7 valence electrons.

mcqs.q: Elements in Period 3, such as sodium and chlorine, possess:
options: Three energy levels, outermost in the third shell
mcqs.why: Period 3 elements possess three energy levels, with their outermost electrons residing in the third shell, as stated for sodium and chlorine in the notes.

lessons.notes_html:
From an element's position in the periodic table we can determine both its occupied energy levels and its number of valence electrons.

Determination of Energy Levels from Period Number

The periodic table is organised to reflect the atomic structure of elements, particularly how electrons occupy various energy levels. The period number of an element indicates how many principal energy levels, or shells, contain electrons. Elements in Period 2, such as lithium and oxygen, have electrons in two energy levels: the first (1s2), followed by the second (2s and 2p). Elements in Period 3, such as sodium and chlorine, possess three energy levels, with their outermost electrons residing in the third shell.

Determination of Valence Electrons from Group Number

From the position of an element in a particular group, we can determine the number of valence electrons, the electrons in the outermost shell. This applies to the main group elements in Groups IA to VIIIA, and these valence electrons play a significant role in determining how an element reacts chemically. In Group IA, lithium has one valence electron with the electronic configuration 1s2 2s1. Oxygen, in Group VIA, has six valence electrons with the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p4. In Period 3, sodium, also in Group IA, has one valence electron in the third shell, while chlorine, in Group VIIA, has seven valence electrons.

Trend Across the Periodic Table

Group I elements have one valence electron, and the count increases across the main groups. As we move down the periodic table, the period number increases, meaning that more energy levels are occupied by electrons. For example, potassium in Period 4 and Group I has four energy levels and one valence electron in the fourth shell, as shown by its electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1.

Key Points

  • Period number gives the number of occupied energy levels.
  • For main group elements (IA to VIIIA), the group number gives the number of valence electrons.
  • Valence electrons decide the chemical reactions of an element.
  • Example: K (Period 4, Group I) has 4 shells and 1 valence electron.
lessons.title: Position of an Element and Its Electron Arrangement

mcqs.q: Metals are located in the periodic table on the:
options: Left side and in the centre
mcqs.why: Metals are located on the left side and in the centre of the periodic table, including Groups IA and IIA and the transition metals in the central block.

mcqs.q: Non-metals are located in the periodic table on the:
mcqs.why: Nonmetals are located on the right side of the periodic table, in the upper parts of Groups IVA to VIIIA, including carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and the noble gases.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen is unusual because, although placed in Group IA, it is:
mcqs.why: Hydrogen, although placed in Group IA, is also a nonmetal, as explicitly noted in the notes on the position of nonmetals in the periodic table.

mcqs.q: Metalloids are located along:
options: The stair-step line separating metals from non-metals
mcqs.why: Metalloids (semi-metals) lie along the stair-step line that separates metals from non-metals, and their position shows their dual behaviour between the two.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only metalloids named in the notes?
mcqs.why: The metalloids named in the notes are boron, silicon, arsenic and tellurium, which have intermediate properties between metals and non-metals.

mcqs.q: The transition metals, such as iron, copper and zinc, are found in:
options: The right side, Groups IVA to VIIIA
mcqs.why: Transition metals are found in the central block (Groups 3 (IIIB) to 12 (IIB)), like iron, copper and zinc, and all transition metals are metals.

mcqs.q: Which elements are given in the notes as metals present in the lower parts of Groups IIIA to VIA?
mcqs.why: Some metals, such as aluminium and lead, are also present in the lower parts of Groups IIIA to VIA, even though the upper parts of those groups contain non-metals.

mcqs.q: Metalloids show properties of:
mcqs.why: Metalloids such as B, Si, As and Te show properties of both metals and non-metals; this intermediate, dual behaviour matches their position on the stair-step line.

mcqs.q: Neon and argon are examples of:
options: Noble gases, which are non-metals on the right side
mcqs.why: Nonmetals on the right side include noble gases like neon and argon, along with elements in the upper parts of Groups IVA to VIIIA such as oxygen and fluorine.

mcqs.q: Lithium, sodium, magnesium and calcium are all:
options: Metals in Groups IA and IIA
mcqs.why: Metals include all elements in Groups IA and IIA, such as lithium, sodium, magnesium and calcium, located on the left side of the periodic table.

lessons.notes_html:
From the position of an element in the periodic table, we can identify whether it is a metal, a non-metal or a metalloid.

Position of Metals in the Periodic Table

Metals are located on the left side and in the centre of the periodic table. They include all elements in Groups IA and IIA, such as lithium, sodium, magnesium and calcium, as well as the transition metals found in the central block (Groups 3 (IIIB) to 12 (IIB)), like iron, copper and zinc. Some metals, such as aluminium and lead, are also present in the lower parts of Groups IIIA to VIA.

Position of Nonmetals in the Periodic Table

Nonmetals are located on the right side of the periodic table. They include elements in the upper parts of Groups IVA to VIIIA, such as carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine, and noble gases like neon and argon. Hydrogen, although placed in Group IA, is also a nonmetal.

Position of Metalloids in the Periodic Table

Metalloids (semi-metals) are located along the stair-step line that separates metals from non-metals. These elements, including boron, silicon, arsenic and tellurium, have intermediate properties between metals and non-metals; their position in the periodic table shows this dual behaviour.

Key Points

  • Metals: left side and centre of the table, including all transition metals.
  • Non-metals: right side of the table; hydrogen is a non-metal despite sitting in Group IA.
  • Metalloids lie on the stair-step line between metals and non-metals.
  • Metalloids such as B, Si, As and Te show properties of both metals and non-metals.
lessons.title: Position of Metals, Non-Metals, and Metalloids in the Periodic Table

mcqs.q: Atomic radius is defined as:
options: The full distance between two nuclei in a molecule
Half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together in a molecule
The radius of the nucleus alone
The distance from the nucleus to the first electron only in ions
mcqs.why: Atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together in a molecule, expressed in nm, angstroms or picometres.

mcqs.q: Across a period (left to right), atomic radius decreases because:
options: Shielding removes the nuclear pull completely
Nuclear charge increases, giving a stronger pull on the electrons
mcqs.why: Across a period atomic radius decreases because of an increase in nuclear charge, resulting in a stronger pull on the electrons and a smaller atomic radius.

mcqs.q: Down a group, atomic radius increases due to:
options: A decrease in nuclear charge to zero
An increase in the number of electron shells and the shielding effect of inner electrons
mcqs.why: Atomic radius increases within a group due to an increase in the number of electron shells and the shielding effect of inner electrons, per the notes.

mcqs.q: The radius of Na+ is 97 pm while the Na atom is 186 pm. By how much is the cation smaller?
mcqs.why: Working: difference = atomic radius - cationic radius = 186 pm - 97 pm = 89 pm. Cations are smaller than their parent atoms due to increased nuclear attraction on the remaining electrons.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage decrease in radius when Na (186 pm) forms Na+ (97 pm)?
mcqs.why: Working: decrease = 186 - 97 = 89 pm; percentage decrease = (89 / 186) x 100 = 47.8%. So the Na+ cation is about 47.8% smaller than the sodium atom.

mcqs.q: The radius of Cl- is 181 pm while the Cl atom is 99 pm. The anion is larger by:
mcqs.why: Working: increase = anionic radius - atomic radius = 181 pm - 99 pm = 82 pm. Anions are larger than parent atoms due to increased electron-electron repulsion.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage increase in radius when Cl (99 pm) forms Cl- (181 pm)?
mcqs.why: Working: increase = 181 - 99 = 82 pm; percentage increase = (82 / 99) x 100 = 82.8%. The chloride anion is therefore about 82.8% larger than the chlorine atom.

mcqs.q: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms because of:
options: Increased attraction between the nucleus and the remaining electrons
mcqs.why: When electrons are removed to form cations, the cationic radius is smaller than the parent atomic radius due to increased attraction between the nucleus and the remaining electrons.

mcqs.q: Across a period, the cationic radius decreases while the anionic radius:
options: Also decreases in every case stated
Increases due to greater electron-electron repulsion
mcqs.why: The notes state the cationic radius decreases left to right due to increased nuclear charge, while the anionic radius increases due to greater electron-electron repulsion.

mcqs.q: Ionic radii down a group:
options: Increase due to an increase in the number of shells
mcqs.why: Cationic and anionic radii increase from top to bottom in a group due to an increase in the number of shells, matching the atomic radius group trend.

lessons.notes_html:
The properties of elements are determined by their electronic configurations, specifically the arrangement of electrons in their outermost shells, known as valence electrons. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, resulting in similar chemical properties. Element properties also show periodic trends within the periods of the periodic table.

Atomic Radius

The atomic radius is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together in a molecule, commonly expressed in nanometres (nm), angstroms (Å) or picometres (pm). Group trend (top to bottom): atomic radius increases within a group due to an increase in the number of electron shells and the shielding effect of inner electrons. Period trend (left to right): atomic radius decreases across a period because of an increase in nuclear charge, resulting in a stronger pull on the electrons and a smaller atomic radius.

Ionic Radius

Ionic radii refer to the average distance of the outermost shell electrons from the centre of the nucleus of an ion. When electrons are removed to form cations (positive ions), the resulting cationic radius is smaller than the parent atomic radius due to increased attraction between the nucleus and the remaining electrons; for example, the radius of Na+ (97 pm) is smaller than that of the Na atom (186 pm). Conversely, when electrons are added to form anions (negative ions), the anionic radius is larger than the parent atomic radius due to increased electron-electron repulsion; for instance, the radius of Cl- (181 pm) is larger than that of its parent atom, Cl (99 pm). Group trend: cationic and anionic radii increase from top to bottom in a group due to an increase in the number of shells. Period trend: the cationic radius decreases from left to right due to an increase in nuclear charge, while the anionic radius increases due to greater electron-electron repulsion.

Key Points

  • Valence electrons determine properties; trends repeat across periods and down groups.
  • Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period.
  • Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger.
  • Ionic radii increase down a group; cationic radii decrease across a period.
lessons.title: Periodic Trends: Atomic Radius and Ionic Radius

mcqs.q: Ionisation energy decreases down a group mainly because electrons farther from the nucleus are:
mcqs.why: Electrons farther from the nucleus are removed more easily, whereas stronger nuclear attraction makes removal harder; this explains why ionisation energy decreases down a group.

mcqs.q: Across a period, ionisation energy generally:
mcqs.why: The principles of distance and effective nuclear charge explain why ionisation energy decreases down a group and increases across a period, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Electron affinity follows which pattern?
options: Increases down a group, decreases across a period
Decreases down a group and increases across a period
mcqs.why: Electron affinity follows the same pattern as ionisation energy: down a group it decreases, and across a period it increases, due to nuclear charge, distance and shielding.

mcqs.q: Electronegativity is defined as the ability of an atom to:
options: Attract a shared pair of electrons in a molecule towards itself
mcqs.why: Electronegativity refers to the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a molecule towards itself, and it has no units.

mcqs.q: Electronegativity decreases down a group because of:
options: An increase in atomic size and the shielding effect of inner shells
A stronger nuclear pull on valence electrons
mcqs.why: Down a group electronegativity decreases due to increased atomic size and shielding, because inner shells block the attraction of the nucleus for the valence electrons.

mcqs.q: Which element is described as so electronegative it can even form compounds with noble gases?
mcqs.why: Fluorine is so electronegative that it can even form compounds with noble gases, which were once considered completely inert; fluorine is the most electronegative element.

mcqs.q: When asked about the definition of electron affinity, the notes say to define:
mcqs.why: The notes specifically instruct: when asked about the definition of electron affinity, define the first electron affinity, the tendency related to gaining the first electron.

mcqs.q: A strong nuclear attraction promotes electron gain, while increased distance and shielding:
options: Reduce the tendency to gain an electron
mcqs.why: The tendency to gain an electron depends on the balance of nuclear charge and distance: strong nuclear attraction promotes gain, whereas increased distance and shielding reduce this tendency.

mcqs.q: Electronegativity has:
mcqs.why: Electronegativity, the pull on a shared pair of electrons in a molecule, has no units, unlike ionisation energy and electron affinity which are energies.

mcqs.q: Across a period, electronegativity increases due to:
options: A decrease in atomic size and an increase in nuclear charge
mcqs.why: Across a period electronegativity increases due to a decrease in atomic size and an increase in nuclear charge, so the nucleus attracts bonding electrons more strongly.

lessons.notes_html:
Three more properties show clear periodic trends: ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.

Ionisation Energy (Recall from Unit 2: Atomic Structure)

The energy required to remove an electron mainly depends on the distance from the nucleus and the effective nuclear charge. Electrons that are farther from the nucleus are removed more easily, whereas a stronger nuclear attraction makes removal more difficult. These principles explain why ionisation energy decreases down a group and increases across a period.

Electron Affinity (Recall from Unit 5: Chemical Energetics)

The tendency of an atom to gain an electron depends on the balance between its nuclear charge and the distance of its valence electrons from the nucleus. A strong nuclear attraction promotes electron gain, whereas increased distance and shielding reduce this tendency. These principles also explain why electron affinity decreases down a group and increases across a period. Note: when asked about the definition of electron affinity, define the first electron affinity.

Electronegativity

Electronegativity refers to the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a molecule towards itself. It has no units. Elements with high electronegativity values, such as fluorine, attract bonding electrons more strongly than elements like sodium that have low electronegativity. Group trend (top to bottom): electronegativity decreases down a group due to an increase in atomic size and the shielding effect, because the inner shells block the attraction of the nucleus for the valence electrons. Period trend (left to right): electronegativity increases across a period, due to a decrease in atomic size and an increase in nuclear charge. Fluorine is so electronegative that it can even form compounds with noble gases, which were once considered completely inert.

Key Points

  • Ionisation energy decreases down a group and increases across a period.
  • Electron affinity follows the same pattern: down a group it decreases, across a period it increases.
  • Electronegativity is the pull on a shared pair of electrons and has no units.
  • Electronegativity decreases down a group and increases across a period; fluorine is the most electronegative element.
lessons.title: Ionisation Energy, Electron Affinity and Electronegativity

mcqs.q: Sodium (Group IA, Period 3) has an electron configuration ending with:
mcqs.why: Sodium is in the s-block in Group IA, Period 3, and its configuration ends with 3s1, indicating one valence electron in the 3s orbital, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Calcium (Group 2, Period 4) has an electron configuration ending with:
mcqs.why: Calcium ends with 4s2, showing two valence electrons in the s subshell, consistent with its s-block position in Group 2 and Period 4.

mcqs.q: Oxygen in Group 16 (VIA), Period 2, has a configuration ending with:
mcqs.why: Oxygen is a p-block element whose configuration ends with 2p4; p-block endings run from np1 to np6 and oxygen has four electrons in the 2p subshell.

mcqs.q: Phosphorus in Period 3, Group 15 (VA) has a configuration ending in:
options: 3p3, three electrons in the p subshell
mcqs.why: Phosphorus has a configuration ending in 3p3, which corresponds to three electrons in the p subshell, as given in the notes for the p-block.

mcqs.q: For d-block elements, the number of d electrons is generally given by:
mcqs.why: The group number minus two generally indicates the number of d electrons; for example iron is 3d6 4s2, and iron is in Group 8, so 8 - 2 = 6 d electrons.

mcqs.q: Iron has the electron configuration:
mcqs.why: Iron has an electron configuration of 3d6 4s2, indicating six electrons in the 3d subshell, filled in the (n-1)d subshell of the d-block transition metals.

mcqs.q: Chromium is an exception to the expected configuration because it has:
mcqs.why: Some elements have exceptions to attain greater stability, such as chromium, which has 3d5 4s1 instead of 3d4 4s2; however, these examples are rare.

mcqs.q: Cerium, an f-block element, has a configuration ending in:
options: 4f1 5d1 6s2, with the 4f orbital starting to fill
mcqs.why: Cerium has a configuration ending in 4f1 5d1 6s2, with the 4f orbital starting to fill; f-block elements fill the (n-2)f subshell and sit at the bottom of the table.

mcqs.q: In the d-block, which subshell is being filled?
mcqs.why: The d-block consists of transition metals, where the (n-1)d subshell is filled, e.g. iron fills 3d while its outer electrons are in 4s.

mcqs.q: The s-block elements are found in which groups?
mcqs.why: Elements in Groups IA and IIA are found in the s-block, where the outer electrons occupy the s subshell, giving endings of ns1 or ns2.

lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table is organised to show how electrons fill the different subshells (s, p, d and f) within an atom. The position of an element in the table (its group and period) provides significant information about its electron configuration, particularly the type of subshell filled by the outermost electrons.

The s-block: Groups 1 (IA) and 2 (IIA)

Elements in Groups IA and IIA are found in the s-block, where the outer electrons occupy the s subshell. Sodium (Group IA, Period 3) has an electron configuration that ends with 3s1, indicating one valence electron in the 3s orbital. Calcium (Group 2, Period 4) ends with 4s2, showing two valence electrons in the s subshell.

The p-block: Groups 13 (IIIA) to 18 (VIIIA)

Elements in Groups 13 (IIIA) to 18 (VIIIA) comprise the p-block, and their outermost electrons occupy the p subshell. Oxygen in Group 16 (VIA), Period 2, has an electron configuration ending with 2p4. Phosphorus in Period 3, Group 15 (VA) has a configuration ending in 3p3, which corresponds to three electrons in the p subshell.

The d-block: Transition Metals (Groups 3 to 12)

The d-block consists of transition metals, where the (n-1)d subshell is filled. Iron has an electron configuration of 3d6 4s2, indicating it contains six electrons in the 3d subshell. The group number minus two generally indicates the number of d electrons. Some elements have exceptions in their electron configurations to attain greater stability, such as chromium, which has 3d5 4s1 instead of 3d4 4s2; however, these examples are rare.

The f-block: Lanthanides and Actinides

The f-block elements are positioned separately at the bottom of the periodic table. They include the lanthanides and actinides, where electrons occupy the (n-2)f subshell. For example, cerium has a configuration ending in 4f1 5d1 6s2, with the 4f orbital starting to fill.

Key Points

  • Group and period reveal which subshell the outermost electrons occupy.
  • s-block endings: ns1 or ns2 (Na ends 3s1; Ca ends 4s2).
  • p-block endings: np1 to np6 (O ends 2p4; P ends 3p3).
  • d-block: d electrons = group number - 2 (Fe is 3d6 4s2); Cr is an exception (3d5 4s1).
  • f-block: the (n-2)f subshell fills (Ce ends 4f1 5d1 6s2).
lessons.title: Deducing Electron Configuration from Periodic Table Position

mcqs.q: The equation for sodium reacting with oxygen is:
mcqs.why: The key equations table gives sodium with oxygen as 4Na(s) + O2(g) -> 2Na2O(s), producing sodium oxide, a basic oxide of the Group 1 metal.

mcqs.q: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to produce:
mcqs.why: Magnesium with oxygen follows 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s), producing magnesium oxide, as listed in the key equations for this lesson.

mcqs.q: Sodium reacts with chlorine according to:
mcqs.why: Sodium with chlorine is 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) -> 2NaCl(s), producing sodium chloride; magnesium instead gives MgCl2 by Mg(s) + Cl2(g) -> MgCl2(s).

mcqs.q: Sodium reacts with water to produce:
options: Sodium hydroxide (a strong base) and hydrogen gas
mcqs.why: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g): sodium reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide, a strong base, and hydrogen gas.

mcqs.q: Magnesium reacts with water to produce:
options: Mg(OH)2 and H2, by Mg(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Mg(OH)2(s) + H2(g)
mcqs.why: Magnesium with water follows Mg(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Mg(OH)2(s) + H2(g), producing slightly soluble magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Which gas is produced in BOTH reactions of sodium and magnesium with water?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen gas is produced in both reactions with water: sodium gives NaOH + H2 and magnesium gives Mg(OH)2 + H2, as shown in the key equations.

mcqs.q: How is sodium's reaction with water described, compared with magnesium's?
options: Sodium does not react with water at all
Magnesium reacts more vigorously than sodium
mcqs.why: The notes state sodium reacts vigorously with water to produce the strong base NaOH, while magnesium simply reacts to give slightly soluble Mg(OH)2.

mcqs.q: The chloride formed when magnesium reacts with chlorine is:
mcqs.why: Mg(s) + Cl2(g) -> MgCl2(s): magnesium produces magnesium chloride, MgCl2, because magnesium forms Mg2+ ions and needs two chloride ions.

mcqs.q: Magnesium hydroxide formed from magnesium and water is described as:
mcqs.why: Magnesium reacts with water to produce slightly soluble magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, unlike sodium hydroxide which is a strong, soluble base.

mcqs.q: The oxide formed when sodium reacts with oxygen is:
mcqs.why: Sodium reacts with oxygen to produce sodium oxide, Na2O, by 4Na(s) + O2(g) -> 2Na2O(s); both metals form oxides, Na2O and MgO.

lessons.notes_html:
Sodium and magnesium are reactive metals that form oxides, chlorides and hydroxides when they react with oxygen, chlorine and water.

Key Equations

ReactionEquation
Sodium with oxygen4Na(s) + O2(g) → 2Na2O(s)
Magnesium with oxygen2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s)
Sodium with chlorine2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s)
Magnesium with chlorineMg(s) + Cl2(g) → MgCl2(s)
Sodium with water2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
Magnesium with waterMg(s) + 2H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s) + H2(g)

Notes on the Reactions

  • With oxygen: sodium reacts to produce sodium oxide; magnesium reacts to produce magnesium oxide.
  • With chlorine: sodium produces sodium chloride; magnesium produces magnesium chloride.
  • With water: sodium reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide, a strong base, and hydrogen gas. Magnesium reacts with water to produce slightly soluble magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

Key Points

  • Both metals form oxides (Na2O, MgO) and chlorides (NaCl, MgCl2).
  • Sodium reacts vigorously with water, giving the strong base NaOH.
  • Magnesium gives Mg(OH)2, which is only slightly soluble.
  • Hydrogen gas is produced in both reactions with water.
lessons.title: Reactions of Sodium and Magnesium with Oxygen, Chlorine, and Water

mcqs.q: Sodium has an oxidation state of +1 in Na2O because it:
options: Loses its one valence electron to reach a stable noble gas configuration
mcqs.why: Sodium is a Group 1 member with one valence electron; it loses this electron to reach a stable noble gas configuration, giving an oxidation state of +1 in sodium oxide.

mcqs.q: In magnesium oxide, magnesium has an oxidation state of +2 because it:
options: Loses both of its two valence electrons
mcqs.why: Magnesium is a Group 2 member with two valence electrons; it loses both to achieve a stable configuration, resulting in an oxidation state of +2 in MgO.

mcqs.q: Oxygen has an oxidation state of -2 in both Na2O and MgO because it:
options: Gains two electrons to fill its octet
mcqs.why: Oxygen is more electronegative with six valence electrons, so it gains two electrons to fill its octet, obtaining an oxidation state of -2 in both oxides.

mcqs.q: In NaCl, chlorine has an oxidation state of -1 because it:
options: Accepts one electron to complete its outer shell
mcqs.why: In sodium chloride, sodium donates its single valence electron to chlorine, which accepts one electron to complete its outer shell, giving chlorine an oxidation state of -1.

mcqs.q: In MgCl2, magnesium donates its two valence electrons:
options: One to each of the two chlorine atoms
mcqs.why: In magnesium chloride, magnesium donates two valence electrons, one to each of the two chlorine atoms, giving +2 for magnesium and -1 for each chloride ion.

options: The number of valence electrons it loses
The number of neutrons it has
mcqs.why: The key points state the oxidation number of a metal equals the number of valence electrons it loses: Group 1 metals show +1 and Group 2 metals show +2.

mcqs.q: Group 2 metals show an oxidation state of:
mcqs.why: Group 2 metals show +2 because they lose their two valence electrons, as magnesium does in both MgO and MgCl2, while Group 1 metals show +1.

mcqs.q: Atoms lose or gain electrons in these reactions in order to:
options: Reach a stable noble gas configuration
mcqs.why: Atoms lose or gain electrons to reach a stable noble gas configuration: sodium loses one, magnesium loses two, oxygen gains two and chlorine gains one electron.

mcqs.q: In the table of oxidation states, Na2O is listed as:
mcqs.why: The notes' table lists Na2O as Na: +1 and O: -2, because each sodium loses one electron and oxygen gains two electrons to form O2-.

mcqs.q: Chlorine gains one electron (-1), while oxygen gains two electrons (-2), because:
options: Each gains the number of electrons needed to complete its outer shell
Both gain the same number always
mcqs.why: Chlorine accepts one electron to complete its outer shell (-1), while oxygen, with six valence electrons, gains two to fill its octet (-2), per the notes.

lessons.notes_html:
The variation in the oxidation numbers of sodium and magnesium in their oxides and chlorides can be explained by their electronic configurations and positions in the periodic table, which determine the number of electrons in their outermost (valence) shells.

Oxidation States in Oxides

Sodium is a Group 1 (IA) member and has one electron in its outermost (valence) shell. To reach a stable noble gas configuration, sodium loses this electron, which gives it an oxidation state of +1 in sodium oxide (Na2O). Oxygen is more electronegative and has six valence electrons, so it gains two electrons to fill its octet, obtaining an oxidation state of -2. In magnesium oxide, magnesium is a Group 2 (IIA) member with two valence electrons; it loses both electrons to achieve a stable configuration, resulting in an oxidation state of +2, while oxygen gains two electrons to form O2-, just like in sodium oxide.

Oxidation States in Chlorides

In sodium chloride (NaCl), sodium shows an oxidation state of +1 by donating its single valence electron to chlorine, which accepts one electron to complete its outer shell, resulting in an oxidation state of -1 for chlorine. In magnesium chloride (MgCl2), magnesium donates two valence electrons, one to each of the two chlorine atoms, giving a +2 oxidation state for magnesium and a -1 oxidation state for each chloride ion.

CompoundMetal Oxidation StateNon-metal Oxidation State
Na2ONa: +1O: -2
MgOMg: +2O: -2
NaClNa: +1Cl: -1
MgCl2Mg: +2Cl: -1 (each)

Key Points

  • Oxidation number of a metal equals the number of valence electrons it loses.
  • Group 1 metals show +1; Group 2 metals show +2.
  • Oxygen gains two electrons (-2); chlorine gains one electron (-1).
  • Atoms lose or gain electrons to reach a stable noble gas configuration.
lessons.title: Variation in the Oxidation Number of Oxides and Chlorides of Sodium and Magnesium

mcqs.why: Sodium oxide reacts vigorously and exothermically with water, producing a strong alkaline solution of sodium hydroxide with pH 12 to 14.

Na2O, because NaOH is a strong alkali that forms completely

lessons.notes_html:
Sodium and magnesium form basic oxides (sodium oxide, Na2O, and magnesium oxide, MgO) when they react with oxygen. Due to variations in solubility and reactivity, these oxides show different behaviours when reacting with water, resulting in solutions with distinct pH values.

Reaction of Sodium Oxide with Water

Sodium oxide reacts vigorously and exothermically with water, producing a strong alkaline solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH):

Na2O(s) + H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq)

The resulting sodium hydroxide solution is highly basic, producing a pH range of 12 to 14, depending on the concentration.

Reaction of Magnesium Oxide with Water

Magnesium oxide, a sparingly soluble base, reacts with water to form a suspension of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, which is partly soluble in water:

MgO(s) + H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s)

The solution produced is weakly alkaline, with a pH level ranging from 8 to 10, due to the partial dissociation of magnesium hydroxide in water.

Key Points

  • Na2O and MgO are both basic oxides, but they differ in solubility and strength.
  • Na2O + water gives NaOH, a strong alkali with pH 12-14.
  • MgO + water gives Mg(OH)2, only partly soluble, a weak alkali with pH 8-10.
  • The difference in pH comes from how completely each hydroxide forms and dissociates.

mcqs.why: Acting as an acid, Al(OH)3 reacts with strong bases to produce aluminate ions; with NaOH it produces sodium aluminate: Al(OH)3 + NaOH -> Na[Al(OH)4](aq).

mcqs.q: Magnesium hydroxide is a weak base because of its:
options: Limited dissociation and lower solubility in water
mcqs.why: The lower solubility and weaker basicity of Mg(OH)2 result from its limited dissociation: Mg(OH)2(s) -> Mg2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) occurs only to a small extent.

mcqs.q: Magnesium oxide reacts with water:
options: Slowly, dissolving only partially to form Mg(OH)2
Not at all under any conditions
mcqs.why: Magnesium oxide is significantly less reactive with water than Na2O: it reacts slowly and dissolves only partially, forming magnesium hydroxide, a weak base.

options: Carbon dioxide and water in every case
mcqs.why: Both hydroxides neutralise acids to form a salt and water: NaOH gives NaCl with HCl, and Mg(OH)2 gives MgCl2 with HCl, per the notes.

mcqs.q: The pH of sodium hydroxide solution is typically:
mcqs.why: NaOH completely dissolves and dissociates into Na+ and OH-, giving a very high pH typically ranging from 12 to 14, unlike weak Mg(OH)2 at pH 8-10.

lessons.notes_html:
The oxides and hydroxides of sodium and magnesium behave as bases, while aluminium hydroxide shows the special amphoteric behaviour of reacting with both acids and bases.

Basic Behaviour of Sodium Oxide and Sodium Hydroxide

Sodium oxide, a strong base, reacts vigorously with water to produce sodium hydroxide (NaOH), which completely dissolves in water to create a strongly alkaline solution:

Na2O(s) + H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq)

Sodium hydroxide is highly soluble in water, dissociating completely into sodium ions (Na+) and hydroxide ions (OH-), giving a very high pH, typically ranging from 12 to 14:

NaOH(s) ⇌ Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) (in H2O)

This strong base readily neutralises acids to produce a salt and water, showing typical base behaviour:

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)

Basic Behaviour of Magnesium Oxide and Magnesium Hydroxide

Magnesium oxide is significantly less reactive with water. It reacts slowly and dissolves only partially, forming magnesium hydroxide:

MgO(s) + H2O(l) → Mg(OH)2(s)

The lower solubility and weaker basicity of magnesium hydroxide, in comparison to NaOH, result from the limited dissociation of Mg(OH)2 in water:

Mg(OH)2(s) ⇌ Mg2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) (in H2O)

Although it has limited solubility, the hydroxide ions produced can still neutralise acids, showing weak base characteristics:

Mg(OH)2(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + 2H2O(l)

Amphoteric Behaviour of Aluminium Hydroxide

Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, which means it can react with both acids and bases. It acts as a base and reacts with strong acids to form salts:

Al(OH)3(s) + 3HCl(aq) → AlCl3(aq) + 3H2O(l)

It also acts as an acid and reacts with strong bases to produce aluminate ions; with sodium hydroxide it produces sodium aluminate:

Al(OH)3(aq) + NaOH(aq) → Na[Al(OH)4](aq)

Key Points

  • NaOH is a strong base: fully soluble and completely dissociated, pH 12-14.
  • Mg(OH)2 is a weak base: sparingly soluble and only slightly dissociated.
  • Both hydroxides neutralise acids to form a salt and water.
  • Al(OH)3 is amphoteric: it reacts with acids (forming AlCl3) and with bases (forming aluminate).
lessons.title: Acid-Base Behaviour of Oxides and Hydroxides of Sodium, Magnesium, and Aluminium

mcqs.why: NaCl simply dissolves and dissociates into Na+ and Cl-; these ions do not react further with water, so the solution stays neutral at about pH 7.

mcqs.q: The equation AlCl3(s) + 3H2O(l) -> Al(OH)3(s) + 3HCl(aq) shows that aluminium chloride:
mcqs.why: This hydrolysis equation from the notes shows AlCl3 forming Al(OH)3 and HCl in water; the acid produced explains the acidic pH of 3 to 4.

lessons.notes_html:
Sodium chloride (NaCl), aluminium chloride (AlCl3) and phosphorus trichloride (PCl3) react differently with water, giving solutions of very different pH.

1. Sodium Chloride

Sodium chloride is an ionic compound that dissolves easily in water without undergoing hydrolysis. It dissociates completely into sodium and chloride ions:

NaCl(s) ⇌ Na+(aq) + Cl-(aq) (in H2O)

These ions do not react further with water, so the solution remains neutral with a pH close to 7.

2. Aluminium Chloride

Aluminium chloride is a covalent compound in its anhydrous state. It forms hydrated ions in aqueous solution and hydrolyses in water, forming hydrochloric acid (HCl) and hydrated aluminium ions, which makes the solution acidic:

AlCl3(s) + 3H2O(l) → Al(OH)3(s) + 3HCl(aq)

Al3+(aq) + 3H2O(l) → Al(OH)3(s) + 3H+(aq)

The presence of H+ ions makes aluminium chloride solution usually acidic, with a pH ranging from 3 to 4.

3. Phosphorus Trichloride

Phosphorus trichloride is a covalent compound that reacts violently with water during hydrolysis, producing phosphorus acid (H3PO3) and hydrogen chloride (HCl):

PCl3(l) + 3H2O(l) → H3PO3(aq) + 3HCl(aq)

ChlorideBondingBehaviour in WaterpH of Solution
NaClIonicDissolves; no hydrolysisAbout 7 (neutral)
AlCl3Covalent (anhydrous)Hydrolyses to give HCl3 to 4 (acidic)
PCl3CovalentViolent hydrolysis to H3PO3 and HClStrongly acidic

Key Points

  • NaCl simply dissolves and dissociates; the solution stays neutral (pH about 7).
  • AlCl3 hydrolyses, releasing H+ ions; the solution is acidic (pH 3-4).
  • PCl3 reacts violently with water, forming H3PO3 and HCl.
  • Ionic chlorides dissolve unchanged; covalent chlorides hydrolyse to give acidic solutions.

lessons.notes_html:
The physical and chemical properties of the oxides and chlorides of sodium and magnesium show that all four compounds have ionic bonding.

Bonding in Sodium and Magnesium Oxides

  • Sodium oxide (Na2O): a white, hygroscopic solid that reacts violently with water to produce a highly basic (alkaline) sodium hydroxide solution. It has a high melting point and forms a crystalline solid. These characteristics show that sodium oxide is an ionic compound, in which sodium atoms lose one electron each to become Na+ ions, while oxygen gains two electrons to form O2- ions. The strong electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions makes a stable ionic lattice.
  • Magnesium oxide (MgO): a white, powdery solid with an exceptionally high melting point; it is slightly soluble in water, forming a slightly alkaline solution of magnesium hydroxide. Magnesium donates two electrons to form Mg2+ ions, while oxygen forms O2- ions. The strong ionic bonding indicates its thermal stability and high melting point.

Bonding in Sodium and Magnesium Chlorides

  • Sodium chloride (NaCl): a white, crystalline solid that dissolves readily in water and conducts electricity when melted or in solution, showing ionic bonding. Sodium loses one electron to produce Na+, while chlorine gains one electron to form Cl- ions; the ions are held together in a giant ionic lattice, which explains the high melting point and solubility in water.
  • Magnesium chloride (MgCl2): a deliquescent white solid that dissolves easily in water, conducts electricity when in aqueous solution and has a high melting point, all typical properties of ionic compounds. Magnesium forms Mg2+ ions by losing two electrons, while each chlorine atom gains one electron to become a Cl- ion, arranged in a crystalline lattice.

Key Points

  • Na2O, MgO, NaCl and MgCl2 are all ionic compounds.
  • Signs of ionic bonding: high melting points, crystalline lattices, conductivity when molten or in solution.
  • Electrons are transferred from the metal to the non-metal (Na to Na+, Mg to Mg2+, O to O2-, Cl to Cl-).
  • Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions holds the lattice together.

mcqs.q: Properties of other group members can be predicted from one member because group members share:

options: White, highly soluble ionic solids that produce strongly alkaline solutions with water
mcqs.why: Group IA properties are consistent: other alkali metals like lithium and potassium will also form white, highly soluble ionic solids producing strongly alkaline solutions with water.

mcqs.why: Sodium forms ionic compounds such as sodium oxide (Na2O) and sodium chloride (NaCl); Na2O with water produces NaOH, a strong base, raising the solution pH.

mcqs.why: Magnesium belongs to Group IIA (the alkaline earth metals); it loses two valence electrons to form Mg2+ ions, giving MgO and MgCl2.

mcqs.why: MgO reacts slightly with water to give weakly soluble Mg(OH)2 and a mildly alkaline solution; this is typical of Group 2, whose hydroxides are only mildly alkaline.

mcqs.q: Calcium, strontium and barium are predicted to behave like magnesium because they are:
options: In the same period as magnesium
mcqs.why: Calcium, strontium and barium are Group 2 elements like magnesium, so they form +2 ions and similar oxides and chlorides, with reactivity increasing down the group.

mcqs.q: The Group 1 prediction from periodicity is that all alkali metals form:
options: Ionic oxides and chlorides; oxides give strong alkalis with water
mcqs.why: Group 1 prediction: all form ionic oxides and chlorides, and their oxides give strong alkalis with water, as sodium does in forming NaOH from Na2O.

mcqs.q: When sodium oxide reacts with water, the pH of the solution:
options: Increases, because NaOH is a strong base
mcqs.why: Na2O with water produces sodium hydroxide, a strong base, which increases the pH of the solution; these properties are consistent throughout Group IA.

mcqs.q: Magnesium loses two valence electrons to form:
options: Mg2+ ions, giving MgO and MgCl2
mcqs.why: Magnesium loses two valence electrons to form Mg2+ ions, resulting in compounds such as magnesium oxide (MgO) and magnesium chloride (MgCl2).

lessons.notes_html:
Because elements in the same group have the same valence electron arrangement, the known properties of one member can be used to predict the characteristic properties of the others. This is the power of chemical periodicity.

Group 1: Alkali Metals

Sodium is a member of the alkali metals. It readily loses its electron to form Na+ ions, resulting in the formation of ionic compounds such as sodium oxide (Na2O) and sodium chloride (NaCl). When sodium oxide reacts with water, it produces sodium hydroxide (NaOH), a strong base, which increases the pH of the solution. These properties are consistent throughout Group IA. Therefore, it can be predicted that other alkali metals like lithium and potassium will also form white, highly soluble ionic solids that produce strongly alkaline solutions upon reaction with water.

Group 2: Alkaline Earth Metals

Magnesium belongs to Group IIA (the alkaline earth metals). It loses two valence electrons to form Mg2+ ions, resulting in compounds such as magnesium oxide (MgO) and magnesium chloride (MgCl2). Magnesium oxide reacts slightly with water to produce magnesium hydroxide, which is a weakly soluble compound that results in a mildly alkaline solution. These characteristics are typical of Group 2 elements. This periodic trend suggests that calcium, strontium and barium will show similar behaviours, with increased reactivity and solubility of their hydroxides as we move down the group.

Key Points

  • Group members share properties because they share the same valence electron count.
  • Group 1 prediction: all form ionic oxides and chlorides; oxides give strong alkalis with water.
  • Group 2 prediction: all form +2 ions; hydroxides are only mildly alkaline.
  • Down Group 2, reactivity and hydroxide solubility increase.
lessons.title: Prediction of Characteristic Properties Using Chemical Periodicity

lessons.notes_html:
The nature, position and identity of an unknown element can be deduced step by step from the behaviour of its oxides and chlorides.

Nature of the Elements

The nature of an unknown element can be deduced from the behaviour of its oxides and chlorides. If an oxide reacts with water to produce a basic solution, the element is metallic in nature. For example, one element forms a strongly basic oxide, while another forms a weakly basic oxide; both indicate metallic characteristics.

Oxidation State and Group Position

The oxidation state further indicates the group placement of the elements. An element that forms a +1 ion is characteristic of Group IA, while one that forms a +2 ion is typical of Group IIA.

Bonding Characteristics

The bonding in their oxides and chlorides is ionic because both elements combine with highly electronegative atoms like oxygen and chlorine. The low electronegativities of these metals, compared to oxygen and chlorine, promote electron transfer and confirm their placement in the s-block of the periodic table.

Periodic Table Placement

The unknown elements can be identified from their physical and chemical properties: the element with a +1 oxidation state and a strongly basic oxide is identified as sodium (Na), Group IA, while the element with a +2 oxidation state and a weakly basic oxide is magnesium (Mg), Group IIA.

Key Points

  • A basic oxide points to a metallic element.
  • Oxidation state +1 means Group IA; +2 means Group IIA.
  • Ionic oxides and chlorides with O and Cl confirm a low-electronegativity s-block metal.
  • Worked deduction: +1 with a strongly basic oxide = sodium; +2 with a weakly basic oxide = magnesium.
lessons.title: Deducing the Nature, Position in the Periodic Table, and Identity of Unknown Elements

mcqs.q: The first ionisation energy of lithium is 520.3 kJ/mol and of caesium is 375.7 kJ/mol. The decrease down Group 1 is:
mcqs.why: Working: decrease = IE(Li) - IE(Cs) = 520.3 - 375.7 = 144.6 kJ/mol. Ionisation energy of alkali metals decreases down the group due to increased atomic size.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage decrease in first ionisation energy from Li (520.3) to Cs (375.7 kJ/mol)?
mcqs.why: Working: decrease = 520.3 - 375.7 = 144.6 kJ/mol; percentage decrease = (144.6 / 520.3) x 100 = 27.8%. So IE falls by about 27.8% from Li to Cs.

mcqs.q: The first ionisation energy falls from Na (495.8) to K (418.9 kJ/mol) by:
mcqs.why: Working: decrease = 495.8 - 418.9 = 76.9 kJ/mol. This fits the Group 1 trend of decreasing first ionisation energy down the group as atomic size increases.

mcqs.q: Alkali metals are powerful reducing agents because they have:
options: The lowest first ionisation energies of all elements, with a loosely bound ns1 electron
mcqs.why: Alkali metals have one loosely bound ns1 valence electron and possess the lowest first ionisation energies of all elements, making them powerful reducing agents.

mcqs.q: The electron affinity of Group 1 elements decreases down the group because:
options: Atomic radius increases and the added electron is more shielded and farther from the nucleus
mcqs.why: Electron affinity decreases down Group 1 due to increased atomic radius and shielding: the added electron is more shielded and farther away, so less energy is released.

mcqs.q: The first ionisation energy of fluorine is 1680 kJ/mol and of iodine is 1008 kJ/mol. The decrease is:
mcqs.why: Working: decrease = 1680 - 1008 = 672 kJ/mol. Halogen ionisation energy decreases down the group as atomic size increases with new energy levels.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage decrease in halogen first IE from F (1680) to I (1008 kJ/mol)?
mcqs.why: Working: decrease = 1680 - 1008 = 672 kJ/mol; percentage decrease = (672 / 1680) x 100 = 40.0%. So halogen IE falls by 40.0% from fluorine to iodine.

mcqs.q: Which halogen has the greatest electron affinity, and what is its value in the table?
mcqs.why: Chlorine, not fluorine, has the greatest electron affinity at -349 kJ/mol; the order is Cl greatest, then F (-328), then Br (-325), then I (-295).

mcqs.q: Fluorine's electron affinity is anomalously lower than chlorine's because:
options: Repulsion between electrons in fluorine's compact 2p orbitals and the added electron reduces its tendency to attract an electron
mcqs.why: Fluorine's small size gives high electron density; repulsion between electrons already in its compact 2p orbitals and the added electron reduces its electron affinity below chlorine's.

mcqs.q: Down Group VIIA, ionisation energy decreases because:
options: Outermost electrons move closer to the nucleus
Atomic size increases with new energy levels, so outermost electrons are farther and less strongly attracted
mcqs.why: Down the halogen group, size increases due to added energy levels, so ionisation energy decreases as outermost electrons are farther from and less attracted to the nucleus.

lessons.notes_html:
The first ionisation energies and electron affinities of the Group IA (alkali metal) and Group VIIA (halogen) elements show regular trends down each group.

Trends in First Ionisation Energy of the Group 1 Elements

Alkali metals have one electron in the valence shell (ns1). This ns1 electron is loosely bound to the nucleus and can be easily detached. Therefore, they possess the lowest first ionisation energies of all the elements in the periodic table, making them powerful reducing agents. The ionisation energy of alkali metals decreases down the group due to an increase in atomic size.

ElementLiNaKRbCs
Ionisation energy (kJ/mol)520.3495.8418.9403.0375.7
Electron affinity (kJ/mol)-59.6-52.9-48.4-47.9-45.5

Trends in Electron Affinity of the Group 1 Elements

The electron affinity of alkali metals decreases down the group because of an increase in atomic radius and the shielding effect: the added electron is more shielded from the nucleus and farther from it, so less energy is released when an electron is added to form a negative ion.

Trends in Ionisation Energy of the Group VIIA Elements

Down the group, the size of the atom increases due to the addition of new energy levels. This leads to a decrease in ionisation energy, as the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and less strongly attracted to it.

ElementFClBrI
Ionisation energy (kJ/mol)1680125611421008
Electron affinity (kJ/mol)-328-349-325-295

Trends in Electron Affinity of Group VIIA Elements

Electron affinity values decrease from chlorine to iodine. However, the electron affinity of fluorine is less than that of chlorine. This is due to the smaller size of the fluorine atom: when an extra electron is added, high electron density is produced around the fluoride ion, and the repulsion between the electrons already present in the relatively compact 2p orbitals of fluorine and the electron being added reduces its tendency to attract an electron. Hence chlorine, not fluorine, has the greatest electron affinity; the order of electron affinity values of the halogens is: Cl greatest, then F, then Br, then I.

Key Points

  • Group 1 first IE decreases down the group (Li 520.3 to Cs 375.7 kJ/mol); alkali metals are strong reducing agents.
  • Group 1 electron affinity also decreases down the group as radius and shielding increase.
  • Halogen IE decreases down the group (F 1680 to I 1008 kJ/mol) as atomic size increases.
  • Halogen electron affinity decreases from Cl to I, but F is anomalously lower than Cl because of electron repulsion in its compact 2p orbitals.
lessons.title: Trends in the Ionisation Energies and Electron Affinities of the Group IA and Group VIIA Elements

chapters.title: Unit 9: p-Block Elements: Nitrogen, Sulphur, and Halogens

mcqs.q: What percentage of the Earth's atmosphere is nitrogen, as stated in the notes?

mcqs.q: Why does the strong triple bond make nitrogen unreactive?
