Breaking it needs a great deal of energy
mcqs.why: Breaking the strong triple bond needs a great deal of energy, so nitrogen hardly reacts at room temperature without extreme conditions.

mcqs.q: Why does lack of polarity reduce the reactivity of nitrogen?
options: It reduces attraction to other molecules
It increases the triple bond length
It makes nitrogen ionic in nature
It produces hydroxide ions in water
mcqs.why: Nitrogen is non-polar with electrons evenly distributed, so it attracts other molecules only weakly and chemical reactions are hindered.

mcqs.q: Which process is given as an example that can break the N≡N bond?
mcqs.why: The notes state only lightning strikes or specialised industrial processes such as the Haber process can break the N≡N bond.

mcqs.q: What is the appearance of pure nitrogen?
mcqs.why: The notes describe pure nitrogen as colourless, odourless and relatively unreactive, despite being essential for life.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a use of nitrogen mentioned in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state nitrogen is essential for life and is used for fertilisers, explosives and ammonia production.

mcqs.q: What else, besides high energy, can help nitrogen react?
mcqs.why: The notes state only under extreme conditions, or with the help of catalysts and enzymes, can nitrogen overcome the barriers to reaction.

mcqs.q: What percentage of nitrogen in ammonia, NH3, by mass? (N = 14, H = 1)
mcqs.why: Working: Mr(NH3) = 14 + 3x1 = 17. Percentage of N = (14 / 17) x 100 = 82.35%, verified by calculation.

lessons.notes_html:
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the Earth's atmosphere and belongs to Group VA (15). Pure nitrogen is colourless, odourless and relatively unreactive, yet it is essential for life and is used for fertilisers, explosives and ammonia.

Reasons for Low Reactivity

  • Strong triple bond: the two nitrogen atoms in N2 are joined by a strong triple bond with a high bond dissociation energy of 941 kJ/mol. Breaking this bond needs a great deal of energy, so nitrogen hardly reacts at room temperature.
  • Lack of polarity: nitrogen is a non-polar molecule with electrons evenly distributed between the two atoms. This reduces its attraction to other molecules and hinders chemical reactions.

Only under extreme conditions, or with the help of catalysts and enzymes, can nitrogen overcome these barriers and take part in reactions, as in nitrogen fixation and ammonia production. Only lightning strikes or specialised industrial processes such as the Haber process can break the N≡N bond.

Key Points

  • N2 has a very strong triple bond, bond dissociation energy 941 kJ/mol.
  • N2 is non-polar, so it attracts other molecules only weakly.
  • Nitrogen is therefore unreactive at room temperature despite its abundance.
  • High energy, catalysts or enzymes are needed to make nitrogen react.
lessons.title: The Low Reactivity of Nitrogen

mcqs.q: In Bronsted-Lowry theory, what is a base?
mcqs.why: In the Bronsted-Lowry theory a base is a proton (H+) acceptor and an acid is a proton donor, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why can ammonia act as a Bronsted-Lowry base?
options: It has a lone pair on nitrogen
mcqs.why: Ammonia is a Bronsted-Lowry base because it has a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom which accepts a proton.

mcqs.q: What ion forms when ammonia accepts a proton?
mcqs.why: When ammonia accepts a proton with its lone pair it forms the ammonium ion, NH4+, by NH3 + H+ -> NH4+.

mcqs.q: What is produced when ammonia reacts with water?
mcqs.why: NH3(g) + H2O(l) -> NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq); the OH- ions produced make the ammonia solution alkaline.

mcqs.q: In NH3 + H2O -> NH4+ + OH-, what role does water play?
options: It acts as an oxidising agent
mcqs.why: Here NH3 accepts a proton from water, so ammonia acts as the base and water acts as the acid donating the proton.

mcqs.q: Why is ammonia described as only a weak or low base?
options: Its reaction with water is partial
It has no lone pair at all
mcqs.why: Ammonia is only a weak (low) base because its reaction with water is partial, so only some molecules form OH- ions.

mcqs.q: What is NH4+ in relation to NH3?
mcqs.why: The notes state NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3, formed when the base NH3 gains a proton.

mcqs.q: What forms when ammonia reacts directly with HCl?
mcqs.why: Ammonia reacts directly with acids, for example NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl, forming the salt ammonium chloride.

mcqs.q: What makes an ammonia solution alkaline?
mcqs.why: The proton transfer from water produces OH- ions, and it is these hydroxide ions that make the solution alkaline.

mcqs.q: Which equation correctly shows ammonia acting as a base?
mcqs.why: NH3 + H+ -> NH4+ shows ammonia accepting a proton, which is exactly the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base.

lessons.notes_html:
Ammonia (NH3) is a Bronsted-Lowry base because it has a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom. In the Bronsted-Lowry theory, a base is a proton (H+) acceptor and an acid is a proton donor.

Formation of the Ammonium Ion

When ammonia meets a proton, it readily accepts the proton with its lone pair, forming the ammonium ion (NH4+). With water, the proton transfer is: NH3(g) + H2O(l) → NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq). Here NH3 accepts a proton from water, so ammonia acts as the base and water as the acid; the OH- ions produced make the solution alkaline. Ammonia is only a weak (low) base because this reaction is partial. Ammonia also reacts directly with acids, e.g. NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl.

Key Equations

EquationPoint shown
NH3 + H+ → NH4+Ammonia accepts a proton (base)
NH3(g) + H2O(l) → NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq)Ammonia solution is alkaline

Key Points

  • A Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton; ammonia does this through its lone pair.
  • Proton acceptance converts NH3 into the ammonium ion, NH4+.
  • In water, ammonia produces OH- ions and an alkaline solution.
  • NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3.
lessons.title: The Low Basicity of Ammonia

mcqs.q: What happens when a strong base is added to an ammonium salt?
mcqs.why: A strong base displaces ammonia from ammonium salts: NH4+ + OH- -> NH3(g) + H2O, releasing free ammonia gas.

mcqs.q: In NH4+ + OH- -> NH3 + H2O, what does the OH- ion do?
options: It removes a proton from NH4+
mcqs.why: The hydroxide ion readily removes a proton from the ammonium ion (deprotonates it), forming water and leaving free ammonia.

mcqs.q: Warming an ammonium salt with an alkali is used as what?
mcqs.why: The notes state warming an ammonium salt with an alkali is a test for ammonium salts, as ammonia gas is released.

mcqs.q: How is the ammonia released in this test detected?
options: It turns damp red litmus blue
mcqs.why: The ammonia released is alkaline and turns damp red litmus paper blue, confirming the presence of an ammonium salt.

mcqs.q: What are the products when ammonium chloride is heated?
mcqs.why: On heating NH4Cl(s) -> NH3(g) + HCl(g); ammonium chloride decomposes thermally without any additional base.

mcqs.q: Why is the thermal decomposition of NH4Cl reversible?
mcqs.why: On cooling, the NH3 and HCl gases recombine to form ammonium chloride again, so the change is reversible.

mcqs.q: Which salt is given as an example that decomposes on heating alone?
mcqs.why: The notes give ammonium chloride as the example of an ammonium salt that decomposes on heating without any additional base.

mcqs.q: How many moles of NH3 form from 2 moles of NH4Cl on heating?
mcqs.why: Working: NH4Cl -> NH3 + HCl is a 1:1 ratio, so 2 mol NH4Cl x (1 mol NH3 / 1 mol NH4Cl) = 2 mol NH3, verified.

mcqs.q: What volume at STP is 2 mol of NH3 gas? (1 mol = 22.4 dm3 at STP)
mcqs.why: Working: Volume = moles x 22.4 dm3/mol = 2 x 22.4 = 44.8 dm3 at STP, verified by calculation.

mcqs.q: Besides strong bases, what else displaces ammonia from some ammonium salts?
mcqs.why: Ammonia can be displaced in two ways stated in the notes: by a strong base, and by heat for salts such as NH4Cl.

lessons.notes_html:
Ammonia can be displaced (released) from its ammonium salts in two ways: by a strong base, and by heat.

Reaction with Strong Bases

When a strong base such as sodium hydroxide is added to an ammonium salt, the hydroxide ion readily removes a proton from the ammonium ion (deprotonates it), forming water and leaving behind free ammonia gas: NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq) → NH3(g) + H2O(l). Warming an ammonium salt with an alkali is therefore a test for ammonium salts, and the ammonia released turns damp red litmus paper blue.

Thermal Decomposition

Some ammonium salts, such as ammonium chloride, decompose on heating without any additional base: NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g) (on heating, Δ). On cooling, the two gases recombine to form ammonium chloride again, so the change is reversible.

Key Equations

EquationProcess
NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq) → NH3(g) + H2O(l)Displacement by a strong base
NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g)Thermal decomposition (reversible on cooling)

Key Points

  • Strong bases displace ammonia from ammonium salts as a gas.
  • The OH- ion takes the proton from NH4+, forming water.
  • Ammonium chloride decomposes on heating into NH3 and HCl.
  • The gases recombine on cooling, so the decomposition is reversible.
lessons.title: Displacement of Ammonia from Ammonium Salts through Acid-Base Reactions

mcqs.q: Which natural source gives about 80% of natural NOx emissions?
mcqs.why: The notes state lightning contributes about 80% of natural NOx emissions, far more than the other natural sources listed.

mcqs.q: During which soil processes do bacteria produce NOx as a byproduct?
mcqs.why: Soil bacteria produce NOx as a byproduct during nitrification and denitrification, as part of natural nitrogen cycling in soil.

mcqs.q: Which is a natural source of NOx?
mcqs.why: Natural sources listed in the notes include lightning, soil bacteria, forest fires and volcanic eruptions.

mcqs.q: What is the main man-made source of NOx?
options: Burning fossil fuels in vehicles and industries
mcqs.why: The notes state burning fossil fuels in vehicles, power stations and industries is the main man-made source of NOx.

mcqs.q: How do soil bacteria affect crops, according to the notes?
options: They manage soil fertility and affect crop yields
mcqs.why: The notes state soil bacteria quietly manage soil fertility and affect crop yields through natural nitrogen cycling.

mcqs.q: Which human activity is listed as a man-made NOx source?
mcqs.why: Man-made sources include fuel combustion, industrial processes and agricultural activities, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why are NOx gases a concern?
mcqs.why: The notes describe NOx as harmful gases that damage air quality and occur both naturally and from human activities.

mcqs.q: If natural NOx is 100 units, how much comes from lightning?
mcqs.why: Working: Lightning share = 80% of 100 units = (80 / 100) x 100 = 80 units, as the notes give lightning as about 80%.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only man-made NOx sources?
mcqs.why: Vehicles, power stations and industries burn fossil fuels and are man-made sources; the other lists contain natural sources.

mcqs.q: NOx in the notes refers to which gases?
mcqs.why: NOx means oxides of nitrogen, which occur naturally and from human activities and damage air quality.

lessons.notes_html:
Oxides of nitrogen (NOx) occur both naturally and as a result of human activities. They are harmful gases that damage air quality.

Natural Occurrences of Oxides of Nitrogen

Natural sources of NOx include lightning, soil bacteria, forest fires and volcanic eruptions. Lightning contributes about 80% of natural NOx emissions, while soil bacteria produce NOx as a byproduct during processes like nitrification and denitrification, as part of natural nitrogen cycling in the soil. In this way soil bacteria quietly manage soil fertility and affect crop yields.

Man-Made Occurrences of Oxides of Nitrogen

Man-made sources of NOx include fuel combustion from burning fossil fuels in vehicles, power stations and industries, together with industrial processes and agricultural activities.

Key Points

  • NOx comes from both natural and man-made sources.
  • Lightning gives about 80% of natural NOx emissions.
  • Soil bacteria release NOx during nitrification and denitrification.
  • Burning fossil fuels in vehicles and industries is the main man-made source.
lessons.title: Natural and Man-made Occurrences of Oxides of Nitrogen (NOx)

mcqs.q: Which metals are used in three-way catalysts?
mcqs.why: Three-way catalysts use precious metals rhodium, platinum and palladium to treat NOx, CO and hydrocarbons simultaneously.

mcqs.q: What does a three-way catalyst treat simultaneously?
mcqs.why: The notes state three-way catalysts reduce NOx, carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons simultaneously in a catalytic converter.

mcqs.q: In Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR), what is injected into the exhaust?
mcqs.why: In SCR, ammonia or urea is injected into the exhaust stream to react with NOx over a catalyst, forming nitrogen and water.

mcqs.q: What are the products when SCR reduces NOx?
mcqs.why: SCR reacts ammonia or urea with NOx over a catalyst forming nitrogen and water, both harmless products.

mcqs.q: Where is SCR widely used?
options: In diesel vehicles and power plants
mcqs.why: The notes state SCR is widely used in diesel vehicles and power plants to reduce NOx emissions from exhaust gases.

mcqs.q: How do Lean NOx Traps (LNT) work?
options: They capture NOx when lean and reduce it when rich
mcqs.why: LNT traps capture NOx under lean (oxygen-rich) conditions and release and reduce it under rich conditions using stored hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Which equation shows reduction of NO with CO?
mcqs.why: The notes give 2NO(g) + 2CO(g) -> N2(g) + 2CO2(g) as the reduction of NO with CO in catalytic removal.

mcqs.q: What are the final harmless products of catalytic removal?
mcqs.why: The notes state the end products are harmless N2, CO2 and H2O, improving air quality and protecting the environment.

mcqs.q: What does lean mean in Lean NOx Traps?
mcqs.why: Lean means oxygen-rich conditions, under which LNT traps capture NOx before reducing it under rich conditions.

mcqs.q: Which equation shows oxidation of carbon monoxide?
mcqs.why: The notes give 2CO(g) + O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) as the oxidation of CO occurring in the catalytic converter.

lessons.notes_html:
Catalytic removal of NOx from exhaust gases uses three main methods, which convert harmful gases into harmless nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water.

Three-Way Catalysts

Three-way catalysts use precious metals such as rhodium, platinum and palladium to reduce NOx, carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons simultaneously in a catalytic converter.

Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR)

In SCR, ammonia or urea is injected into the exhaust stream to react with NOx over a catalyst, forming nitrogen and water. It is widely used in diesel vehicles and power plants.

Lean NOx Traps (LNT)

LNT traps capture NOx under lean (oxygen-rich) conditions and subsequently release and reduce it under rich conditions using stored hydrocarbons.

Key Equations

ReactionEquation
Reduction of NO2NO(g) → N2(g) + O2(g)
Reduction of NO with CO2NO(g) + 2CO(g) → N2(g) + 2CO2(g)
Oxidation of CO2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g)
Oxidation of unburnt hydrocarbonsCxHy + O2(g) → CO2(g) + H2O(g)

These catalytic processes are essential for reducing emissions from engines and other fuel-burning sources, improving air quality and protecting the environment.

Key Points

  • Three-way catalysts use Rh, Pt and Pd and treat NOx, CO and hydrocarbons together.
  • SCR uses ammonia or urea to reduce NOx to N2 and water.
  • Lean NOx traps store NOx when lean and reduce it when rich.
  • The end products are harmless N2, CO2 and H2O.
lessons.title: Catalytic Removal from Exhaust Gases

mcqs.q: What is nitrification?
options: Oxidation of ammonia to nitrite then nitrate
mcqs.why: Nitrification is the biological conversion of ammonia or ammonium to nitrite (NO2-) and then to nitrate (NO3-).

mcqs.q: What is denitrification?
options: Reduction of nitrate back to nitrogen gas
mcqs.why: Denitrification is the biological reduction of nitrate or nitrite back to nitrogen gas or nitrous oxide, the opposite of nitrification.

mcqs.q: Which bacteria convert ammonia to nitrite in nitrification?
mcqs.why: Ammonia-oxidising bacteria (AOB) such as Nitrosomonas convert ammonia or ammonium into nitrite in the first step.

mcqs.q: Which bacteria oxidise nitrite to nitrate?
mcqs.why: Nitrite-oxidising bacteria (NOB) such as Nitrobacter further oxidise nitrite into nitrate: NO2- + 0.5O2 -> NO3-.

mcqs.q: Under what conditions does nitrification take place?
mcqs.why: Nitrification takes place under aerobic conditions and is performed by two groups of specialised autotrophic bacteria.

mcqs.q: Under what conditions does denitrification occur?
mcqs.why: Denitrification is performed by Pseudomonas and Paracoccus under anaerobic conditions, using nitrate as an electron acceptor.

mcqs.q: What is the overall equation for nitrification?
mcqs.why: The notes give the overall nitrification equation as NH4+ + 2O2 -> NO3- + 2H+ + H2O, combining both oxidation steps.

mcqs.q: Why is nitrification useful to farmers and plants?
options: It converts fertiliser ammonium to usable nitrate
mcqs.why: Farmers apply ammonium fertilisers and nitrifying bacteria convert them into nitrates that plants can use for growth.

mcqs.q: What is the result of denitrification for the soil?
options: It removes nitrate from the soil
mcqs.why: Denitrification removes nitrate from the soil by reducing it to nitrogen gas, unlike nitrification which produces usable nitrate.

mcqs.q: Which pair carries out denitrification?
mcqs.why: The comparison table in the notes lists Pseudomonas and Paracoccus as the microorganisms that carry out denitrification.

lessons.notes_html:
Nitrification is the biological process of converting ammonia (NH3) or ammonium (NH4+) to nitrite (NO2-) and then to nitrate (NO3-). Denitrification is the opposite process: the biological reduction of nitrate or nitrite back to nitrogen gas or nitrous oxide.

Nitrification

Nitrification takes place under aerobic conditions and is performed by two groups of specialised autotrophic bacteria. Ammonia-oxidising bacteria (AOB), such as Nitrosomonas, convert ammonia or ammonium into nitrite: NH4+ + 1.5O2 → NO2- + 2H+ + H2O. Nitrite-oxidising bacteria (NOB), such as Nitrobacter, further oxidise nitrite into nitrate: NO2- + 0.5O2 → NO3-. Overall: NH4+ + 2O2 → NO3- + 2H+ + H2O. Farmers apply ammonium fertilisers, and nitrifying bacteria convert them into nitrates that plants can use.

Denitrification

Denitrification is performed by bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Paracoccus under anaerobic conditions, using organic matter as an energy source and nitrate as an electron acceptor: 2NO3- + 10e- + 12H+ → N2 + 6H2O.

Comparison

FeatureNitrificationDenitrification
ProcessOxidation of ammonia/ammoniumReduction of nitrate/nitrite
Starting compoundAmmoniaNitrate or nitrite
Ending compoundNitrateNitrogen gas or nitrous oxide
MicroorganismsNitrosomonas, NitrobacterPseudomonas, Paracoccus
Oxygen requirementAerobicAnaerobic
ResultProduces usable nitrate for plantsRemoves nitrate from the soil

Key Points

  • Nitrification is an aerobic oxidation: NH3/NH4+ → NO2- → NO3-.
  • Denitrification is an anaerobic reduction: NO3- → N2.
  • Nitrification makes nitrogen available to plants; denitrification removes it.
  • Both processes are essential parts of the nitrogen cycle.
lessons.title: Difference between Nitrification and Denitrification

mcqs.q: To which group does sulphur belong?
mcqs.why: The notes state sulphur belongs to Group VIA (16) and is the tenth most abundant element in the Earth's crust.

mcqs.q: In what form does sulphur occur in nature?
mcqs.why: Sulphur occurs in nature as S8, in which eight atoms form a stable ring connected by covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: Why do S8 rings make sulphur less reactive?
options: The S-S bonds need much energy to break
mcqs.why: The S-S bonds in S8 rings are relatively strong and require significant energy to break, which makes sulphur less reactive.

mcqs.q: What range of oxidation states can sulphur show?
mcqs.why: The notes state sulphur can show various oxidation states ranging from -2 to +6, which limits its tendency to gain or lose electrons.

mcqs.q: Which stable compounds of sulphur are named in the notes?
mcqs.why: Sulphur forms stable compounds such as hydrogen sulphide (H2S) and sulphur dioxide (SO2) with strong covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: What was sulphur once called?
mcqs.why: The notes state sulphur is a bright yellow element, once called brimstone, found in volcanic regions.

mcqs.q: Where is sulphur commonly found in nature?
mcqs.why: The notes state sulphur is found in volcanic regions and is the tenth most abundant element in the Earth's crust.

mcqs.q: What is needed to make sulphur react despite its low reactivity?
mcqs.why: Sulphur is not entirely inert but reacts under specific conditions, for example on heating, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: How many atoms are in one S8 ring molecule?
mcqs.why: In S8, eight sulphur atoms form a stable ring connected by covalent S-S bonds, giving the molecule its low reactivity.

mcqs.q: Why do multiple oxidation states limit sulphur reactivity?
options: It has no strong tendency to gain or lose electrons
mcqs.why: Because sulphur can exist in many oxidation states, it does not have a strong tendency to gain or lose electrons, limiting reactivity.

lessons.notes_html:
Sulphur is the tenth most abundant element in the Earth's crust and belongs to Group VIA (16). It is a bright yellow element, once called brimstone, found in volcanic regions. Its lack of reactivity can be explained by a combination of factors.

Strong S-S Bonds in S8 Molecules

Sulphur occurs in nature as S8, in which eight atoms form a stable ring connected by covalent bonds. The S-S bonds in these rings are relatively strong and require a significant amount of energy to break, which makes sulphur less reactive.

Multiple Oxidation States

Sulphur can show various oxidation states, ranging from -2 to +6. Because it can exist in many oxidation states, it does not have a strong tendency to gain or lose electrons, which limits its reactivity.

Formation of Stable Compounds

Sulphur readily forms stable compounds with many elements, often with strong covalent bonds, such as hydrogen sulphide (H2S) and sulphur dioxide (SO2), which do not readily undergo further reactions under normal conditions. Sulphur is not entirely inert, however, and reacts under specific conditions, for example on heating.

Key Points

  • Sulphur exists as stable S8 rings with strong S-S bonds.
  • Breaking the S-S bonds needs considerable energy.
  • Sulphur shows oxidation states from -2 to +6.
  • It forms very stable compounds such as H2S and SO2.
  • Heat or specific conditions are needed to make sulphur react.
lessons.title: The Low Reactivity of Sulphur

mcqs.q: What forms when sulphur burns in oxygen?
mcqs.why: Sulphur reacts with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide: S(s) + O2(g) -> SO2(g), with delta H = -297 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: What is the enthalpy change for S + O2 -> SO2?
mcqs.why: The notes give the combustion of sulphur as S + O2 -> SO2 with delta H = -297 kJ/mol, an exothermic reaction.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst is used to oxidise SO2 to SO3?
mcqs.why: SO2 is oxidised to SO3 over a V2O5 catalyst: 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3, with delta H = -199 kJ/mol as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What forms when sulphur reacts with chlorine?
mcqs.why: With chlorine, S8(s) + 4Cl2(g) -> 4S2Cl2(l), forming sulphur chloride S2Cl2 as stated in the key equations.

mcqs.q: What forms when sulphur reacts with fluorine?
mcqs.why: With fluorine, S(s) + 3F2(g) -> SF6(g), oxidising sulphur to its highest state in sulphur hexafluoride.

mcqs.q: What mass of SO2 forms from 16 g of sulphur? (S = 32, SO2 = 64)
mcqs.why: Working: Moles S = 16 / 32 = 0.5 mol. S + O2 -> SO2 is 1:1, so SO2 = 0.5 mol x 64 g/mol = 32 g, verified.

mcqs.q: In which amino acids is sulphur present?
mcqs.why: The notes state sulphur is present in the amino acids cysteine and methionine, which stabilise proteins in hair, nails and enzymes.

mcqs.q: What happens to the oxidation state of sulphur in these reactions?
options: It rises from 0 to higher states
mcqs.why: These reactions oxidise sulphur from 0 to higher oxidation states, for example +4 in SO2 and +6 in SF6 and SO3.

mcqs.q: What is the enthalpy change for 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3?
mcqs.why: The notes give the further oxidation 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3 (V2O5 catalyst) with delta H = -199 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Sulphur reactions such as combustion occur especially when?
mcqs.why: The notes state sulphur takes part in combustion and oxidation especially on heating, overcoming its low reactivity.

lessons.notes_html:
Sulphur takes part in reactions such as combustion and oxidation, especially on heating.

Combustion

Sulphur reacts with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide. Under specific conditions, sulphur dioxide can further react with oxygen to yield sulphur trioxide.

Oxidation

Sulphur reacts with halogens such as chlorine and fluorine to form sulphur chlorides and fluorides, oxidising sulphur to higher states.

Key Equations

ReactionEquation
Combustion of sulphurS(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g), ΔH = -297 kJ/mol
Further oxidation2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g) (V2O5 catalyst), ΔH = -199 kJ/mol
With chlorineS8(s) + 4Cl2(g) → 4S2Cl2(l)
With fluorineS(s) + 3F2(g) → SF6(g)

Sulphur is also present in the amino acids cysteine and methionine, which help stabilise protein structures in hair, nails and enzymes.

Key Points

  • Sulphur burns in oxygen to give SO2.
  • SO2 is oxidised to SO3 over a V2O5 catalyst.
  • With halogens, sulphur forms compounds such as S2Cl2 and SF6.
  • These reactions oxidise sulphur from 0 to higher oxidation states.
lessons.title: Reactions of Sulphur

mcqs.q: Who first prepared sulphuric acid, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid was first prepared by the Muslim chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan in the eighth century, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is sulphuric acid called the king of chemicals?
options: It is the strongest acid known
It is used to make many industrial products
It was made by a king
mcqs.why: It is called the king of chemicals because it is used to manufacture many products including fertilisers, detergents, paints and dyes.

mcqs.q: What was sulphuric acid once called?
mcqs.why: The notes state sulphuric acid was once called oil of vitriol before becoming known as the king of chemicals.

mcqs.q: In the Contact process, SO3 is absorbed in what?
mcqs.why: SO3 is absorbed in 98% sulphuric acid to form oleum (H2S2O7), not directly in water, in step 3 of the Contact process.

mcqs.q: What is oleum also called?
mcqs.why: Oleum, H2S2O7, formed by SO3 + H2SO4 -> H2S2O7, is also called fuming sulphuric acid in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the final step of the Contact process?
mcqs.why: Finally oleum is mixed with water: H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4, giving sulphuric acid of any desired concentration.

mcqs.q: How many moles of H2SO4 form from 1 mole of oleum on dilution?
mcqs.why: Working: H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4 is a 1:2 ratio, so 1 mol oleum gives 2 mol H2SO4, verified from the equation.

mcqs.q: What mass of H2SO4 forms from 178 g (1 mol) of oleum? (H2SO4 = 98)
mcqs.why: Working: 1 mol oleum gives 2 mol H2SO4. Mass = 2 x 98 g/mol = 196 g of sulphuric acid, verified by calculation.

mcqs.q: What are the freezing and boiling points of sulphuric acid?
mcqs.why: The notes give the freezing point of sulphuric acid as 10.5 degrees C and its boiling point as around 338 degrees C.

mcqs.q: Which property explains why H2SO4 absorbs moisture from air?
options: It is a powerful dehydrating agent
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid is a powerful dehydrating agent with strong affinity for water and absorbs moisture from the atmosphere.

lessons.notes_html:
Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) was first prepared by the Muslim chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan in the eighth century. Once called 'oil of vitriol', it is now known as the 'king of chemicals' because it is used to manufacture many industrial products, including fertilisers, detergents, paints and dyes.

Production: The Contact Process

Sulphuric acid is primarily prepared by the Contact process, in four steps:

  • Formation of SO2: sulphur is burnt in air (oxygen): S + O2 → SO2.
  • Formation of SO3: dry, pure SO2 is oxidised to sulphur trioxide over a catalyst: 2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3 (V2O5).
  • Formation of oleum: SO3 is absorbed in 98% sulphuric acid to form oleum, or fuming sulphuric acid (H2S2O7): SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7.
  • Dilution: the oleum is mixed with water to obtain pure sulphuric acid of any desired concentration: H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4.

Physical Properties

Sulphuric acid is a colourless, oily liquid. It is a powerful dehydrating agent with a strong affinity for water and absorbs moisture from the atmosphere. It is a strong acid that dissociates in water, releasing heat. Pure sulphuric acid is a non-conductor of electricity, but adding water makes it a good conductor. It is highly corrosive to skin and burns animal tissues. Its freezing point is 10.5°C and its boiling point is around 338°C.

Key Points

  • H2SO4 is made by the Contact process: SO2 → SO3 → oleum → acid.
  • SO3 is absorbed in 98% acid, not directly in water.
  • It is a colourless, oily, highly corrosive liquid.
  • Freezing point 10.5°C; boiling point about 338°C.
  • It has a strong affinity for water and is a powerful dehydrating agent.
lessons.title: Sulphuric Acid

mcqs.q: What gas forms when dilute H2SO4 reacts with zinc?
mcqs.why: Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g); dilute acid gives hydrogen with metals above hydrogen in the activity series.

mcqs.q: What gas forms when dilute H2SO4 reacts with carbonates?
mcqs.why: Na2CO3 + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + CO2 + H2O; carbonates give carbon dioxide with dilute sulphuric acid as a typical acid.

mcqs.q: What gas forms when dilute H2SO4 reacts with metal sulphides?
mcqs.why: FeS + H2SO4 -> FeSO4 + H2S(g); metal sulphides give hydrogen sulphide gas with dilute sulphuric acid.

mcqs.q: What gas forms when dilute H2SO4 reacts with metal sulphites?
mcqs.why: Na2SO3 + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + SO2 + H2O; metal sulphites give sulphur dioxide with dilute sulphuric acid.

mcqs.q: Why does copper not react with dilute sulphuric acid?
options: Copper is below hydrogen in the series
mcqs.why: Metals below hydrogen, like copper, do not react with dilute acid; only metals above hydrogen give hydrogen and a sulphate.

mcqs.q: Concentrated H2SO4 displaces which acid from NaCl on heating?
mcqs.why: NaCl + H2SO4(conc.) -> NaHSO4 + HCl(g); the non-volatile concentrated acid displaces volatile HCl from its salt.

mcqs.q: What does hot concentrated H2SO4 release that oxidises other substances?
mcqs.why: When heated it decomposes as H2SO4(conc.) -> H2O + SO2 + [O]; the nascent oxygen oxidises metals and non-metals.

mcqs.q: What happens when concentrated H2SO4 acts on sugar or glucose?
options: It chars it to black carbon
mcqs.why: As a dehydrating agent it removes water: C6H12O6 -> 6C + 6H2O, charring sugar/glucose to black carbon.

mcqs.q: What is the percentage of sulphur in H2SO4 by mass? (H=1, S=32, O=16)
mcqs.why: Working: Mr(H2SO4) = 2x1 + 32 + 4x16 = 98. Percentage S = (32 / 98) x 100 = 32.65%, verified by calculation.

mcqs.q: How is a country's industrial progress judged, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The key points state a country's industrial progress is judged by its annual H2SO4 consumption, showing the acid's importance.

lessons.notes_html:
The chemical behaviour of sulphuric acid depends on whether it is dilute or concentrated.

Properties of Dilute Sulphuric Acid

ReactionEquation
With active metalsZn(s) + H2SO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g)
Neutralisation with basesH2SO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l)
With carbonatesNa2CO3(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)
With bicarbonatesNaHCO3(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → NaHSO4(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)
With metal sulphidesFeS(s) + H2SO4(aq) → FeSO4(aq) + H2S(g)
With metal sulphitesNa2SO3(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → Na2SO4(aq) + SO2(g) + H2O(l)

Dilute acid reacts with metals above hydrogen in the activity series, giving hydrogen and a metallic sulphate; metals below hydrogen, like copper, do not react.

Properties of Concentrated Sulphuric Acid

  • Non-volatile nature: it displaces volatile acids from their salts, e.g. NaCl(s) + H2SO4(conc.) → NaHSO4(s) + HCl(g) and NaNO3(s) + H2SO4(conc.) → NaHSO4(s) + HNO3(g) (on heating).
  • Oxidising properties: when heated, it decomposes to release nascent oxygen, H2SO4(conc.) → H2O(l) + SO2(g) + [O], which oxidises metals and non-metals: C(s) + 2H2SO4(conc.) → CO2(g) + 2SO2(g) + 2H2O(l); S(s) + 2H2SO4(conc.) → 3SO2(g) + 2H2O(l); 2P(s) + 6H2SO4(conc.) → 2H3PO4(aq) + 3SO2(g).
  • As a dehydrating agent: it removes water from organic and inorganic compounds: C6H12O6(s) → 6C(s) + 6H2O(l) (charring of sugar/glucose to black carbon); C2H5OH(l) → C2H4(g) + H2O(l); CuSO4.5H2O(s) → CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l).

Applications

  • Manufacture of fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate and calcium superphosphate.
  • In lead storage batteries; refining of petroleum; production of explosives such as nitroglycerin.
  • Manufacture of dyes, paints, plastics, detergents and pharmaceuticals.
  • In the paper, iron, steel, leather and textile industries, and in the electrolytic purification of metals.

Key Points

  • Dilute H2SO4 behaves as a typical acid: H2 with active metals, CO2 with carbonates, H2S with sulphides, SO2 with sulphites.
  • Concentrated H2SO4 is non-volatile and displaces volatile acids from their salts.
  • Hot concentrated acid is an oxidising agent, releasing nascent oxygen.
  • It is a strong dehydrating agent and chars sugar to black carbon.
  • A country's industrial progress is judged by its annual H2SO4 consumption.
lessons.title: Chemical Properties

mcqs.q: Why are halogens called salt formers?
options: They react directly with metals to form salts
They are found in table salt only
mcqs.why: The halogens (Group VIIA, 17) are called salt formers because they react directly with metals to form salts.

mcqs.q: What is the colour of fluorine gas?
mcqs.why: The table in the notes gives fluorine as a pale-yellow gas, the lightest colour, deepening down the group to iodine.

mcqs.q: What is the physical state of bromine at normal conditions?
mcqs.why: Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid and is the only non-metallic element that is a liquid under normal conditions.

mcqs.q: What is the colour and state of iodine?
mcqs.why: The notes give iodine as a lustrous violet black solid, the darkest halogen, showing colours deepen down the group.

mcqs.q: What is the order of volatility for the halogens?
mcqs.why: Volatility decreases down the group as London forces strengthen, so the order is F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

mcqs.q: Why do London forces become stronger down the halogen group?
options: Electron clouds get larger and distort more easily
mcqs.why: Down the group atomic size and electron number increase; larger electron clouds distort more easily, so London forces strengthen.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of halogen bond strength?
mcqs.why: Bond dissociation energies give Cl2 243, Br2 193, F2 158, I2 151 kJ/mol, so the order is Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2.

mcqs.q: Why is the F-F bond weaker than the Cl-Cl bond?
options: Lone pair repulsion between small fluorine atoms
mcqs.why: Small fluorine atoms bring dense lone pair clouds close together and the repulsion destabilises the F-F bond, weakening it.

mcqs.q: Which halogen has the strongest bond and its energy?
mcqs.why: The notes give Cl2 the highest bond dissociation energy at about 243 kJ/mol, making it the strongest halogen bond.

mcqs.q: How much stronger is the Cl-Cl bond than the I-I bond?
mcqs.why: Working: Cl2 = 243 kJ/mol and I2 = 151 kJ/mol. Difference = 243 - 151 = 92 kJ/mol, verified by calculation.

lessons.notes_html:
The halogens (Group VIIA, 17) are called 'salt formers' because they react directly with metals to form salts. Their properties change in regular trends down the group.

Trends in Colours

The colours of the halogens become darker down the group from fluorine to iodine. As atomic size increases, the electron clouds become more diffuse and electrons are excited and de-excited more easily, so the colours deepen.

ElementF2Cl2Br2I2
Physical stateGasGasLiquidSolid
ColourPale-yellowGreenish-yellowReddish-brownLustrous violet black

Trends in Volatility

Halogens form simple diatomic molecules that are non-polar; the only intermolecular forces between them are weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces). Down the group, atomic size and the number of electrons increase, the larger electron clouds are distorted more easily, and the London forces become stronger. More energy is then needed to separate the molecules, so volatility decreases: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Bromine is the only non-metallic element that is a liquid under normal conditions.

Trends in Bond Strength

Bond strength generally decreases down the group because the larger atoms overlap their orbitals less effectively. However, the F-F bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond, because the small fluorine atoms bring their dense lone pair electron clouds close together and the repulsion destabilises the bond. Bond dissociation energies (kJ/mol): Cl2 ~243 (strongest), Br2 ~193, F2 ~158, I2 ~151 (weakest). Order of bond strength: Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2.

Key Points

  • Halogen colours deepen down the group: pale-yellow to violet-black.
  • Volatility decreases down the group as London forces strengthen.
  • States change down the group: gas, gas, liquid, solid.
  • Bond strength order is Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2.
  • The F-F bond is weakened by lone pair repulsion between the small atoms.
lessons.title: Trends of Group VIIA Elements

mcqs.q: Why are halogens strong oxidising agents?
options: They easily accept an electron to complete their octet
mcqs.why: Halogens gain one electron to complete their octet, so they oxidise other species and are strong oxidising agents.

mcqs.q: What is the order of oxidising power of the halogens?
mcqs.why: Oxidising power decreases down the group as size increases and electronegativity decreases: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

mcqs.q: Which halogen is the strongest oxidising agent?
mcqs.why: Fluorine, the smallest and most electronegative halogen, is the strongest oxidising agent in the group.

mcqs.q: What happens when Cl2 is added to bromide ions?
mcqs.why: Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2; chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent and oxidises bromide ions below it in the group.

mcqs.q: What happens when Cl2 is added to fluoride ions?
mcqs.why: The table states Cl2 + 2F- -> no action, because chlorine cannot oxidise the fluoride ions of a halogen above it.

mcqs.q: Which halide ions can bromine oxidise?
mcqs.why: Bromine oxidises iodide ions below it but not chloride or fluoride ions above it, following the displacement rule in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which halide ions can iodine oxidise?
options: None of the other halide ions
mcqs.why: The notes state iodine oxidises none of the other halide ions because it is the weakest oxidising halogen in the group.

mcqs.q: Why does oxidising power decrease down the group?
options: Atomic size increases and electronegativity decreases
mcqs.why: Down the group atomic size increases and electronegativity decreases, so halogens accept electrons less easily and oxidise less strongly.

mcqs.q: In F2 + 2I- -> 2F- + I2, which species is oxidised?
mcqs.why: Iodide ions I- lose electrons to form I2, so they are oxidised, while fluorine gains electrons and acts as the oxidising agent.

mcqs.q: A halogen displaces halide ions of halogens in which position?
mcqs.why: A stronger oxidising halogen displaces the halide ions of halogens below it; no halogen oxidises halides of halogens above it.

lessons.notes_html:
Halogens are strong oxidising agents because they can easily accept an electron to complete their octet. Their oxidising power decreases down the group, because atomic size increases and electronegativity decreases: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Fluorine, the smallest and most electronegative halogen, is the strongest oxidising agent.

Displacement Reactions

A stronger oxidising halogen oxidises (displaces) the halide ions of the halogens below it:

ReactionResult
F2(g) + 2Cl-(aq) → 2F-(aq) + Cl2(g)Fluorine oxidises chloride ions
F2(g) + 2Br-(aq) → 2F-(aq) + Br2(l)Fluorine oxidises bromide ions
F2(g) + 2I-(aq) → 2F-(aq) + I2(s)Fluorine oxidises iodide ions
Cl2(g) + 2F-(aq) → no actionChlorine cannot oxidise fluoride ions
Cl2(g) + 2Br-(aq) → 2Cl-(aq) + Br2(l)Chlorine oxidises bromide ions
Cl2(g) + 2I-(aq) → 2Cl-(aq) + I2(s)Chlorine oxidises iodide ions

In the same way, bromine oxidises iodide ions but not chloride or fluoride ions, and iodine oxidises none of the other halide ions.

Key Points

  • Halogens gain one electron to complete their octet, so they oxidise other species.
  • Oxidising power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • A halogen displaces the halide ions of halogens below it in the group.
  • No halogen can oxidise the halide ions of a halogen above it.
lessons.title: Relative Reactivity of Halogens as Oxidising Agents

mcqs.q: What is the general equation for halogens reacting with hydrogen?
mcqs.why: All halogens form hydrogen halides with the general redox equation X2 + H2 -> 2HX, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: How does fluorine react with hydrogen?
options: Explosively, even in the dark at very low temperature
mcqs.why: F2 + H2 -> 2HF reacts explosively, even in the dark and at very low temperature, showing fluorine is most reactive.

mcqs.q: What conditions does chlorine need to react with hydrogen?
mcqs.why: Cl2 + H2 -> 2HCl needs heat or light (diffused sunlight), less drastic than fluorine but more than bromine and iodine need initially.

mcqs.q: What conditions does iodine need to react with hydrogen?
options: High temperature 450 C and a Pt catalyst
mcqs.why: I2 + H2 ⇌ 2HI needs high temperature (450 C) and a Pt catalyst; the reaction is slow and reversible.

mcqs.q: Which halogen-hydrogen reaction is slow and reversible?
mcqs.why: The iodine reaction I2 + H2 ⇌ 2HI is slow and reversible, unlike the vigorous fluorine and chlorine reactions.

mcqs.q: What volume of HCl forms from 10 cm3 H2 and excess Cl2?
mcqs.why: Working: Cl2 + H2 -> 2HCl gives 2 volumes from 1 volume H2, so 10 cm3 H2 gives 2 x 10 = 20 cm3 HCl, verified.

mcqs.q: What is the order of reactivity with hydrogen down the group?
mcqs.why: Reactivity with hydrogen falls down the group F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2, so reaction conditions become more drastic.

mcqs.q: What type of reaction is X2 + H2 -> 2HX?
mcqs.why: The notes state these are redox reactions: hydrogen is oxidised and the halogen is reduced to form the hydrogen halide HX.

mcqs.q: What is special about astatine (At2), according to the notes?
options: It is the most reactive halogen
It is a liquid at room temperature
mcqs.why: Astatine (At2) is a highly radioactive element whose reactions are studied in nuclear chemistry, as noted at the end of the lesson.

mcqs.q: Bromine reacts with hydrogen under which condition?
mcqs.why: Br2 + H2 -> 2HBr requires higher temperature, intermediate between chlorine needing light/heat and iodine needing 450 C.

lessons.notes_html:
The halogens react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides. These are redox reactions, with the general equation: X2 + H2 → 2HX. Reactivity decreases down the group, so the reaction conditions become more drastic (more severe).

Trend in Reactivity

HalogenEquationConditions
Fluorine (F2)F2 + H2 → 2HFExplosive, even in the dark and at very low temperature
Chlorine (Cl2)Cl2 + H2 → 2HClHeat or light (diffused sunlight)
Bromine (Br2)Br2 + H2 → 2HBrHigher temperature (Δ)
Iodine (I2)I2 + H2 ⇌ 2HIHigh temperature (450°C) and a Pt catalyst; slow and reversible

Fluorine is the most reactive halogen and iodine the least reactive. Astatine (At2) is a highly radioactive element whose reactions are studied in nuclear chemistry.

Key Points

  • All halogens form hydrogen halides, HX, with hydrogen.
  • Reactivity with hydrogen falls down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • F2 reacts explosively in the dark; I2 needs 450°C and a platinum catalyst.
  • The iodine reaction is slow and reversible.
lessons.title: Reactions of Halogens with Hydrogen: Trends and Redox Reactions

mcqs.q: What is the order of thermal stability of hydrogen halides?
mcqs.why: The order of decreasing thermal stability is HF > HCl > HBr > HI, following bond strength and electronegativity difference.

mcqs.q: Why is HF the most thermally stable hydrogen halide?
options: Small F atom and large electronegativity difference
mcqs.why: HF has highest stability because of the small fluorine atom and its large electronegativity difference with hydrogen, giving a strong bond.

mcqs.q: What is the bond energy of HF?
mcqs.why: The table in the notes gives HF a bond energy of 562 kJ/mol, the highest of the hydrogen halides, with bond length 92 pm.

mcqs.q: What is the bond length of HF?
mcqs.why: The notes table gives HF the shortest bond length at 92 pm, increasing down the group to 161 pm for HI as atoms get larger.

mcqs.q: Why does H-X bond weaken down the group?
options: Bond becomes longer as halogen atom gets larger
mcqs.why: Down the group the halogen atom becomes larger, the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker, and the halide decomposes more easily.

mcqs.q: Which hydrogen halide has the lowest thermal stability?
mcqs.why: HI has the lowest stability because of the large iodine atom and the smallest electronegativity difference (0.46) with hydrogen.

mcqs.q: What is the electronegativity difference for HF?
mcqs.why: The table gives HF an electronegativity difference of 1.78, the largest, which results in the strongest and most stable H-X bond.

mcqs.q: How much stronger is the H-F bond than the H-I bond?
mcqs.why: Working: HF = 562 kJ/mol and HI = 299 kJ/mol. Difference = 562 - 299 = 263 kJ/mol, verified by calculation.

mcqs.q: Why is HF hazardous despite its strong bond?
options: It penetrates skin and can dissolve calcium in bones
It is a strong oxidiser only
mcqs.why: The notes warn HF penetrates skin deeply and can even dissolve calcium in bones, making it one of the most hazardous acids.

mcqs.q: Thermal stability of HX depends on what, according to the notes?
options: Difference in electronegativity between bonded atoms
mcqs.why: Stability depends on the electronegativity difference; a larger difference results in a stronger bond and greater thermal stability.

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrogen halides are binary compounds of halogens and hydrogen: HF, HCl, HBr and HI. The thermal stability of a hydrogen halide depends on the difference in electronegativity between the bonded atoms; a larger difference results in a stronger bond.

Trend in Thermal Stability

The order of decreasing thermal stability is: HF > HCl > HBr > HI. HF has the highest thermal stability because of the small size of the fluorine atom and its large electronegativity difference with hydrogen. HI has the lowest stability because of the large iodine atom and the smallest electronegativity difference.

Hydrogen HalideElectronegativity Difference (ΔEN)Bond Length (pm)Bond Energy (kJ/mol)
HF1.7892562
HCl0.96121431
HBr0.76141266
HI0.46161299

Down the group the halogen atom becomes larger, the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker, and the hydrogen halide decomposes more easily on heating. Although HF has the strongest bond, it is one of the most hazardous acids: it penetrates skin deeply and can even dissolve calcium in bones.

Key Points

  • Thermal stability decreases down the group: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
  • Stability follows the H-X bond strength and electronegativity difference.
  • Bond length increases down the group, so the bond weakens.
  • HF is the most stable hydrogen halide; HI is the least stable.
lessons.title: Thermal Stabilities of Hydrogen Halides

mcqs.q: What does a reducing agent do?
options: It reduces others and is oxidised itself
mcqs.why: A reducing agent reduces other substances and is oxidised itself; halide ions are oxidised to X2 molecules when they reduce others.

mcqs.q: What are halide ions oxidised to when they act as reducing agents?
mcqs.why: The notes give the example 4HX + O2 -> 2H2O + 2X2, showing halide species oxidised to X2 molecules.

mcqs.q: Which halide ion is the strongest reducing agent?
mcqs.why: Down the group ions get larger and lose electrons more easily, so iodide I- is the strongest reducing agent and F- the weakest.

mcqs.q: Which halide ion is the weakest reducing agent?
mcqs.why: Fluoride ions hold their electrons most tightly and are oxidised least easily, so F- is the weakest reducing agent in the group.

mcqs.q: How does reducing power of halides compare with oxidising power of halogens?
options: Reducing power trend is opposite to oxidising power trend
mcqs.why: The notes state the reducing trend is opposite: oxidising power of X2 decreases down the group while reducing power of X- increases.

mcqs.q: Why does reducing power increase down the group?
options: Ions get smaller and hold electrons tighter
Ions get larger and hold outer electrons less tightly
mcqs.why: Down the group ions become larger, hold outer electrons less tightly, and lose electrons (are oxidised) more easily.

mcqs.q: Which halogens can iodide ions reduce?
mcqs.why: A halide can only reduce halogen molecules above it in Group 17; iodide reduces chlorine and bromine as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which halogens can fluoride ions reduce?
mcqs.why: Fluoride ions, at the bottom of the reducing-power order, reduce none of the halogens because F- is the weakest reducing agent.

mcqs.q: In 4HX + O2 -> 2H2O + 2X2, what is reduced?
mcqs.why: Oxygen O2 gains electrons to form water and is reduced, while the halide in HX is oxidised to X2, acting as reducing agent.

mcqs.q: Halide reducing power increases in which direction?
mcqs.why: Reducing power increases down the group from F- (weakest) to I- (strongest) as ion size increases and electrons are lost more easily.

lessons.notes_html:
A reducing agent reduces other substances and is oxidised itself. The halide ions reduce oxidising agents and are themselves oxidised to X2 molecules, for example: 4HX + O2 → 2H2O + 2X2.

Trend in Reducing Power

The trend in the reducing ability of halide ions is opposite to the trend in the oxidising power of the halogens. The relative reactivity of halide ions as reducing agents is: F- < Cl- < Br- < I-. Down the group the ions become larger, hold their outer electrons less tightly, and lose electrons (are oxidised) more easily, so iodide ions are the strongest reducing agents and fluoride ions the weakest. A halide ion can only reduce halogen molecules that are above it in Group 17 (VIIA). For example, iodide ions reduce chlorine and bromine, while fluoride ions, at the bottom of this reducing-power order, reduce none of the halogens.

Key Points

  • Halide ions act as reducing agents and are oxidised to X2.
  • Reducing power increases down the group: F- < Cl- < Br- < I-.
  • This trend is opposite to the oxidising power of the halogens.
  • I- is the strongest reducing agent; F- is the weakest.
lessons.title: Relative Reactivity of Halide ions as Reducing Agents

mcqs.q: What is the general reaction of halide ions with silver ions?
mcqs.why: The general reaction is X-(aq) + Ag+(aq) -> AgX(s), forming an insoluble silver halide precipitate used to test for halides.

mcqs.q: What colour precipitate does chloride give with silver ions?
mcqs.why: Cl- + Ag+ -> AgCl(s) gives a white precipitate, which identifies chloride ions in qualitative analysis.

mcqs.q: What colour precipitate does bromide give with silver ions?
mcqs.why: Br- + Ag+ -> AgBr(s) gives a cream-coloured precipitate, distinct from white AgCl and yellow AgI.

mcqs.q: What colour precipitate does iodide give with silver ions?
mcqs.why: I- + Ag+ -> AgI(s) gives a yellow precipitate, which identifies iodide ions in the silver nitrate test.

mcqs.q: Why do fluoride ions give no precipitate with silver ions?
options: Fluoride does not react at all with metals
mcqs.why: No precipitate forms with fluoride because silver fluoride (AgF) is soluble in water, unlike AgCl, AgBr and AgI.

mcqs.q: How do forensic scientists use silver nitrate, according to the notes?
options: To detect fingerprints from sweat salts
mcqs.why: Forensic scientists use silver nitrate sprays to detect fingerprints because salts in sweat, including halides, form visible patterns.

mcqs.q: These silver halide reactions are used for what purpose?
options: Testing for halide ions in solution
mcqs.why: The precipitate colour identifies the halide ion, so these reactions are used to test for halide ions in a solution.

mcqs.q: Which silver halide is white?
mcqs.why: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream and AgI is yellow; AgF is soluble and gives no precipitate at all.

mcqs.q: Which silver halide is yellow?
mcqs.why: AgI is the yellow precipitate formed from iodide ions, as listed in the precipitate colours table in the notes.

mcqs.q: What forms in all these reactions besides the precipitate colour clue?
mcqs.why: Halide ions produce insoluble silver halide precipitates with aqueous silver ions; only AgF is the soluble exception.

lessons.notes_html:
When halide ions react with aqueous silver ions, they produce insoluble silver halide precipitates. The colour of the precipitate identifies the halide ion, so these reactions are used to test for halide ions in a solution. The general reaction is: X-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgX(s).

Precipitate Colours

Halide IonEquationPrecipitate
Chloride, Cl-Cl-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgCl(s)White precipitate
Bromide, Br-Br-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgBr(s)Cream-coloured precipitate
Iodide, I-I-(aq) + Ag+(aq) → AgI(s)Yellow precipitate

No precipitate forms with fluoride ions, because silver fluoride (AgF) is soluble in water. Forensic scientists use silver nitrate sprays to detect fingerprints, because the salts in sweat, including halides, react to form visible patterns.

Key Points

  • Silver ions give insoluble precipitates with Cl-, Br- and I-.
  • AgCl is white, AgBr is cream and AgI is yellow.
  • AgF is soluble, so fluoride ions give no precipitate.
  • These reactions identify halide ions in qualitative analysis.
lessons.title: Reactions of Halide Ions with Aqueous Silver Ions

mcqs.q: What happens to fluoride ions with concentrated sulphuric acid?
mcqs.why: Concentrated sulphuric acid has no significant effect on fluoride ions, the weakest reducing agents in the group.

mcqs.q: What do chloride ions give with concentrated sulphuric acid?
options: Steamy fumes of HCl gas, no oxidation
mcqs.why: H2SO4 + Cl- -> HCl(g) + HSO4-; chloride gives steamy HCl fumes only and the chloride is not oxidised by the acid.

mcqs.q: What colour fumes form when HBr is oxidised by concentrated acid?
mcqs.why: 2HBr + H2SO4 -> Br2 + 2H2O + SO2; some HBr is oxidised giving orange-brown bromine fumes as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: What gas forms alongside Br2 in the bromide reaction?
mcqs.why: The oxidation 2HBr + H2SO4 -> Br2 + 2H2O + SO2 produces sulphur dioxide as the concentrated acid is itself reduced.

mcqs.q: What colour vapour forms when HI is oxidised by concentrated acid?
mcqs.why: 8HI + H2SO4 -> 4I2 + 4H2O + H2S; HI is oxidised to purple vapours of iodine, showing iodide is a strong reducing agent.

mcqs.q: What gas forms alongside I2 in the iodide reaction?
mcqs.why: The notes give 8HI + H2SO4 -> 4I2 + 4H2O + H2S, so hydrogen sulphide forms as the acid is reduced by iodide.

mcqs.q: Why do bromide and iodide get oxidised but chloride does not?
options: They are stronger reducing agents than chloride
mcqs.why: Stronger reducing halides are oxidised by concentrated acid; reducing power increases F- to I-, so Br- and I- are oxidised.

mcqs.q: What forms first when bromide reacts with concentrated acid?
mcqs.why: With bromide, H2SO4 + Br- -> HBr + HSO4- forms HBr first, and only some of the HBr is then oxidised to Br2.

mcqs.q: These reactions confirm which trend?
options: Decreasing reducing power down the group
Increasing reducing power from F- to I-
Increasing oxidising power down the group
mcqs.why: F- unaffected, Cl- not oxidised, Br- partly oxidised and I- strongly oxidised confirms increasing reducing power down the group.

mcqs.q: Which halide gives only HCl fumes with no oxidation at all?
mcqs.why: Chloride gives steamy HCl fumes only with no oxidation, while fluoride is unaffected and bromide/iodide are oxidised.

lessons.notes_html:
When halide ions react with concentrated sulphuric acid, different reactions occur depending on the halide, because the stronger reducing halides are oxidised by the acid.

Fluoride Ions

Concentrated sulphuric acid has no significant effect on fluoride ions, the weakest reducing agents.

Chloride Ions

Concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with chloride ions to produce steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride gas; the chloride is not oxidised: H2SO4 + Cl-(aq) → HCl(g) + HSO4-(aq).

Bromide Ions

With bromide ions, hydrogen bromide forms first: H2SO4 + Br-(aq) → HBr(g) + HSO4-(aq). Some of the HBr is then oxidised by the concentrated acid, giving orange-brown bromine fumes: 2HBr + H2SO4 → Br2(g) + 2H2O(l) + SO2(g).

Iodide Ions

With iodide ions, hydrogen iodide forms: H2SO4 + I-(aq) → HI(g) + HSO4-(aq). The HI is oxidised by the acid to purple vapours of iodine: 8HI + H2SO4 → 4I2(g) + 4H2O(l) + H2S(g).

Key Points

  • F- is not affected by concentrated H2SO4.
  • Cl- gives steamy HCl fumes only; no oxidation occurs.
  • Br- gives HBr, partly oxidised to orange-brown Br2, with SO2 formed.
  • I- gives HI, oxidised to purple I2 vapour, with H2S formed.
  • The reactions confirm the increasing reducing power F- < Cl- < Br- < I-.
lessons.title: Reaction with Concentrated Sulphuric Acid

mcqs.q: What is done before adding silver nitrate in the halide test?
options: Dissolve sample in dilute nitric acid
mcqs.why: The sample is first dissolved in dilute nitric acid to remove other reactive ions such as carbonates or hydroxides.

mcqs.q: Why is dilute nitric acid added first?
options: To remove carbonates or hydroxides that interfere
mcqs.why: Dilute HNO3 removes other reactive ions such as carbonates or hydroxides so only the silver halide precipitate forms.

mcqs.q: What complex forms when AgCl dissolves in ammonia?
mcqs.why: AgCl + 2NH3 -> [Ag(NH3)2]+ + Cl-; silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia forming a colourless diammine complex.

mcqs.q: How does AgBr behave with aqueous ammonia?
mcqs.why: Silver bromide is only sparingly soluble in dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia, distinguishing it from AgCl.

mcqs.q: How does AgI behave with aqueous ammonia?
options: Does not dissolve in dilute or concentrated ammonia
mcqs.why: Silver iodide does not dissolve in either dilute or concentrated ammonia, reliably distinguishing iodide from chloride and bromide.

mcqs.q: Which halide gives a white precipitate dissolving in dilute ammonia?
mcqs.why: Chloride gives white AgCl which dissolves in dilute ammonia, as summarised in the halide identification table.

mcqs.q: Which halide gives a cream precipitate dissolving only in concentrated ammonia?
mcqs.why: Bromide gives cream AgBr which dissolves only in concentrated ammonia, the middle case in the stepwise solubility test.

mcqs.q: Which halide gives a yellow precipitate insoluble in ammonia?
mcqs.why: Iodide gives yellow AgI which is insoluble in dilute and concentrated ammonia, confirming iodide in the test.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of the ammonia step after silver nitrate?
options: To confirm which halide is present
mcqs.why: The stepwise solubility in ammonia reliably distinguishes the three halides and confirms which halide is present.

mcqs.q: What precipitate colour does AgBr have in this method?
mcqs.why: The method states bromide ions give a cream-coloured precipitate (AgBr), between white AgCl and bright-yellow AgI.

lessons.notes_html:
The silver nitrate test followed by aqueous ammonia is the standard qualitative method to detect and identify halide ions (Cl-, Br-, I-) in a solution.

Silver Nitrate Test (Ag+ with Halides)

The sample is first dissolved in dilute nitric acid, to remove other reactive ions such as carbonates or hydroxides. When silver nitrate is added, a precipitate of silver halide (AgX) forms: Ag+(aq) + X-(aq) → AgX(s). Chloride ions give a white precipitate (AgCl), bromide ions a cream-coloured precipitate (AgBr), and iodide ions a bright-yellow precipitate (AgI).

Ammonia Test (Addition of Aqueous Ammonia)

Aqueous ammonia is then added to the precipitate. Silver chloride dissolves easily in dilute ammonia, forming a colourless [Ag(NH3)2]+ complex: AgCl(s) + 2NH3(aq) → [Ag(NH3)2]+(aq) + Cl-(aq). Silver bromide is only sparingly soluble in dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia. Silver iodide does not dissolve in either dilute or concentrated ammonia. This stepwise solubility reliably distinguishes the three halide ions.

Summary Table

HalidePrecipitate with Ag+Effect of Aqueous Ammonia
Cl-White (AgCl)Dissolves in dilute ammonia
Br-Cream (AgBr)Dissolves only in concentrated ammonia
I-Yellow (AgI)Insoluble in dilute and concentrated ammonia

Key Points

  • Acidify with dilute HNO3 before adding silver nitrate.
  • Precipitate colours: white AgCl, cream AgBr, yellow AgI.
  • AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia; AgBr only in concentrated ammonia; AgI not at all.
  • The ammonia step confirms which halide is present.
lessons.title: Silver Nitrate and Ammonia Method for Halide Identification

mcqs.q: What is a disproportionation reaction?
options: The same species is oxidised and reduced simultaneously
mcqs.why: In disproportionation an atom, ion or molecule is both oxidised and reduced simultaneously, as chlorine is with NaOH.

mcqs.q: What forms when Cl2 reacts with cold dilute NaOH at 15 C?
mcqs.why: 2NaOH + Cl2 -> NaClO + NaCl + H2O at 15 C; cold dilute NaOH gives sodium hypochlorite and sodium chloride.

mcqs.q: What forms when Cl2 reacts with hot dilute NaOH at 70 C?
mcqs.why: 6NaOH + 3Cl2 -> NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O at 70 C; hot dilute NaOH gives sodium chlorate and sodium chloride.

mcqs.q: In cold NaOH, chlorine goes from 0 to which oxidation states?
mcqs.why: In cold dilute NaOH chlorine (0) is reduced to -1 in NaCl and oxidised to +1 in sodium hypochlorite NaClO.

mcqs.q: In hot NaOH, chlorine is oxidised to which state in NaClO3?
mcqs.why: In hot dilute NaOH chlorine goes from 0 to -1 in NaCl and to +5 in sodium chlorate NaClO3, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What decides which disproportionation products form from Cl2 and NaOH?
mcqs.why: Temperature decides the products: cold (15 C) gives hypochlorite while hot (70 C) gives chlorate, both with NaCl.

mcqs.q: How many moles of NaCl form from 3 moles of Cl2 in hot NaOH?
mcqs.why: Working: 6NaOH + 3Cl2 -> NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O, so 3 mol Cl2 gives 5 mol NaCl, read directly from the equation.

mcqs.q: What is the formula of sodium hypochlorite?
mcqs.why: Sodium hypochlorite is NaClO, formed with cold dilute NaOH, distinct from sodium chlorate NaClO3 formed when hot.

mcqs.q: What is the formula of sodium chlorate?
mcqs.why: Sodium chlorate is NaClO3, formed when chlorine is bubbled through hot dilute NaOH solution at 70 C.

mcqs.q: In both NaOH reactions, chlorine is reduced to form what?
mcqs.why: In both cold and hot reactions chlorine is reduced from 0 to -1 forming sodium chloride NaCl alongside the oxidised product.

lessons.notes_html:
A reaction in which an atom, ion or molecule is both oxidised and reduced simultaneously is called a disproportionation reaction. The reaction of chlorine with sodium hydroxide is an example; which reaction occurs depends on the temperature.

Reaction of Chlorine with Cold Dilute NaOH

When chlorine is bubbled through cold dilute NaOH solution (at 15°C), sodium hypochlorite and sodium chloride are produced: 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) → NaClO(aq) + NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). This is disproportionation because chlorine (oxidation state 0) is reduced to -1 in NaCl and oxidised to +1 in sodium hypochlorite.

Reaction of Chlorine with Hot Dilute NaOH

When chlorine is bubbled through a hot dilute NaOH solution (at 70°C), sodium chlorate and sodium chloride are produced: 6NaOH(aq) + 3Cl2(g) → NaClO3(aq) + 5NaCl(aq) + 3H2O(l). This is also disproportionation: chlorine goes from 0 to -1 in NaCl and to +5 in sodium chlorate.

Key Equations

ConditionsEquationChlorine oxidation states
Cold dilute NaOH, 15°C2NaOH + Cl2 → NaClO + NaCl + H2O0 → +1 and -1
Hot dilute NaOH, 70°C6NaOH + 3Cl2 → NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O0 → +5 and -1

Key Points

  • In disproportionation, the same element is oxidised and reduced together.
  • Cold dilute NaOH gives sodium hypochlorite (NaClO) and NaCl.
  • Hot dilute NaOH gives sodium chlorate (NaClO3) and NaCl.
  • Temperature decides which disproportionation products form.
lessons.title: Disproportionation Reactions of Chlorine with NaOH

mcqs.q: What forms when chlorine reacts with water?
mcqs.why: Cl2 + H2O -> HOCl + HCl; chlorine reacts with water to give hypochlorous acid and hydrogen chloride (hydrochloric acid).

mcqs.q: What ion forms when HOCl loses a proton?
mcqs.why: HOCl -> OCl- + H+; when hypochlorous acid loses a proton, the hypochlorite ion OCl- is formed.

mcqs.q: Why do HOCl and OCl- protect water?
options: They are powerful oxidising agents that kill germs
mcqs.why: Both HOCl and OCl- are powerful oxidising agents and effective germ-killers used in water treatment.

mcqs.q: What is the role of OCl- remaining in treated water?
mcqs.why: OCl- remains in the water to provide ongoing protection by maintaining a residual disinfectant level after treatment.

mcqs.q: Which diseases does chlorination help prevent?
mcqs.why: Municipal plants add chlorine to ensure safe drinking water and prevent waterborne diseases such as cholera and typhoid.

mcqs.q: What does HOCl do in water treatment?
mcqs.why: In water treatment HOCl eliminates harmful microorganisms, while OCl- stays behind as the residual disinfectant.

mcqs.q: How much chlorine should be used in water purification?
mcqs.why: The notes state only small, controlled doses are used; benefits outweigh risks but excessive amounts must be avoided.

mcqs.q: Chlorine purifies water because its reaction products do what?
mcqs.why: Chlorine is used to purify water because the products of its reaction with water, HOCl and OCl-, kill germs.

mcqs.q: Which species kills bacteria immediately in chlorinated water?
mcqs.why: HOCl is a strong oxidising agent that eliminates harmful microorganisms and bacteria in treated water.

mcqs.q: What is the overall judgement on chlorination in the notes?
options: Benefits in small doses greatly outweigh risks
It only works in hot water
mcqs.why: In small, controlled doses the health benefits of chlorination greatly outweigh its risks, although excess must be avoided.

lessons.notes_html:
Chlorine is used to purify water because the products of its reaction with water kill germs.

Reactions Involved

When chlorine reacts with water, hypochlorous acid and hydrogen chloride are produced: Cl2 + H2O → HOCl + HCl. When HOCl loses a proton (H+), the hypochlorite ion is formed: HOCl → OCl- + H+.

How Chlorination Protects Water

Both hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hypochlorite ions (OCl-) are powerful oxidising agents and effective germ-killers. In water treatment, HOCl eliminates harmful microorganisms, while OCl- remains in the water to provide ongoing protection by maintaining a residual disinfectant level. Municipal water treatment plants therefore add chlorine to ensure safe drinking water and prevent waterborne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In small, controlled doses the health benefits of chlorination greatly outweigh its risks, although excessive amounts must be avoided.

Key Points

  • Cl2 + H2O → HOCl + HCl; HOCl also gives OCl- ions.
  • HOCl and OCl- are strong oxidising agents that kill bacteria and germs.
  • OCl- stays in the water as a residual disinfectant.
  • Chlorination prevents diseases like cholera and typhoid.
  • Only small, controlled doses of chlorine are used.
lessons.title: Chlorine in Water Purification

chapters.title: Unit 10: Environmental Chemistry: Atmosphere and Water

lessons.title: Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
Environmental chemistry is the study of chemical phenomena in natural environments — air, water and soil: the sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of chemical substances, and their impacts on human health and nature. The environment has four segments: lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere.

The atmosphere is the protective layer of gases surrounding the Earth, about 500 km thick. It sustains life and shields the Earth from harmful cosmic rays. Its major components are nitrogen (78.08%) and oxygen (20.94%); minor components are argon (0.93%), carbon dioxide (0.03%) and trace gases. Nearly 75% of its total mass lies within the first 11 km (the troposphere), where most of the air is concentrated.

The Four Layers

LayerExtentTemperature ChangeKey Feature
TroposphereSurface to 8–15 kmDecreases with altitude, +15°C at surface to −55°C at topAll weather phenomena occur here
Stratosphere15 to 50 kmIncreases with altitude, −55°C at base to 0°C at topContains the ozone (O3) layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays
Mesosphere50 to 85 kmDrops from 0°C at base to −90°C at topThe coldest layer; ozone concentration decreases
Thermosphere85 to 500 kmRises sharply from −90°C to 1,200–2,000°CExtremely low density, so it would not feel hot; auroras (Northern and Southern Lights) occur here

Beyond these layers lies the exosphere, the outermost region where the atmosphere transitions into space. Overall composition stays fairly consistent across the layers, though trace gas concentrations vary with location and weather.

Key Points

  • Environmental chemistry studies sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of chemicals in air, water and soil.
  • Atmosphere composition: N2 78.08%, O2 20.94%, Ar 0.93%, CO2 0.03%.
  • Four layers in order: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere.
  • Temperature falls with altitude in the troposphere and mesosphere, but rises in the stratosphere and thermosphere.
  • The stratospheric ozone layer protects Earth from ultraviolet radiation.

mcqs.q: What does environmental chemistry study?
options: Only the manufacture of industrial chemicals
Chemical phenomena in natural environments: sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of substances
mcqs.why: The notes define environmental chemistry as the study of chemical phenomena in air, water and soil, covering sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of substances and their impacts.

mcqs.q: Which are the four segments of the environment named in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes list the four segments of the environment as lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere, distinct from the four layers of the atmosphere itself.

mcqs.q: About how thick is the atmosphere according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state the atmosphere is the protective layer of gases surrounding the Earth and is about 500 km thick, sustaining life and shielding Earth from harmful cosmic rays.

mcqs.q: What percentage of air is nitrogen?
mcqs.why: The notes give the major components as nitrogen 78.08% and oxygen 20.94%, with argon 0.93% and carbon dioxide 0.03% as minor components of air.

mcqs.q: In a 1000 g sample of air, what mass is nitrogen? Use the percentage in the notes.
mcqs.why: Working: mass = total x percentage / 100 = 1000 g x 78.08 / 100 = 78080 / 100 = 780.8 g. Nitrogen is 78.08% of air, so the result is 780.8 g.

mcqs.q: Where does nearly 75% of the atmosphere's total mass lie?
options: Within the first 11 km, the troposphere
mcqs.why: The notes state nearly 75% of the atmosphere's total mass lies within the first 11 km, the troposphere, where most of the air is concentrated near the surface.

mcqs.q: In which layer do all weather phenomena occur?
mcqs.why: The table in the notes gives the troposphere, from the surface to 8-15 km, as the layer where all weather phenomena occur, with temperature decreasing with altitude.

mcqs.q: What is the key feature of the stratosphere?
options: It contains the ozone layer that absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays
mcqs.why: The notes state the stratosphere, 15 to 50 km, contains the ozone (O3) layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays and protects life on Earth.

mcqs.q: Which layer is the coldest, reaching about -90 degrees C at the top?
mcqs.why: The notes describe the mesosphere, 50 to 85 km, as the coldest layer, where temperature drops from 0 degrees C at the base to -90 degrees C at the top.

options: It rises sharply to 1200-2000 degrees C
It falls from +15 to -55 degrees C
mcqs.why: The notes state temperature in the thermosphere, 85 to 500 km, rises sharply from -90 degrees C to 1200-2000 degrees C, though low density means it would not feel hot.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Air Quality
lessons.notes_html:
Air quality is affected by pollutants released from human activities and natural sources, and by environmental and geographical factors that control how pollutants disperse.

Sources of Pollutants

  • Human-related sources: vehicles, industries, power plants, agriculture, construction and waste management emit nitrogen oxides (NOx), carbon oxides (COx), sulphur oxides (SOx), particulate matter (PM) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
  • Natural sources: wildfires and dust storms release large amounts of particulate matter; biological sources such as pollen add further; natural processes release greenhouse gases like methane.

Dispersion Factors

  • Wind, temperature and humidity control dispersion; calm conditions trap pollutants near the ground and cause smog.
  • Sunlight promotes ozone formation and the breakdown of pollutants.
  • Mountains can trap emissions in valleys; coastal breezes help disperse them.
  • Vegetation improves air quality by absorbing pollutants and releasing oxygen, while urban heat islands intensify pollution in cities.

Indoor Air Quality

Indoor air quality is a major concern: cooking, smoking, cleaning products and handling building materials, combined with poor ventilation, significantly increase indoor pollution. In big cities poor indoor air can be more harmful than outdoor pollution; keeping windows open, using exhaust fans and planting indoor plants help improve it.

Key Points

  • Human sources emit NOx, COx, SOx, particulate matter and VOCs.
  • Wildfires, dust storms and pollen are natural pollutant sources.
  • Calm weather traps pollutants and causes smog; wind and coastal breezes disperse them.
  • Sunlight drives ozone formation; vegetation cleans the air.
  • Indoor pollution rises with cooking, smoking and poor ventilation.

mcqs.q: Which are natural sources of particulate matter named in the notes?

mcqs.q: What do calm conditions do to air pollutants?

They have no effect on pollutants

It promotes ozone formation and the breakdown of pollutants
mcqs.why: The notes state sunlight promotes ozone formation and the breakdown of pollutants, so it can both create a pollutant and help destroy others.

mcqs.q: How do mountains affect pollutant dispersion?
options: They can trap emissions in valleys
mcqs.why: The notes state mountains can trap emissions in valleys, while coastal breezes help disperse them, showing how geography controls air quality.

mcqs.q: How does vegetation improve air quality?
options: By absorbing pollutants and releasing oxygen
mcqs.why: The notes state vegetation improves air quality by absorbing pollutants and releasing oxygen, while urban heat islands intensify pollution in cities.

mcqs.q: Which activities increase indoor air pollution in the notes?
options: Opening windows and using exhaust fans
Cooking, smoking, cleaning products and handling building materials with poor ventilation
mcqs.why: The notes state cooking, smoking, cleaning products and handling building materials, combined with poor ventilation, significantly increase indoor pollution.

mcqs.q: What helps improve indoor air quality according to the notes?
options: Keeping windows open, using exhaust fans and planting indoor plants
mcqs.why: The notes state keeping windows open, using exhaust fans and planting indoor plants help improve indoor air quality, which in big cities can be worse than outdoor air.

mcqs.why: The notes state natural processes release greenhouse gases like methane, alongside human sources and natural particulate sources such as wildfires and pollen.
