mcqs.why: The notes state urban heat islands intensify pollution in cities, in contrast to vegetation which improves air quality by absorbing pollutants.

lessons.title: Sources and Effects of Common Air Pollutants
lessons.notes_html:
Air pollution occurs when harmful substances, called pollutants, are released into the atmosphere. Common pollutants, their sources and effects are:

PollutantSourceEffects
Ozone (O3)Not emitted directly; forms when sunlight reacts with gases from vehicles and factories (ground-level ozone)Chest pain, coughing, difficulty breathing; damages plants; major component of smog
Lead (Pb)Once in gasoline; now mainly old paint, dust and soilHarmful even in small amounts, especially to children: damages brain, slows learning, heart and blood issues
Mercury (Hg)Burning coal, mining and industrial processesAccumulates in lakes, rivers and fish; harms brain and nervous system, especially in pregnant women and small children
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs)Combustion of wood, coal, oil or wasteRespiratory issues, weakened immune system, increased cancer risk
Persistent organic pollutants (POPs)Outdated pesticides, industrial waste, specific productsRemain in the environment for long periods; accumulate in bodies; disrupt hormones, cause cancer, affect child development
Greenhouse gasesCO2, CH4 and N2O released from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and farmsTrap heat and cause climate change: rising temperatures, extreme weather, melting ice, rising sea levels
Ozone-depleting substances (CFCs)Old air conditioners, refrigerators and aerosol spraysDestroy the protective ozone layer; more UV reaches Earth, raising skin cancer and eye problems
Volatile organic compounds (VOCs)Paint, cleaning products, burning wood, vehicle exhaustIrritate eyes, nose and throat; make breathing difficult; help form smog and ground-level ozone
Heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd)Power plants, smelters and vehiclesDamage brain, kidneys, heart and other organs; especially harmful to children and infants

Primary and Secondary Pollutants

Primary pollutants are emitted directly from a source, e.g. total suspended particulates (smoke, dust, fumes) and oxides of carbon, nitrogen and sulphur from industrial chimneys and automobile exhaust. Secondary pollutants are created in the atmosphere by reactions (oxidation, photochemical reactions) involving primary pollutants, e.g. hydrogen peroxide, ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), sulphuric and nitric acids and their salts.

Key Points

  • Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant and a main part of smog; stratospheric ozone is protective.
  • Lead and mercury attack the brain and nervous system, worst in children.
  • POPs persist for long periods and accumulate in living bodies.
  • Greenhouse gases trap heat; CFCs deplete the ozone layer — two different problems.
  • Primary pollutants are emitted directly; secondary pollutants form by reactions in the air.

lessons.title: Impact of Human Activities on the Atmosphere
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities have greatly changed the Earth's atmosphere, primarily due to the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.

Burning of Fossil Fuels

When fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas are burned, they emit a large amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) into the atmosphere. This gas traps heat, leading to global warming and climate change. The excess CO2 warms the Earth's surface, resulting in melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather patterns.

Deforestation

Deforestation is cutting down trees for agriculture, construction or other human activities. Trees absorb CO2 and produce oxygen, helping to maintain a balanced atmosphere. When forests are destroyed, this natural purification process is lost, leading to higher levels of CO2 in the air. This enhances the greenhouse effect and worsens climate change.

Key Points

  • Burning coal, oil and natural gas is the main human source of extra CO2.
  • Excess CO2 traps heat and causes global warming and climate change.
  • Effects include melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather.
  • Trees absorb CO2 and release oxygen; cutting them removes this natural purification.
  • Deforestation therefore raises atmospheric CO2 and strengthens the greenhouse effect.

mcqs.q: What is the main human source of extra CO2 in the notes?
options: Burning coal, oil and natural gas
mcqs.why: The notes state burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas emits a large amount of carbon dioxide and is the main human source of extra CO2.

mcqs.q: What does excess CO2 do in the atmosphere?
options: It destroys the ozone layer directly
It traps heat, leading to global warming and climate change
It forms acid rain on its own
mcqs.why: The notes state CO2 traps heat, leading to global warming and climate change, with melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather patterns as results.

options: Melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather patterns
mcqs.why: The notes state the excess CO2 warms the Earth's surface, resulting in melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather patterns around the world.

mcqs.why: The notes state when forests are destroyed the natural purification process is lost, leading to higher CO2 levels, which enhances the greenhouse effect and worsens climate change.

mcqs.why: The notes state human activities have greatly changed the atmosphere primarily due to the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation, both raising atmospheric CO2.

options: It raises atmospheric CO2 and strengthens the greenhouse effect
mcqs.why: The key points state deforestation raises atmospheric CO2 and strengthens the greenhouse effect, because trees that would absorb CO2 have been removed.

mcqs.q: Which fuels are named as fossil fuels in this lesson?
mcqs.why: The notes name coal, oil and natural gas as the fuels burned that emit large amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere when used for energy.

mcqs.q: What warms as a result of excess CO2, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state the excess CO2 warms the Earth's surface, resulting in melting ice, rising sea levels and unusual weather patterns linked to climate change.

lessons.title: Ozone Depletion
lessons.notes_html:
In the stratosphere, ozone (O3) is formed naturally from oxygen, but it is broken down by chlorine atoms released from chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), causing ozone layer depletion.

Formation of Ozone

Diatomic oxygen absorbs an ultraviolet photon and splits into two oxygen free radicals. Each radical reacts with another O2 molecule to form triatomic oxygen (ozone). M is a third body (N2 or O2) that absorbs the excess energy released, stabilising the ozone.

Destruction of Ozone by CFCs

Ultraviolet radiation breaks down CFCs, releasing chlorine atoms. A chlorine atom reacts with ozone to form chlorine monoxide and O2; the chlorine monoxide then reacts with an oxygen atom, regenerating the chlorine atom. The cycle repeats, so one chlorine atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules.

Key Equations

StepEquation
O2 photolysisO2(g) —hv→ O•(g) + O•(g)
Ozone formationO•(g) + O2(g) + M(N2 or O2) → O3(g) + M
CFC breakdownCCl2F2 —UV→ CClF2 + Cl•
Ozone attackCl• + O3 → ClO• + O2
Chlorine regeneratedClO• + O• → Cl• + O2
Net reactionO3 + O• → 2O2

Ozone depletion lets more harmful UV radiation reach the Earth, causing skin cancer, eye damage, weakening of the immune system and reduced crop yields.

Key Points

  • Ozone forms when O2 splits under UV and O atoms combine with O2 in the presence of a third body M.
  • CFCs release chlorine atoms under UV radiation in the stratosphere.
  • Chlorine acts as a catalyst: it is regenerated and destroys thousands of O3 molecules.
  • Net reaction of the depletion cycle: O3 + O• → 2O2.
  • Effects of depletion: skin cancer, eye damage, weak immunity and lower crop yields.

mcqs.q: Where does ozone depletion take place?
options: In the stratosphere, where ozone is broken down by chlorine from CFCs
mcqs.why: The notes state that in the stratosphere ozone is formed naturally from oxygen but is broken down by chlorine atoms released from chlorofluorocarbons, causing depletion.

mcqs.q: How does ozone formation begin?
options: O2 absorbs a UV photon and splits into two oxygen free radicals
mcqs.why: The notes state diatomic oxygen absorbs an ultraviolet photon and splits into two oxygen free radicals, each of which then reacts with O2 to form ozone.

mcqs.q: What is M in the ozone formation step?
options: A third body, N2 or O2, that absorbs excess energy and stabilises the ozone
mcqs.why: The notes state M is a third body, N2 or O2, that absorbs the excess energy released in O + O2 forming O3, stabilising the ozone molecule.

mcqs.q: What breaks down CFCs in the stratosphere?
mcqs.why: The notes state ultraviolet radiation breaks down CFCs such as CCl2F2, releasing chlorine atoms that then attack ozone molecules in a repeating cycle.

mcqs.q: What does a chlorine atom form when it reacts with ozone?
mcqs.why: The notes give the step Cl + O3 forming ClO (chlorine monoxide) and O2; the chlorine monoxide then reacts with an oxygen atom to regenerate chlorine.

mcqs.q: Why can one chlorine atom destroy thousands of ozone molecules?
options: Because chlorine is regenerated in the cycle and acts as a catalyst
Because chlorine is used up quickly
Because each CFC holds thousands of chlorines
mcqs.why: The notes state the chlorine monoxide reacts with an oxygen atom regenerating the chlorine atom, so the cycle repeats and one chlorine destroys thousands of ozone molecules.

mcqs.q: What is the net reaction of the ozone depletion cycle?
mcqs.why: The notes list the net reaction of the depletion cycle as O3 + O radical forming 2O2, summarising ozone attack plus chlorine regeneration steps together.

mcqs.q: Which equation shows CFC breakdown in the notes?
options: O2 under hv gives O + O
O + O2 + M gives O3 + M
CCl2F2 under UV gives CClF2 + Cl radical
mcqs.why: The notes give the CFC breakdown step as CCl2F2 under UV forming CClF2 plus a chlorine radical, which is the chlorine that then destroys ozone.

mcqs.q: What are the effects of ozone depletion listed in the notes?
options: Skin cancer, eye damage, weakened immune system and reduced crop yields
Floods and sea level rise only
mcqs.why: The notes state ozone depletion lets more harmful UV reach Earth, causing skin cancer, eye damage, weakening of the immune system and reduced crop yields.

mcqs.q: Which gas is the starting material for natural ozone formation?
mcqs.why: The notes state ozone forms when O2 splits under UV and the oxygen atoms combine with O2 in the presence of a third body M to form O3.

lessons.title: Industrial Smog
lessons.notes_html:
Smog is a combination of smoke and fog. Industrial smog (also called London smog or grey smog) creates a yellow-brown colour near ground level. It is a mixture of fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and some VOCs, and is common in cities with heavy industry and power plants, especially cold, damp urban areas. The Great Smog of London (1952) killed about 4,000 people in a few days. Smog harms humans, plants and animals, causing asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, lung infections and even cancer.

Reactions Forming Industrial Smog

Combustion of coal and oil releases sulphur dioxide, which is further oxidised to sulphur trioxide. The trioxide reacts with water in fog to form sulphuric acid. These acidic droplets, combined with particulates such as soot and ash, create the thick, grey smog characteristic of industrial pollution.

Key Equations

StepEquation
Sulphur burns in oxygenS(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g)
Oxidation of SO22SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g)
Acid formation in fogSO3(g) + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq)

Key Points

  • Industrial (London/grey) smog = fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and VOCs near ground level.
  • It forms mainly where coal and oil are burned in heavy industry and power plants.
  • The key acid formed is H2SO4, from SO2 → SO3 → H2SO4 in fog water.
  • It is worst in cold, damp conditions.
  • Health effects: asthma, bronchitis, emphysema, lung infections and cancer.

mcqs.q: What is smog, and what is industrial smog also called?
options: A mix of rain and snow, called acid smog
A combination of smoke and fog, also called London smog or grey smog
A mix of ozone and dust only
mcqs.why: The notes define smog as a combination of smoke and fog, and industrial smog is also called London smog or grey smog, with a yellow-brown colour near ground level.

mcqs.q: What does industrial smog contain?
options: Fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and some VOCs
mcqs.why: The notes state industrial smog is a mixture of fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and some VOCs, common in cities with heavy industry and power plants.

mcqs.q: What happened in the Great Smog of London in 1952?
options: About 4,000 people were killed in a few days
mcqs.why: The notes state the Great Smog of London in 1952 killed about 4,000 people in a few days, showing how deadly industrial smog can be.

mcqs.q: Which health effects are linked to industrial smog?
options: Asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, lung infections and even cancer
mcqs.why: The notes state smog harms humans, plants and animals, causing asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, lung infections and even cancer in exposed populations.

mcqs.q: What is formed when sulphur burns in oxygen?
mcqs.why: The notes give the first smog reaction as sulphur burning in oxygen: S(s) + O2(g) forms SO2(g), the sulphur dioxide released by burning coal and oil.

mcqs.q: How is SO3 formed from SO2 in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give the oxidation step as 2SO2(g) + O2(g) forming 2SO3(g); the trioxide then reacts with water in fog to form sulphuric acid.

mcqs.q: What acid forms when SO3 reacts with water in fog?
mcqs.why: The notes give SO3(g) + H2O(l) forming H2SO4(aq); these acidic droplets with soot and ash create the thick grey smog of industrial pollution.

mcqs.q: Where and when is industrial smog worst?
options: In cold, damp urban areas with heavy industry and power plants
mcqs.why: The notes state industrial smog is common in cities with heavy industry and power plants, especially cold, damp urban areas where coal and oil are burned.

mcqs.q: What colour does industrial smog create near ground level?
mcqs.why: The notes state industrial smog creates a yellow-brown colour near ground level, as a mixture of fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and some VOCs.

mcqs.q: What combines with acidic droplets to create thick grey smog?
options: Particulates such as soot and ash
mcqs.why: The notes state the acidic droplets, combined with particulates such as soot and ash, create the thick grey smog characteristic of industrial pollution.

lessons.title: Photochemical Smog
lessons.notes_html:
Photochemical smog (sometimes called Los Angeles smog or brown smog) is created when oxides of nitrogen react with volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight. It produces a mixture of hundreds of hazardous secondary pollutants, including ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), aldehydes and peroxybenzoyl nitrate (PBzN), and appears as a yellow-brown haze. It is common in cities with many automobiles and a sunny, warm, dry climate, developing on hot, sunny days in heavy traffic.

Reactions Forming Photochemical Smog

StepReaction
1. N2 and O2 combine at high temperature in vehicle enginesN2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g)
2. Nitric oxide oxidises in air2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g)
3. NO2 undergoes photolysis in sunlight (UV)NO2(g) —hv (sunlight)→ NO(g) + O•(g)
4. Oxygen radical forms ozoneO•(g) + O2(g) → O3(g)
5. Ozone reacts with VOCs and NO2 to give secondary pollutants such as PANVOCs(g) + O3(g) + NO2(g) → CH3CO3NO2(g) (peroxyacetyl nitrate, PAN)

Similar reactions generate aldehydes, peroxybenzoyl nitrate (PBzN) and other oxidants, which give the brownish haze and toxic effects. Health hazards include headaches, eye irritation, asthma, lung tissue damage, bronchial infections, pulmonary oedema (fluid in the lungs) and lung cancer.

Key Points

  • Photochemical (Los Angeles/brown) smog needs NOx + VOCs + sunlight.
  • Its harmful products are secondary pollutants: O3, PAN, aldehydes and PBzN.
  • NO2 photolysis is the step that starts ozone formation.
  • It forms in sunny, warm, dry cities with heavy automobile traffic.
  • Unlike industrial smog, it is not based on sulphur compounds and coal smoke.

mcqs.q: What is needed to create photochemical smog?
options: Oxides of nitrogen reacting with VOCs in the presence of sunlight
CFCs and UV in the stratosphere
mcqs.why: The notes state photochemical smog is created when oxides of nitrogen react with volatile organic compounds in the presence of sunlight, producing many secondary pollutants.

mcqs.q: What is photochemical smog also called?
options: Los Angeles smog or brown smog
mcqs.why: The notes state photochemical smog is sometimes called Los Angeles smog or brown smog, unlike industrial smog which is called London or grey smog.

mcqs.q: Which pollutants are produced in photochemical smog?
options: Ozone, PAN, aldehydes and peroxybenzoyl nitrate (PBzN)
mcqs.why: The notes state photochemical smog produces hundreds of hazardous secondary pollutants including ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate, aldehydes and peroxybenzoyl nitrate, as a yellow-brown haze.

mcqs.q: What is the first reaction forming photochemical smog?
options: N2 and O2 combine at high temperature in vehicle engines to give 2NO
mcqs.why: The notes list step 1 as N2(g) + O2(g) forming 2NO(g) at high temperature in vehicle engines; the NO then oxidises to NO2 in air.

mcqs.q: What does NO2 do in sunlight?
options: It undergoes photolysis to give NO and an oxygen radical
mcqs.why: The notes give step 3 as NO2 under hv (sunlight) forming NO plus an oxygen radical; that radical then reacts with O2 to form ozone.

mcqs.q: How does ozone form in photochemical smog?
mcqs.why: The notes give step 4 as the oxygen radical forming ozone: O radical + O2(g) forms O3(g), following photolysis of NO2 in sunlight.

mcqs.q: What is PAN and how is it shown forming?
options: A sulphur acid from SO3 and water
A lead compound from old paint
Peroxyacetyl nitrate, from VOCs + O3 + NO2 giving CH3CO3NO2
mcqs.why: The notes give step 5 as VOCs + O3 + NO2 forming CH3CO3NO2, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), one of the secondary pollutants of photochemical smog.

mcqs.q: Where and when does photochemical smog commonly develop?
options: Cold damp industrial cities in winter
Cities with many automobiles and a sunny, warm, dry climate, on hot sunny days in heavy traffic
mcqs.why: The notes state photochemical smog is common in cities with many automobiles and a sunny, warm, dry climate, developing on hot, sunny days in heavy traffic.

mcqs.q: Which health hazards are listed for photochemical smog?
options: Headaches, eye irritation, asthma, lung tissue damage and pulmonary oedema
mcqs.why: The notes list headaches, eye irritation, asthma, lung tissue damage, bronchial infections, pulmonary oedema (fluid in the lungs) and lung cancer as hazards.

mcqs.q: How does photochemical smog differ from industrial smog?
options: It is based on sulphur compounds and coal smoke
It is not based on sulphur compounds and coal smoke; it needs NOx, VOCs and sunlight
mcqs.why: The key points state that unlike industrial smog, photochemical smog is not based on sulphur compounds and coal smoke; it needs NOx plus VOCs plus sunlight.

lessons.title: Acid Rain
lessons.notes_html:
Acid rain (more accurately, acid precipitation) is created when SO2, NO2 and CO2 combine with water molecules in the atmosphere, resulting in mild solutions of sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3) and carbonic acid (H2CO3). It can also fall as snow, sleet, fog, dew, hail, or as dry material that settles to Earth. Normal rainwater is slightly acidic, with pH 5.3 to 6.0, because CO2 and H2O combine to produce weak carbonic acid; when the pH of rainwater drops below this range, it becomes acid rain.

Reactions of Acid Rain Formation

Acid FormedEquations
Carbonic acid (normal rain)CO2(g) + H2O(l) → H2CO3(aq)
Sulphuric acid (acid rain)2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g); SO3(g) + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq)
Nitric acid (acid rain)2NO2(g) + H2O(l) → HNO2(aq) + HNO3(aq); 4NO2(g) + 2H2O(l) + O2(g) → 4HNO3(aq)

SO2 comes mainly from burning fossil fuels such as coal and oil; oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO2) are produced by vehicle engines and power plants.

Harmful Effects of Acid Rain

Acid rain damages forests, buildings and monuments. Its low pH dissolves metals such as iron (Fe) and aluminium (Al) from the soil, contaminating water sources and potentially causing kidney damage and nervous disorders in humans.

Key Points

  • Acid rain contains H2SO4 and HNO3 formed from SO2 and NO2 in the atmosphere.
  • Normal rain is already slightly acidic (pH 5.3–6.0) due to carbonic acid.
  • Rain below this pH range is classified as acid rain.
  • Main sources: fossil fuel burning (SO2) and vehicle engines and power plants (NOx).
  • It damages forests, buildings and monuments, and leaches toxic metals from soil into water.

mcqs.q: What is acid rain more accurately called, and what does it contain?
options: Acid precipitation, with mild H2SO4, HNO3 and H2CO3 solutions
mcqs.why: The notes state acid rain, more accurately acid precipitation, forms when SO2, NO2 and CO2 combine with water giving mild solutions of sulphuric, nitric and carbonic acids.

mcqs.q: What is the pH range of normal rainwater in the notes?
options: pH 5.3 to 6.0, slightly acidic due to carbonic acid
mcqs.why: The notes state normal rainwater is slightly acidic with pH 5.3 to 6.0 because CO2 and H2O combine to produce weak carbonic acid; below this range it is acid rain.

mcqs.q: A rain sample has pH 5.0. How is it classified using the notes range?
options: Acid rain, because 5.0 is below the normal range 5.3 to 6.0
mcqs.why: Working: normal range from notes = pH 5.3 to 6.0. Compare: 5.0 < 5.3, difference = 5.3 - 5.0 = 0.3 below the lower limit. Result: the sample is acid rain.

mcqs.q: Which reaction forms carbonic acid in normal rain?
mcqs.why: The notes give the carbonic acid reaction as CO2(g) + H2O(l) forming H2CO3(aq), which makes normal rainwater slightly acidic even without pollution.

mcqs.q: Which steps form sulphuric acid in acid rain?
options: 2SO2 + O2 gives 2SO3, then SO3 + H2O gives H2SO4
mcqs.why: The notes give sulphuric acid formation as 2SO2(g) + O2(g) forming 2SO3(g), followed by SO3(g) + H2O(l) forming H2SO4(aq) in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Which equation forms nitric acid in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give nitric acid formation including 4NO2(g) + 2H2O(l) + O2(g) forming 4HNO3(aq), and also 2NO2 + H2O forming HNO2 plus HNO3.

mcqs.q: Where do SO2 and nitrogen oxides for acid rain mainly come from?
options: SO2 from burning fossil fuels; NO and NO2 from vehicle engines and power plants
SO2 from farms; NOx from forests
mcqs.why: The notes state SO2 comes mainly from burning fossil fuels such as coal and oil, while oxides of nitrogen are produced by vehicle engines and power plants.

mcqs.q: In what other forms can acid precipitation fall?
options: As snow, sleet, fog, dew, hail, or as dry material that settles to Earth
mcqs.why: The notes state acid precipitation can also fall as snow, sleet, fog, dew or hail, or as dry material that settles to Earth, not only as liquid rain.

mcqs.q: What does acid rain damage, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state acid rain damages forests, buildings and monuments, and its low pH also dissolves metals from soil, contaminating water sources.

mcqs.q: Which metals does acid rain dissolve from soil, and what harm can follow?
options: Gold and silver, causing skin cancer

Calcium and magnesium only, with no harm

mcqs.why: The notes state the low pH dissolves metals such as iron and aluminium from the soil, contaminating water sources and potentially causing kidney damage and nervous disorders in humans.

lessons.title: Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
The greenhouse effect is the process by which thermal infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface is absorbed and trapped by certain gases in the atmosphere, such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone, preventing heat from escaping into space. Some solar radiation is reflected by the Earth and atmosphere, most is absorbed by the surface, and the infrared radiation re-emitted by the surface is absorbed and re-emitted in all directions by greenhouse gas molecules.

Global Warming

Global warming (also known as climate change) is the gradual increase in the overall temperature of the Earth's atmosphere, caused by gases accumulating in the air and preventing heat from escaping into space. The natural greenhouse effect maintains average global temperatures at about 15°C; without it, average temperatures might have been around −17°C, at which life would not have been able to exist. Greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, thus play a crucial role in keeping the Earth warm and sustaining life.

Share of Global Greenhouse Gas Emissions

GasShare
Carbon dioxide (fossil fuel and industrial processes)65%
Carbon dioxide (forestry and other land use)11%
Methane16%
Nitrous oxide6%
Fluorinated gases2%

Key Points

  • Greenhouse gases absorb and trap infrared radiation from the Earth's surface.
  • Main greenhouse gases: CO2, water vapour, CH4, N2O and O3.
  • The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth at about 15°C instead of about −17°C.
  • Global warming is the gradual rise in temperature from extra accumulated greenhouse gases.
  • CO2 is the largest contributor to emissions (65% from fossil fuels and industry, 11% from land use).

mcqs.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: Reflection of all sunlight back to space
Thermal infrared radiation from Earth's surface is absorbed and trapped by certain gases, preventing heat escaping to space
Cooling of Earth by water vapour only
mcqs.why: The notes define the greenhouse effect as thermal infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface being absorbed and trapped by gases such as CO2, water vapour, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone.

mcqs.q: Which are the main greenhouse gases listed in the notes?
options: CO2, water vapour, CH4, N2O and O3
mcqs.why: The key points list the main greenhouse gases as CO2, water vapour, CH4, N2O and O3, which absorb and trap infrared radiation from Earth's surface.

mcqs.q: What average temperature does the natural greenhouse effect maintain, and what would it be without it?
options: About 15 degrees C; without it about -17 degrees C
About 25 degrees C; without it 0 degrees C
About 5 degrees C; without it -5 degrees C
About 30 degrees C; without it 15 degrees C
mcqs.why: The notes state the natural greenhouse effect maintains average global temperatures at about 15 degrees C; without it temperatures might have been around -17 degrees C.

mcqs.q: By how much does the natural greenhouse effect warm the Earth? Use the temperatures in the notes.
mcqs.why: Working: warming = temperature with effect - temperature without effect = 15 - (-17) = 15 + 17 = 32. Result: the natural greenhouse effect warms Earth by 32 degrees C.

mcqs.q: What share of emissions is CO2 from fossil fuel and industrial processes?
mcqs.why: The notes table gives carbon dioxide from fossil fuel and industrial processes as 65% of global greenhouse gas emissions, the largest single share listed.

mcqs.q: What share is methane in the emissions table?
mcqs.why: The notes table gives methane a 16% share of global greenhouse gas emissions, second after total carbon dioxide when both CO2 categories are combined.

mcqs.q: What is global warming as defined in the notes?
options: A sudden cooling of the atmosphere
The formation of the ozone layer

lessons.title: Causes of Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
The main cause of global warming is the build-up of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere from human activities, especially the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation.

Greenhouse Gases

  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), water vapour and ozone trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere, thereby enhancing the greenhouse effect.
  • CO2 contributes 76% to total global warming (65% from fossil fuel and industrial processes plus 11% from forestry and other land use).
  • CH4 contributes 16% and N2O 6%.
  • Fluorinated gases (2%) play a significant role despite their small share, because of their high heat absorption potential.

Anything that adds greenhouse gases — burning coal, oil and gas, cutting forests that would absorb CO2, and farm emissions — strengthens the heat-trapping blanket and raises global temperatures.

Key Points

  • Global warming is caused by enhanced greenhouse gas concentrations.
  • CO2 is the biggest contributor at 76% of total global warming.
  • CH4 (16%) and N2O (6%) are the next largest contributors.
  • Fluorinated gases are only 2% but absorb heat very strongly.
  • Fossil fuel burning and deforestation are the human activities behind the increase.

lessons.title: Consequences of Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
Global warming is the slow rise in Earth's average temperature. If it remains unchecked, temperatures might increase by up to 5°C by the end of the century, leading to serious environmental and societal issues.

Drowning of Coastal Cities

Melting glaciers and polar ice caps are causing rising sea levels, which threaten to submerge low-lying coastal areas and cities. As temperatures continue to rise, sea levels will rise further, leading to increased flooding and the displacement of populations.

Seasonal Shifting

Global warming disrupts natural climate cycles, resulting in changes to seasonal timing, such as earlier springs or delayed winters.

Change in Rainfall Pattern

Changes in global temperatures greatly influence precipitation patterns, causing some regions to experience severe droughts while others face increased rainfall and flooding.

Winds and Storms

Higher global temperatures result in more frequent and intense extreme weather events, including hurricanes, cyclones, strong winds and storms.

Key Points

  • Unchecked warming could raise temperatures by up to 5°C by 2100.
  • Melting ice raises sea levels, flooding and drowning low-lying coastal cities.
  • Seasons shift: earlier springs and delayed winters.
  • Rainfall patterns change — droughts in some regions, floods in others.
  • Extreme weather (hurricanes, cyclones, storms) becomes more frequent and intense.

lessons.title: Technologies and Strategies for Air Quality Improvement
lessons.notes_html:
Air pollution can be reduced by controlling emissions at source, switching to renewable energy, using energy efficiently and choosing greener transport.

Emissions Control Technologies

TechnologyFunction
Catalytic convertersDevices in vehicles that convert harmful pollutants in the exhaust system into less toxic substances
Smokestack filtersUsed in industrial facilities to trap particulate matter and prevent its release into the atmosphere
ScrubbersDevices that employ a chemical process to remove pollutants from industrial exhaust gases

Renewable Energy Sources

  • Solar power: sunlight captured by solar panels and converted to electricity; clean and renewable, it decreases dependence on fossil fuels and reduces greenhouse gas emissions (e.g. Quaid-e-Azam Solar Park, Bahawalpur).
  • Wind power: turbines capture the kinetic energy of air and produce electricity without carbon emissions.
  • Hydropower: electricity from flowing water (rivers or dams) turning turbines; dependable and renewable, with no direct air pollution or greenhouse gases.

Energy Efficiency and Green Transportation

  • Improving fuel efficiency: vehicles with higher fuel efficiency, and hybrid and electric options, reduce transportation emissions.
  • Energy-efficient appliances: efficient appliances and lighting minimise overall energy consumption and emissions.
  • Public transit: expanding public transport reduces the number of individual vehicles on the road.
  • Cycling infrastructure: bicycle-friendly infrastructure promotes cycling as an alternative mode of transportation.

Key Points

  • Catalytic converters clean vehicle exhaust; filters trap particulates; scrubbers chemically remove pollutants.
  • Solar, wind and hydropower produce energy without burning fossil fuels.
  • Fuel-efficient, hybrid and electric vehicles cut transport emissions.
  • Energy-efficient appliances and lighting reduce total energy demand.
  • Public transit and cycling reduce the number of polluting vehicles.

lessons.title: Types of Water Pollution
lessons.notes_html:
Water pollution is any physical, chemical or biological change in the quality of water, resulting from the addition of harmful substances, that affects living organisms. Water pollution is classified by the source of contamination into two primary categories: point source and nonpoint source pollution.

Point Source Pollution

Point source pollution originates from a specific, single source, making monitoring and regulation easier. Examples include industrial discharges from factories, municipal wastewater from sewage treatment plants, and oil spills from tankers or pipelines; also wastewater from manufacturers, oil refineries or treatment facilities, leaks from septic systems, chemical spills and illegal dumping. The EPA regulates point source pollution by setting discharge limits for facilities. Despite its localised origin, it can affect extended stretches of waterways and oceans — the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill released approximately 4.9 million barrels of oil into the Gulf of Mexico.

Nonpoint Source Pollution

Nonpoint source pollution originates from diffuse sources, making it more challenging to trace back to a specific origin. Examples include agricultural runoff (fertilisers, pesticides and animal waste), urban runoff (oil, grease, heavy metals and debris), atmospheric deposition (heavy metals and acidic compounds), residential runoff (pollutants from lawns, gardens and residential areas) and transportation runoff (oil, heavy metals, tyre particles and exhaust-related pollutants). Rain can carry tiny rubber particles from vehicle tyres into rivers; tyre wear releases more microplastics into oceans than plastic bags and bottles combined.

Key Points

  • Point source = one identifiable source, e.g. a factory discharge pipe or an oil spill from a tanker.
  • Point sources are easier to monitor and regulate through discharge limits.
  • Nonpoint source = diffuse sources spread over an area, e.g. farm and urban runoff.
  • Nonpoint pollution is harder to trace and control.
  • Both types can damage long stretches of waterways and oceans.

mcqs.why: The notes define water pollution as any physical, chemical or biological change in the quality of water, resulting from harmful substances, that affects living organisms.

lessons.title: Common Water Pollutants
lessons.notes_html:
Water pollution occurs when harmful substances are introduced into water bodies, adversely affecting living organisms and disrupting ecological balance. The most common types of water pollutants are:

Pollutant TypeExamples and Effects
Suspended solids and sedimentsSilt, clay, coal dust, plankton and industrial wastes; cause turbidity, reduce sunlight penetration and harm aquatic vegetation and animals
Dissolved solidsOrganic and inorganic compounds dissolved in water — calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chlorides, sulphates, carbonates; excess dissolved solids (salts, metals, fertilisers, pesticides) disturb growth of aquatic life and make water unsafe for drinking
Toxic elements and heavy metalsMercury, cadmium, lead, arsenic, chromium, nickel and zinc from industrial effluents, mining and waste disposal; toxic even in small amounts to humans and aquatic life
Pesticides and agricultural runoffDDT, endosulfan, atrazine and chlorpyrifos enter water via agricultural runoff; these persistent organic pollutants accumulate in the food chain
Volatile organic compounds (VOCs)Benzene, toluene and xylene from industrial discharges, solvents and fuels; toxic and carcinogenic
Oil and greaseOil spills and industrial runoff cover the water surface, lowering oxygen availability for aquatic life
Thermal pollutionHot water discharged from thermal or nuclear power plants (often 10–15°C warmer) raises water temperature, reduces dissolved oxygen and harms aquatic life

Key Points

  • Suspended solids make water turbid and block sunlight for aquatic plants.
  • Heavy metals are toxic even in very small amounts and enter through industry and mining.
  • Pesticides such as DDT are persistent and accumulate in the food chain.
  • Oil films on the surface cut off oxygen for aquatic organisms.
  • Thermal pollution lowers dissolved oxygen by warming the water.

lessons.title: Water Treatment
lessons.notes_html:
Water treatment is the process of making raw water suitable for drinking and other domestic uses by removing foreign materials. Its purpose is to eliminate contaminants and organisms through a combination of biological, chemical and physical methods, ensuring the water is safe for consumption. Contaminated water is a primary source of infectious diseases such as amoebiasis, dysentery, cholera, typhoid, jaundice, malaria and paratyphoid fever.

Steps of Water Treatment

StepPurpose
1. PretreatmentWater passes through screens to eliminate large debris and floating materials such as leaves and sticks
2. CoagulationChemicals induce clumping of small suspended particles, aiding removal of colloidal clay precipitates
3. SedimentationWater rests in sedimentation tanks so large or heavy particles settle, reducing the overall load of impurities
4. FiltrationWater is filtered through layers of sand and gravel to remove fine particles and organic matter
5. Carbon adsorptionWater passes over beds of activated charcoal, which eliminate unpleasant tastes, odours and certain organic contaminants
6. ChlorinationChlorine or chlorine compounds are added to kill harmful microorganisms — the final, critical disinfection step
7. UV disinfectionUltraviolet light disrupts the DNA of microorganisms, preventing reproduction and rendering them harmless

The treated water is then stored and distributed for home consumption (Fig. 10.7 sequence: intake → coagulation → sedimentation → filtration → disinfection → treated water storage → distribution).

Key Points

  • Water treatment combines physical, chemical and biological methods to make water safe.
  • Order of steps: pretreatment → coagulation → sedimentation → filtration → carbon adsorption → disinfection.
  • Coagulation clumps fine suspended particles so they can settle out.
  • Activated charcoal removes tastes, odours and organic contaminants.
  • Chlorination and UV light disinfect by killing or inactivating microorganisms.

lessons.title: Human Impact on Water Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities, particularly in agriculture and industrial processes, significantly and complexly impact water resources. These impacts affect both the quantity of water available and its quality, which in turn has consequences for ecosystems and human communities.

Agriculture's Impact on Water Resources

Farming uses a large amount of the world's freshwater supply for irrigation, which can lead to water scarcity and further deplete water sources like rivers and aquifers; inefficient irrigation practices worsen the problem by putting additional strain on water sources. Chemicals from fertilisers and pesticides used in farming can contaminate rivers and streams, harming ecosystems and posing risks to wildlife and human health. Deforestation and unsustainable farming practices lead to soil erosion, which pollutes waterways with sediment and reduces water quality.

Industrial Processes and Water Resources

Industries use significant amounts of water for cooling, manufacturing and other processes, which can strain water resources, especially in areas already facing water scarcity. Industrial activities release pollutants like heavy metals and toxic chemicals into waterways, making them unsuitable for various purposes. Excess heat generated by industrial processes can disrupt aquatic ecosystems and create uninhabitable zones for many species. Additionally, both agriculture and industry contribute to climate change, further worsening water scarcity and altering hydrological cycles.

Key Points

  • Agriculture is the largest user of freshwater, mainly for irrigation.
  • Inefficient irrigation depletes rivers and aquifers and causes scarcity.
  • Fertilisers and pesticides from farms contaminate rivers and streams.
  • Industry uses water for cooling and manufacturing and discharges heavy metals and toxic chemicals.
  • Industrial waste heat creates uninhabitable zones for aquatic species.

lessons.title: Strategies for Conservation and Preservation of Water Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Water conservation involves promoting responsible water use in homes, businesses and agriculture, encouraging water-efficient technologies and appliances, and implementing methods like rainwater harvesting and efficient irrigation to conserve water.

Strategies for Conservation and Preservation (Table 10.1)

StrategyFocusKey ExamplesBenefits
Water conservationReduce demandLow-flow appliances, smart irrigation, rainwater harvesting, research in advanced water-saving technologiesLess pressure on water sources; reduces stress during droughts and floods
Watershed managementProtect sourcesRiparian buffers, wetland restoration, erosion control, runoff managementSustained water supplies, improved water quality, remote sensing for informed management
Pollution controlSafeguard purityRegulations on discharges, advanced wastewater treatment, responsible chemical use, septic tank filters, storm water managementMinimises water pollution, protects ecosystems and human health, stronger legislation holds polluters accountable
Infrastructure investmentModernise and optimiseLeak detection, smart systems, efficient storage and desalination, replacing aging pipesReduced water losses, increased efficiency and resilience, equitable access to water
Education and awarenessEmpower individuals and communitiesWater conservation campaigns, educational workshops, media outreach, integrating water education into schoolsFosters individual responsibility; builds a sustainable, water-conscious society

Key Points

  • Conservation reduces demand through efficient appliances, smart irrigation and rainwater harvesting.
  • Watershed management protects the sources of water themselves.
  • Pollution control safeguards purity through discharge regulations and wastewater treatment.
  • Modern infrastructure cuts losses from leaks and aging pipes.
  • Education builds a water-conscious society that sustains all other strategies.

mcqs.why: The notes state watershed management protects sources through riparian buffers, wetland restoration, erosion control and runoff management, sustaining supplies and water quality.

mcqs.why: The notes state infrastructure investment modernises systems through leak detection, smart systems, efficient storage and desalination, and replacing aging pipes to reduce losses.

options: Reduced water losses, increased efficiency and resilience, and equitable access to water
mcqs.why: Table 10.1 lists benefits of infrastructure investment as reduced water losses, increased efficiency and resilience, and equitable access to water for all communities.

It fosters individual responsibility and builds a sustainable, water-conscious society
mcqs.why: The notes state education and awareness through campaigns, workshops, media outreach and school education foster individual responsibility and build a water-conscious society.

options: Less pressure on water sources and reduced stress during droughts and floods
mcqs.why: Table 10.1 states conservation benefits include less pressure on water sources and reduced stress during droughts and floods, because demand has been lowered.

mcqs.why: Table 10.1 states pollution control benefits include stronger legislation holding polluters accountable, minimising water pollution and protecting ecosystems and human health.

lessons.title: The Influence of Chemical Properties on Water Quality and Pollution
lessons.notes_html:
The physical, biological and chemical properties of drinking water — including its molecular structure, polarity, ability to form hydrogen bonds and role as a solvent — play a critical role in determining water quality and potential pollution. Even minor variations in these parameters can have significant implications for human health.

Chemical Properties of Water

  • Molecular structure and polarity: H2O is a polar molecule due to the electronegativity difference between oxygen and hydrogen. This polarity makes water an excellent solvent, attracting polar molecules and dissolving substances — essential for transporting nutrients and minerals in living organisms.
  • Hydrogen bonding: water molecules form (weak) hydrogen bonds due to their polarity, giving properties like high surface tension, cohesion, adhesion, capillary action and water transport in plants.
  • Solvent properties: water is a universal solvent that transports nutrients and minerals, but it is also susceptible to pollution from acid rain, industrial discharges and runoff, as it can dissolve and carry harmful chemicals.

Relation to Water Quality

  • pH level: drinking water should be near neutral (pH 7); deviations can harm aquatic life and human health.
  • Dissolved oxygen (DO): aquatic organisms rely on dissolved oxygen for respiration; pollution such as organic matter from sewage or agricultural runoff can deplete oxygen levels.
  • Ion concentrations: elevated nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers cause nutrient pollution, leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion; vital minerals like calcium and magnesium are beneficial in moderation.

Relation to Water Pollution

  • Solubility: water's ability to dissolve substances makes it vulnerable to pollution from agricultural runoff, industrial waste and urban wastewater.
  • Bioaccumulation: pollutants like pesticides or heavy metals accumulate in the tissues of organisms over time, especially when absorption exceeds breakdown or excretion.
  • Chemical reactions: pollutants can react in water, forming toxic by-products; industrial discharges may produce harmful compounds.

Key Points

  • Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, making it a universal solvent.
  • The same solvent power that carries nutrients also carries pollutants.
  • Water quality is judged by pH, dissolved oxygen and ion concentrations.
  • Excess nitrates and phosphates cause algal blooms and oxygen depletion.
  • Bioaccumulation builds up pesticides and heavy metals in organism tissues over time.

mcqs.q: Why is water a polar molecule?
options: Because it has no charge difference
Due to the electronegativity difference between oxygen and hydrogen
mcqs.why: The notes state H2O is a polar molecule due to the electronegativity difference between oxygen and hydrogen, making water an excellent solvent for polar substances.

mcqs.q: What does water's polarity make it able to do?
options: Act as an excellent solvent, attracting polar molecules and dissolving substances
mcqs.why: The notes state polarity makes water an excellent solvent, attracting polar molecules and dissolving substances, essential for transporting nutrients and minerals in living organisms.

mcqs.q: What do hydrogen bonds give water?
options: High surface tension, cohesion, adhesion, capillary action and water transport in plants
mcqs.why: The notes state water molecules form weak hydrogen bonds due to polarity, giving properties like high surface tension, cohesion, adhesion, capillary action and transport in plants.

mcqs.q: Why is water called a universal solvent, and what is the risk?
options: It dissolves nothing, so it stays pure
It transports nutrients and minerals but can also dissolve and carry harmful chemicals and pollutants
mcqs.why: The notes state water is a universal solvent transporting nutrients and minerals, but it is also susceptible to pollution from acid rain, discharges and runoff as it carries harmful chemicals.

mcqs.q: What pH should drinking water be near?
options: Near neutral, pH 7; deviations can harm aquatic life and human health
mcqs.why: The notes state drinking water should be near neutral at pH 7, and deviations from this can harm aquatic life and human health, so pH judges water quality.

mcqs.q: Why is dissolved oxygen important in water quality?
options: Aquatic organisms rely on it for respiration; pollution from sewage or runoff can deplete it
mcqs.why: The notes state aquatic organisms rely on dissolved oxygen for respiration, and pollution such as organic matter from sewage or agricultural runoff can deplete oxygen levels.

mcqs.q: What do elevated nitrates and phosphates cause?
options: Nutrient pollution, leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion
mcqs.why: The notes state elevated nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers cause nutrient pollution, leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion that harms aquatic life.

mcqs.q: Which minerals are beneficial in moderation in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state vital minerals like calcium and magnesium are beneficial in moderation, unlike excess nitrates and phosphates which cause nutrient pollution.

mcqs.q: What is bioaccumulation?
options: Pollutants like pesticides or heavy metals accumulating in organism tissues over time when absorption exceeds breakdown or excretion
Pollutants breaking down quickly in water
mcqs.why: The notes define bioaccumulation as pollutants like pesticides or heavy metals accumulating in the tissues of organisms over time, especially when absorption exceeds breakdown or excretion.

mcqs.q: How can pollutants become more harmful inside water?
options: Pollutants can react in water, forming toxic by-products and harmful compounds
mcqs.why: The notes state pollutants can react in water forming toxic by-products, and industrial discharges may produce harmful compounds beyond the original pollutants released.

lessons.title: Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons and their derivatives are organic compounds. Compounds of only carbon and hydrogen are hydrocarbons; those also containing O, N, S, P or halogens are derivatives of hydrocarbons. Their study is organic chemistry.

Functional Group

A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that mainly determines the chemical behaviour of the molecule. Double and triple bonds are also functional groups. Compounds with the same functional group show similar properties: methanol CH3OH, ethanol CH3CH2OH and propanol CH3CH2CH2OH are alike because of the —OH group. The functional group is the reactive part; the hydrocarbon part is inert. A compound with two or more functional groups is a polyfunctional compound.

Key Formulae

ClassFunctional groupExampleSuffix/Prefix
Alkanes— (R—H)CH3—CH3, ethane-ane
AlkenesC=CH2C=CH2, ethene-ene
AlkynesC≡CCH≡CH, ethyne-yne
Alkyl halides—XCH3CH2Cl, chloroethanehalo-
Alcohols—OHCH3CH2OH, ethanol-ol
Ethers—O—CH3—O—CH3, methoxymethane—
Aldehydes—CHOCH3CHO, ethanal-al
KetonesC=O (carbonyl)propan-2-one-one
Carboxylic acids—COOHCH3COOH, ethanoic acid-oic acid
Esters—COORmethyl ethanoate-oate
Amides—CONH2ethanamide-amide
Amines—NH2methanamine-amine
Nitriles—CNCH3—C≡N, ethanenitrile-nitrile

Key Points

  • Functional group decides chemical behaviour, nomenclature and classification.
  • Same functional group = similar chemical properties.
  • Ethanol (—OH) is in alcoholic beverages; acetic acid (—COOH) gives vinegar its sour flavour; formaldehyde (—CHO) preserves specimens.
  • Phenols have —OH on an aromatic ring; acyl halides —COX take suffix -oyl halide; acid anhydrides take -oic anhydride.

mcqs.q: What is a functional group?
options: An atom or group of atoms that mainly determines the chemical behaviour of a molecule
The inert hydrocarbon part of a molecule
Any carbon atom in a chain
A molecule containing only carbon and hydrogen
mcqs.why: The notes define a functional group as an atom or group of atoms that mainly determines the chemical behaviour of the molecule.

mcqs.q: Which compounds are hydrocarbons?
options: Compounds containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
Compounds of only carbon and hydrogen
mcqs.why: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen; compounds also containing O, N, S, P or halogens are derivatives of hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Why do methanol, ethanol and propanol show similar properties?
options: They have the same number of carbon atoms
They have the same molecular mass
They all contain the —OH functional group
mcqs.why: Methanol CH3OH, ethanol CH3CH2OH and propanol are alike because they share the same functional group, —OH.

mcqs.q: In an organic molecule, which part is described as inert?
mcqs.why: The functional group is the reactive part of the molecule, while the hydrocarbon part is inert.

mcqs.q: What is a polyfunctional compound?
options: A compound with two or more functional groups
A compound with only one carbon atom
A compound with no functional group
A compound made only of hydrogen
mcqs.why: A compound with two or more functional groups is called a polyfunctional compound, as stated in the lesson notes.

mcqs.q: Which suffix is used for carboxylic acids?
mcqs.why: Carboxylic acids such as ethanoic acid CH3COOH take the suffix -oic acid in the functional group table.

mcqs.q: Ethanol owes its presence in alcoholic beverages to which group, and acetic acid its sour flavour to which group?
options: —OH in ethanol and —COOH in acetic acid
mcqs.why: Ethanol contains the —OH group and is found in alcoholic beverages; acetic acid contains —COOH, which gives vinegar its sour flavour.

mcqs.q: Which functional group is present in ethanal, CH3CHO?
mcqs.why: Ethanal contains the aldehyde group —CHO, and aldehydes take the suffix -al in their names.

mcqs.q: Double and triple bonds are also considered as:
mcqs.why: The notes state that double and triple bonds are also functional groups, alongside groups such as —OH and —COOH.

mcqs.q: Phenols are compounds in which —OH is attached to:
mcqs.why: Phenols have the —OH group attached to an aromatic ring, which distinguishes them from ordinary alcohols.

lessons.title: Homologous Series
lessons.notes_html:
A homologous series is a group of organic compounds in which each member differs from the next by a methylene group (—CH2—). Its members are called homologs.

Alkane Series

NameC atomsMolecular formulaCondensed formula
Methane1CH4CH4
Ethane2C2H6CH3CH3
Propane3C3H8CH3CH2CH3
Butane4C4H10CH3(CH2)2CH3
Pentane5C5H12CH3(CH2)3CH3
Hexane6C6H14CH3(CH2)4CH3
Heptane7C7H16CH3(CH2)5CH3
Octane8C8H18CH3(CH2)6CH3
Nonane9C9H20CH3(CH2)7CH3
Decane10C10H22CH3(CH2)8CH3

General Characteristics

  • Same functional group, same general formula, same types of elements.
  • Similar chemical properties; different physical properties because molecular masses differ.
  • Successive members differ by CH2; molecular mass differs by 14 units (CH2 = 12 + 2 = 14).
  • All members are prepared by the same general methods.

Key Formulae

ClassGeneral formula
AlkaneCnH2n+2
AlkeneCnH2n
AlkyneCnH2n-2
AlcoholCnH2n+1OH
Alkyl halideCnH2n+1X (X = F, Cl, Br, I)

Here n is the number of carbon atoms.

Key Points

  • Homologs differ by —CH2— and 14 mass units.
  • Chemical properties stay similar down the series.
  • Physical properties change gradually with molecular mass.
  • One general formula represents the whole series.

mcqs.q: In a homologous series, each member differs from the next by:
mcqs.why: Members of a homologous series differ from the next member by a methylene group, —CH2—, and are called homologs.

mcqs.q: By how many mass units do successive homologs differ?
mcqs.why: The mass of —CH2— is 12 + 2 = 14, so successive members of a homologous series differ by 14 mass units.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of alkanes?
mcqs.why: Alkanes follow the general formula CnH2n+2, where n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

mcqs.q: Which formula represents heptane in the alkane table?
mcqs.why: Heptane has 7 carbon atoms; using CnH2n+2 gives C7H16, matching the alkane series table in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why do homologs have different physical properties?
mcqs.why: Homologs share the same functional group but their physical properties differ because their molecular masses differ.

mcqs.q: What is the molecular formula of nonane?
mcqs.why: Nonane has 9 carbons; CnH2n+2 gives H = 2(9)+2 = 20, so the molecular formula of nonane is C9H20.

mcqs.q: Which general formula belongs to alkynes?
mcqs.why: The key formulae table gives CnH2n-2 as the general formula for the alkyne homologous series.

mcqs.q: Members of a homologous series are prepared by:
options: A different method for each member
mcqs.why: One general characteristic of a homologous series is that all its members are prepared by the same general methods.

mcqs.q: What is the condensed formula of pentane as given in the table?
mcqs.why: Pentane has 5 carbons, written in condensed form as CH3(CH2)3CH3 in the alkane series table.

mcqs.q: In the general formulas, the letter n stands for:
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that in these general formulas, n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
The system for naming compounds is called nomenclature. Two primary systems name organic compounds: the Common System and the IUPAC System. Common names are often shorter and useful when the IUPAC name is lengthy, e.g. tartaric acid for 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid.

IUPAC System

To avoid memorising millions of names, a commission of 34 chemists from nine countries met in Geneva (Switzerland) in 1892 and developed the Geneva system. The group became the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), pronounced eye-you-pack. Its rules are continually revised. The fundamental principle: each different compound should have a distinct and unambiguous name.

Parts of an IUPAC Name

  • Root: number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain.
  • Suffix: the family of the compound.
  • Prefix: identity, position and number of substituents on the chain.

Key Points

  • Nomenclature = the naming system for compounds.
  • IUPAC began with the Geneva meeting of 1892.
  • One compound, one distinct unambiguous IUPAC name.
  • Every IUPAC name has root + suffix, with prefixes for substituents.

mcqs.q: What is nomenclature in organic chemistry?
mcqs.why: Nomenclature is the system used for naming compounds; the two primary systems are the Common System and the IUPAC System.

mcqs.q: The IUPAC system began with a meeting in which city and year?
mcqs.why: A commission of 34 chemists from nine countries met in Geneva, Switzerland, in 1892 and developed the Geneva system.

mcqs.q: What does the root in an IUPAC name indicate?
options: The number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain
mcqs.why: The root of an IUPAC name shows the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain of the molecule.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the prefix in an IUPAC name?
options: It shows the family of the compound
It gives the identity, position and number of substituents
mcqs.why: The prefix gives the identity, position and number of substituents attached to the main carbon chain.

mcqs.q: What is the fundamental principle of IUPAC naming?
options: Each different compound should have a distinct and unambiguous name
Every name should be as short as possible
Names should be based on discoverers
mcqs.why: The fundamental IUPAC principle is that each different compound should have a distinct and unambiguous name.

mcqs.q: Tartaric acid is the common name for which IUPAC name?
mcqs.why: The notes give tartaric acid as a common name that is shorter and useful where the IUPAC name, 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid, is lengthy.

mcqs.q: How is IUPAC pronounced, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The group became the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), pronounced eye-you-pack.

mcqs.q: What does the suffix in an IUPAC name show?
mcqs.why: The suffix in an IUPAC name indicates the family to which the compound belongs, such as -ane, -ene or -ol.

mcqs.q: How many chemists and countries formed the original Geneva commission?
mcqs.why: The notes state that a commission of 34 chemists from nine countries met in Geneva in 1892 to develop the system.

mcqs.q: Why are common names still sometimes used?
options: They are more accurate than IUPAC names
They are often shorter and useful when the IUPAC name is lengthy
IUPAC names are forbidden in industry
Common names show substituent positions better
mcqs.why: Common names are often shorter and remain useful when the systematic IUPAC name is lengthy, as with tartaric acid.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Straight Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
The first four alkanes keep common names: methane, ethane, propane and butane. Names of larger alkanes use a Latin or Greek prefix for the number of carbon atoms, followed by -ane.

Common-System Prefixes for Isomers

In the common system all isomeric alkanes share one parent name, e.g. pentane for the three C5H12 isomers. Prefixes n-, iso- and neo- distinguish them.

  • n- (normal): all carbons in one continuous unbranched chain, e.g. n-pentane CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, n-hexane.
  • iso-: one methyl group on the second carbon of the chain, e.g. isopentane, isohexane.
  • neo-: two methyl groups on the second carbon, e.g. neohexane, neoheptane.

Key Formulae

C atomsRootParent nameC atomsRootParent name
1MethMethane11UndecUndecane
2EthEthane12DodecDodecane
3PropPropane13TridecTridecane
4ButButane14TetradecTetradecane
5PentPentane15PentadecPentadecane
6HexHexane16HexadecHexadecane
7HeptHeptane17HeptadecHeptadecane
8OctOctane18OctadecOctadecane
9NonNonane19NonadecNonadecane
10DecDecane20EicosEicosane

Skeletal formula: a zigzag line; each end and corner is a carbon, e.g. ethane is one line segment, propane two segments.

Key Points

  • Root + -ane names a straight-chain alkane.
  • n- = unbranched; iso- = one methyl at C-2; neo- = two methyls at C-2.
  • First four names (methane to butane) are retained common names.

mcqs.q: The first four alkanes, which keep their common names, are:
mcqs.why: The first four alkanes keep common names: methane, ethane, propane and butane; larger alkanes use Latin or Greek prefixes plus -ane.

mcqs.q: In the common system, the prefix n- (normal) means:
options: One methyl group on the second carbon
All carbons in one continuous unbranched chain
Two methyl groups on the second carbon
mcqs.why: The prefix n- means all carbons lie in one continuous unbranched chain, as in n-pentane CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3.

mcqs.q: What does the prefix iso- indicate in the common system?
options: Two methyl groups on the second carbon
One methyl group on the second carbon of the chain
mcqs.why: The iso- prefix indicates one methyl group on the second carbon of the chain, as in isopentane and isohexane.

mcqs.q: Neo-hexane and neoheptane are named with neo- because they have:
options: One methyl group on the first carbon
A triple bond in the chain
Two methyl groups on the second carbon
mcqs.why: The neo- prefix is used when there are two methyl groups on the second carbon of the chain, as in neohexane.

mcqs.q: What is the parent name for an alkane with 12 carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: The root for 12 carbons is Dodec, giving the parent name dodecane in the root table of the notes.

mcqs.q: In a skeletal formula, each end and each corner of the zigzag line represents:
mcqs.why: In a skeletal formula each end and corner of the zigzag line is a carbon; ethane is one segment and propane is two segments.

mcqs.q: How many isomeric alkanes share the parent name pentane in the common system example?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in the common system all isomeric alkanes share one parent name, e.g. pentane for the three C5H12 isomers.

mcqs.q: What is the root word for a 20-carbon alkane?
mcqs.why: The table gives Eicos as the root for 20 carbon atoms, so the parent alkane name is eicosane.

mcqs.q: Names of larger straight-chain alkanes are formed by:
options: A Latin or Greek prefix for the carbon number, followed by -ane
mcqs.why: Larger alkanes use a Latin or Greek prefix showing the number of carbon atoms, followed by the suffix -ane.

mcqs.q: Which root corresponds to 9 carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: The root for 9 carbon atoms is Non, giving nonane as the parent name in the straight-chain alkane table.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Branched Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Branched-chain alkanes are named by the IUPAC rules below.

Rules

  • (i) Select the longest continuous chain as parent (stem) name. It may turn a corner; e.g. the worked example gives an 8-carbon parent, octane.
  • (ii) Number from the end closer to the substituents: 3-methylhexane, not 4-methylhexane.
  • (iii) Show the substituent position by its carbon number: 4-methyloctane.
  • (iv) Identical substituents take di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-: 2,4-dimethylpentane.
  • (v) If the first substituent is equidistant from both ends, give the lower number to the second substituent (first point of difference): 2,4,7-trimethyloctane, not 2,5,7-trimethyloctane.
  • (vi) Different substituents are listed alphabetically: 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane. Ignore di-, tri-, sec-, tert- in alphabetising; iso- and cyclo- are not ignored. If numbering ties both ways, the first-listed substituent alphabetically gets the lower number.
  • (vii) Between equal-length chains, choose the one with more substituents: 3-ethyl-2-methylheptane, not 3-isopropylheptane.

Branch name and parent name are written as one word; numbers are separated by commas, and a hyphen separates number from word.

Key Points

  • Longest chain first, then lowest locants.
  • Alphabetical order for different substituents.
  • di-/tri- show repeated identical substituents.
  • More substituents wins when chains are equal in length.

mcqs.q: What is the first rule for naming a branched-chain alkane?
options: Select the longest continuous chain as the parent name
Number from the middle of the chain
mcqs.why: Rule (i) is to select the longest continuous chain as the parent (stem) name; the chain may turn a corner.

mcqs.q: Why is CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH2CH3-type naming written 3-methylhexane rather than 4-methylhexane in the example?
options: Numbering is done from the end closer to the substituents
The longest chain is hexane either way
Methyl groups are always at position 3
mcqs.why: Rule (ii) says to number from the end closer to the substituents, giving 3-methylhexane rather than 4-methylhexane.

mcqs.q: Which prefixes show identical substituents appearing more than once?
mcqs.why: Identical substituents take the multiplying prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- and penta-, as in 2,4-dimethylpentane.

mcqs.q: Different substituents in a branched alkane name are listed:
mcqs.why: Rule (vi) requires different substituents to be listed alphabetically, as in 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane.

mcqs.q: When alphabetising substituents, which prefixes are IGNORED?
mcqs.why: The notes say to ignore di-, tri-, sec- and tert- when alphabetising, but iso- and cyclo- are not ignored.

mcqs.q: If the first substituent is equidistant from both ends, the lower number goes to:
options: The second substituent (first point of difference)
mcqs.why: Rule (v): if the first substituent is equidistant, give the lower number to the second substituent — 2,4,7-trimethyloctane, not 2,5,7-.

mcqs.q: Between two equal-length chains, the parent chain chosen is the one with:
options: A methyl group at the end
mcqs.why: Rule (vii): between equal-length chains choose the one with more substituents — 3-ethyl-2-methylheptane, not 3-isopropylheptane.

mcqs.q: In an alkane name, numbers are separated by ___ and a ___ separates a number from a word.
mcqs.why: Branch and parent names form one word; numbers are separated by commas, and a hyphen separates a number from a word.

mcqs.q: The worked example in the rules gives an 8-carbon parent chain. Its parent name is:
mcqs.why: The worked example under rule (i) gives an 8-carbon parent chain, so the parent (stem) name is octane.

mcqs.q: If numbering ties both ways for different substituents, the lower number goes to:
mcqs.why: Rule (vi) states that if numbering ties both ways, the first-listed substituent alphabetically gets the lower number.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Cycloalkanes are named by IUPAC rules for rings.

Rules

  • (i) Add prefix cyclo- to the alkane with the same number of carbons as the ring: cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane. They are drawn as geometric figures — triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon; each corner is one carbon with two hydrogens.
  • (ii) A single substituent needs no position number, as all positions are equivalent: methylcyclopropane, ethylcyclobutane.
  • (iii) With two or more substituents, number the ring for the lowest possible numbers and name substituents alphabetically: 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane; 1-ethyl-2-methylcyclopentane; 1-ethyl-2,5-dimethylcyclohexane.
  • (iv) If the substituent chain has more carbons than the ring, the chain is the parent and the ring is a substituent: 1-cyclopropylbutane, 2-cyclobutylpentane.

Key Points

  • cyclo- + alkane name = cycloalkane.
  • Mono-substituted rings need no locant.
  • Lowest locants, then alphabetical order, for several substituents.
  • Larger chain beats the ring as parent.

mcqs.q: How is a cycloalkane named?
options: By adding the prefix cyclo- to the alkane with the same number of carbons as the ring
By adding the suffix -ring to the alkane name
By using the name of the corresponding alkene
By counting only the ring hydrogens
mcqs.why: Rule (i): add the prefix cyclo- to the alkane with the same number of carbons as the ring, e.g. cyclopropane and cyclohexane.

mcqs.q: Cyclopentane is drawn as which geometric figure?
mcqs.why: Cycloalkanes are drawn as geometric figures: cyclopentane is a pentagon, each corner being one carbon with two hydrogens.

mcqs.q: Why does methylcyclopropane need no position number for its substituent?
options: The ring has only one carbon
With a single substituent all ring positions are equivalent
Numbers are not used in ring compounds
mcqs.why: Rule (ii): a single substituent needs no position number because all positions on the ring are equivalent.

mcqs.q: With two or more substituents on a ring, the ring is numbered to give:
options: Numbers starting at the largest substituent
The lowest possible numbers, with substituents named alphabetically
mcqs.why: Rule (iii) requires numbering for the lowest possible locants and naming substituents alphabetically, e.g. 1-ethyl-2-methylcyclopentane.

mcqs.q: If a substituent chain has more carbons than the ring, then:
options: The chain is the parent and the ring is named as a substituent
The ring is always the parent
mcqs.why: Rule (iv): if the substituent chain has more carbons than the ring, the chain is the parent, e.g. 1-cyclopropylbutane.

mcqs.q: Which name follows the rules for a cyclohexane ring with an ethyl group at C-1 and methyl groups at C-2 and C-5?
mcqs.why: The book example is 1-ethyl-2,5-dimethylcyclohexane: lowest locants are used and substituents are listed alphabetically.

mcqs.q: Each corner of a drawn cycloalkane ring represents:
mcqs.why: In the geometric figures for cycloalkanes, each corner is one carbon atom carrying two hydrogen atoms.

mcqs.q: 2-cyclobutylpentane is an example of:
options: A case where the chain has more carbons than the ring, so the chain is the parent
mcqs.why: In 2-cyclobutylpentane the five-carbon chain is the parent and the four-carbon ring is a substituent, following rule (iv).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the correct name for a three-carbon ring with two methyl groups on adjacent carbons?
mcqs.why: The book example for two substituents on a ring is 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane, using the lowest possible locants.

mcqs.q: Ethylcyclobutane illustrates which rule?
options: A single substituent on a ring needs no position number
The lowest-locant rule for many substituents
mcqs.why: Ethylcyclobutane is given under rule (ii): a single substituent needs no locant because all ring positions are equivalent.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alkenes and Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes

  • Select the longest continuous chain containing the C=C bond; position of the double bond follows the root, then suffix -ene: CH2=CH—CH2—CH3 is butene (parent).
  • Number from the end closest to the double bond; give its position by the lower-numbered carbon. Two- and three-carbon alkenes need no number. Example: pent-2-ene.
  • Name substituents as in alkanes: 4-methylpent-2-ene.
  • Two or more double bonds: -diene, -triene, -tetraene replace -ene, e.g. buta-1,3-diene CH2=CH—CH=CH2.

Alkynes

  • Select the longest chain containing C≡C; suffix -yne: CH3—C≡C—CH3 is butyne (parent).
  • Number from the end nearest the triple bond; position by the lower carbon: pent-2-yne. Two-/three-carbon alkynes need no numbering.
  • Substituents as usual, triple bond lowest: 4-methylhex-2-yne.
  • Several triple bonds: -diyne, -triyne, -tetrayne, e.g. buta-1,3-diyne.
  • Both double and triple bonds: root ends in -en, suffix -yne for the whole molecule. Number from the end closest to either bond; if equidistant, the double bond gets the lower number: pent-1-en-4-yne, pent-1-en-3-yne, pent-3-en-1-yne.

Key Points

  • Parent chain must contain the multiple bond.
  • Multiple bond gets the lowest possible locant.
  • -diene/-diyne etc. show several multiple bonds.
  • In enynes, a tie is broken in favour of the double bond.

mcqs.q: For an alkene, the parent chain must:
mcqs.why: Alkene naming selects the longest continuous chain containing the C=C bond, and the suffix -ene follows the root.

mcqs.q: How is an alkene chain numbered?
options: From the end closest to the largest substituent
From the end closest to the double bond
mcqs.why: Alkenes are numbered from the end closest to the double bond, giving its position by the lower-numbered carbon, e.g. pent-2-ene.

mcqs.q: Which alkenes need no number for the double bond position?
mcqs.why: The notes state that two- and three-carbon alkenes need no number for the position of the double bond.

mcqs.q: CH2=CH—CH=CH2 is named:
mcqs.why: Two double bonds take the suffix -diene, so CH2=CH—CH=CH2 is buta-1,3-diene, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: For alkynes, the suffix used is:
mcqs.why: Alkynes select the longest chain containing C≡C and use the suffix -yne, e.g. CH3—C≡C—CH3 is butyne.

mcqs.q: 4-methylhex-2-yne shows that in alkynes:
options: The methyl group gets the lowest number
The triple bond is given the lowest possible locant, with substituents named as usual
The suffix is written before the root
mcqs.why: In 4-methylhex-2-yne the chain is numbered from the end nearest the triple bond so the triple bond gets the lowest locant.

mcqs.q: Several triple bonds in a molecule are shown by suffixes such as:
mcqs.why: Several triple bonds take the suffixes -diyne, -triyne and -tetrayne, e.g. buta-1,3-diyne in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a molecule with both a double and a triple bond, if the two bonds are equidistant from the ends:
options: The triple bond gets the lower number
The compound is named as an alkane
The double bond gets the lower number
mcqs.why: For enynes, numbering starts near either bond, but if they are equidistant the double bond gets the lower number.

mcqs.q: In enyne names such as pent-1-en-4-yne, the root ends in ___ and the suffix is ___:
mcqs.why: When both double and triple bonds are present, the root ends in -en and the suffix -yne is used for the whole molecule.

mcqs.q: 4-methylpent-2-ene is an example of:
options: An alkene named with its substituent following alkane rules
mcqs.why: The notes use 4-methylpent-2-ene to show that alkene substituents are named as in alkanes, with the double bond locant shown.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Haloalkanes and Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Haloalkanes (Alkyl Halides)

Select the longest chain including the halogen as parent. Number from the end closest to the halogen for its lowest number. Name the halogen as a prefix — fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo — with its position number. Several identical halogens take di-, tri-, tetra-; different halogens are written alphabetically.

Examples: bromoethane CH3—CH2—Br; 2-chloropropane; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane.

Alcohols

The longest chain containing —OH is the parent; suffix -ol replaces the final -e of the alkane. Number from the end closer to —OH so it gets the lowest number, and show its position. Other substituents follow standard rules, with priority to —OH in numbering. Several —OH groups take -diol, -triol and the final -e is retained.

Examples: ethanol CH3—CH2—OH; propan-2-ol; 3-methylbutan-1-ol; pentane-2,4-diol; 4-bromo-3-chloro-2-methylbutan-1-ol.

Key Points

  • Halogens are always prefixes, never the suffix.
  • Alcohol suffix is -ol; —OH controls numbering.
  • Multiple —OH groups: -diol, -triol, keeping the -e.
  • Different halogens are listed alphabetically.

mcqs.q: In haloalkanes, the halogen is always named as:
mcqs.why: Halogens are always prefixes (fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo) with a position number; they are never the suffix.

mcqs.q: How is a haloalkane chain numbered?
options: From the end farthest from the halogen
From the end closest to the halogen, for its lowest number
mcqs.why: The longest chain including the halogen is the parent, numbered from the end closest to the halogen for its lowest number.

mcqs.q: 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane shows that different halogens are:
mcqs.why: Different halogens are written alphabetically, as in the book example 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane (bromo before chloro).

mcqs.q: For alcohols, the parent chain is:
options: The shortest chain in the molecule
The chain with the most carbons overall
The longest chain containing the —OH group
mcqs.why: For alcohols the longest chain containing —OH is the parent, and the suffix -ol replaces the final -e of the alkane.

mcqs.q: Several —OH groups in an alcohol are shown by:
options: -diol, -triol, with the final -e of the alkane retained
mcqs.why: Several —OH groups take -diol or -triol and the final -e is retained, as in pentane-2,4-diol.

mcqs.q: In alcohol numbering, priority is given to:
options: The —OH group, so it gets the lowest number
mcqs.why: Alcohol chains are numbered from the end closer to —OH so that the —OH group gets the lowest possible number.

mcqs.q: CH3—CH2—Br is named:
mcqs.why: The book example for CH3—CH2—Br is bromoethane; a two-carbon chain needs no locant for a single halogen.

mcqs.q: 3-methylbutan-1-ol shows the —OH group at:
mcqs.why: In 3-methylbutan-1-ol the locant 1 before -ol shows the —OH group is on carbon-1 of the butane chain.

mcqs.q: Several identical halogens in a haloalkane take:
mcqs.why: Several identical halogens take di-, tri- and tetra- prefixes, just like identical alkyl substituents in alkanes.

mcqs.q: Propan-2-ol is the name for an alcohol in which —OH is:
options: On the middle carbon (carbon-2) of propane
mcqs.why: Propan-2-ol is listed in the notes: the locant 2 shows the —OH group sits on the second carbon of the propane chain.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes
