The longest chain containing the —CHO group is the parent. Suffix -al replaces the final -e of the alkane. The —CHO carbon is always carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single aldehyde group. Other substituents follow standard rules.

Examples: methanal HCHO; ethanal CH3CHO; propanal; 3-methylbutanal; 4-bromo-3-chloro-2-methylbutanal.

Ketones

The longest chain containing the carbonyl group (C=O) is the parent. Suffix -one replaces the final -e. Number from the end nearer the carbonyl group and place its locant before the name. Substituents follow standard rules.

Examples: propan-2-one CH3—CO—CH3; butan-2-one; 2-methylpentan-3-one; 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one.

Note the contrast: an aldehyde group is terminal (at the chain end, —CHO with a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon), while a ketone carbonyl is bonded to two carbons inside the chain. That is why aldehydes never need a locant for one group, but ketones from butan-2-one onwards do; propan-2-one needs none because the carbonyl can only sit on the middle carbon.

Key Points

  • Aldehyde carbon is always C-1; suffix -al.
  • Ketone suffix is -one with a locant for C=O.
  • Carbonyl carbon in a ketone lies inside the chain.
  • Substituents are numbered from the functional-group end.

mcqs.q: In aldehydes, the —CHO carbon is always:
options: Carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single aldehyde group
The last carbon of the chain
mcqs.why: The —CHO carbon is always carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single aldehyde group; the suffix -al replaces the final -e.

mcqs.q: HCHO is named:
mcqs.why: HCHO is methanal, the one-carbon aldehyde listed first among the aldehyde examples in the notes.

mcqs.q: For ketones, the suffix ___ replaces the final -e of the alkane:
mcqs.why: Ketones use the suffix -one, and the chain is numbered from the end nearer the carbonyl group, e.g. butan-2-one.

mcqs.q: Why does propan-2-one need no locant in practice?
options: Because it has only two carbons
Because the carbonyl can only sit on the middle carbon
mcqs.why: In propan-2-one the carbonyl can only sit on the middle carbon, so no locant is strictly needed, unlike butan-2-one onwards.

mcqs.q: An aldehyde group differs from a ketone carbonyl because the aldehyde group is:
options: Terminal, at the chain end, with a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon
Always in the middle of the chain
mcqs.why: An aldehyde group is terminal (—CHO with a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon), while a ketone carbonyl is bonded to two carbons inside the chain.

mcqs.q: 2-methylpentan-3-one shows the carbonyl group at:
mcqs.why: In 2-methylpentan-3-one the locant 3 before -one places the carbonyl carbon at position 3 of the pentane chain.

mcqs.q: 3-methylbutanal is an aldehyde with:
options: A methyl substituent on carbon-3 of a four-carbon chain
Five carbons in the main chain
mcqs.why: 3-methylbutanal has a four-carbon parent chain including the —CHO carbon, with a methyl substituent on carbon-3.

mcqs.q: Ketone chains are numbered from:
options: The end farthest from the carbonyl
The end nearer the carbonyl group
mcqs.why: Ketones are numbered from the end nearer the carbonyl group, and the carbonyl locant is placed before the name.

mcqs.q: CH3—CO—CH3 is named:
mcqs.why: CH3—CO—CH3 is propan-2-one, the three-carbon ketone given as the first ketone example in the notes.

mcqs.q: In aldehyde and ketone names, substituents are numbered from:
options: The end opposite the functional group
mcqs.why: The key points state that substituents are numbered from the functional-group end in aldehydes and ketones.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Ethers and Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Ethers

Ethers are alkoxy derivatives of hydrocarbons. The larger alkyl chain is the parent alkane; the smaller alkyl group on oxygen is an alkoxy substituent. Number from the end closer to oxygen and show the alkoxy position by its locant.

Examples: methoxymethane CH3—O—CH3; methoxyethane CH3—O—CH2—CH3; 2-methoxypropane; 2-ethoxybutane.

Amines

Amines are alkyl derivatives of ammonia. The longest chain containing —NH2 is the parent; suffix -amine replaces the final -e. Number from the end closest to —NH2 for its lowest number; the locant is not needed when —NH2 is at carbon-1 in a primary amine. Several —NH2 groups take -diamine, -triamine, retaining the final -e.

Examples: methanamine CH3—NH2; ethanamine; propan-2-amine; butane-2,3-diamine. In secondary and tertiary amines, extra alkyl groups on nitrogen are N-substituents: N-methylethanamine; N,N-dimethylmethanamine; N-ethyl-N-methylpropan-2-amine.

Key Points

  • Ether: larger group = parent, smaller = alkoxy prefix.
  • Amine suffix is -amine; —NH2 controls numbering.
  • Groups on nitrogen are named with the locant N-.

mcqs.q: In naming an ether, the parent alkane is:
options: The larger alkyl chain; the smaller group on oxygen is the alkoxy substituent
mcqs.why: Ethers are alkoxy derivatives: the larger alkyl chain is the parent alkane and the smaller group on oxygen is an alkoxy substituent.

mcqs.q: CH3—O—CH2—CH3 is named:
mcqs.why: CH3—O—CH2—CH3 is methoxyethane: the larger ethyl chain is the parent and the smaller methyl group on oxygen is methoxy-.

mcqs.q: An ether chain is numbered from:
options: The end closer to oxygen, showing the alkoxy position by its locant
Carbon-1 at the alkoxy group always
mcqs.why: Ether numbering starts from the end closer to oxygen, and the alkoxy position is shown by its locant, e.g. 2-methoxypropane.

mcqs.q: Amines are described in the notes as:
mcqs.why: Amines are alkyl derivatives of ammonia; the longest chain containing —NH2 is the parent and the suffix is -amine.

mcqs.q: Several —NH2 groups in an amine take the suffixes:
mcqs.why: Several —NH2 groups take -diamine or -triamine with the final -e retained, as in butane-2,3-diamine.

mcqs.q: In amine numbering, the —NH2 group should get:
options: The same number as the longest branch
mcqs.why: Amine chains are numbered from the end closest to —NH2 so it gets its lowest number; the locant is unneeded at carbon-1 in a primary amine.

mcqs.q: CH3—NH2 is named:
options: Methylamine as the systematic -amine name given
mcqs.why: CH3—NH2 is methanamine, the first amine example in the notes, formed with the suffix -amine replacing the final -e.

mcqs.q: Extra alkyl groups attached to the nitrogen atom of an amine are named as:
mcqs.why: In secondary and tertiary amines, extra alkyl groups on nitrogen are N-substituents, e.g. N-methylethanamine and N,N-dimethylmethanamine.

mcqs.q: 2-ethoxybutane shows an ethoxy group at:
mcqs.why: In 2-ethoxybutane the locant 2 shows the ethoxy substituent is attached at carbon-2 of the parent butane chain.

mcqs.q: Propan-2-amine has its —NH2 group:
mcqs.why: Propan-2-amine is listed in the notes; the locant 2 places the —NH2 group on the middle carbon of propane.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Nitriles and Carboxylic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Nitriles

Select the longest chain that includes the —C≡N group and add suffix -nitrile to the parent name. The nitrile carbon is always carbon-1, so no separate locant is needed for a simple nitrile. Substituents follow standard rules; several —C≡N groups take dinitrile, trinitrile.

Examples: ethanenitrile CH3—C≡N; propanenitrile; 2-methylpropanenitrile; 2-ethylpropane-1,3-dinitrile.

Carboxylic Acids

The longest chain containing —COOH is the parent; suffix -oic acid replaces the final -e. The —COOH carbon is always carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single carboxyl group. Substituents follow the lowest-locant rule.

Examples: ethanoic acid CH3COOH (common name acetic acid, vinegar); propanoic acid; 2-methylpropanoic acid.

Counting the functional carbon in the chain length is the common trap in both classes: CH3—C≡N has two carbons in total, so it is ethanenitrile, not methanenitrile; likewise CH3COOH is ethanoic acid. The book's household example makes the point — CH3COOH is commonly called acetic acid (vinegar), while its systematic IUPAC name is ethanoic acid, and systematic naming avoids such confusion in science and industry.

Key Points

  • Nitrile and carboxyl carbons are both counted as C-1.
  • Suffixes: -nitrile and -oic acid.
  • No locant is needed for one —CN or one —COOH group.

mcqs.q: For nitriles, the parent chain must include:
options: The —C≡N group, with the suffix -nitrile added
Only the alkyl part of the molecule
mcqs.why: Nitriles select the longest chain that includes the —C≡N group and add the suffix -nitrile to the parent name.

mcqs.q: Why does a simple nitrile need no separate locant for the —CN group?
options: Because nitriles have no carbon in the group
Because the nitrile carbon is always carbon-1
Because locants are never used with triple bonds
Because the group is always in the middle
mcqs.why: The nitrile carbon is always carbon-1, so no separate locant is needed for a simple nitrile, just as for carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: CH3—C≡N is named ethanenitrile and NOT methanenitrile because:
options: Nitrile names always add one carbon
The methyl group is counted twice
The nitrile carbon is counted in the chain length, giving two carbons in total
mcqs.why: Counting the functional carbon is the common trap: CH3—C≡N has two carbons in total, so it is ethanenitrile, not methanenitrile.

mcqs.q: CH3COOH has the systematic IUPAC name:
options: Acetic acid as its systematic name
mcqs.why: CH3COOH is ethanoic acid; acetic acid (vinegar) is its common name, and systematic naming avoids such confusion.

mcqs.q: Several —C≡N groups in one molecule take the suffixes:
mcqs.why: Several nitrile groups take dinitrile or trinitrile, as in the book example 2-ethylpropane-1,3-dinitrile.

mcqs.q: For carboxylic acids, the suffix -oic acid:
options: Is added without changing the alkane name
Replaces the final -e of the alkane
Is used only for cyclic acids
mcqs.why: For carboxylic acids the suffix -oic acid replaces the final -e, e.g. CH3COOH is ethanoic acid from ethane.

mcqs.q: 2-methylpropanoic acid has how many carbons in its parent chain (including the —COOH carbon)?
mcqs.why: Propanoic acid has a three-carbon parent chain including the —COOH carbon; the methyl group is a substituent on carbon-2.

mcqs.q: The —COOH carbon in a carboxylic acid is always:
options: Given a locant in every name
Carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single carboxyl group
mcqs.why: The —COOH carbon is always carbon-1, so no locant is needed for a single carboxyl group in a carboxylic acid.

mcqs.q: Propanenitrile contains how many carbon atoms in total?
mcqs.why: Propanenitrile's parent chain has three carbons including the —C≡N carbon, which is counted as carbon-1.

mcqs.q: 2-methylpropanenitrile shows that nitrile substituents:
options: Are numbered from the far end
Follow the standard substituent rules, with the nitrile carbon as C-1
mcqs.why: In 2-methylpropanenitrile the methyl substituent is on carbon-2, counting the nitrile carbon as carbon-1, following standard rules.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Acyl Halides, Amides and Esters
lessons.notes_html:
Acyl Halides

Replace the suffix -ic acid in the parent carboxylic acid name with -yl halide. Examples: methanoyl chloride H—CO—Cl; propanoyl bromide; butanoyl bromide.

Amides

Replace the suffix -oic acid of the parent acid with -amide. Examples: methanamide H—CO—NH2; ethanamide CH3—CO—NH2; propanamide; 4-chloropentanamide.

Esters

An ester name has two words. The first word is the alkyl group bonded to the oxygen atom; the second is obtained by replacing -ic acid in the parent acid name with -ate. Examples: methyl methanoate H—CO—OCH3; ethyl ethanoate CH3—CO—OCH2CH3; methyl propanoate.

Key Formulae

ClassGroupSuffix change
Acyl halide—COX-ic acid → -yl halide
Amide—CONH2-oic acid → -amide
Ester—COOR-ic acid → -ate, alkyl group first

Key Points

  • All three classes are named from the parent carboxylic acid.
  • Ester names are two words: alkyl + alkanoate.
  • Acyl halide: -oyl chloride / bromide etc.

mcqs.q: Acyl halides are named from the parent carboxylic acid by replacing -ic acid with:
mcqs.why: Acyl halides replace the suffix -ic acid in the parent carboxylic acid name with -yl halide, e.g. propanoyl bromide.

mcqs.q: H—CO—Cl is named:
mcqs.why: H—CO—Cl is methanoyl chloride, the one-carbon acyl halide example given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Amides are named by replacing -oic acid of the parent acid with:
mcqs.why: Amides replace the suffix -oic acid of the parent acid with -amide, e.g. CH3—CO—NH2 is ethanamide.

mcqs.q: An ester name consists of two words. They are:
options: The acid name first, then the alkyl group
The alkanoate first, then the alkyl group
The alkyl group bonded to oxygen first, then the -ate part from the acid
mcqs.why: An ester name has two words: first the alkyl group bonded to the oxygen atom, then the part obtained by replacing -ic acid with -ate.

mcqs.q: CH3—CO—OCH2CH3 is named:
mcqs.why: CH3—CO—OCH2CH3 is ethyl ethanoate: the ethyl group is on oxygen and the acid part comes from ethanoic acid.

mcqs.q: H—CO—OCH3 is named:
mcqs.why: H—CO—OCH3 is methyl methanoate, the first ester example in the notes, with methyl as the alkyl word.

mcqs.q: 4-chloropentanamide is an amide in which chlorine is:
options: Part of an acyl chloride group
mcqs.why: In 4-chloropentanamide the chloro- prefix with locant 4 shows chlorine is a substituent on carbon-4 of the pentanamide chain.

mcqs.q: All three classes in this lesson — acyl halides, amides and esters — are named from:
mcqs.why: The key points state that all three classes are named from the parent carboxylic acid by changing its suffix.

mcqs.q: Butanoyl bromide is an acyl halide derived from the acid with how many carbons?
mcqs.why: Butanoyl bromide comes from butanoic acid, which has four carbons including the carbonyl carbon of the —COBr group.

mcqs.q: Propanamide is formed from propanoic acid by replacing -oic acid with -amide. Its formula group is:
mcqs.why: Amides contain the —CONH2 group; propanamide is listed among the amide examples in the notes.

lessons.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Acid Anhydrides and Compounds with Multiple Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Acid Anhydrides

Symmetrical anhydrides: replace acid in the parent acid name with anhydride — methanoic anhydride, ethanoic anhydride. Unsymmetrical (mixed) anhydrides, from two different acids, are named by alphabetising both acid names and replacing acid with anhydride: ethanoic methanoic anhydride; ethanoic propanoic anhydride.

Multiple Functional Groups

Prioritise functional groups by a set hierarchy; the highest-priority group gives the suffix, the others are named as prefixes, in alphabetical order.

Priority order (book): Carboxylic acids (—COOH) > Esters (—COOR) > Amides (—CONH2) > Nitriles (—CN) > Aldehydes (—CHO) > Ketones (>C=O) > Alcohols (—OH) > Amines (—NH2) > Alkenes (C=C) > Alkynes (C≡C) > Alkanes (C—C) > Halides (—X).

Examples: 2-chloropropanal (—CHO wins over Cl); 3-bromo-2-hydroxybutanoic acid; 3-hydroxybutanal; 4-hydroxy-2-methylhexan-3-one (ketone suffix, —OH as hydroxy- prefix).

Key Points

  • Only the top-priority group becomes the suffix.
  • Lower groups appear as prefixes: hydroxy-, halo-, etc.
  • Mixed anhydrides list both acids alphabetically.
  • Carboxylic acid has the highest priority in the book list.

mcqs.q: A symmetrical acid anhydride is named by replacing 'acid' in the parent acid name with:
mcqs.why: Symmetrical anhydrides replace 'acid' with 'anhydride', e.g. methanoic anhydride and ethanoic anhydride.

mcqs.q: An unsymmetrical (mixed) anhydride from ethanoic acid and methanoic acid is named:
options: Methanoic ethanoic anhydride in size order
Ethanoic methanoic anhydride, alphabetising both acid names
mcqs.why: Mixed anhydrides are named by alphabetising both acid names and replacing 'acid' with anhydride: ethanoic methanoic anhydride.

mcqs.q: In a compound with several functional groups, the suffix is given by:
options: The group present in largest amount
The highest-priority group in the hierarchy
mcqs.why: The highest-priority group gives the suffix; the others are named as prefixes in alphabetical order.

mcqs.q: According to the book's priority order, which group has the HIGHEST priority?
mcqs.why: The book's priority order starts with carboxylic acids (—COOH), followed by esters, amides, nitriles and the rest.

mcqs.q: In 2-chloropropanal, the suffix comes from the aldehyde group because:
options: —CHO has higher priority than the halide —Cl
Chlorine can never be a prefix
mcqs.why: The book example 2-chloropropanal shows —CHO winning over Cl: the aldehyde gives the suffix and chlorine is a prefix.

mcqs.q: In 4-hydroxy-2-methylhexan-3-one, the —OH group is named as the prefix:
mcqs.why: The ketone takes the suffix in 4-hydroxy-2-methylhexan-3-one, so the lower-priority —OH group appears as the hydroxy- prefix.

mcqs.q: In the book's priority order, where do halides (—X) stand?
options: At the top of the list
mcqs.why: The priority order ends with alkanes (C—C) and then halides (—X), so halides have the lowest priority in the book list.

mcqs.q: 3-hydroxybutanal contains which two functional groups?
options: An aldehyde (suffix) and an —OH shown as hydroxy-
mcqs.why: 3-hydroxybutanal is a book example: the aldehyde group gives the -al suffix and the —OH group is named as the hydroxy- prefix.

mcqs.q: Between an alkene (C=C) and an alkyne (C≡C), which has higher priority in the book list?
mcqs.why: The book's order places alkenes (C=C) above alkynes (C≡C), both below amines and above alkanes and halides.

mcqs.q: 3-bromo-2-hydroxybutanoic acid shows that in a carboxylic acid compound, other groups are named:
options: As prefixes, in alphabetical order (bromo before hydroxy)
In order of their locants only
mcqs.why: The —COOH group takes the suffix; bromo- and hydroxy- appear as prefixes in alphabetical order in 3-bromo-2-hydroxybutanoic acid.

lessons.title: Empirical and Molecular Formulae
lessons.notes_html:
The symbolic representation of a compound is its formula (chemical formula): empirical, molecular, structural, displayed and skeletal.

Empirical Formula

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Examples: glucose CH2O, benzene CH, hydrogen peroxide HO, ammonia NH3, water H2O.

Molecular Formula

The molecular formula shows the total number of atoms in a molecule: glucose C6H12O6, benzene C6H6, hydrogen peroxide H2O2, ammonia NH3, water H2O.

Key Formulae

QuantityFormula
Moles of an elementMole = Percentage of an Element / Atomic Mass
Value of nn = Molecular Formula Mass / Empirical Formula Mass
Molecular formulaMolecular formula = n × Empirical Formula

Determination

  • Empirical: (i) divide each percentage by its atomic mass to get moles (assume 100 g); (ii) divide all moles by the smallest to get the simple ratio; (iii) multiply fractions to whole numbers; (iv) write ratios as subscripts.
  • Example 11.1: 92.3% C, 7.69% H → moles C = 92.3/12 ≈ 7.69, H = 7.69/1 = 7.69; ratio 1:1; empirical formula CH.
  • Molecular: find n, then multiply. Example 11.2: acetylene, empirical CH (mass 13), molecular mass 26 → n = 26/13 = 2 → C2H2.

Key Points

  • Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual atom counts.
  • Molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of empirical.
  • Percentages are treated as grams in a 100 g sample.

mcqs.q: The empirical formula of a compound shows:
options: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
The total number of atoms in a molecule
The arrangement of atoms and bonds
mcqs.why: The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, e.g. glucose is CH2O and benzene is CH.

mcqs.q: What is the molecular formula of glucose, whose empirical formula is CH2O?
mcqs.why: Glucose has empirical formula CH2O but its molecular formula, showing the total atoms in a molecule, is C6H12O6.

mcqs.q: A compound contains 92.3% C and 7.69% H. Moles of C in 100 g are 92.3/12 ≈ 7.69 and moles of H are 7.69/1 = 7.69. Its empirical formula is:
mcqs.why: Working: moles C = 92.3 / 12 ≈ 7.69; moles H = 7.69 / 1 = 7.69; ratio = 7.69 : 7.69 = 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH (book Example 11.1).

mcqs.q: For acetylene, empirical formula CH (mass 13) and molecular mass 26, the value of n is:
mcqs.why: Working: n = molecular formula mass / empirical formula mass = 26 / 13 = 2, so the molecular formula is 2 × CH = C2H2 (book Example 11.2).

mcqs.q: In empirical formula determination, percentages are treated as:
options: Percentages of the smallest element only
mcqs.why: The method assumes a 100 g sample, so each percentage is treated as grams, then divided by the atomic mass to get moles.

mcqs.q: The first step in finding an empirical formula from percentage composition is:
options: Divide each percentage by its atomic mass to get moles
Divide by the largest mole value
mcqs.why: Step (i): divide each percentage by its atomic mass to get moles, using Mole = Percentage of an Element / Atomic Mass.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen peroxide has empirical formula HO. Its molecular formula is:
mcqs.why: The notes pair empirical HO with molecular H2O2 for hydrogen peroxide: the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple (n = 2) of the empirical formula.

mcqs.q: After finding the moles of each element, the next step is to:
options: Multiply by the atomic masses again
Round each mole value to zero
Divide all moles by the smallest mole value to get the simple ratio
mcqs.why: Step (ii): divide all moles by the smallest value to get the simple ratio, then multiply fractions up to whole numbers if needed.

mcqs.q: Benzene has molecular formula C6H6. Its empirical formula is:
mcqs.why: C6H6 reduces to the simplest whole-number ratio 1 : 1, so benzene's empirical formula is CH, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: The molecular formula is obtained from the empirical formula by:
options: Multiplying the empirical formula by n, where n = molecular mass / empirical mass
mcqs.why: Molecular formula = n × Empirical Formula, where n = Molecular Formula Mass / Empirical Formula Mass, a whole number.

lessons.title: Condensed, Structural, Displayed and Skeletal Formulae
lessons.notes_html:
Condensed Formula

The condensed formula is a structural formula that indicates the number and type of atoms but gives no indication of the bonds between them. Example: propanol is CH3CH2CH2OH.

Structural Formula

The structural formula is the most detailed representation of a molecule, showing the arrangement of atoms and the bonds between them. For propanol (C3H7OH) it shows each C bonded in a chain, hydrogens on each carbon, and —O—H at the end, all joined by single bonds. Its two types are displayed formula and skeletal formula.

Displayed Formula

The displayed formula is a simplified structural formula that explicitly draws each atom and bond, giving a clear visual picture of the spatial arrangement, e.g. propanol drawn with every H, C and O and every bond shown.

Skeletal Formula

The skeletal formula emphasises the carbon skeleton and functional groups, using lines for carbon—carbon bonds while omitting carbon and hydrogen atoms. Hydrogens on carbon are excluded; only heteroatoms (atoms other than C and H) and the skeleton are shown, e.g. propanol as a two-segment zigzag ending in —OH.

Key Points

  • Condensed: atoms counted, bonds not shown.
  • Structural/displayed: every atom and bond shown.
  • Skeletal: lines only; C and its H atoms are understood.
  • Heteroatoms are always written in a skeletal formula.

mcqs.q: A condensed formula indicates the number and type of atoms but does NOT show:
mcqs.why: The condensed formula gives the number and type of atoms but no indication of the bonds between them, e.g. propanol is CH3CH2CH2OH.

mcqs.q: Which formula is described as the most detailed representation of a molecule?
mcqs.why: The structural formula is the most detailed representation, showing the arrangement of atoms and the bonds between them.

mcqs.q: The two types of structural formula named in the notes are:
mcqs.why: The structural formula has two types: the displayed formula and the skeletal formula, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: In a skeletal formula, which atoms are always written explicitly?
options: Heteroatoms (atoms other than C and H)
mcqs.why: Skeletal formulas omit carbon and its hydrogens, but heteroatoms such as oxygen are always written, e.g. propanol ends in —OH.

mcqs.q: The displayed formula differs from the skeletal formula because it:
options: Explicitly draws each atom and every bond
Uses no bond lines at all
mcqs.why: The displayed formula explicitly draws each atom and bond, giving a clear visual picture of the spatial arrangement.

mcqs.q: Propanol in skeletal form is drawn as:
options: A full drawing of every H, C and O
mcqs.why: Propanol's skeletal formula is a two-segment zigzag (three carbons) ending in —OH, with C and its H atoms understood.

mcqs.q: CH3CH2CH2OH is an example of which type of formula for propanol?
mcqs.why: CH3CH2CH2OH is propanol's condensed formula: it counts the atoms in groups but shows no bonds between them.

mcqs.q: In a skeletal formula, the lines represent:
mcqs.why: The skeletal formula uses lines for carbon—carbon bonds while omitting carbon and hydrogen atoms from the drawing.

mcqs.q: Why are hydrogens attached to carbon excluded in a skeletal formula?
options: They are understood to be present on each carbon
Propanol has no hydrogens on carbon
They are shown as lines instead
mcqs.why: In skeletal formulas hydrogens on carbon are excluded because they are understood; only heteroatoms and the skeleton are shown.

mcqs.q: The structural formula of propanol (C3H7OH) shows:
options: Each C bonded in a chain, hydrogens on each carbon, and —O—H at the end, all joined by single bonds
A zigzag with no atoms labelled
mcqs.why: Propanol's structural formula shows each carbon in a chain, hydrogens on each carbon and —O—H at the end, joined by single bonds.

lessons.title: Saturated and Unsaturated Compounds, Fission and Free Radicals
lessons.notes_html:
Saturated and Unsaturated

Saturated compounds contain only single bonds between carbon atoms and the maximum possible hydrogens, e.g. butane. Unsaturated compounds contain at least one multiple bond (double or triple) and fewer hydrogens, e.g. butene and butyne.

Homolytic and Heterolytic Fission

Homolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks with each atom keeping one electron, forming two free radicals: Cl2 → 2Cl•. Heterolytic fission: one atom takes both electrons, forming ions: H—Cl → H+ + Cl-.

Free Radical

A free radical is a highly reactive species with an unpaired electron; it initiates chain reactions. Examples: methyl radical •CH3 and chlorine radical •Cl.

Initiation, Propagation and Termination

  • Initiation: first step, generates free radicals: Cl2 → 2Cl•.
  • Propagation: radicals react with molecules, making new radicals and continuing the chain: Cl• + CH4 → HCl + •CH3.
  • Termination: radicals combine to form a stable molecule, ending the chain: •CH3 + •Cl → CH3Cl.

Key Points

  • Homolytic = one electron each, radicals; heterolytic = both to one atom, ions.
  • Radicals carry an unpaired electron and are very reactive.
  • Chain sequence: initiation → propagation → termination.

mcqs.q: Saturated compounds are those which contain:
options: Only single bonds between carbon atoms, with the maximum possible hydrogens
mcqs.why: Saturated compounds contain only single bonds between carbons and the maximum possible hydrogens, e.g. butane.

mcqs.q: Butene and butyne are unsaturated because they:
options: Contain at least one multiple bond and fewer hydrogens
mcqs.why: Unsaturated compounds contain at least one multiple bond (double or triple) and fewer hydrogens than the saturated compound.

mcqs.q: In homolytic fission, a covalent bond breaks so that:
options: Both electrons go to one atom, forming ions
No electrons are shared at all
Each atom keeps one electron, forming two free radicals
The bond does not actually break
mcqs.why: Homolytic fission: each atom keeps one electron of the bond, forming two free radicals, e.g. Cl2 → 2Cl•.

mcqs.q: H—Cl → H+ + Cl- is an example of:
mcqs.why: Heterolytic fission gives both bonding electrons to one atom, forming ions: H—Cl → H+ + Cl-, as in the notes.

mcqs.q: A free radical is best described as:
options: A highly reactive species with an unpaired electron
A stable ion with a full octet and a charge
A species with a paired electron pair only
mcqs.why: A free radical is a highly reactive species with an unpaired electron; examples are •CH3 and •Cl, and it initiates chain reactions.

mcqs.q: Which step of a radical chain reaction generates the free radicals at the start?
mcqs.why: Initiation is the first step and generates free radicals, e.g. Cl2 → 2Cl•, which then start the chain reaction.

mcqs.q: Cl• + CH4 → HCl + •CH3 is an example of which chain step?
mcqs.why: In propagation, radicals react with molecules making new radicals and continuing the chain: Cl• + CH4 → HCl + •CH3.

mcqs.q: Termination of a radical chain occurs when:
options: Two radicals combine to form a stable molecule, ending the chain
mcqs.why: In termination, radicals combine to form a stable molecule, e.g. •CH3 + •Cl → CH3Cl, which ends the chain.

mcqs.q: The methyl radical is written as:
mcqs.why: The methyl radical •CH3 is given in the notes as an example of a free radical with an unpaired electron.

mcqs.q: The correct order of a free-radical chain reaction is:
mcqs.why: The chain sequence in the key points is initiation → propagation → termination, in that order.

lessons.title: Nucleophiles, Electrophiles and Types of Reaction
lessons.notes_html:
Nucleophile and Electrophile

A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates a pair of electrons and is attracted to electron-deficient sites, e.g. OH- attacking carbon in haloalkanes. An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that accepts a pair of electrons and is attracted to electron-rich sites, e.g. the carbocation CH3+.

Addition, Substitution and Elimination

  • Addition: atoms are added with nothing removed, e.g. hydrogenation of ethene: CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3 (Ni catalyst, 150-200°C as printed in this section).
  • Substitution: atoms or groups are replaced, e.g. CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (hv).
  • Elimination: atoms or groups are removed, e.g. dehydrohalogenation: CH3CH2Br + NaOH → CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O (heat).

Hydrolysis and Condensation

Hydrolysis: a compound reacts with water and its bonds break: C12H22O11 + H2O → 2C6H12O6 (maltose → glucose, H+). Enzymes hydrolyse starch and proteins in digestion. Condensation: two or more molecules join into a larger molecule, often losing a small molecule such as water — esterification: CH3COOH + C2H5OH → CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (H+). Condensation makes polyester and nylon.

Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state, e.g. combustion: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O. Reduction is gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation state, e.g. CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3 (Pt, 45-100°C). LiAlH4 reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols: R—CHO → R—CH2—OH.

Key Points

  • Nucleophile donates an electron pair; electrophile accepts one.
  • Addition adds, substitution swaps, elimination removes.
  • Hydrolysis splits with water; condensation joins with loss of water.
  • Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains them.

mcqs.q: A nucleophile is a species that:
options: Is electron-rich, donates a pair of electrons and is attracted to electron-deficient sites
mcqs.why: A nucleophile is electron-rich, donates a pair of electrons and attacks electron-deficient sites, e.g. OH- attacking carbon in haloalkanes.

mcqs.q: Which species is given in the notes as an example of an electrophile?
mcqs.why: An electrophile accepts a pair of electrons; the notes give the carbocation CH3+ as the example of an electrophile.

mcqs.q: Hydrogenation of ethene, CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3, is which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: In addition, atoms are added with nothing removed; hydrogenation of ethene over Ni at 150-200°C is the book's addition example.

mcqs.q: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (hv) is an example of:
mcqs.why: In substitution, atoms or groups are replaced: a hydrogen of methane is replaced by chlorine, giving CH3Cl + HCl.

mcqs.q: Dehydrohalogenation of CH3CH2Br with NaOH and heat, giving CH2=CH2, is:
options: An elimination reaction, because atoms/groups are removed
mcqs.why: Elimination removes atoms or groups: CH3CH2Br + NaOH → CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O on heating, as in the notes.

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis is a reaction in which:
options: Two molecules join with loss of water
A compound reacts with water and its bonds break
Electrons are lost by a species
Hydrogen is added across a double bond
mcqs.why: In hydrolysis a compound reacts with water and its bonds break, e.g. maltose C12H22O11 + H2O → 2C6H12O6.

mcqs.q: Esterification, CH3COOH + C2H5OH → CH3COOC2H5 + H2O, is an example of:
mcqs.why: Condensation joins molecules into a larger molecule with loss of a small molecule such as water; esterification is the example given.

mcqs.q: Oxidation, in terms of electrons, is:
options: Loss of hydrogen only in every case
Loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state
mcqs.why: Oxidation is loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state, e.g. combustion 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O.

mcqs.q: LiAlH4 reduces an aldehyde R—CHO to:
mcqs.why: The notes state that LiAlH4 reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols: R—CHO → R—CH2—OH, a reduction (gain of electrons / H).

mcqs.q: Enzymes hydrolyse which substances during digestion, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state that enzymes hydrolyse starch and proteins in digestion, splitting them by reaction with water.

lessons.title: Importance of Catenation in Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Catenation (from Latin catena, chain) is the ability of atoms of the same element to bond with each other to form chains or rings. It is especially significant for carbon.

Why Carbon Catenates Best

  • Carbon has four valence electrons and a small size, so it forms strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.
  • Its C—C bonds are stable, giving long chains, branched structures and rings.
  • This diversity is the basis of organic and biomolecules — proteins, nucleic acids and carbohydrates.
  • Silicon, boron and sulphur also catenate, but to a lesser extent because their bonds are weaker; they form only smaller chains or rings.

Forms shown in the book: straight chain, branched chain and cyclic chain of carbon atoms.

The book illustrates catenation with three arrangements of linked carbon atoms: a straight chain of four carbons in a row, a branched chain with one carbon attached below the chain, and a cyclic chain forming a ring. One mole of carbon atoms joined end-to-end would make a chain long enough to wrap around the Earth's equator millions of times, showing the scale of diversity catenation allows.

Key Points

  • Catenation = self-linking into chains and rings.
  • Strong, stable C—C bonds make carbon unique.
  • Catenation explains the huge number of organic compounds.
  • Other elements catenate only weakly by comparison.

mcqs.q: Catenation is the ability of atoms of the same element to:
options: Bond with each other to form chains or rings
mcqs.why: Catenation (from Latin catena, chain) is the self-linking of atoms of the same element into chains or rings.

mcqs.q: Why does carbon catenate better than other elements?
options: It has six valence electrons and a large size
It has four valence electrons and a small size, forming strong covalent C—C bonds
Its C—C bonds are weak and unstable
It forms ionic bonds with itself
mcqs.why: Carbon has four valence electrons and a small size, so it forms strong, stable covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: The diversity produced by catenation is the basis of:
options: Organic and biomolecules such as proteins, nucleic acids and carbohydrates
mcqs.why: Stable C—C chains, branches and rings underlie organic and biomolecules — proteins, nucleic acids and carbohydrates.

mcqs.q: Silicon, boron and sulphur catenate less than carbon because:
options: Their bonds are weaker, so they form only smaller chains or rings
mcqs.why: Silicon, boron and sulphur also catenate but to a lesser extent because their bonds are weaker, giving only smaller chains or rings.

mcqs.q: Which three forms of carbon chains are shown in the book for catenation?
options: Straight chain, branched chain and cyclic chain
mcqs.why: The book shows three arrangements: a straight chain, a branched chain and a cyclic chain (ring) of carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: The word catenation comes from the Latin word 'catena', meaning:
mcqs.why: The notes state that catenation comes from the Latin catena, meaning chain, reflecting the chain-forming ability.

mcqs.q: According to the book's illustration, one mole of carbon atoms joined end-to-end would make a chain long enough to:
options: Wrap around the Earth's equator millions of times
mcqs.why: The book illustrates that one mole of carbons joined end-to-end could wrap around the Earth's equator millions of times.

mcqs.q: In the book's branched-chain illustration of catenation, the branch is shown as:
options: A second long chain of equal length
A double bond in the chain
One carbon attached below the main chain
mcqs.why: The book draws a straight chain of four carbons, a branched chain with one carbon attached below it, and a cyclic ring.

mcqs.q: Catenation mainly explains:
options: The huge number of organic compounds
mcqs.why: The key points state that catenation explains the huge number of organic compounds known.

mcqs.q: Carbon's C—C bonds are described in the notes as:
options: Stable, giving long chains, branched structures and rings
mcqs.why: Carbon's C—C bonds are stable, which gives long chains, branched structures and rings in organic compounds.

lessons.title: Nucleophilic Substitution and Electrophilic Addition
lessons.notes_html:
Curly arrows show the movement of a pair of electrons in a reaction.

Nucleophilic Substitution (SN)

A nucleophile (Nu-) attacks and replaces a leaving group (X) on the substrate. Two types: SN2, one-step bimolecular, and SN1, two-step unimolecular. In SN2 the nucleophile attacks carbon from the back side, displacing the functional group; one group is substituted by another. The curly arrow starts at the nucleophile and goes to the electrophilic centre (the electron-deficient carbon, δ+ next to X δ-); a second arrow shows the C—X bond electrons moving onto X, which leaves as X-.

Electrophilic Addition (Alkene Hydrogenation)

A double bond reacts with an electrophile (which accepts an electron pair) to form a new functional group. Curly arrows show pi electrons moving from the double bond to the electrophilic centre, usually a positively charged atom such as H+. A carbocation forms, then a nucleophile such as X- attacks it, giving new sigma bonds at both carbons. Hydrogenation of vegetable oils to margarine is given as an everyday electrophilic addition.

Key Points

  • Curly arrow = movement of an electron pair, from electron-rich to electron-poor.
  • SN2 is one step with back-side attack; SN1 is two steps.
  • Electrophilic addition passes through a carbocation.
  • The pi bond supplies the electrons in electrophilic addition.

mcqs.q: A curly arrow in a reaction mechanism shows:
options: The movement of a pair of electrons
The movement of a single electron only
The movement of atoms in space
mcqs.why: Curly arrows show the movement of a pair of electrons in a reaction, from electron-rich to electron-poor centres.

mcqs.q: SN2 differs from SN1 because SN2 is:
options: One-step and bimolecular, with back-side attack
mcqs.why: SN2 is a one-step bimolecular substitution in which the nucleophile attacks carbon from the back side, displacing the leaving group.

mcqs.q: In nucleophilic substitution, the curly arrow starts at the nucleophile and goes to:
options: The electrophilic centre, the electron-deficient carbon (δ+ next to X δ-)
mcqs.why: The arrow starts at the nucleophile and goes to the electrophilic centre; a second arrow shows the C—X bond electrons moving onto X.

mcqs.q: In electrophilic addition to an alkene, the first intermediate formed is:
mcqs.why: Pi electrons move to the electrophile (often H+), forming a carbocation, which a nucleophile such as X- then attacks.

mcqs.q: In electrophilic addition, the electrons that attack the electrophile come from:
options: The pi bond of the double bond
A sigma bond of the chain
mcqs.why: The pi bond supplies the electrons in electrophilic addition: pi electrons move from the double bond to the electrophilic centre.

mcqs.q: SN1 is described in the notes as:
options: An addition to a double bond
mcqs.why: The notes classify SN1 as two-step unimolecular, in contrast to the one-step bimolecular SN2 mechanism.

mcqs.q: When the C—X bond breaks in nucleophilic substitution, the bonding electrons:
options: Move onto X, which leaves as X-
mcqs.why: A second curly arrow shows the C—X bond electrons moving onto X, which leaves as the anion X-.

mcqs.q: Which everyday process is given as an example of electrophilic addition?
options: Chlorination of methane in UV light
Hydrogenation of vegetable oils to margarine
mcqs.why: The notes give hydrogenation of vegetable oils to margarine as an everyday example of electrophilic addition.

mcqs.q: After the carbocation forms in electrophilic addition, the next step is:
options: A nucleophile such as X- attacks it, giving new sigma bonds at both carbons
mcqs.why: The carbocation is attacked by a nucleophile such as X-, so new sigma bonds form at both carbons of the former double bond.

mcqs.q: In SN2, the nucleophile attacks the carbon from:
options: The same side as the leaving group
The back side, opposite the leaving group
Above the plane only in rings
mcqs.why: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks carbon from the back side, displacing the functional/leaving group in a single step.

lessons.title: Elimination, Free-radical Substitution and Nucleophilic Addition
lessons.notes_html:
Elimination Reaction

Atoms or groups are removed from neighbouring carbon atoms of a saturated substrate, forming a double bond. A base abstracts a proton (H+) from the β-carbon while a leaving group such as halide departs from the adjacent α-carbon; simultaneous removal creates C=C, e.g. a primary alkyl halide + OH- → ethene + H2O + X-.

Free-radical Substitution

A covalent bond breaks to give highly reactive free radicals, which then replace atoms or groups in a molecule — a substitution reaction. Example: chlorination of methane, CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. The same radical chemistry lets CFCs release chlorine radicals that damage the ozone layer.

Nucleophilic Addition

A nucleophile (Nu-) adds to a multiple bond in the substrate, such as a double bond. The main examples are additions to carbonyl groups, e.g. HCN adding to ethanal: CH3—CHO + H—CN → CH3—CH(OH)—CN. Curly arrows show the nucleophile (CN-) attacking the carbonyl carbon while the C=O pi electrons move onto oxygen.

Key Points

  • Elimination removes H from β-C and X from α-C to form C=C.
  • Free-radical substitution works through radical intermediates.
  • Nucleophilic addition is typical of carbonyl compounds.
  • Mechanism arrows always follow the electron pairs.

mcqs.q: In an elimination reaction forming C=C, the proton (H+) is removed from:
options: The β-carbon, while the leaving group departs from the adjacent α-carbon
The α-carbon, while the leaving group leaves the β-carbon
A carbon far from the leaving group
mcqs.why: A base abstracts H+ from the β-carbon while the leaving group departs from the adjacent α-carbon, creating the C=C double bond.

mcqs.q: Free-radical substitution of methane with chlorine gives:
mcqs.why: Chlorination of methane is the example: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, proceeding through free-radical intermediates.

mcqs.q: Nucleophilic addition is typical of which class of compounds?
mcqs.why: Nucleophilic addition is typical of carbonyl compounds, e.g. HCN adding to ethanal to give CH3—CH(OH)—CN.

mcqs.q: In the addition of HCN to ethanal, the CN- nucleophile attacks:
options: The carbonyl carbon, while the C=O pi electrons move onto oxygen
mcqs.why: Curly arrows show CN- attacking the carbonyl carbon while the C=O pi electrons move onto oxygen, giving CH3—CH(OH)—CN.

mcqs.q: The radical chemistry of CFCs is mentioned because CFCs:
options: Release chlorine radicals that damage the ozone layer
Act as nucleophiles in the ozone layer
Are used as bases in elimination
mcqs.why: The same radical chemistry lets CFCs release chlorine radicals that damage the ozone layer, as noted in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Elimination reactions start from what type of substrate, according to the notes?
options: An unsaturated substrate with a triple bond
A saturated substrate, removing atoms/groups from neighbouring carbons
mcqs.why: Elimination removes atoms or groups from neighbouring carbons of a saturated substrate, forming a double bond.

mcqs.q: A primary alkyl halide reacting with OH- to give ethene + H2O + X- is an example of:
mcqs.why: Removing H from the β-carbon and X from the α-carbon to form ethene is an elimination reaction, as in the book example.

mcqs.q: In free-radical substitution, the intermediates that replace atoms or groups are:
mcqs.why: A covalent bond breaks to give highly reactive free radicals, which then replace atoms or groups in the molecule.

mcqs.q: The product of HCN addition to ethanal, CH3—CH(OH)—CN, contains which new groups on the former carbonyl carbon?
options: —OH and —CN both attached to that carbon
—OH only, with CN lost as gas
mcqs.why: The product CH3—CH(OH)—CN shows both —OH (from the carbonyl oxygen) and —CN attached to the former carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: Mechanism curly arrows in all three reactions of this lesson always follow:
options: The direction of the leaving group
mcqs.why: The key points state that mechanism arrows always follow the electron pairs, showing where each pair of electrons moves.

lessons.title: Planarity in Organic Molecules: Impact on Structure and Reactivity
lessons.notes_html:
A molecule is planar when its atoms lie in a single plane, bonded so they occupy the same flat plane without significant deviation. Planarity is important for structure and reactivity.

Planar Example: Benzene

Benzene's carbon atoms form a hexagonal ring and all its atoms lie in one plane. This planar arrangement enhances its stability and aromatic properties. Planar molecules may contain single, double or triple bonds.

Non-planar Molecules

Not all organic molecules are planar. Steric hindrance, bulky substituents and ring strain make some non-planar. Cyclohexane adopts a non-planar, puckered conformation — shown in the book as the boat conformation and the chair conformation.

The book draws benzene in two ways: a full structural form with alternating double bonds in a six-carbon ring, and the skeletal hexagon with a circle/double-bond representation. In both, every carbon and hydrogen lies flat. Planarity therefore links directly to how a molecule packs, how stable it is, and how it reacts — flat aromatic systems behave very differently from puckered saturated rings such as cyclohexane.

Key Points

  • Planar = all atoms in one flat plane.
  • Benzene is planar, which aids its stability and aromatic character.
  • Bulky groups and ring strain can force non-planar shapes.
  • Cyclohexane is puckered (chair and boat forms).

mcqs.q: A molecule is planar when:
options: All its atoms lie in a single plane
Its atoms form a tetrahedral shape
mcqs.why: A molecule is planar when its atoms lie in a single plane, occupying the same flat plane without significant deviation.

mcqs.q: Benzene is planar, and this arrangement enhances its:
mcqs.why: Benzene's carbons form a hexagonal ring with all atoms in one plane; this enhances its stability and aromatic properties.

mcqs.q: Which factors can make a molecule non-planar?
options: The presence of a double bond
Steric hindrance, bulky substituents and ring strain
mcqs.why: Not all molecules are planar: steric hindrance, bulky substituents and ring strain make some molecules non-planar.

mcqs.q: Cyclohexane adopts which shapes because it is non-planar?
mcqs.why: Cyclohexane adopts a non-planar, puckered conformation, shown in the book as the boat conformation and the chair conformation.

mcqs.q: Planar molecules may contain which types of bonds?
mcqs.why: The notes state that planar molecules may contain single, double or triple bonds; planarity is about atom positions, not bond type.

mcqs.q: In both drawings of benzene in the book, every carbon and hydrogen:
options: Is puckered out of the plane
mcqs.why: Whether drawn with alternating double bonds or as a skeletal hexagon, every carbon and hydrogen of benzene lies flat in one plane.

mcqs.q: Planarity links directly to which properties of a molecule?
options: Only its state at room temperature
How it packs, how stable it is, and how it reacts
mcqs.why: Planarity links to how a molecule packs, its stability and its reactivity; flat aromatics behave very differently from puckered rings.

mcqs.q: Benzene's carbon atoms form which ring shape?
mcqs.why: Benzene's carbon atoms form a hexagonal ring, and all of its atoms lie in one plane, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Which molecule is given as the planar example in this lesson?
mcqs.why: Benzene is the planar example: a hexagonal ring in which all atoms lie in a single plane, aiding stability and aromatic character.

mcqs.q: Cyclohexane is described as puckered rather than flat because of:
options: Ring strain forcing a non-planar shape
mcqs.why: Bulky groups and ring strain can force non-planar shapes; cyclohexane is puckered into chair and boat forms instead of lying flat.

lessons.title: Structural Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different properties are isomers; the phenomenon is isomerism, e.g. n-butane and isobutane, both C4H10. Two main types: stereoisomerism and structural isomerism. Octane C8H18 has 18 structural isomers.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas — a different arrangement of atoms. They divide into five types:

Key Formulae

TypeDifferenceBook example
Chain (skeleton)Different carbon chainn-pentane, isopentane, neopentane (C5H12)
PositionDifferent position of same functional group1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane (C4H9Cl); but-1-ene and but-2-ene (C4H8)
Functional groupDifferent functional groupEthanol CH3CH2OH and dimethyl ether CH3OCH3 (C2H6O); methyl acetate and propanoic acid (C3H6O2)
MetamersDifferent distribution of carbons on either side of the functional groupDiethyl ether and methyl-n-propyl ether; trimethylamine and ethylmethylamine
TautomersDifferent positions of protons and electrons; keto and enol forms in dynamic equilibriumPropan-2-one (keto) ⇌ propen-2-ol (enol), as drawn in the book

Metamers belong to the same homologous series. Tautomerism matters in biology: keto—enol tautomerism affects DNA base pairing, and errors can cause mutations.

Key Points

  • Structural isomers differ in atom arrangement, not just in space.
  • Five types: chain, position, functional group, metamers, tautomers.
  • Tautomers interconvert rapidly and exist in dynamic equilibrium.
  • Metamers keep the same functional group and series.

mcqs.q: Isomers are compounds that have:
options: The same molecular formula but different properties
Different molecular formulas but the same properties
The same structure but different formulas
mcqs.why: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different properties are isomers; n-butane and isobutane (both C4H10) are the example.

mcqs.q: How many structural isomers does octane, C8H18, have according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state that octane C8H18 has 18 structural isomers, showing how isomer numbers grow with chain length.

mcqs.q: Structural isomers differ in:
options: Their structural formula — a different arrangement of atoms
mcqs.why: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas, i.e. a different arrangement of atoms.

mcqs.q: n-pentane, isopentane and neopentane (C5H12) are examples of:
mcqs.why: They differ in their carbon chain arrangement, so they are chain (skeleton) isomers, the first type in the book's table.

mcqs.q: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane (C4H9Cl) are:
options: Position isomers, differing in the position of the same functional group
mcqs.why: They have the same functional group at different positions, so they are position isomers, as are but-1-ene and but-2-ene.

mcqs.q: Ethanol CH3CH2OH and dimethyl ether CH3OCH3 (both C2H6O) are:
options: Functional group isomers, with different functional groups
mcqs.why: They contain different functional groups (—OH versus ether —O—) with the same formula C2H6O, so they are functional group isomers.

mcqs.q: Metamers differ in:
options: The position of a double bond
The distribution of carbons on either side of the functional group
The position of protons and electrons
mcqs.why: Metamers show a different distribution of carbons on either side of the functional group, e.g. diethyl ether and methyl-n-propyl ether.

mcqs.q: Tautomers, such as propan-2-one (keto) and propen-2-ol (enol), exist in:
options: Dynamic equilibrium, differing in positions of protons and electrons
mcqs.why: Tautomers differ in the positions of protons and electrons and interconvert rapidly in dynamic equilibrium (keto ⇌ enol).

mcqs.q: Metamers belong to:
mcqs.why: The notes state that metamers belong to the same homologous series and keep the same functional group.

mcqs.q: Why does tautomerism matter in biology, according to the notes?
options: It changes the colour of DNA
Keto—enol tautomerism affects DNA base pairing, and errors can cause mutations
It makes proteins fold into rings
mcqs.why: Keto—enol tautomerism affects DNA base pairing, and errors arising from it can cause mutations, as stated in the lesson.

lessons.title: Stereoisomers (Configurational Isomers)
lessons.notes_html:
Stereoisomers have the same molecular and structural formulas but differ in the arrangement of atoms or groups in space; the phenomenon is stereoisomerism. Two types: geometric isomers and optical isomers; this unit discusses only geometric isomers.

Geometric Isomers (cis-trans Isomers)

Geometric isomers have restricted rotation, caused by a C=C double bond or by single bonds in cyclic compounds. The cis isomer (Latin cisoid, same side) has similar groups on the same side of the double bond; the trans isomer (transoid, opposite side) has them on opposite sides.

Example: cis-but-2-ene has both H atoms on the same side; trans-but-2-ene has them opposite. Cis and trans are distinct compounds with different physical properties. Trans is more stable: in cis, bulky groups on the same side repel each other, lowering stability.

Cyclic example: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane has both methyl groups on the same side of the ring; trans has them on opposite sides.

Key Points

  • Stereoisomers differ only in spatial arrangement.
  • Geometric isomerism needs restricted rotation.
  • cis = same side; trans = opposite sides.
  • Trans isomers are generally more stable than cis.

mcqs.q: What are stereoisomers?
options: Compounds with the same molecular and structural formulas but different arrangement of atoms or groups in space
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulas
Compounds with different molecular formulas but similar properties
Compounds that differ only in the number of carbon atoms
mcqs.why: Stereoisomers share both molecular and structural formulas; they differ only in how atoms or groups are arranged in space.

mcqs.q: How many types of stereoisomers are named in the notes, and which type does this unit discuss?
options: Two types — chain and position — and only chain isomers are discussed
Two types — geometric and optical — and only geometric isomers are discussed
Three types — geometric, optical and functional — all discussed equally
mcqs.why: The notes name geometric and optical isomers as the two types of stereoisomers, and state that this unit discusses only geometric isomers.

mcqs.q: What is required for geometric (cis-trans) isomerism to occur?
options: Free rotation about a C—C single bond in an open chain
The presence of a triple bond in an open chain
Restricted rotation, caused by a C=C double bond or by single bonds in cyclic compounds
A difference in the molecular formula of the two compounds
mcqs.why: Geometric isomerism needs restricted rotation; the notes give the C=C double bond and single bonds in cyclic compounds as its causes.

mcqs.q: In a cis isomer, where are the similar groups placed?
options: On opposite sides of the double bond
On different carbon atoms far apart in the chain
One inside the ring and one outside the ring
On the same side of the double bond
mcqs.why: Cis comes from the Latin cisoid, meaning same side: in the cis isomer the similar groups lie on the same side of the double bond.

mcqs.q: In a trans isomer, where are the similar groups placed?
options: On opposite sides of the double bond
On the same side of the double bond
Both on the same carbon atom
Trans isomers have no similar groups at all
mcqs.why: Trans comes from transoid, meaning opposite side: the similar groups lie on opposite sides of the double bond in a trans isomer.

mcqs.q: How are the hydrogen atoms arranged in cis-but-2-ene?
options: The H atoms are on opposite sides of the double bond
Both H atoms are on the same side of the double bond
Both H atoms are attached to the same carbon atom
But-2-ene has no hydrogen atoms on its double-bond carbons
mcqs.why: The book example states that cis-but-2-ene has both H atoms on the same side, while trans-but-2-ene has them opposite.

mcqs.q: Which is generally more stable, a cis or a trans isomer, and why?
options: The cis isomer, because groups on the same side attract each other strongly
Both are always equally stable in every case
The trans isomer, because in cis the bulky groups on the same side repel each other and lower stability
The cis isomer, because repulsion between groups raises its stability
mcqs.why: The notes state trans is more stable: in the cis form, bulky groups on the same side repel each other, which lowers stability.

mcqs.q: In cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane, where are the two methyl groups?
options: On opposite sides of the ring
Both attached to the same ring carbon
One methyl group is inside the ring and one is outside
Both on the same side of the ring
mcqs.why: The cyclic example in the notes: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane has both methyl groups on the same side of the ring; trans has them opposite.

mcqs.q: Cis and trans isomers are best described as:
options: Distinct compounds with different physical properties
The same compound drawn in two different ways
Compounds that always have identical physical properties
mcqs.why: The notes stress that cis and trans are distinct compounds and that they show different physical properties.

mcqs.q: The phenomenon shown by stereoisomers is called:
mcqs.why: Compounds differing only in spatial arrangement are stereoisomers, and the phenomenon itself is called stereoisomerism.

lessons.title: Hydrocarbons
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds, composed solely of carbon and hydrogen, joined by covalent bonds: methane CH4, ethylene C2H4, acetylene C2H2 and benzene C6H6. They are classified as aliphatic or aromatic, depending on the presence of a benzene ring.

Aliphatic Hydrocarbons

Straight-chained, branched or cyclic but non-aromatic hydrocarbons are aliphatic. Most are volatile and flammable. Saturated: only single bonds — alkanes and cycloalkanes, e.g. ethane CH3—CH3, cyclopropane (triangle). Unsaturated: at least one double or triple bond — alkenes, e.g. ethene CH2=CH2, and alkynes, e.g. ethyne HC≡CH.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons containing at least one benzene ring are aromatic: benzene, toluene, m-xylene and naphthalene.

In a straight chain, a carbon is never bonded to more than two carbons; in a branched compound a carbon may bond to three or four carbons at a time.

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons contain C and H only.
  • Aliphatic = non-aromatic chains, branches or rings.
  • Aromatic = contains a benzene ring.
  • Aliphatic splits into saturated and unsaturated.

mcqs.q: What are hydrocarbons?
options: The simplest organic compounds, composed solely of carbon and hydrogen joined by covalent bonds
Compounds containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only
Compounds made only of carbon atoms
Compounds containing carbon and a halogen
mcqs.why: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen joined by covalent bonds; the notes give methane CH4, ethylene C2H4, acetylene C2H2 and benzene C6H6.

mcqs.q: How are hydrocarbons classified as aliphatic or aromatic?
options: Depending on the number of hydrogen atoms they contain
Depending on the presence of a benzene ring
Depending on whether they are gases or liquids
Depending on the length of the carbon chain only
mcqs.why: The notes classify hydrocarbons as aliphatic or aromatic depending on the presence of a benzene ring.

mcqs.q: Which hydrocarbons are called aliphatic?
options: Any hydrocarbon containing a benzene ring
Only straight-chain hydrocarbons with triple bonds
Straight-chained, branched or cyclic but non-aromatic hydrocarbons
Only hydrocarbons that are solids at room temperature
mcqs.why: Aliphatic hydrocarbons are straight-chained, branched or cyclic but non-aromatic; most of them are volatile and flammable.

mcqs.q: Which pair is a correct example of saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons?
mcqs.why: Saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons have only single bonds — alkanes and cycloalkanes — such as ethane and cyclopropane (drawn as a triangle).

mcqs.q: Unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons are those that contain:
options: At least one double or triple bond, e.g. alkenes and alkynes
Only single bonds between carbon atoms
A benzene ring in every molecule
mcqs.why: Unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbons contain at least one double or triple bond; the notes give alkenes such as ethene and alkynes such as ethyne.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only aromatic hydrocarbons given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Aromatic hydrocarbons contain at least one benzene ring; the notes list benzene, toluene, m-xylene and naphthalene as examples.

mcqs.q: In a straight chain, a carbon atom is never bonded to more than how many other carbons?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a straight chain a carbon is never bonded to more than two carbons.

mcqs.q: In a branched compound, a carbon atom may bond to how many carbons at a time?
mcqs.why: The notes contrast branched compounds, where a carbon may bond to three or four carbons at a time, with straight chains.

mcqs.q: Most aliphatic hydrocarbons are described in the notes as:
options: Solids with very high melting points
mcqs.why: The notes describe most aliphatic hydrocarbons as volatile and flammable.

mcqs.q: Which formula–name pairing is correct as given in the notes?
options: Acetylene is C2H4 and benzene is C6H12
Acetylene is C2H2 and benzene is C6H6
Methane is CH6 and ethylene is C2H2
Benzene is C6H6 and methane is C2H4
mcqs.why: The opening examples pair methane CH4, ethylene C2H4, acetylene C2H2 and benzene C6H6 — so acetylene C2H2 and benzene C6H6 is correct.

lessons.title: Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes

Alkanes contain only single bonds between carbon atoms. They are also called paraffins, from Latin parum (little) + affin (affinity) — little affinity, the least reactive. Petroleum and natural gas are usually composed of alkanes.

Cycloalkanes

Cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which carbons are linked by single covalent bonds to form a ring; they are also called cycloparaffins. Their formula has two hydrogens fewer than the corresponding alkane because of the ring, e.g. cyclopropane (triangle) and cyclobutane (square).

Key Formulae

ClassGeneral formula
AlkanesCnH2n+2
CycloalkanesCnH2n

Petroleum and natural gas, the main fossil sources studied later in this unit, consist largely of alkanes, which is why alkane chemistry underlies fuels and petrochemicals. Cycloalkanes occur alongside them in crude oil. Despite sharing single bonds, a cycloalkane is not an alkane isomer series member: its ring closes the chain, so it follows CnH2n, the same general formula as alkenes.

Key Points

  • Alkanes: single bonds only, general formula CnH2n+2.
  • Paraffin means little affinity — alkanes are least reactive.
  • Cycloalkanes are ring alkanes with formula CnH2n.
  • Ring formation costs two hydrogen atoms.

mcqs.q: Alkanes contain which kind of bonds between carbon atoms?
options: At least one double bond in every molecule
A mixture of double and triple bonds
mcqs.why: Alkanes contain only single bonds between carbon atoms, which is why they are the saturated open-chain hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Why are alkanes also called paraffins?
options: From a Latin word meaning wax, because they are all waxy solids
From Latin parum (little) + affin (affinity) — little affinity, because they are the least reactive
From the name of the scientist who discovered them
Because they are found only in paraffin wax
mcqs.why: Paraffin comes from parum, little, plus affin, affinity: alkanes show little affinity, i.e. they are the least reactive hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Petroleum and natural gas are usually composed of which hydrocarbons?
mcqs.why: The notes state that petroleum and natural gas, the main fossil sources, are usually composed of alkanes.

mcqs.q: Cycloalkanes are also called:
mcqs.why: Cycloalkanes are saturated ring hydrocarbons with single covalent bonds, and the notes give cycloparaffins as their other name.

mcqs.q: How does the formula of a cycloalkane compare with the corresponding alkane?
options: It has two hydrogens fewer because of the ring
It has two hydrogens more because of the ring
It has exactly the same number of hydrogens
It has four hydrogens fewer because of the ring
mcqs.why: Ring formation costs two hydrogen atoms, so a cycloalkane has two hydrogens fewer than the corresponding alkane.

mcqs.q: Using the alkane general formula CnH2n+2, what is the molecular formula of the alkane with n = 5?
mcqs.why: Working: general formula CnH2n+2 with n = 5 gives H = 2n + 2 = 2(5) + 2 = 12, so the alkane is C5H12.

mcqs.q: Using the cycloalkane general formula CnH2n, what is the molecular formula of the cycloalkane with n = 4?
mcqs.why: Working: general formula CnH2n with n = 4 gives H = 2n = 2(4) = 8, so the cycloalkane (cyclobutane) is C4H8.

mcqs.q: How are cyclopropane and cyclobutane drawn in the notes?
options: Cyclopropane as a square and cyclobutane as a pentagon
Cyclopropane as a pentagon and cyclobutane as a triangle
Cyclopropane as a triangle and cyclobutane as a square
mcqs.why: The notes draw cyclopropane as a triangle and cyclobutane as a square, each corner representing one ring carbon.

mcqs.q: A cycloalkane follows the same general formula as which other class?
mcqs.why: The notes point out that a cycloalkane is not an alkane-series member: closing the ring gives CnH2n, the same general formula as alkenes.

mcqs.q: Why does a cycloalkane not belong to the alkane series even though it has only single bonds?
options: Because its bonds are double bonds, not single bonds
Its ring closes the chain, so it follows CnH2n instead of CnH2n+2
Because it contains a benzene ring
Because it contains one carbon atom fewer than an alkane
mcqs.why: Despite sharing single bonds, the ring closes the chain, so cycloalkanes follow CnH2n rather than the alkane formula CnH2n+2.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of Alkanes — Ethane

Ethane (C2H6), the second alkane, has two carbons joined by a single covalent bond, each carbon bonded to three hydrogens. The atoms arrange so the bonds are as far apart as possible: each carbon is tetrahedral, with bond angles of approximately 109.5°. The molecule can rotate freely about the C—C single bond — a characteristic feature of alkanes.

Structure of Cycloalkanes — Cyclopropane

Cyclopropane is the simplest cycloalkane. Cycloalkanes are written with a line-angle formula: a regular polygon with as many sides as ring carbons — triangle for cyclopropane, square for cyclobutane, pentagon for cyclopentane, hexagon for cyclohexane. Cyclopropane has significant bond angle strain (60° instead of 109.5°), which makes it highly reactive; it was once used as an anaesthetic.

Key Points

  • Ethane carbons are tetrahedral, angle about 109.5°.
  • Free rotation occurs about C—C single bonds.
  • Cycloalkanes are drawn as polygons (line-angle formula).
  • Cyclopropane is strained and unusually reactive.

mcqs.q: In ethane (C2H6), how is each carbon atom bonded?
options: Each carbon is joined to the other carbon by a single covalent bond and bonded to three hydrogens
Each carbon is bonded to four hydrogens and to no other carbon
The two carbons are joined by a double bond, each with two hydrogens
Each carbon is bonded to one hydrogen and one oxygen
mcqs.why: Ethane, the second alkane, has two carbons joined by a single covalent bond, each carbon bonded to three hydrogens — 2 carbons and 6 hydrogens in C2H6.

mcqs.q: What is the shape and bond angle around each carbon in ethane?
options: Trigonal planar, with bond angles of approximately 120°
Tetrahedral, with bond angles of approximately 109.5°
Square planar, with bond angles of 90°
mcqs.why: The atoms arrange so the bonds are as far apart as possible: each carbon in ethane is tetrahedral with bond angles of approximately 109.5°.

mcqs.q: Which movement is a characteristic feature of alkanes such as ethane?
options: No rotation of any kind about the C—C bond
Rotation that requires breaking the C—C bond first
Free rotation about the C—C single bond
Free rotation about a C=C double bond
mcqs.why: The notes state that the ethane molecule can rotate freely about the C—C single bond, a characteristic feature of alkanes.

mcqs.q: Which is the simplest cycloalkane?
mcqs.why: Cyclopropane is the simplest cycloalkane, a three-carbon ring drawn as a triangle in the line-angle formula.

mcqs.q: In the line-angle formula of a cycloalkane, what does the polygon show?
options: A regular polygon with as many sides as there are ring carbons
A polygon whose sides show the number of hydrogen atoms
A circle showing the ring has no carbons at its corners
A polygon with six sides for every cycloalkane
mcqs.why: Cycloalkanes are written as a regular polygon with as many sides as ring carbons: triangle, square, pentagon and hexagon for 3, 4, 5 and 6 carbons.

mcqs.q: Which polygon represents cyclopentane and which represents cyclohexane?
options: Cyclopentane is a hexagon and cyclohexane is a pentagon
Cyclopentane is a pentagon and cyclohexane is a hexagon
Cyclopentane is a triangle and cyclohexane is a square
mcqs.why: In the line-angle formula, cyclopentane (5 ring carbons) is a pentagon and cyclohexane (6 ring carbons) is a hexagon.

mcqs.q: Cyclopropane has bond angles of 60° instead of the ideal 109.5°. What is the size of this angle difference?
mcqs.why: Working: angle difference = ideal angle − ring angle = 109.5° − 60° = 49.5°. This large strain is why cyclopropane is highly reactive.

mcqs.q: Because of its significant bond angle strain, cyclopropane is:
options: More stable than all other cycloalkanes
Unable to react with any reagent
mcqs.why: The notes state that cyclopropane has significant bond angle strain (60° instead of 109.5°), which makes it highly reactive.

mcqs.q: Cyclopropane was once used for which purpose mentioned in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes record that cyclopropane, because of its unusual reactivity, was once used as an anaesthetic.

mcqs.q: Why do the bonds around each carbon in ethane point as far apart as possible?
options: Because each carbon carries a positive charge that attracts hydrogens
The atoms arrange themselves so the bonds are as far apart as possible, giving the tetrahedral arrangement
Because the hydrogens are joined to each other in a ring
Because ethane contains a double bond that forces a flat shape
mcqs.why: The notes explain that in ethane the atoms arrange so the bonds are as far apart as possible, which produces the tetrahedral carbon with 109.5° angles.

lessons.title: The Unreactive Nature of Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes are generally unreactive to polar reagents. Carbon electronegativity is 2.5 and hydrogen 2.1 — a difference of only about 0.4 — so the C—H bond is nearly non-polar, and the C—C bond, with no electronegativity difference, is completely non-polar. Alkane molecules therefore lack partial positive or negative charges that could attract polar reagents.

In methane, ethane and propane, bonding involves only strong sigma bonds formed by head-on orbital overlap. These bonds are stable and difficult to break under normal conditions. With non-polar character and strong bonding, alkanes show little or no electrophilic or nucleophilic behaviour and stay largely unreactive to polar reagents.

Reactions of alkanes usually need extreme conditions: high temperature, strong oxidising agents or catalysts. They do react in specific cases, e.g. halogenation when exposed to light.

Key Points

  • C—H is nearly non-polar; C—C is non-polar.
  • No partial charges, so polar reagents are not attracted.
  • Strong sigma bonds are hard to break.
  • Alkane reactions need heat, light, strong oxidisers or catalysts.

mcqs.q: What are the electronegativity values of carbon and hydrogen given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give carbon electronegativity as 2.5 and hydrogen as 2.1, a difference of only about 0.4.

mcqs.q: What is the electronegativity difference across the C—H bond?
mcqs.why: Working: difference = 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4. Because this difference is so small, the C—H bond is nearly non-polar.

mcqs.q: Because the electronegativity difference is so small, the C—H bond is:
mcqs.why: With a difference of only about 0.4 between carbon (2.5) and hydrogen (2.1), the C—H bond is nearly non-polar.

mcqs.q: The C—C bond in alkanes is best described as:
options: Strongly polar, because carbon attracts electrons from carbon
Ionic, because electrons are transferred between carbons
Nearly non-polar with a large partial charge
Completely non-polar, because there is no electronegativity difference
mcqs.why: The C—C bond has no electronegativity difference at all, so the notes describe it as completely non-polar.

mcqs.q: Why are polar reagents not attracted to alkane molecules?
options: Alkane molecules lack partial positive or negative charges that could attract polar reagents
Because alkanes are always gases that escape from reagents
Because alkanes contain charged carbon atoms that repel all reagents
Because polar reagents dissolve only in water
mcqs.why: With nearly non-polar C—H and non-polar C—C bonds, alkane molecules have no partial charges to attract polar reagents.

mcqs.q: The bonds in methane, ethane and propane are strong sigma bonds formed by:
options: Overlap that occurs only in ring compounds
mcqs.why: In methane, ethane and propane, bonding involves only strong sigma bonds formed by head-on orbital overlap, which are stable and hard to break.

mcqs.q: How do alkanes behave towards electrophiles and nucleophiles?
options: They are strongly attacked by both electrophiles and nucleophiles
They show little or no electrophilic or nucleophilic behaviour
mcqs.why: Because of their non-polar character and strong bonding, alkanes show little or no electrophilic or nucleophilic behaviour.

mcqs.q: Reactions of alkanes usually need which conditions?
options: Ordinary room temperature and pressure in the dark
No conditions at all — they react instantly
Extreme conditions: high temperature, strong oxidising agents or catalysts
mcqs.why: The notes state that alkane reactions usually need extreme conditions such as high temperature, strong oxidising agents or catalysts.

mcqs.q: Alkanes do react in one specific case mentioned in the notes. Which is it?
options: Addition of bromine water in the dark
Reaction with dilute alkalis at room temperature
mcqs.why: The notes give halogenation when exposed to light as a specific case where alkanes do react, despite their general unreactivity.

mcqs.q: Overall, alkanes are generally unreactive towards which kind of reagents?
options: Free radicals under UV light only
Strong oxidising agents at high temperature
mcqs.why: The section concludes that alkanes are generally unreactive to polar reagents because their bonds are non-polar and strong.

lessons.title: Radical Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
A radical (free radical) is a highly reactive species with an unpaired electron, formed by homolysis of a covalent bond. Heterolysis: both bonding electrons stay with one atom, A—B → A+ + :B-. Homolysis: each atom keeps one electron, A—B → A• + B• (shown with single-headed curly arrows).

Reaction Mechanism — Chlorination of Methane

  • Initiation: Cl2 undergoes homolytic fission in heat or light: Cl—Cl → Cl• + Cl• (UV).
  • Propagation: Cl• + CH4 → •CH3 + HCl; then •CH3 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl•. Further substitution gives CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4 step by step, each step regenerating Cl•.
  • Termination: two radicals combine: •CH3 + •CH3 → CH3—CH3; •Cl + •Cl → Cl2; •CH3 + •Cl → CH3Cl. This reduces the radicals available and ends the chain.

Chlorination of Ethane

Same mechanism: initiation Cl2 → 2Cl• (hv); propagation Cl• + CH3CH3 → •CH2CH3 + HCl, then •CH2CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + Cl•; termination gives CH3CH2CH2CH3, Cl2 or CH3CH2Cl. Propagation differs slightly because ethane has secondary-type hydrogens in the book's wording.

Key Points

  • Free-radical chain: initiation, propagation, termination.
  • UV light or heat starts homolysis of Cl2.
  • Methane chlorination can continue to CCl4.
  • Termination removes radicals by combining them.

mcqs.q: A free radical is best defined as:
options: A highly reactive species with an unpaired electron, formed by homolysis of a covalent bond
A stable ion carrying a full positive charge
A species with a complete pair of bonding electrons shared equally forever
An atom that has gained two electrons
mcqs.why: The notes define a radical (free radical) as a highly reactive species with an unpaired electron, formed by homolysis of a covalent bond.

mcqs.q: In heterolysis of a bond A—B, what happens to the bonding electrons?
options: Each atom keeps one electron, giving two radicals
Both bonding electrons stay with one atom, giving A+ + :B-
Both electrons are lost to the surroundings
The electrons move onto the hydrogen atom only
mcqs.why: Heterolysis: both bonding electrons stay with one atom, A—B → A+ + :B-, forming ions rather than radicals.

mcqs.q: In homolysis of a bond A—B, what is formed?
options: Two ions, A+ and B-, shown with double-headed arrows
One radical and one stable molecule only
Two radicals, A• + B•, each atom keeping one electron, shown with single-headed curly arrows
A carbocation and a carbanion pair
mcqs.why: Homolysis: each atom keeps one electron, A—B → A• + B•, and the notes show this with single-headed curly arrows.

mcqs.q: What happens in the initiation step of methane chlorination?
options: CH4 splits into ions in the dark
Two methyl radicals combine to form ethane
HCl is formed from H2 and Cl2
Cl2 undergoes homolytic fission in heat or UV light: Cl—Cl → Cl• + Cl•
