mcqs.why: Initiation is the homolytic fission of chlorine in heat or light (UV): Cl—Cl → Cl• + Cl•, generating the first radicals.

mcqs.q: Which equation is a propagation step in the chlorination of methane?
mcqs.why: In propagation, a chlorine radical attacks methane: Cl• + CH4 → •CH3 + HCl, producing a methyl radical that continues the chain.

mcqs.q: What happens in the second propagation step of methane chlorination?
options: •CH3 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl•, regenerating a chlorine radical
CH4 + Cl2 → C + 4HCl in one step
Cl• + Cl• → Cl2, ending the chain
mcqs.why: The methyl radical reacts with chlorine: •CH3 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl•. The regenerated Cl• keeps the chain going.

mcqs.q: How far can the chlorination of methane continue?
options: It always stops after forming CH3Cl
It stops at CH2Cl2 because no hydrogens remain
Step by step through CH2Cl2 and CHCl3 to CCl4, each step regenerating Cl•
It gives only CHCl3 directly in one step
mcqs.why: Further substitution gives CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4 step by step, each step regenerating the Cl• radical.

mcqs.q: Which equation shows a termination step?
mcqs.why: Termination combines two radicals into a stable molecule: •CH3 + •CH3 → CH3—CH3. Other examples are •Cl + •Cl → Cl2 and •CH3 + •Cl → CH3Cl.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of termination steps on the chain reaction?
options: They reduce the radicals available and end the chain
They generate more radicals and speed the chain up
mcqs.why: Termination removes radicals by combining them into stable molecules, which reduces the radicals available and ends the chain.

mcqs.q: In the chlorination of ethane, the first propagation step gives which radical?
options: •CH3, from breaking ethane into two methyl radicals
Cl• only, with no carbon radical formed
mcqs.why: For ethane the same mechanism applies: Cl• + CH3CH3 → •CH2CH3 + HCl, then •CH2CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + Cl•.

lessons.title: Identification of Organic Redox Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Organic redox reactions involve changes in oxidation states, identified by the gain or loss of oxygen and/or hydrogen.

Oxidation

Oxidation increases oxygen content or decreases hydrogen content, e.g. converting alcohols to aldehydes or ketones, and alkanes to alcohols.

  • Alkane to alcohol: CH3CH3 + 1/2 O2(g) → CH3CH2OH (PdCl2/CuCl2, 150-250°C).
  • Alcohol to aldehyde: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4); ethyl alcohol → acetaldehyde.
  • Secondary alcohol to ketone: CH3—CH(OH)—CH3 + [O] → CH3—CO—CH3 + H2O; sec-propyl alcohol → acetone.

Reduction

Reduction decreases oxygen content and/or increases hydrogen content, e.g. aldehydes/ketones are reduced to alcohols and alkenes to alkanes. The book shows acetone with NaBH4/H2O giving isopropyl alcohol under this heading.

In the body, glucose is oxidised in cells to release energy (ATP), just as hydrocarbons burn in engines.

Key Points

  • Oxidation: gain O or lose H.
  • Reduction: lose O or gain H.
  • Alcohol → aldehyde/ketone is oxidation; carbonyl → alcohol is reduction.
  • K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 is the oxidising system used in the examples.

mcqs.q: In organic chemistry, oxidation is identified by:
options: Increase in oxygen content or decrease in hydrogen content
Decrease in oxygen content and increase in hydrogen content
No change in oxygen or hydrogen content
Loss of carbon atoms from the molecule
mcqs.why: The notes identify oxidation by gain of oxygen and/or loss of hydrogen, as in converting alcohols to aldehydes or ketones.

mcqs.q: In organic chemistry, reduction is identified by:
options: Increase in oxygen content or decrease in hydrogen content
Decrease in oxygen content and/or increase in hydrogen content
Gain of oxygen and loss of hydrogen together
mcqs.why: Reduction decreases oxygen content and/or increases hydrogen content, e.g. aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols.

mcqs.q: The conversion of ethane to ethanol, CH3CH3 + 1/2 O2 → CH3CH2OH, is an example of:
options: Reduction — hydrogen is added across a double bond
Substitution — a chlorine replaces a hydrogen
Oxidation — an alkane is converted to an alcohol (PdCl2/CuCl2, 150-250°C)
Hydration — water adds across a double bond
mcqs.why: Converting an alkane to an alcohol increases the oxygen content, so it is oxidation; the notes give PdCl2/CuCl2 at 150-250°C.

mcqs.q: Ethanol is converted to acetaldehyde (ethanal) using which oxidising system?
mcqs.why: The notes oxidise ethyl alcohol to acetaldehyde with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol such as sec-propyl alcohol gives:
mcqs.why: Secondary alcohol to ketone is oxidation: CH3—CH(OH)—CH3 + [O] → CH3—CO—CH3 + H2O; sec-propyl alcohol gives acetone.

mcqs.q: Which pair shows reductions as described in the notes?
options: Alcohols oxidised to aldehydes, and alkanes oxidised to alcohols
Aldehydes/ketones reduced to alcohols, and alkenes reduced to alkanes
Ethanol converted to acetaldehyde with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4
Glucose oxidised in body cells to release energy
mcqs.why: Reduction examples in the notes: aldehydes/ketones are reduced to alcohols and alkenes are reduced to alkanes (gain of hydrogen).

mcqs.q: Acetone treated with NaBH4/H2O gives isopropyl alcohol. This change is:
options: Reduction — the carbonyl compound gains hydrogen and becomes an alcohol
mcqs.why: The book shows acetone with NaBH4/H2O giving isopropyl alcohol under reduction: oxygen content effectively falls as hydrogen is gained.

mcqs.q: In the body, glucose is oxidised in cells in order to:
options: Store hydrogen for later reduction reactions
Convert glucose into a hydrocarbon fuel
Release energy (ATP), just as hydrocarbons burn in engines
mcqs.why: The notes compare the two: in the body glucose is oxidised in cells to release energy (ATP), just as hydrocarbons burn in engines.

mcqs.q: Converting an alcohol into an aldehyde or a ketone is classified as:
mcqs.why: Alcohol → aldehyde/ketone increases oxygen content (or decreases hydrogen), so the key points classify it as oxidation.

mcqs.q: Converting a carbonyl compound (aldehyde/ketone) into an alcohol is classified as:
mcqs.why: Carbonyl → alcohol is the reverse change: hydrogen is gained, so the key points classify it as reduction.

lessons.title: Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one or more carbon—carbon double bonds (C=C). They are also known as olefins, from the French word olefiant, oil-forming, because lower alkenes give oily products with chlorine or bromine.

Alkenes occur in natural gas, coal gas and gasoline in small amounts, and are produced in large quantities by the cracking of petroleum. Ethene was first identified in the 18th century as olefiant gas because it formed oily liquids with chlorine. Ethylene (ethene) is the first member of the series.

Key Formulae

ClassGeneral formula
Alkenes (monoenes)CnH2n

Ethene itself is the starting material for polythene and many other products studied later in this unit, and propene is the second member of the series. Alkenes are also called monoenes when they contain one double bond. Their occurrence is small in nature compared with alkanes, so industry makes them deliberately by cracking long-chain petroleum fractions into shorter, more useful molecules.

Key Points

  • Alkenes contain C=C and are unsaturated.
  • General formula CnH2n; first member is ethene.
  • Main source: cracking of petroleum.
  • Olefins = oil-forming, from their oily halogen products.

mcqs.q: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing:
options: One or more carbon—carbon double bonds (C=C)
At least one triple bond in every molecule
mcqs.why: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one or more C=C double bonds; ethene is the first member of the series.

mcqs.q: Alkenes are also known as olefins. What does this name come from?
options: The Latin word for little affinity
The French word olefiant, oil-forming, because lower alkenes give oily products with chlorine or bromine
The name of the scientist who first made ethene
A Greek word meaning double bond
mcqs.why: Olefins comes from the French olefiant, oil-forming, because lower alkenes give oily products with chlorine or bromine.

mcqs.q: Where do alkenes occur naturally, according to the notes?
options: In natural gas, coal gas and gasoline, in small amounts
They do not occur anywhere in nature
mcqs.why: Alkenes occur in natural gas, coal gas and gasoline in small amounts, and are produced in large quantities by cracking petroleum.

mcqs.q: Alkenes are produced in large quantities by which process?
options: Fractional distillation alone, with no bond breaking
mcqs.why: Industry makes alkenes deliberately by cracking long-chain petroleum fractions into shorter, more useful molecules.

mcqs.q: Ethene was first identified in the 18th century as:
options: Olefiant gas, because it formed oily liquids with chlorine
Laughing gas, because of its effect on people
mcqs.why: Ethene (ethylene) was first identified in the 18th century as olefiant gas because it formed oily liquids with chlorine.

mcqs.q: The first member of the alkene series is:
mcqs.why: Ethylene (ethene) is the first member of the alkene series, and propene is the second member.

mcqs.q: Using the alkene general formula CnH2n, what is the molecular formula of the alkene with n = 3?
mcqs.why: Working: general formula CnH2n with n = 3 gives H = 2n = 2(3) = 6, so the alkene (propene) is C3H6.

mcqs.q: Alkenes containing exactly one double bond are also called:
mcqs.why: The notes state that alkenes are also called monoenes when they contain one double bond.

mcqs.q: Ethene is the starting material for which product mentioned in the notes?
mcqs.why: Ethene itself is the starting material for polythene and many other products studied later in this unit.

mcqs.q: The second member of the alkene series is:
mcqs.why: The notes name ethene as the first member of the series and propene as the second member.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Ethene contains a carbon—carbon double bond made of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The double-bonded carbons are sp2 hybridised: each has three sp2 hybrid orbitals and one pure p-orbital.

  • Each sp2 orbital overlaps with another atom's orbital to form sigma bonds (head-to-head overlap).
  • The remaining p-orbital on one sp2 carbon overlaps side-to-side with the p-orbital of the other to form the pi bond.
  • All six atoms of ethene lie in the same plane: ethene is trigonal planar.
  • HCH and HCC bond angles are approximately 120°.
  • C=C bond length is 134 pm; C—H bond length is 109 pm.

Because the pi bond is made by sideways overlap above and below the C—C line, rotation about C=C is restricted — the two carbons cannot twist without breaking the pi overlap. This is the structural reason behind the geometric (cis-trans) isomerism described in section 11.11, and behind ethene's flat shape: all six atoms must stay in one plane for the p-orbitals to overlap.

Key Points

  • C=C = one sigma + one pi bond.
  • Double-bond carbons are sp2, trigonal planar, about 120°.
  • Sigma forms head-on; pi forms side-on from p-orbitals.
  • Ethene is a flat (planar) molecule.

mcqs.q: The carbon—carbon double bond in ethene is made of:
options: One sigma bond and one pi bond
One sigma bond and two pi bonds
mcqs.why: Ethene contains a C=C double bond made of one sigma bond and one pi bond; the double-bonded carbons are sp2 hybridised.

mcqs.q: The double-bonded carbons in ethene are sp2 hybridised. What does each such carbon have?
options: Four sp3 hybrid orbitals and no p-orbital
Three sp2 hybrid orbitals and one pure p-orbital
Two sp orbitals and two p-orbitals
One sp2 orbital and three p-orbitals
mcqs.why: Each double-bonded carbon is sp2 hybridised: it has three sp2 hybrid orbitals and one pure p-orbital.

mcqs.q: How is the sigma bond between the carbons of ethene formed?
options: By transfer of an electron pair to oxygen
By head-to-head overlap of sp2 orbitals
By overlap of hydrogen 1s orbitals only
mcqs.why: Each sp2 orbital overlaps with another atom's orbital head-to-head to form sigma bonds.

mcqs.q: How is the pi bond in ethene formed?
options: By head-to-head overlap of two sp2 orbitals
By overlap of two hydrogen atoms
By sharing electrons with a neighbouring molecule
By side-to-side overlap of the remaining p-orbital on one carbon with the p-orbital of the other carbon
mcqs.why: The remaining p-orbital on one sp2 carbon overlaps side-to-side with the p-orbital of the other carbon to form the pi bond.

mcqs.q: What is the shape of the ethene molecule and where do its atoms lie?
options: All six atoms lie in the same plane — ethene is trigonal planar
The atoms form a tetrahedral shape in three dimensions
Only the two carbons lie in one plane; the hydrogens are above and below it
The molecule is linear, with all atoms in a straight line
mcqs.why: All six atoms of ethene lie in the same plane: ethene is trigonal planar, with HCH and HCC angles of approximately 120°.

mcqs.q: The HCH and HCC bond angles in ethene are approximately:
mcqs.why: Ethene is trigonal planar at each carbon, so its HCH and HCC bond angles are approximately 120°, not the tetrahedral 109.5°.

mcqs.q: The C=C bond length is 134 pm and the C—H bond length is 109 pm. How much longer is C=C than C—H?
mcqs.why: Working: difference in bond length = 134 pm − 109 pm = 25 pm. So the C=C bond (134 pm) is 25 pm longer than C—H (109 pm).

mcqs.q: Why is rotation about the C=C double bond restricted?
options: Because the sigma bond is too short to allow rotation
Because hydrogen atoms block the rotation physically
Because ethene molecules are joined to each other in a chain
Twisting the carbons would break the sideways pi overlap above and below the C—C line
mcqs.why: The pi bond is made by sideways overlap above and below the C—C line, so the two carbons cannot twist without breaking the pi overlap.

mcqs.q: The restricted rotation about C=C is the structural reason behind which phenomenon?
options: Geometric (cis-trans) isomerism, and behind ethene's flat shape
mcqs.why: The notes link restricted rotation directly to geometric (cis-trans) isomerism and to ethene's flat shape, needed for p-orbital overlap.

mcqs.q: For the p-orbitals in ethene to overlap and form the pi bond, what must be true?
options: The molecule must twist out of plane by 90°
All six atoms must stay in one plane
The hydrogens must move to the same carbon
The sigma bond must break first
mcqs.why: Ethene's flat shape is required: all six atoms must stay in one plane for the p-orbitals on the two carbons to overlap.

lessons.title: Preparation of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are typically produced by β-elimination reactions: two atoms or groups on adjacent carbon atoms are eliminated and a double bond forms.

Dehydration of Alcohols

Removal of H2O from adjacent carbons of an alcohol by heating with a dehydrating agent is dehydration. The best dehydrating reagents are (i) conc. H2SO4, (ii) Al2O3, (iii) P2O5 (printed P2O2 in the book); all work at high temperatures. Ethyl alcohol needs conc. H2SO4 at 170-180°C: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O (OH leaves the α-carbon, H leaves the β-carbon).

Dehydrohalogenation of Alkyl Halides

Removal of HX from adjacent carbons of an alkyl halide by heating with alcoholic KOH is dehydrohalogenation. X is removed from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon: CH2(X)—CH2(H) skeleton + KOH → CH2=CH2 + HX (alcohol, heat), as drawn in the book.

In both methods the carbon skeleton keeps the same number of carbons; only H2O or HX is lost and a single bond becomes a double bond.

Key Points

  • Both methods are β-eliminations forming C=C.
  • Dehydration: conc. H2SO4, 170-180°C for ethanol.
  • Dehydrohalogenation: alcoholic KOH with heat.
  • Leaving atoms come from adjacent (α and β) carbons.

mcqs.q: Alkenes are typically produced by which type of reaction?
options: β-Elimination reactions — two atoms or groups on adjacent carbons are eliminated and a double bond forms
Addition reactions across a triple bond
Substitution of a hydrogen by a halogen in sunlight
mcqs.why: Alkenes are typically produced by β-elimination: atoms or groups on adjacent carbon atoms are eliminated and a double bond forms.

mcqs.q: Dehydration of an alcohol means:
options: Addition of water across a double bond
Removal of H2O from adjacent carbons of an alcohol by heating with a dehydrating agent
Removal of HX from an alkyl halide
Loss of H2 from an alkane at room temperature
mcqs.why: Dehydration is the removal of H2O from adjacent carbons of an alcohol by heating with a dehydrating agent.

mcqs.q: Which reagents are listed as the best dehydrating reagents?
options: Dilute H2SO4 at room temperature, NaOH and water
Conc. H2SO4, Al2O3 and P2O5 (printed P2O2 in the book), all at high temperatures
mcqs.why: The best dehydrating reagents listed are conc. H2SO4, Al2O3 and P2O5 (printed P2O2 in the book); all work at high temperatures.

mcqs.q: Ethyl alcohol gives ethene on heating with conc. H2SO4 at what temperature?
mcqs.why: Ethyl alcohol needs conc. H2SO4 at 170-180°C: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O, with OH leaving the α-carbon and H the β-carbon.

mcqs.q: In the dehydration of an alcohol, which groups leave from which carbons?
options: OH leaves the α-carbon and H leaves the β-carbon
H leaves the α-carbon and OH leaves the β-carbon
Both OH and H leave the same carbon atom
Two hydrogens leave and oxygen stays in the product
mcqs.why: The notes state for dehydration: OH leaves the α-carbon, H leaves the β-carbon, and the double bond forms between them.

mcqs.q: Dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide is carried out by:
options: Heating with alcoholic KOH, removing HX from adjacent carbons
Passing dry HX gas over the halide
Adding H2 with a nickel catalyst
mcqs.why: Removal of HX from adjacent carbons of an alkyl halide by heating with alcoholic KOH is dehydrohalogenation.

mcqs.q: In dehydrohalogenation, the halogen X is removed from which carbon, and H from which?
options: X from the β-carbon and H from the α-carbon
Both X and H from the α-carbon
X from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon
Both X and H from the β-carbon
mcqs.why: As drawn in the book, X is removed from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon, giving CH2=CH2 + HX with alcoholic KOH and heat.

mcqs.q: What happens to the carbon skeleton in both preparation methods?
options: It loses one carbon atom in each reaction
It gains an extra carbon from the reagent
It breaks into two smaller fragments
It keeps the same number of carbons; only H2O or HX is lost and a single bond becomes a double bond
mcqs.why: In both methods the carbon skeleton keeps the same number of carbons; only H2O or HX is lost and a single bond becomes a double bond.

mcqs.q: Both dehydration and dehydrohalogenation are examples of:
options: β-Eliminations forming a C=C double bond
Electrophilic additions to a double bond
Condensation reactions losing water between two molecules
mcqs.why: The key points state that both methods are β-eliminations forming C=C, with leaving atoms coming from adjacent (α and β) carbons.

mcqs.q: The complete equation for preparing ethene from ethanol is:
mcqs.why: Dehydration of ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at 170-180°C gives ethene and water: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the pi bond. The pi bond is formed by parallel (side-to-side) overlapping of p-orbitals.

The pi electrons of the double bond lie much farther from the carbon nuclei and are therefore less firmly bound to them. This makes the pi bond a weak bond compared with the sigma bond, so it breaks much more easily under attack by an electrophilic reagent.

Contrast with Alkanes

FeatureAlkanesAlkenes
BondsOnly strong sigma bondsOne sigma + one weak pi bond at C=C
ReactivityUnreactive to polar reagentsReadily attacked by electrophiles
Typical reactionFree-radical substitution under UVElectrophilic addition

The pi electrons form an exposed electron cloud above and below the double bond. An electrophile is attracted to this electron-rich region, donates nothing and accepts the pi electron pair, so addition begins. Once the pi bond breaks, two new sigma bonds can form, giving a saturated product — the pattern followed by every reaction in section 11.22.

Key Points

  • The exposed pi electrons make alkenes reactive.
  • Pi bond is weaker than sigma bond.
  • Electrophiles attack the pi bond first.
  • Most alkene reactions break the pi bond, keeping sigma intact.

mcqs.q: Why are alkenes more reactive than alkanes?
options: Because of the pi bond, formed by parallel (side-to-side) overlapping of p-orbitals
Because their sigma bonds are weaker than those of alkanes
Because they contain more hydrogen atoms than alkanes
Because their molecules carry a positive charge
mcqs.why: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the pi bond, formed by side-to-side overlapping of p-orbitals.

mcqs.q: Where do the pi electrons of a double bond lie, and what follows from this?
options: Very close to the carbon nuclei, so they are held more tightly than sigma electrons
Much farther from the carbon nuclei, so they are less firmly bound to them
Equally shared between the two hydrogen atoms
mcqs.why: The pi electrons lie much farther from the carbon nuclei and are therefore less firmly bound, making the pi bond weak and easy to break.

mcqs.q: How does the strength of the pi bond compare with the sigma bond?
options: The pi bond is stronger than the sigma bond
Both bonds are exactly equal in strength
The pi bond is a weak bond compared with the sigma bond, so it breaks much more easily
The sigma bond breaks first in every alkene reaction
mcqs.why: The notes state the pi bond is weak compared with the sigma bond, so it breaks much more easily under attack by an electrophilic reagent.

mcqs.q: In the contrast table, alkanes are described as having:
options: One sigma and one weak pi bond at C=C
An exposed electron cloud above the double bond
mcqs.why: The contrast table gives alkanes only strong sigma bonds, while alkenes have one sigma plus one weak pi bond at C=C.

mcqs.q: How do alkenes and alkanes differ towards polar/electrophilic reagents?
options: Alkenes are readily attacked by electrophiles; alkanes are unreactive to polar reagents
Both are equally unreactive to electrophiles
Alkanes are readily attacked by electrophiles; alkenes are unreactive
Neither reacts with any reagent under any conditions
mcqs.why: The table contrasts unreactive alkanes (to polar reagents) with alkenes, which are readily attacked by electrophiles at the pi bond.

mcqs.q: What are the typical reactions of alkanes and alkenes in the contrast table?
options: Alkanes: free-radical substitution under UV; alkenes: electrophilic addition
Alkanes: electrophilic addition; alkenes: free-radical substitution under UV
mcqs.why: Typical reactions from the table: alkanes undergo free-radical substitution under UV, while alkenes undergo electrophilic addition.

mcqs.q: The pi electrons of an alkene form what feature around the double bond?
options: A shield that repels all electrophiles
A ring of positive charge around the carbons
An exposed electron cloud above and below the double bond
A second sigma bond inside the first
mcqs.why: The pi electrons form an exposed electron cloud above and below the double bond, and an electrophile is attracted to this electron-rich region.

mcqs.q: When an electrophile attacks an alkene, what does the electrophile do?
options: It donates a pair of electrons to the pi bond
It removes a hydrogen atom as a radical
It breaks the sigma bond and leaves the pi bond intact
It donates nothing and accepts the pi electron pair, so addition begins
mcqs.why: The notes state an electrophile is attracted to the electron-rich region, donates nothing and accepts the pi electron pair, so addition begins.

mcqs.q: Once the pi bond of an alkene breaks during a reaction, what can happen?
options: Two new sigma bonds can form, giving a saturated product
The molecule must break into two fragments
A new pi bond forms on a different carbon automatically
The carbon skeleton loses one carbon atom
mcqs.why: Once the pi bond breaks, two new sigma bonds can form, giving a saturated product — the pattern followed by every reaction in the next section.

mcqs.q: In most alkene reactions, which bond breaks and which stays intact?
options: The sigma bond breaks, keeping the pi bond intact
The pi bond breaks, keeping the sigma bond intact
Both bonds break in every reaction
Neither bond breaks; only hydrogen atoms move
mcqs.why: The key points state that most alkene reactions break the pi bond, keeping the sigma bond intact.

lessons.title: Hydrogenation and Hydrohalogenation of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The most important reactions of alkenes are addition reactions: two molecules combine into one product and the double bond becomes a single bond.

Catalytic Hydrogenation

H2 adds to an alkene with a catalyst (Pt, Ni or Pd) at moderate pressure 1-5 atm to give an alkane: CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3—CH3; CH3—CH=CH2 + H2 → CH3—CH2—CH3 (Ni, 1-5 atm, 250-300°C). The heat evolved per mole is the heat of hydrogenation, about 120 kJ/mol for each double bond. Hydrogenation of vegetable oils gives margarine and vegetable ghee.

Hydrohalogenation (Electrophilic Addition)

Addition of HX to an alkene gives an alkyl halide, in acetic acid or by passing dry HX gas over the alkene: CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3—CH2—Br (ethyl bromide); propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane. Reactivity order: HI > HBr > HCl > HF.

Mechanism (HBr + ethene): Step 1 — pi electrons attack H of HBr, forming a carbocation + Br-. Step 2 — Br- (nucleophile) attacks the carbocation to give ethyl bromide.

Markovnikov's rule: when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the halide attaches to the carbon with fewer hydrogens and the proton to the carbon with more hydrogens, because the more stable carbocation forms. Propene gives mainly 2-bromopropane via the secondary carbocation, which is more stable than the primary one; 1-bromopropane is the minor product.

Key Points

  • Addition converts C=C into C—C.
  • Hydrogenation needs Ni/Pt/Pd and gives alkanes.
  • Markovnikov: X goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
  • Carbocation stability decides the major product.

mcqs.q: In an addition reaction of an alkene, what happens overall?
options: Two molecules combine into one product and the double bond becomes a single bond
One molecule splits into two products
A group is replaced by another group with nothing added
Atoms are removed and a double bond forms
mcqs.why: Addition reactions: two molecules combine into one product and the double bond becomes a single bond.

mcqs.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene requires which conditions?
options: H2 alone at 400°C with no catalyst
H2 with a catalyst (Pt, Ni or Pd) at moderate pressure 1-5 atm, giving an alkane
mcqs.why: H2 adds to an alkene with a catalyst (Pt, Ni or Pd) at moderate pressure 1-5 atm to give an alkane, e.g. CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3—CH3.

mcqs.q: Propene hydrogenated with Ni at 1-5 atm and 250-300°C gives:
mcqs.why: The book equation: CH3—CH=CH2 + H2 → CH3—CH2—CH3 (Ni, 1-5 atm, 250-300°C) — the double bond becomes single.

mcqs.q: The heat of hydrogenation is about 120 kJ/mol for each double bond. How much heat is evolved when a molecule with 2 double bonds is fully hydrogenated?
mcqs.why: Working: heat evolved = number of double bonds × heat per double bond = 2 × 120 kJ/mol = 240 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: Hydrogenation of vegetable oils gives which products mentioned in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state that hydrogenation of vegetable oils gives margarine and vegetable ghee.

mcqs.q: Hydrohalogenation of an alkene gives which type of product?
options: An alkyl halide, in acetic acid or by passing dry HX gas over the alkene
mcqs.why: Addition of HX to an alkene gives an alkyl halide, e.g. CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3—CH2—Br (ethyl bromide).

mcqs.q: Ethene reacts with HBr to give:
options: Bromoethane with Br on a carbon that had no hydrogens
mcqs.why: The book example: CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3—CH2—Br, ethyl bromide, formed by electrophilic addition of HBr.

mcqs.q: What is the reactivity order of the hydrogen halides towards alkenes?
options: All four react at exactly the same rate
mcqs.why: The notes give the reactivity order for hydrohalogenation as HI > HBr > HCl > HF.

mcqs.q: In the mechanism of HBr addition to ethene, what happens in Step 1 and Step 2?
options: Step 1: pi electrons attack H of HBr, forming a carbocation + Br-; Step 2: Br- attacks the carbocation
Step 1: Br- attacks the double bond; Step 2: H+ leaves as hydrogen gas
Step 1: two radicals form; Step 2: the radicals combine
Step 1: HBr splits into H2 and Br2; Step 2: Br2 adds across the bond
mcqs.why: Mechanism: pi electrons attack H of HBr forming a carbocation and Br-, then the nucleophile Br- attacks the carbocation to give ethyl bromide.

mcqs.q: According to Markovnikov's rule, when HX adds to propene the main product is 2-bromopropane because:
options: The halide attaches to the carbon with more hydrogens via a primary carbocation
The halide attaches to the carbon with fewer hydrogens via the more stable secondary carbocation; 1-bromopropane is minor
Both products form in exactly equal amounts
The primary carbocation is more stable than the secondary one
mcqs.why: Markovnikov's rule: X goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms because the more stable (secondary) carbocation forms; 1-bromopropane is the minor product.

lessons.title: Hydration, Halogenation and Halohydration of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Inductive Effect and Carbocation Stability

The inductive effect is the electron-donating tendency of alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl) that stabilises carbocations: electron density shifts towards the electron-deficient carbon and reduces its charge. Stability order: tertiary (3 alkyl groups) > secondary (2) > primary (1). This explains Markovnikov addition.

Hydration

Addition of water is hydration. Alkenes react with H2O in the presence of H2SO4 at 100°C to form alcohols, via ethyl hydrogensulphate from ethene, which then hydrolyses to ethyl alcohol (ethanol).

Halogenation

Addition of Cl2 or Br2 is halogenation. Alkenes react in an inert solvent such as CCl4 in the dark to form vicinal dihalides, e.g. propene + Cl2 → 1,2-dichloropropane. Mechanism: Step 1 — pi electrons attack X—X, forming a halonium ion + X-. Step 2 — X- attacks to give the vicinal dihalide. Bromine water test: reddish-brown bromine water turns colourless with an alkene, detecting a C=C bond.

Halohydration

Addition of hypohalous acid is halohydration. Aqueous Cl2 or Br2 gives halohydrins with adjacent halo and hydroxyl groups: alkene + X2 + H2O → halohydrin + HX; propene + Cl2 + H2O → 1-chloropropan-2-ol + HCl.

Key Points

  • Carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary.
  • Hydration (H2SO4, 100°C) gives alcohols.
  • Halogenation gives vicinal dihalides; bromine water is decolourised.
  • Halohydration gives a halohydrin (X and OH on adjacent carbons).

mcqs.q: What is the inductive effect as described in the notes?
options: The electron-donating tendency of alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl) that stabilises carbocations
The electron-withdrawing effect of halogen atoms on a ring
The movement of pi electrons in a double bond only
The repulsion between bulky groups on the same side
mcqs.why: The inductive effect is the electron-donating tendency of alkyl groups: electron density shifts towards the electron-deficient carbon and reduces its charge.

mcqs.q: What is the stability order of carbocations given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Stability order: tertiary (3 alkyl groups) > secondary (2) > primary (1). This order explains Markovnikov addition.

mcqs.q: Hydration of an alkene gives which product, and under what conditions?
options: An alkyl halide — with dry HX gas
A vicinal dihalide — with Br2 in CCl4
An alcohol — alkenes react with H2O in the presence of H2SO4 at 100°C
An alkane — with H2 and Ni
mcqs.why: Addition of water is hydration: alkenes react with H2O in the presence of H2SO4 at 100°C to form alcohols.

mcqs.q: How is ethanol formed from ethene by hydration, according to the notes?
options: By direct addition of H2 across the double bond
Via a halohydrin that loses HCl
Via ethyl hydrogensulphate from ethene, which then hydrolyses to ethyl alcohol (ethanol)
mcqs.why: The notes describe ethene forming ethyl hydrogensulphate first, which then hydrolyses to ethyl alcohol (ethanol).

mcqs.q: Halogenation of an alkene gives which product, and under what conditions?
options: A vicinal dihalide — Cl2 or Br2 in an inert solvent such as CCl4 in the dark
An alkyl halide — with one equivalent of HX
mcqs.why: Addition of Cl2 or Br2 in an inert solvent such as CCl4 in the dark forms vicinal dihalides, e.g. propene + Cl2 → 1,2-dichloropropane.

mcqs.q: Propene reacts with Cl2 in CCl4 to give:
mcqs.why: The book example of halogenation: propene + Cl2 → 1,2-dichloropropane, a vicinal dihalide with Cl on adjacent carbons.

mcqs.q: In the mechanism of halogenation, what is formed in Step 1?
options: A carbocation + H-, when pi electrons attack HX
Two free radicals by homolytic fission
A halonium ion + X-, when pi electrons attack X—X; then X- attacks in Step 2
A halohydrin directly in one step
mcqs.why: Halogenation mechanism: Step 1 — pi electrons attack X—X, forming a halonium ion + X-; Step 2 — X- attacks to give the vicinal dihalide.

mcqs.q: The bromine water test for a C=C bond works because:
options: Bromine water turns blue with an alkene
Bromine water forms a white precipitate with an alkene
Bromine water bubbles vigorously with an alkene
Reddish-brown bromine water turns colourless with an alkene
mcqs.why: Bromine water test: reddish-brown bromine water turns colourless with an alkene, detecting a C=C bond.

mcqs.q: Halohydration of an alkene gives a halohydrin, which is:
options: A product with adjacent halo and hydroxyl groups, from alkene + X2 + H2O
A product with two halogen atoms on adjacent carbons
An alcohol with no halogen atom
A product with halo and hydroxyl groups on the same carbon
mcqs.why: Addition of hypohalous acid is halohydration: aqueous Cl2 or Br2 gives halohydrins with adjacent halo and hydroxyl groups, plus HX.

mcqs.q: Propene with Cl2 and H2O gives which halohydrin?
mcqs.why: The book equation: propene + Cl2 + H2O → 1-chloropropan-2-ol + HCl — Cl and OH end up on adjacent carbons.

lessons.title: Epoxidation, Ozonolysis and Polymerization of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Epoxidation

Addition of oxygen to an alkene is epoxidation. With O2 over a silver catalyst at high pressure and temperature it gives epoxides: 2CH2=CH2 + O2 → 2 ethylene oxide (Ag, 300°C); propene similarly gives propylene oxide.

Ozonolysis

Ozonolysis is the reaction of ozone (O3) with alkenes to break the C=C bond. In an inert solvent such as ether, ozone forms an unstable molozonide, which rearranges to an ozonide. Ozonides are explosive and are not isolated; decomposition with zinc and water gives aldehydes and/or ketones: ethylene ozonide + Zn → 2HCHO + ZnO (H2O, 100°C). If a double-bonded carbon is fully substituted, a ketone forms instead. Ozonolysis locates the position of a double bond, since molecules cleave at the double bond.

Polymerization

Small molecules (monomers) combine into large molecules (polymers) in polymerisation. Ethene polymerises with a catalyst at high temperature and pressure to polythene (polyethylene): nCH2=CH2 → —[CH2—CH2]n— (400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2/peroxide).

Key Points

  • Epoxidation adds one O atom across C=C (Ag catalyst).
  • Ozonolysis cleaves C=C to aldehydes/ketones.
  • Ozonolysis finds the double-bond position.
  • Polymerisation: ethene → polythene.

mcqs.q: Epoxidation of an alkene is:
options: Addition of oxygen to an alkene, giving epoxides with O2 over a silver catalyst at high pressure and temperature
Cleavage of the double bond by ozone
Addition of water across the double bond
Joining of many alkene molecules into a polymer
mcqs.why: Addition of oxygen to an alkene is epoxidation: with O2 over a silver catalyst at high pressure and temperature it gives epoxides.

mcqs.q: Ethene is converted to ethylene oxide under which conditions?
options: O3 in ether, then Zn and water
mcqs.why: The book equation for epoxidation: 2CH2=CH2 + O2 → 2 ethylene oxide (Ag, 300°C); propene similarly gives propylene oxide.

mcqs.q: Propene undergoes epoxidation to give:
mcqs.why: The notes state that propene similarly gives propylene oxide on epoxidation with O2 over a silver catalyst.

mcqs.q: Ozonolysis is the reaction of ozone (O3) with alkenes to:
options: Add one oxygen atom across the double bond
Saturate the double bond with hydrogen
Form a halohydrin in aqueous solution
Break the C=C bond, via an unstable molozonide that rearranges to an ozonide
mcqs.why: In an inert solvent such as ether, ozone forms an unstable molozonide, which rearranges to an ozonide, breaking the C=C bond.

mcqs.q: Why are ozonides not isolated during ozonolysis?
options: Ozonides are explosive; they are decomposed with zinc and water to aldehydes and/or ketones
Ozonides dissolve completely in the solvent and vanish
Ozonides are gases that escape from the apparatus
mcqs.why: Ozonides are explosive and are not isolated; decomposition with zinc and water gives aldehydes and/or ketones.

mcqs.q: Decomposition of ethylene ozonide with zinc gives:
mcqs.why: The book equation: ethylene ozonide + Zn → 2HCHO + ZnO (H2O, 100°C) — formaldehyde forms from each CH2 end.

mcqs.q: In ozonolysis, if a double-bonded carbon is fully substituted, what forms instead of an aldehyde?
mcqs.why: The notes state: if a double-bonded carbon is fully substituted, a ketone forms instead of an aldehyde on ozonolysis.

mcqs.q: Ozonolysis is useful because it:
options: Measures the heat of hydrogenation of an alkene
Tests whether bromine water is decolourised
Locates the position of a double bond, since molecules cleave at the double bond
mcqs.why: Because cleavage occurs exactly at the C=C, ozonolysis locates the position of a double bond in the original alkene.

mcqs.q: Polymerisation of ethene gives polythene under which conditions?
options: A catalyst at high temperature and pressure: nCH2=CH2 → —[CH2—CH2]n— (400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2/peroxide)
mcqs.why: Ethene polymerises with a catalyst at high temperature and pressure to polythene (polyethylene): 400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2/peroxide.

mcqs.q: In polymerisation, the small molecules that combine are called ___ and the large molecules formed are ___.
mcqs.why: Small molecules (monomers) combine into large molecules (polymers) in polymerisation, e.g. ethene monomers give polythene.

lessons.title: Conjugation in Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Conjugation (Latin: to link together) describes pi systems, such as double bonds, linked together.

Conjugated Dienes

Dienes in which the double bonds are separated by a single bond are conjugated dienes, e.g. pent-1,3-diene CH2=CH—CH=CH—CH3. The simplest conjugated diene is but-1,3-diene CH2=CH—CH=CH2.

Conjugation

Conjugation occurs whenever p-orbitals overlap on three or more adjacent atoms. In 1,3-butadiene all four carbons are sp2 hybridised, each with a pure p-orbital; the four p-orbitals on adjacent atoms form the conjugated system. With three or more pure p-orbitals on adjacent atoms, electrons delocalise throughout the molecule: pi electron density is spread over all four atoms, lowering the molecule's energy and enhancing its stability. Penta-1,4-diene is not conjugated because its double bonds are not separated by just one single bond, so its p-orbitals cannot overlap continuously.

Key Points

  • Conjugated diene: C=C—C=C pattern.
  • Needs overlapping p-orbitals on adjacent atoms.
  • Delocalisation lowers energy and increases stability.
  • Simplest example: but-1,3-diene.

mcqs.q: The word conjugation comes from Latin meaning:
options: To link together — it describes pi systems, such as double bonds, linked together
mcqs.why: Conjugation (Latin: to link together) describes pi systems, such as double bonds, linked together.

mcqs.q: A conjugated diene is one in which:
options: The double bonds are separated by two single bonds
The double bonds are separated by a single bond
The two double bonds share the same carbon atom
There is only one double bond in the molecule
mcqs.why: Dienes in which the double bonds are separated by a single bond are conjugated dienes, e.g. pent-1,3-diene.

mcqs.q: Which is the simplest conjugated diene?
mcqs.why: The simplest conjugated diene is but-1,3-diene CH2=CH—CH=CH2, with the C=C—C=C pattern.

mcqs.q: Pent-1,3-diene, CH2=CH—CH=CH—CH3, is given in the notes as an example of:
mcqs.why: Pent-1,3-diene has double bonds separated by one single bond, so the notes use it as a conjugated diene example.

mcqs.q: Conjugation occurs whenever:
options: p-Orbitals overlap on three or more adjacent atoms
Sigma bonds overlap head-on between any two carbons
A molecule contains a benzene ring
Double bonds are separated by two or more single bonds
mcqs.why: Conjugation occurs whenever p-orbitals overlap on three or more adjacent atoms, allowing electrons to delocalise.

mcqs.q: In 1,3-butadiene, the hybridisation of the four carbons is:
options: All four carbons are sp3 hybridised
All four carbons are sp2 hybridised, each with a pure p-orbital
Two carbons are sp2 and two are sp hybridised
Only the end carbons are sp2 hybridised
mcqs.why: In 1,3-butadiene all four carbons are sp2 hybridised, each with a pure p-orbital; the four p-orbitals on adjacent atoms form the conjugated system.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of electron delocalisation in a conjugated system?
options: Pi electrons become fixed on one carbon, raising the energy
The molecule becomes less stable than a non-conjugated diene
Pi electron density spreads over all the atoms, lowering the molecule's energy and enhancing its stability
The double bonds are converted into single bonds
mcqs.why: With p-orbitals on adjacent atoms, electrons delocalise throughout the molecule: pi density spreads out, lowering energy and enhancing stability.

mcqs.q: Why is penta-1,4-diene NOT conjugated?
options: It contains no double bonds at all
Its carbons are all sp3 hybridised
It has only four carbon atoms
Its double bonds are not separated by just one single bond, so its p-orbitals cannot overlap continuously
mcqs.why: Penta-1,4-diene is not conjugated because its double bonds are not separated by just one single bond, so p-orbitals cannot overlap continuously.

mcqs.q: The characteristic bond pattern of a conjugated diene is:
mcqs.why: The key points give the conjugated diene pattern as C=C—C=C: two double bonds separated by exactly one single bond.

mcqs.q: For conjugation, the p-orbitals must be:
options: On atoms far apart in the molecule
On adjacent atoms, overlapping continuously (three or more of them)
Present on only one atom of the molecule
Replaced by sp3 orbitals on every carbon
mcqs.why: Conjugation needs overlapping p-orbitals on adjacent atoms — three or more pure p-orbitals — so electrons can delocalise.

lessons.title: Energy and Petrochemicals
lessons.notes_html:
Energy is the foundation of civilisation: it powers homes, fuels industries, drives transport and supports economic growth. Fossil fuels — crude oil, natural gas and coal — are major energy sources and the backbone of the petrochemical industry.

Petrochemicals are vital for modern life: they produce plastics, fibres, fertilisers, medicines, fuels and construction materials. Without them, modern technology, healthcare and infrastructure would not exist. Energy sustains the world, while petrochemicals shape the materials and products of modern life. Nearly 8% of the world's crude oil is not used as fuel but is diverted to produce plastics, fibres, medicines and detergents.

Fossil fuels such as crude oil, natural gas and coal are therefore studied twice in this unit: once as fuels that release energy on burning, and once as raw materials. The petrochemical route is covered in the sections that follow — what petrochemicals are, how they differ from the chemicals derived from them, the raw materials used, fractional distillation of petroleum, the major petrochemicals and their importance, and finally the formation, properties and uses of fossil fuels themselves.

Key Points

  • Fossil fuels supply both energy and petrochemical feedstocks.
  • Petrochemicals underpin plastics, medicines, fertilisers and fibres.
  • About 8% of crude oil goes to non-fuel products.
  • Energy and petrochemicals together sustain modern life.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, energy is the foundation of civilisation because it:
options: Powers homes, fuels industries, drives transport and supports economic growth
Is used only for producing plastics
Replaces the need for raw materials in industry
mcqs.why: The notes open: energy powers homes, fuels industries, drives transport and supports economic growth — it is the foundation of civilisation.

mcqs.q: The major fossil-fuel energy sources named in the notes are:
options: Crude oil, natural gas and coal
mcqs.why: Fossil fuels — crude oil, natural gas and coal — are major energy sources and the backbone of the petrochemical industry.

mcqs.q: Petrochemicals are vital because they produce:
options: Plastics, fibres, fertilisers, medicines, fuels and construction materials
Electricity directly, with no chemical products
mcqs.why: The notes list plastics, fibres, fertilisers, medicines, fuels and construction materials as products of petrochemicals.

mcqs.q: What share of the world's crude oil is diverted to non-fuel products such as plastics, fibres, medicines and detergents?
mcqs.why: The notes state nearly 8% of the world's crude oil is not used as fuel but is diverted to produce plastics, fibres, medicines and detergents.

mcqs.q: Out of 1000 barrels of crude oil, about how many barrels go to non-fuel petrochemical products at the share given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Working: non-fuel share = 8% of 1000 barrels = (8/100) × 1000 = 80 barrels. The notes give the share as nearly 8%.

mcqs.q: Without petrochemicals, the notes say which things would not exist?
mcqs.why: The notes state that without petrochemicals, modern technology, healthcare and infrastructure would not exist.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels are studied twice in this unit — in which two roles?
options: Once as solids and once as liquids
Once as natural products and once as synthetic products
Once as fuels that release energy on burning, and once as raw materials
Once in Pakistan and once worldwide
mcqs.why: Crude oil, natural gas and coal are studied once as fuels that release energy on burning, and once as raw materials for petrochemicals.

mcqs.q: Which sentence best matches the summary in the notes?
options: Petrochemicals sustain the world, while energy shapes its materials
Energy and petrochemicals are the same thing
Petrochemicals are only a minor use of fossil fuels with no wider role
Energy sustains the world, while petrochemicals shape the materials and products of modern life
mcqs.why: The notes summarise: energy sustains the world, while petrochemicals shape the materials and products of modern life.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels form the backbone of which industry?
mcqs.why: The notes call crude oil, natural gas and coal major energy sources and the backbone of the petrochemical industry.

mcqs.q: The petrochemical sections that follow in the unit cover, among other topics:
options: Only the drilling of oil wells
What petrochemicals are, their raw materials, fractional distillation of petroleum, major petrochemicals and fossil fuels themselves
Only the prices of petrol and diesel
The chemistry of silicon and boron compounds
mcqs.why: The route listed: what petrochemicals are, derived chemicals, raw materials, fractional distillation, major petrochemicals, and fossil fuels themselves.

lessons.title: Difference between Petrochemical and Derived Chemicals
lessons.notes_html:
Petrochemicals are chemicals derived from petroleum or natural gas through cracking and refining, e.g. ethylene, propylene, benzene, toluene and xylene. They are not used directly by consumers but are essential across industries. Chemicals derived from petrochemicals are secondary products made by processing primary petrochemicals: plastics, synthetic rubber, solvents, detergents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals for pharmaceuticals and textiles.

Key Formulae

FeaturePetrochemicalsChemicals derived from them
SourcePrimary products directly from petroleum or natural gasSecondary products made using petrochemicals as raw materials
NatureBasic building blocks, often simple organic compoundsComplex and varied, for specific purposes
ApplicationsLimited direct consumer applicationsWide range: plastics, pharmaceuticals, textiles, etc.
ProcessingInitial processes like cracking and refiningFurther refined and combined for specific uses
ExamplesEthylene, propylene, benzene, toluene, xylenePlastics, synthetic rubber, solvents, detergents, pharmaceuticals

Key Points

  • Petrochemicals are primary building blocks.
  • Derived chemicals are the finished, consumer-facing products.
  • Ethylene and propylene are petrochemicals; plastics are derived.

mcqs.q: Petrochemicals are best defined as:
options: Chemicals derived from petroleum or natural gas through cracking and refining, e.g. ethylene, propylene, benzene, toluene and xylene
Finished consumer products such as plastics and detergents
mcqs.why: Petrochemicals are primary chemicals derived from petroleum or natural gas through cracking and refining: ethylene, propylene, benzene, toluene, xylene.

mcqs.q: How are petrochemicals used by consumers?
options: They are sold directly to consumers as finished goods
They are not used directly by consumers, but are essential across industries
mcqs.why: The notes state petrochemicals are not used directly by consumers but are essential across industries as building blocks.

mcqs.q: Chemicals derived from petrochemicals are:
options: Primary products taken directly from crude oil
The raw materials from which petrochemicals are made
Secondary products made by processing primary petrochemicals — plastics, synthetic rubber, solvents, detergents and pharmaceuticals
mcqs.why: Derived chemicals are secondary products made by processing primary petrochemicals: plastics, synthetic rubber, solvents, detergents, pharmaceuticals.

mcqs.q: In the comparison table, the SOURCE of petrochemicals is:
options: Secondary products made using other chemicals as raw materials
Primary products directly from petroleum or natural gas
mcqs.why: Table: petrochemicals are primary products directly from petroleum or natural gas; derived chemicals are secondary products made using petrochemicals.

mcqs.q: In the comparison table, the NATURE of petrochemicals is:
options: Basic building blocks, often simple organic compounds
Complex and varied, made for specific purposes
Finished products with a single fixed use
mcqs.why: Table: petrochemicals are basic building blocks, often simple organic compounds; derived chemicals are complex and varied, for specific purposes.

mcqs.q: In the comparison table, the APPLICATIONS of derived chemicals are:
options: Limited, with no direct consumer applications
mcqs.why: Table: petrochemicals have limited direct consumer applications, while derived chemicals have a wide range — plastics, pharmaceuticals, textiles, etc.

mcqs.q: In the comparison table, the PROCESSING of petrochemicals involves:
options: Further refining and combining for specific uses
No processing at all — they are used as dug out
Initial processes like cracking and refining
mcqs.why: Table: petrochemicals come from initial processes like cracking and refining; derived chemicals are further refined and combined for specific uses.

mcqs.q: Which pairing is correct according to the key points?
options: Plastics are petrochemicals; ethylene is a derived chemical
Both plastics and ethylene are raw materials from wells
Detergents are petrochemicals; benzene is a derived chemical
Ethylene and propylene are petrochemicals; plastics are derived chemicals
mcqs.why: Key points: petrochemicals are primary building blocks and derived chemicals are finished, consumer-facing products — ethylene/propylene are petrochemicals; plastics are derived.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only examples of petrochemicals from the table?
mcqs.why: The table's examples of petrochemicals are ethylene, propylene, benzene, toluene and xylene; the other lists are derived chemicals.

mcqs.q: Derived chemicals serve industries including:
options: Pharmaceuticals and textiles, as industrial chemicals
No industries — they are laboratory curiosities
mcqs.why: The notes describe derived chemicals as including industrial chemicals for pharmaceuticals and textiles, besides plastics, rubber, solvents and detergents.

lessons.title: Raw Materials for the Petrochemical Industry
lessons.notes_html:
Main Raw Materials

  • Crude oil: a complex mixture of alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons; the primary source, refined into naphtha, gasoline, diesel and fuel oil.
  • Natural gas: mainly methane, with ethane, propane and butane; feedstock especially for ethylene and propylene.
  • Coal: converted into syngas (hydrogen + carbon monoxide), then used to make methanol and ammonia.
  • Naphtha: a volatile hydrocarbon fraction from distillation of crude oil, used to produce ethylene and propylene.
  • Refinery off-gases: methane, ethane, propane and butane from refining, used as plant feedstocks.
  • Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG): propane + butane from natural gas processing or refining; fuel for cooking, heating and power, and feedstock for propylene and butadiene.
  • Aromatics: benzene, toluene and xylene (BTX) from catalytic reforming of naphtha or extraction; used for styrene, phenol and other aromatics.
  • Hydrogen: from natural gas by steam reforming; essential for hydrogenation and hydrocracking.

Key Points

  • Crude oil and natural gas are the main feedstocks.
  • Naphtha and refinery gases feed olefin production.
  • BTX aromatics come from reforming naphtha.
  • Coal works through syngas to methanol and ammonia.

mcqs.q: Crude oil, the primary raw material, is described as:
options: A complex mixture of alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons, refined into naphtha, gasoline, diesel and fuel oil
A pure compound containing only methane
A mixture of only aromatic hydrocarbons
A solid that is converted into syngas
mcqs.why: Crude oil is a complex mixture of alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons; it is the primary source for the petrochemical industry.

mcqs.q: Natural gas used as a feedstock consists mainly of:
options: Methane, with ethane, propane and butane; it is a feedstock especially for ethylene and propylene
mcqs.why: Natural gas is mainly methane, with ethane, propane and butane, and is a feedstock especially for ethylene and propylene.

mcqs.q: Coal is used in the petrochemical industry by first converting it into:
options: Naphtha, then reformed into BTX aromatics
Syngas (hydrogen + carbon monoxide), then used to make methanol and ammonia
mcqs.why: Coal is converted into syngas (hydrogen + carbon monoxide), which is then used to make methanol and ammonia.

mcqs.q: Naphtha is best described as:
options: A gas obtained from natural gas processing only
The heaviest residue left after distillation
A volatile hydrocarbon fraction from distillation of crude oil, used to produce ethylene and propylene
mcqs.why: Naphtha is a volatile hydrocarbon fraction from distillation of crude oil, used to produce ethylene and propylene.

mcqs.q: Refinery off-gases used as plant feedstocks consist of:
options: Methane, ethane, propane and butane from refining
mcqs.why: Refinery off-gases — methane, ethane, propane and butane from refining — are used as plant feedstocks.

mcqs.q: Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is:
options: Pure methane compressed into cylinders for cooking
Propane + butane from natural gas processing or refining; a fuel for cooking, heating and power, and a feedstock for propylene and butadiene
A liquid form of benzene used as a solvent

lessons.title: Fractional Distillation of Petroleum
lessons.notes_html:
Fractional distillation separates petroleum by boiling points. Crude oil is heated to about 400°C to vaporise it; vapours rise through a tall column with trays or packing and cool, so hydrocarbons condense at different heights. Each fraction has similar boiling points: lighter fractions condense higher up, middle fractions in the middle, heavier fractions lower down.

Key Formulae

Ligroin / light naphthaC6-C7, 60-100°CNonpolar solvent
PetrolC5-C10, 40-200°CMotor fuel
Kerosene oilC12-C18, 150-275°CJet fuel, lamps, domestic heating
Diesel oilC12-C20, 250-400°C (text)Diesel engines, buses, trucks, machinery
Lubricating oilC20-C30 and higherReduces friction in machines
Paraffin waxC23-C35 and higher, m.p. 50-60°CPolishes, candles, cosmetics

The figure also shows fuel oil between diesel and lubricating oil. Lubricating oil is obtained by vacuum distillation of the residue.

Key Points

  • Separation is by boiling point in a fractionating column.
  • Light fractions rise highest; heavy residue stays lowest.
  • Petrol, kerosene and diesel are the main fuel fractions.
  • Asphalt is the final non-volatile residue.

lessons.title: Role and Significance of Petrochemicals in the Modern World
lessons.notes_html:
Petrochemicals are chemical products derived primarily from petroleum and natural gas; they are the building blocks for countless everyday products.

Major Petrochemicals

  • Ethylene: polyethylene (plastics, packaging), ethylene glycol (antifreeze, polyester).
  • Propylene: polypropylene, acrylonitrile (synthetic fibres), propylene oxide (polyurethanes).
  • Benzene: styrene (polystyrene), phenol (resins), aniline (dyes, rubber processing).
  • Toluene: solvent; makes benzene, explosives and other chemicals.
  • Xylenes: terephthalic acid for PET plastics and fibres.
  • Butadiene: synthetic rubber for tyres; styrene for plastics and synthetic rubber. Methanol and ammonia are also listed as major petrochemicals.

Importance

  • Plastics and packaging: polyethylene and polypropylene for packaging and containers.
  • Agriculture: ammonia and urea fertilisers raise crop yields and food security.
  • Healthcare: pharmaceuticals, syringes, antiseptics, PVC IV bags.
  • Textiles: polyester, nylon and acrylic fibres.
  • Transport: fuels, lubricants, tyre rubber, lightweight plastic parts.
  • Construction: PVC pipes, insulation foams, paints, adhesives, sealants.

Key Points

  • Ethylene and propylene are the top building blocks.
  • Petrochemicals serve packaging, farming, health, textiles, transport and construction.
  • Butadiene is the key petrochemical for synthetic rubber.

lessons.title: Fossil Fuels: Formation, Properties, Uses, and Importance in the Modern World
lessons.notes_html:
Formation of Fossil Fuels

Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — formed from ancient plants and organisms buried and subjected to heat and pressure over millions of years; some coal is 300-400 million years old. Coal originates from plants in swampy environments; oil and natural gas come from marine organisms in ancient seas.

Properties

  • Coal: solid; properties vary with carbon content and compression; contains C, H, S, O and other elements.
  • Oil (petroleum): liquid mixture of hydrocarbons of various molecular weights, from underground reservoirs; light to heavy crude.
  • Natural gas: gaseous, mainly methane; found with oil, or from coal seams and shale. Cleaner than coal but still releases CO2 when burned.

Uses

  • Coal: electricity, industrial heating, steel, chemical feedstock.
  • Oil: transport fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel), heating, electricity, and raw material for petrochemicals, plastics, lubricants, pharmaceuticals.
  • Natural gas: heating, electricity, industrial processes, feedstock for chemicals and fertilisers.

Importance

Fossil fuels provide energy for electricity, transport, heating and industry worldwide; they drove industrialisation and economic growth, supply feedstocks for plastics, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and synthetic materials, create large employment, are major international trade commodities, and ensure national and global energy security.

Key Points

  • Formed over millions of years under heat and pressure.
  • Coal from land plants; oil and gas from marine organisms.
  • They are both fuels and petrochemical feedstocks.
  • Natural gas is cleaner than coal but still emits CO2.

lessons.notes_html:
Halogen derivatives of alkanes are called haloalkanes (halogenoalkanes or alkyl halides). They consist of a halogen atom covalently bonded to a saturated carbon atom within an alkyl group, with the general formula CnH2n+1X, where X is F, Cl, Br or I. They are classified as primary (1°), secondary (2°) or tertiary (3°) alkyl halides, depending on whether the halogen atom is directly bonded to a primary, secondary or tertiary carbon atom. Fluorocarbons, a type of haloalkane, are used as refrigerants and propellants, though many have been phased out because of their role in ozone depletion.

Structure of a Haloalkane

Take methyl chloride as the example. The carbon atom to which the halogen is bonded is sp3 hybridised. The halogen atom has one half-filled p orbital. The carbon-halogen σ-bond is formed by head-to-head overlap of one sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon and one half-filled p orbital of the halogen atom. Each carbon-hydrogen σ-bond is formed by head-to-head overlap of one sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon and one half-filled s orbital of hydrogen. The H-C-H and H-C-Cl bond angles are nearly 109.5°, so the arrangement of atoms or groups around the carbon atom is tetrahedral.

Key Points

  • Haloalkanes have the general formula CnH2n+1X (X = F, Cl, Br, I).
  • They are primary, secondary or tertiary according to the carbon holding the halogen.
  • The carbon bonded to the halogen is sp3 hybridised; the molecule is tetrahedral.
  • The C-X σ-bond forms by sp3-p overlap; C-H bonds form by sp3-s overlap.
  • Bond angles around the carbon are about 109.5°.
lessons.title: Structure of Haloalkanes

lessons.notes_html:
The molecular structure of a haloalkane strongly affects its reactivity. The main factors are steric hindrance, carbon-halogen bond polarity, carbon-halogen bond strength, leaving group ability and the nature of the nucleophile.

Steric Hindrance

Steric hindrance is caused by bulky alkyl groups surrounding the halogen in tertiary halogenoalkanes, making it difficult for nucleophiles to approach the carbon atom. Tertiary haloalkanes therefore react more slowly in nucleophilic substitution than primary and secondary haloalkanes.

Bond Polarity of Carbon-Halogen Bond

The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C-X bond is polarised: carbon carries a partial positive charge and is open to attack by a nucleophile. The greater the electronegativity difference between carbon and halogen, the greater the polarity of the C-X bond.

HalomethaneElectronegativity of HalogenEN Difference between C and XDipole Moment (Debye)
CH3F3.983.98 - 2.55 = 1.431.85
CH3Cl3.163.16 - 2.55 = 0.611.87
CH3Br2.962.96 - 2.55 = 0.411.81
CH3I2.662.66 - 2.55 = 0.111.62

Carbon-Halogen Bond Strength

Weaker C-X bonds are broken more easily and are more susceptible to nucleophilic attack. Bond energy measures bond strength: the greater the bond energy, the stronger the bond and the less reactive the C-X bond.

BondBond Energy (kJ/mol)
C-F485
C-Cl327
C-Br285
C-I213

The order of reactivity of alkyl halides is: RI greater than RBr greater than RCl greater than RF.

Key Points

  • Bulky groups in tertiary haloalkanes hinder nucleophilic attack and slow substitution.
  • The C-X bond is polar because halogens are more electronegative than carbon.
  • Bond strength falls C-F greater than C-Cl greater than C-Br greater than C-I.
  • Reactivity rises as the C-X bond weakens: RI greater than RBr greater than RCl greater than RF.
  • Reactivity is decided by steric hindrance, bond polarity, bond strength, leaving group ability and the nucleophile.
lessons.title: Influence of Molecular Structure on Reactivity

lessons.notes_html:
Haloalkanes can be synthesised by three main routes: free-radical substitution of alkanes, electrophilic addition to alkenes, and substitution of the -OH group of alcohols.

Free-Radical Substitution of Alkanes

A hydrogen atom in an alkane is substituted by a halogen atom (chlorine or bromine) under ultraviolet (UV) light. Ethane gives chloroethane or bromoethane:

CH3CH3 + Cl2 →(UV light) CH3CH2Cl + HCl
CH3CH3 + Br2 →(UV light) CH3CH2Br + HBr

Electrophilic Addition of Alkene with Halogen or Hydrogen Halide

A halogen (X2) or hydrogen halide (HX) adds across the double bond of an alkene at room temperature to form a halogenoalkane:

CH2=CH2 + Cl2 →(room temperature) CH2Cl-CH2Cl (1,2-dichloroethane)
CH2=CH2 + HCl →(room temperature) CH3-CH2Cl (chloroethane)

With Br2 the product is 1,2-dibromoethane, and with HBr it is bromoethane.

From Alcohols

The hydroxyl group (-OH) of an alcohol is substituted by a halogen atom. The reagent and conditions decide the product; the major product is typically an alkyl halide:

ReactionConditionsProducts
ROH + HXH2SO4 or H3PO4RX + H2O
ROH + KBrH2SO4 or H3PO4RBr + KOH
3ROH + PCl3-3RCl + H3PO3
ROH + PCl5HeatRCl + POCl3 + HCl
ROH + SOCl2PyridineRCl + SO2 + HCl

Key Points

  • Alkanes + Cl2 or Br2 in UV light give haloalkanes by free-radical substitution.
  • Alkenes + X2 or HX at room temperature give haloalkanes by electrophilic addition.
  • Alcohols give haloalkanes with HX, KBr/H2SO4 or H3PO4, PCl3, PCl5 with heat, or SOCl2.
  • In each alcohol reaction the -OH group is replaced by the halogen.
lessons.title: Haloalkane Synthesis

mcqs.q: In nucleophilic substitution of haloalkanes, the nucleophile:

lessons.notes_html:
In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile replaces the halogen atom of a haloalkane. These reactions are widely used in organic synthesis.

Reaction with Aqueous NaOH

Halogenoalkanes react with aqueous NaOH on heating to produce alcohols; the halogen atom is replaced by an -OH group:

R-X + NaOH →(H2O, heat) R-OH + NaX

Reaction with KCN

With potassium cyanide in aqueous ethanol, heated, the halogen is replaced by the -CN group, producing alkyl cyanides or nitriles. This lengthens the carbon chain by one carbon:

R-X + KCN →(aq. ethanol, heat) R-CN + KX

Reaction with NH3

With an alcoholic solution of ammonia, heated in a sealed tube, haloalkanes yield a mixture of amines: the first product is a primary alkylamine, which reacts further to give dialkylamine and then trialkylamine:

R'-X + NH3 →(ethanol, heat) R'-NH2 + HX
R''-X + R'-NH2 →(ethanol, heat) R'-NH-R'' + HX

Reaction with AgNO3

In ethanol, the halide ion displaced from a haloalkane reacts with silver nitrate to form a silver halide precipitate; this is the test used to identify the halogen present. Example: CH3CH2-Br + AgNO3 →(ethanol) CH3CH2-ONO2 + AgBr. Precipitate colours: AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI bright yellow; fluoroalkanes give no visible precipitate (AgF is colourless/soluble). The rate of reaction increases down the group: iodoalkanes react fastest, then bromoalkanes, then chloroalkanes.

Key Points

  • Aqueous NaOH (heat) converts haloalkanes to alcohols.
  • KCN in aqueous ethanol (heat) gives nitriles and adds one carbon to the chain.
  • NH3 in ethanol (heat, sealed tube) gives a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
  • AgNO3 in ethanol identifies the halogen: white (Cl), cream (Br), bright yellow (I) precipitates.
  • Rate with AgNO3: RI fastest, then RBr, then RCl; RF gives no precipitate.
lessons.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions of Haloalkanes

mcqs.q: Conditions that favour elimination over substitution for bromoethane are:
mcqs.why: NaOH in ethanol with heat gives elimination; the same reagent in water gives substitution to the alcohol instead.

mcqs.q: The two atoms removed in bromoethane elimination come from:
mcqs.why: A hydrogen and a bromine are removed from adjacent carbon atoms, alpha and beta, to form the double bond.

mcqs.q: Products of CH3CH2-Br + NaOH (ethanol, heat) besides ethene are:
mcqs.why: The equation gives CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O, so besides ethene the other products are sodium bromide and water.

lessons.notes_html:
When bromoethane is mixed with sodium hydroxide in ethanol and heated, a hydrogen atom and a bromine atom are removed from adjacent carbon atoms. This process, called elimination, forms a double bond between the two carbon atoms:

CH3CH2-Br + NaOH →(ethanol, heat) CH2=CH2 + NaBr + H2O

The carbon bonded to the leaving group (such as bromine) is called the alpha (α) carbon, and the carbon adjacent to it is the beta (β) carbon. In elimination, a hydrogen atom is removed from the beta carbon and the leaving group departs from the alpha carbon.

Note the contrast of conditions: aqueous NaOH with heat gives substitution (an alcohol), while NaOH in ethanol with heat gives elimination (an alkene). Elimination reactions of haloalkanes are important in industry because they produce alkenes, which serve as precursors for polymers like polyethylene.

Key Points

  • Elimination removes H from the β-carbon and X from the α-carbon, forming a C=C double bond.
  • Bromoethane + NaOH in ethanol, heated, gives ethene + NaBr + H2O.
  • Solvent decides the reaction: aqueous NaOH → substitution; ethanolic NaOH → elimination.
  • Elimination is an industrial route to alkenes for polymer manufacture.

lessons.notes_html:
Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. They are classified as primary, secondary and tertiary depending on the number of alkyl groups bonded to the nitrogen atom. The nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons, which controls the basicity and reactivity of amines.

ClassAlkyl Groups on NGeneral FormExample Form
Primary amineOneR-NH2CH3NH2 (methylamine)
Secondary amineTwoR-NH-R(CH3)2NH (dimethylamine)
Tertiary amineThreeR-N(R)-R(CH3)3N (trimethylamine)

Amines occur widely in nature: caffeine and nicotine are alkaloids, naturally occurring amines found in tea, coffee and tobacco, and neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin and adrenaline are also amines.

Key Points

  • Amines are ammonia derivatives: one, two or three H atoms replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
  • Primary = one alkyl group on N; secondary = two; tertiary = three.
  • The lone pair on nitrogen makes amines basic and nucleophilic.
  • Many natural products, such as caffeine, nicotine and adrenaline, are amines.

mcqs.q: Amines are basic because the lone pair on nitrogen can:

mcqs.why: Electron-releasing alkyl groups increase electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more readily available for acids.

mcqs.q: In aqueous solution, basicity order of aliphatic amines is:
mcqs.why: In aqueous solution (about 25°C) the order is 2° greater than 1° greater than 3° greater than NH3, due to combined effects.

mcqs.q: pKb values: (CH3)2NH 3.27, CH3NH2 3.34, (CH3)3N 4.20, NH3 4.74. The strongest base is:
mcqs.why: Smaller pKb means stronger base; (CH3)2NH has pKb 3.27, the smallest listed, so it is the strongest methylamine base.

mcqs.q: Larger pKb value means:
options: Smaller tendency to accept a proton from water, so weaker base
mcqs.why: The notes state the larger the pKb, the smaller the tendency to accept a proton from water, so the weaker the base.

mcqs.q: Hydration effect: as alkyl groups on nitrogen increase, H-bonding capacity of the substituted ammonium ion:
mcqs.why: In water the ion is stabilised by solvation (H-bonding); more alkyl groups decrease its H-bonding capacity, affecting basicity order.

mcqs.q: CH3NH2(aq) + H2O(l) gives:
mcqs.why: Methylamine accepts a proton from water to form methylammonium ions and hydroxide ions; only a small fraction is protonated.

mcqs.q: CH3NH2 + HCl gives:
mcqs.why: Amines neutralise acids to produce water-soluble ammonium salts, e.g. methylammonium chloride from methylamine and HCl.

mcqs.q: Treatment of RNH3+Cl- with NaOH does what?
options: Reproduces the free amine RNH2 + NaCl + H2O
mcqs.why: The salt reaction is reversible: NaOH regenerates the free amine, RNH3+Cl- + NaOH → RNH2 + NaCl + H2O.

mcqs.q: Steric effect on basicity: more alkyl groups increase steric hindrance, making it:
options: Harder for the amine to accept a proton
mcqs.why: More alkyl groups increase steric hindrance, making proton acceptance harder - one reason aqueous order is not simply 3° > 2° > 1°.

lessons.notes_html:
Amines are basic because of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton. Alkanamines are generally more basic than ammonia because the electron-releasing alkyl groups increase the electron density on nitrogen, making the lone pair more readily available for sharing with acids. In aqueous solution (about 25°C), the basicity order of aliphatic amines is 2° greater than 1° greater than 3° greater than NH3. For the methylamines: (CH3)2NH (pKb = 3.27) greater than CH3NH2 (pKb = 3.34) greater than (CH3)3N (pKb = 4.20) greater than NH3 (pKb = 4.74). The larger the pKb value, the smaller the tendency to accept a proton from water, so the weaker the base.

Basic strength in aqueous solution depends not only on the electron-releasing effect of alkyl groups but also on steric and hydration effects:

  • Hydration effect: in aqueous solution the substituted ammonium ion is stabilised by solvation (hydrogen bonding) with water molecules; as the number of alkyl groups on nitrogen increases, the capacity for hydrogen bonding of the ion decreases.
  • Steric effect: as the number of alkyl groups increases, steric hindrance increases, making it harder for the amine to accept a proton.

Reactions of Amines as Bases

With water: alkyl amines (RNH2) act as weak bases; they accept a proton from water to form alkylammonium ions and hydroxide ions. The reaction is reversible, so only a small fraction of molecules is protonated: CH3NH2(aq) + H2O(l) → CH3NH3+(aq) + OH-(aq). The methylamines are highly soluble in water and act as weak bases.

With acids: amines neutralise acids to produce water-soluble ammonium salts, e.g. RNH2(aq) + HCl(aq) → RNH3+Cl-(aq); CH3NH2 + HCl → CH3NH3+Cl- (methylammonium chloride). The reaction is reversible: treatment of the salt with a strong base such as NaOH reproduces the free amine: RNH3+Cl-(aq) + NaOH(aq) → RNH2(aq) + NaCl(aq) + H2O(l).

Key Points

  • Basicity comes from the lone pair on nitrogen accepting a proton.
  • Alkyl groups release electrons (+I effect), so alkanamines are stronger bases than ammonia.
  • In water the order is 2° greater than 1° greater than 3° greater than NH3, due to hydration and steric effects.
  • Smaller pKb means a stronger base: (CH3)2NH is the strongest of the methylamines.
  • Amines form soluble ammonium salts with acids; NaOH regenerates the free amine from the salt.
lessons.title: Basicity of Amines

mcqs.why: Main reactions arise from the nitrogen lone pair attacking electron-deficient (positive or slightly positive) centres of other molecules.

mcqs.why: The notes state reactivity order primary greater than secondary greater than tertiary amine for reactivity and nucleophilicity.

mcqs.why: The extra hydrogen on nitrogen in primary amines enables them to undergo reactions like oxidation and substitution.

mcqs.q: Secondary amines compared with primary amines are:
options: Less reactive than primary but still capable of nucleophilic substitution
mcqs.why: Secondary amines are less reactive than primary amines but still capable of nucleophilic substitution reactions.

mcqs.q: Tertiary amines are less nucleophilic because:
options: Their lone pair is less available to participate in reactions
They have no lone pair at all
mcqs.why: Tertiary amines are less nucleophilic because the lone pair on nitrogen is less available to participate in reactions.

mcqs.q: Amines can act as both:
mcqs.why: The lesson opens: amines can act as both bases and nucleophiles, both roles driven by the nitrogen lone pair.

mcqs.q: Amines are useful intermediates, for example in production of:
options: Antihistamine medications that help alleviate allergies
mcqs.why: Amines are useful intermediates, e.g. in production of antihistamine medications that help alleviate allergies, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Electron-deficient centres attacked by amines are described as:
options: Positive or slightly positive parts of other molecules
mcqs.why: Lone pair electrons attack electron-deficient centres (positive or slightly positive parts) of other molecules in amine reactions.

mcqs.q: Which amine type is described as least nucleophilic in the comparison?
mcqs.why: Tertiary amines are the least nucleophilic in the order 1° > 2° > 3° because their lone pair is least available.

mcqs.q: Secondary amines still act as nucleophiles in which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: The comparison states secondary amines are still capable of nucleophilic substitution reactions despite being less reactive than primary.

lessons.notes_html:
Amines can act as both bases and nucleophiles. The main reactions of amines arise from the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom: these electrons attack the electron-deficient centres (positive or slightly positive parts) of other molecules.

Comparing Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Amines

  • Primary amines are the most reactive. The extra hydrogen atom on the nitrogen enables them to undergo reactions like oxidation and substitution.
  • Secondary amines are less reactive than primary amines but are still capable of nucleophilic substitution reactions.
  • Tertiary amines are less nucleophilic than primary and secondary amines because the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is less available to participate in reactions.

So the reactivity and nucleophilicity order is: primary amine greater than secondary amine greater than tertiary amine. Amines are also useful intermediates, for example in the production of antihistamine medications that help alleviate allergies.

Key Points

  • Amine reactions are driven by the nitrogen lone pair attacking electron-deficient centres.
  • Primary amines are the most reactive; they can undergo oxidation and substitution.
  • Secondary amines still act as nucleophiles in substitution reactions.
  • Tertiary amines are the least nucleophilic because their lone pair is least available.
  • Reactivity order: 1° greater than 2° greater than 3°.
lessons.title: Reactivity of Amines
