mcqs.why: Alkyl halides with ammonia in a sealed tube, heated, undergo ammonolysis to produce primary, secondary and tertiary amines.

mcqs.q: With CH3I, the sequence NH3 → CH3NH2 → (CH3)2NH → (CH3)3N ends with CH3I giving:
mcqs.why: Final step (CH3)3N + CH3I → [(CH3)4N]+I- tetramethylammonium iodide, completing the stepwise alkylation sequence.

mcqs.q: Primary amine is the major product in ammonolysis when:
mcqs.why: Excess NH3 favours the primary amine; conversely excess alkyl halide favours tertiary amine and quaternary salt formation.

mcqs.q: Tertiary amine is the major product when:
mcqs.why: When alkyl halide is in excess, further alkylation dominates and the tertiary amine (and quaternary salt) is the major product.

mcqs.q: Reduction of nitro compounds gives which amine type only?
mcqs.why: Reduction of nitro compounds (LiAlH4, Zn/HCl, H2/Ni or H2/Pt) gives primary amines only, unlike ammonolysis mixtures.

mcqs.q: CH3NO2 + 3H2 with Pt catalyst gives:
mcqs.why: The notes give CH3NO2 + 3H2 (Pt) → CH3NH2 + 2H2O, reduction of a nitro compound to a primary amine.

mcqs.q: Reagents listed for reducing nitro compounds include:
mcqs.why: Nitro reduction uses LiAlH4, or Zn/HCl, or H2/Ni, or H2/Pt - all listed as alternatives in the notes.

mcqs.q: The ammonium salt from ammonolysis gives back the free amine on treatment with:
mcqs.why: The resulting ammonium salt, on treatment with a base, regenerates the amine - parallel to salt behaviour in the basicity lesson.

mcqs.q: First step with methyl iodide is NH3 + CH3I →:
mcqs.why: First alkylation step is NH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI, then the primary amine reacts further with more CH3I stepwise.

mcqs.q: Conditions for alkylation of ammonia by alkyl halides are:
options: Aqueous or alcoholic ammonia in a sealed tube, when heated
Room temperature in open air only
mcqs.why: Alkyl halides react with aqueous or alcoholic solutions of ammonia in a sealed tube, when heated, to produce amines.

lessons.notes_html:
Alkylation of Ammonia by Alkyl Halides

Alkyl halides react with aqueous or alcoholic solutions of ammonia in a sealed tube, when heated, to produce primary, secondary and tertiary amines. The cleavage of the carbon-halogen bond by the ammonia molecule is known as ammonolysis. With methyl iodide the sequence is:

NH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI
CH3NH2 + CH3I → (CH3)2NH + HI
(CH3)2NH + CH3I → (CH3)3N + HI
(CH3)3N + CH3I → [(CH3)4N]+I- (tetramethylammonium iodide)

The primary amine is the major product when ammonia is present in excess; conversely, the tertiary amine is the major product when the alkyl halide is in excess. The resulting ammonium salt, on treatment with a base, regenerates the amine.

Reduction of Nitro Compounds

Nitro compounds are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4, or Zn/HCl, or H2/Ni, or H2/Pt:

CH3NO2 + 6[H] →(LiAlH4) CH3NH2 + 2H2O
CH3NO2 + 3H2 →(Pt) CH3NH2 + 2H2O

Key Points

  • Ammonolysis: alkyl halides + ammonia (sealed tube, heat) give amines step by step.
  • Excess NH3 favours the primary amine; excess alkyl halide favours the tertiary amine and quaternary salt.
  • Ammonium salts give back the free amine on treatment with a base.
  • Reduction of nitro compounds (LiAlH4, Zn/HCl, H2/Ni or H2/Pt) gives primary amines only.
lessons.title: Preparation of Amines

options: C6H5NH2, -NH2 directly attached to a benzene ring, a primary aromatic amine
mcqs.why: Phenylamine C6H5NH2 is a primary aromatic amine with -NH2 directly attached to a benzene ring; its common name is aniline.

mcqs.q: The old and still commonly used name for phenylamine is:
mcqs.why: Its old and still commonly used name is aniline, also present in names of many of its derivatives.

mcqs.q: In phenylamine, the nitrogen lone pair is:

mcqs.why: The lone pair is partially delocalised into the benzene ring, increasing electron density mainly at 2, 4 and 6 positions.

mcqs.why: Delocalisation reduces lone pair availability for protons; resonance stabilisation makes aniline less basic than ammonia and alkylamines.

mcqs.why: The notes state electron density increases mainly at the 2, 4 and 6 positions due to lone pair delocalisation into the ring.

mcqs.q: Compared with benzene, phenylamine toward electrophilic substitution is:
mcqs.why: Phenylamine is more reactive than benzene toward electrophilic substitution because the -NH2 lone pair activates the ring.

mcqs.q: Aniline basicity compared with ammonia, as stated in the notes, is:
options: Less basic than ammonia and alkylamines as well
mcqs.why: Resonance stabilisation makes aniline less basic than ammonia and alkylamines, a distinctive consequence of delocalisation.

mcqs.q: Distinctive reactivity of phenylamine is due to:
options: Its aromatic amine structure with delocalised lone pair
mcqs.why: Phenylamine shows distinctive reactivity due to its aromatic amine structure; the lone pair delocalisation drives both ring activation and weak basicity.

mcqs.q: The amino group in phenylamine is:

mcqs.why: An amino group (-NH2) is directly attached to a benzene ring in phenylamine, defining it as a primary aromatic amine.

lessons.notes_html:
Phenylamine, C6H5NH2, is a primary aromatic amine in which an amino group (-NH2) is directly attached to a benzene ring. Its old and still commonly used name is aniline, which is also present in the names of many of its derivatives.

Reactivity of Phenylamine (Aniline)

Phenylamine shows distinctive reactivity due to its aromatic amine structure. The lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is partially delocalised into the benzene ring, increasing the electron density mainly at the 2, 4 and 6 positions. This activates the ring toward electrophilic substitution, making phenylamine more reactive than benzene.

However, the delocalisation of the lone pair reduces the availability of nitrogen to accept protons. Consequently, phenylamine is a weaker base than aliphatic amines; resonance stabilisation makes aniline less basic than ammonia and alkylamines as well.

Key Points

  • Phenylamine (aniline) is C6H5NH2, a primary aromatic amine.
  • Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.
  • Electron density rises at the 2, 4 and 6 positions, so the ring is activated for electrophilic substitution.
  • Because the lone pair is delocalised, aniline is a much weaker base than aliphatic amines.
lessons.title: Phenylamine (Aniline)

mcqs.why: In conc. nitric/sulphuric acids the amino group gets protonated; it is therefore first protected by acylation, then nitration is controlled.

mcqs.q: Density of phenylamine at room temperature is approximately:
mcqs.why: Its density is approximately 1.02 g/cm3 at room temperature, listed alongside mp -6°C and bp 184°C.

mcqs.q: The -NH2 group in electrophilic aromatic substitution directs mainly to:
options: Ortho and para positions, activating the ring as an electron-donating group
mcqs.why: The -NH2 group is electron-donating and activates the ring; substitution occurs mainly at ortho and para positions.

mcqs.q: Main uses of phenylamine listed include:
options: Azo dyes, drugs such as paracetamol, and agrochemicals
mcqs.why: Aniline is a precursor for azo dyes, drugs such as paracetamol and sulpha drugs, and agrochemicals like herbicides and fungicides.

lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties

  • Phenylamine is a colourless to pale yellow liquid with a strong, unpleasant odour.
  • It is slightly soluble in water but much more soluble in organic solvents like ethanol, ether and benzene.
  • Its melting point is approximately -6°C and its boiling point is around 184°C.
  • Its density is approximately 1.02 g/cm3 at room temperature.

Chemical Properties

Salt formation: aniline reacts with acids, such as hydrochloric acid, to form anilinium salts, showing its basic character: C6H5NH2 + HCl → C6H5NH3+Cl- (anilinium chloride).

Electrophilic aromatic substitution: the -NH2 group is electron-donating and activates the ring; substitution occurs mainly at the ortho and para positions. With bromine water at room temperature, aniline immediately forms 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine: C6H5NH2 + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3NH2 + 3HBr. Direct nitration with concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids is unfavourable because the amino group gets protonated; the amino group is therefore first protected by acylation, and then controlled nitration is performed.

Acylation (protection): the amino group attacks acid chlorides or anhydrides to form stable amides instead of the ring undergoing substitution: phenylamine + ethanoyl chloride → N-phenylethanamide + HCl; phenylamine + ethanoic anhydride → N-phenylethanamide + ethanoic acid. This acylation protects the amino group, preventing unwanted reactions on the ring.

Applications of Phenylamine (Aniline)

  • Essential precursor for synthesising azo dyes, used to colour textiles, leather and paper (the famous purple dye mauveine was accidentally discovered from aniline in the 1850s).
  • Used in manufacturing drugs such as paracetamol (acetaminophen), sulpha drugs and other medicinal compounds.
  • Used to synthesise agrochemicals, including herbicides, fungicides and plant growth regulators.

Key Points

  • Aniline: pale yellow oily liquid, mp -6°C, bp 184°C, slightly soluble in water.
  • It forms anilinium salts with acids, e.g. anilinium chloride with HCl.
  • Bromine water instantly gives 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine (ortho/para substitution).
  • For nitration, the -NH2 group is first protected by acylation to N-phenylethanamide.
  • Main uses: azo dyes, drugs such as paracetamol, and agrochemicals.
lessons.title: Properties of Phenylamine

mcqs.q: Azo compounds contain the azo group:
options: -N=N- connecting two aryl or alkyl groups
mcqs.why: Azo compounds contain the azo group (-N=N-) which connects two aryl or alkyl groups, general formula R-N=N-R'.

mcqs.q: General structural formula of azo compounds is:
options: R-N=N-R' where R and R' can be aryl or alkyl
mcqs.why: General formula is R-N=N-R', where R and R' can be aryl (aromatic) or alkyl groups, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Vivid colours of azo compounds are due to:
options: The azo group plus extended conjugation letting the molecule absorb more visible light
mcqs.why: The azo group is responsible for vivid colours; aromatic groups intensify colour via extended conjugation absorbing more visible light.

mcqs.q: Methyl Orange and Methyl Red are azo compounds used as:
options: Acid-base indicators for titration experiments in laboratories
mcqs.why: Methyl Orange and Methyl Red are azo compounds used in laboratories as acid-base indicators for titration experiments.

mcqs.q: Reduction of azobenzene with Sn/HCl and 4[H] gives:
options: 2 phenylamine, by breaking the -N=N- bond into two -NH2 groups
No reaction, azo is stable to reduction
mcqs.why: Azobenzene + 4[H] (Sn/HCl) → 2 phenylamine; the -N=N- bond breaks resulting in two -NH2 groups on the products.

mcqs.q: Electrophilic substitution on azo aromatic rings is generally limited because the azo group is:
mcqs.why: Substitution is generally limited because the azo group is mildly electron-withdrawing, unless -OH or -NH2 groups are present on the ring.

mcqs.q: Nitration of 4-hydroxyazobenzene gives, as the example in the notes:
mcqs.why: With -OH present, substitution occurs ortho/para to that group; nitration gives 2-nitro-4-hydroxyazobenzene as the example.

mcqs.q: Azo compounds are largely stable under:
mcqs.why: The notes state azo compounds are largely stable under neutral and basic conditions, despite being reducible by Sn/HCl.

mcqs.q: Tartrazine and Sunset Yellow are azo examples used as:
options: Food colorants (Tartrazine E102 may cause allergies in some individuals)
mcqs.why: Azo compounds are used in food colorants e.g. Tartrazine and Sunset Yellow; Tartrazine E102 may cause allergies in some individuals.

mcqs.q: Azo pigments, being water-insoluble, are used in:
options: Paints, plastics, rubber and printing inks for light and thermal stability
mcqs.why: Water-insoluble azo pigments go into paints, plastics, rubber and inks because of excellent light and thermal stability.

lessons.notes_html:
Azo compounds are a class of organic compounds containing the azo group (-N=N-), which connects two aryl or alkyl groups. The general structural formula is R-N=N-R', where R and R' can be aryl (aromatic) or alkyl groups. The azo group is responsible for the vivid colours (red, orange, yellow, blue) of azo compounds. When the groups attached to the azo group are aromatic rings, the colour intensifies because of the extended conjugation of double bonds, which lets the molecule absorb more visible light; hence azo compounds are used as dyes. Examples: azobenzene (yellow to orange-red) and the yellow azo dye; Methyl Orange and Methyl Red are azo compounds used in laboratories as acid-base indicators for titration experiments.

Reactivity of Azo Compounds

  • Electrophilic substitution on the aromatic rings is generally limited because the azo group is mildly electron-withdrawing. If electron-donating groups such as -OH or -NH2 are present on the ring, substitution can occur at the ortho and para positions relative to those groups, e.g. nitration of 4-hydroxyazobenzene gives 2-nitro-4-hydroxyazobenzene.
  • Reduction: azo compounds can be converted into aromatic amines. Using tin and hydrochloric acid, the -N=N- bond breaks, resulting in two -NH2 groups: azobenzene + 4[H] →(Sn/HCl) 2 phenylamine.
  • Azo compounds are largely stable under neutral and basic conditions.

Uses of Azo Compounds as Dyes and Pigments

  • Azo dyes are widely used in the textile, leather and paper industries for their vibrant and diverse colours.
  • They are also used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and food colorants, e.g. Tartrazine and Sunset Yellow (note: Tartrazine, E102, may cause allergies in some individuals).
  • Azo pigments are water-insoluble and are used in paints, plastics, rubber and printing inks because of their excellent light and thermal stability.

Key Points

  • Azo compounds contain the -N=N- group joining two aryl or alkyl groups: R-N=N-R'.
  • The azo group plus extended conjugation gives strong colours, so they are used as dyes.
  • Methyl Orange and Methyl Red are azo indicators used in titrations.
  • Reduction with Sn/HCl cleaves -N=N- to give aromatic amines.
  • Azo dyes colour textiles, leather, paper and foods; azo pigments go into paints, plastics, rubber and inks.
lessons.title: Azo Compounds

mcqs.q: An alcohol is a compound in which a hydroxyl group —OH is bonded to what?
mcqs.why: The notes define alcohols as compounds with a hydroxyl group bonded to a saturated carbon atom.

mcqs.q: A monohydric alcohol contains how many hydroxyl groups?
mcqs.why: Monohydric alcohols contain a single hydroxyl group, for example ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, is classified as which type of alcohol?
mcqs.why: In ethanol the —OH is on a primary carbon bonded to only one other carbon and at least two H atoms.

mcqs.q: Propan-2-ol is the standard example of which class?
mcqs.why: Propan-2-ol has —OH on a secondary carbon bonded to two other carbons and one H atom, so it is secondary.

mcqs.q: Methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol because its —OH carbon is bonded to what?
options: One other carbon and two H atoms
Three other carbons and no H atoms
Two other carbons and one H atom
mcqs.why: A tertiary carbon carries —OH, is bonded to three other carbons and has no H atoms, as in methylpropan-2-ol.

mcqs.q: Glycol (ethane-1,2-diol) is an example of what?
mcqs.why: Polyhydric alcohols with two —OH groups are diols; glycol is ethane-1,2-diol, given as the example.

mcqs.q: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) contains how many —OH groups?
options: Three —OH groups, making it a triol
mcqs.why: Three —OH groups make a triol; glycerol is propane-1,2,3-triol and is used because it retains water.

mcqs.q: Which alcohols dehydrate most easily at low temperatures?
mcqs.why: Reactivity depends on class: tertiary alcohols dehydrate easily at low temperatures, while primary need severe conditions.

mcqs.q: Ethanol is used in which roles according to the notes?
options: As a solvent, fuel additive and in medicines
mcqs.why: Ethanol is used as a solvent, a fuel additive and in medicines, as stated in the introduction to alcohols.

mcqs.q: Glycerol is used in toothpaste, moisturisers and cough syrups because it does what?
mcqs.why: Glycerol retains water, which is why it is used in toothpaste, moisturisers and cough syrups in the notes.

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are compounds in which a hydroxyl group (—OH) is bonded to a saturated carbon atom. Ethanol is used as a solvent, a fuel additive and in medicines; methanol and glycerol are used in pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and polymer production. By number of hydroxyl groups, alcohols are monohydric or polyhydric.

Monohydric Alcohols

Monohydric alcohols contain a single hydroxyl group, e.g. ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol. They are classified by the carbon carrying the —OH group:

  • Primary (1°) alcohol: —OH on a primary carbon, bonded to only one other carbon and at least two H atoms, e.g. ethanol, CH3CH2OH.
  • Secondary (2°) alcohol: —OH on a secondary carbon, bonded to two other carbons and one H atom, e.g. propan-2-ol.
  • Tertiary (3°) alcohol: —OH on a tertiary carbon, bonded to three other carbons and no H atoms, e.g. methylpropan-2-ol.

Reactivity depends on this class: tertiary alcohols dehydrate easily at low temperatures, while primary alcohols need severe conditions.

Alcohols with Multiple Hydroxy Groups (Polyhydric Alcohols)

Polyhydric alcohols contain two or more hydroxyl groups. Two —OH groups = a diol, e.g. glycol (ethane-1,2-diol); three —OH groups = a triol, e.g. glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol); more than three = a polyol. Glycerol is used in toothpaste, moisturisers and cough syrups because it retains water.

Key Points

  • Alcohol = —OH group bonded to a saturated carbon atom.
  • Monohydric alcohols have one —OH; polyhydric alcohols have two or more.
  • Primary, secondary and tertiary depend on the carbon attached to —OH.
  • Ethanol (1°), propan-2-ol (2°) and methylpropan-2-ol (3°) are the standard examples.
  • Diols have two —OH groups; triols have three; polyols have more.
lessons.title: Alcohols

mcqs.q: Steam adds to an alkene to give an alcohol using which catalyst?
mcqs.why: Electrophilic addition of steam to an alkene uses an H3PO4 catalyst: R—CH=CH2 + HOH gives the alcohol.

mcqs.q: Cold dilute acidified KMnO4 converts ethene into what product?
mcqs.why: Cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII) converts an alkene to a diol, here ethane-1,2-diol from ethene.

mcqs.q: A halogenoalkane is converted to an alcohol by which reagents and conditions?
options: Aqueous NaOH or KOH, with heat
mcqs.why: Substitution of a halogenoalkane uses aqueous NaOH or KOH and heat, e.g. CH3CH2Br + KOH gives ethanol + KBr.

mcqs.q: Reduction of an aldehyde with NaBH4 or LiAlH4 gives which type of alcohol?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes reduce to primary alcohols: CH3CHO gives CH3CH2OH, while ketones give secondary alcohols.

mcqs.q: Reduction of a ketone such as CH3COCH3 gives what?
mcqs.why: Ketones reduce to secondary alcohols; CH3COCH3 gives propan-2-ol, as shown in the preparations table.

mcqs.q: Which reducing agent can reduce carboxylic acids and esters to alcohols?
mcqs.why: LiAlH4 is a strong reducing agent that reduces acids and esters, unlike NaBH4 which reduces only aldehydes and ketones.

mcqs.q: NaBH4 reduction requires what type of solvent?
options: A polar solvent such as water or ethanol
mcqs.why: NaBH4 needs a polar solvent such as water or ethanol, while LiAlH4 for acids and esters is used in ether.

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis of an ester with NaOH gives an alcohol plus what?
options: The sodium salt of the acid, e.g. CH3COONa
mcqs.why: With NaOH, ester hydrolysis gives the alcohol plus the sodium salt: CH3COOCH2CH3 gives ethanol + CH3COONa.

mcqs.q: In the reduction CH3COOH + 4[H] -> CH3CH2OH + H2O, how many [H] are used per acid molecule?
mcqs.why: Working: the equation in the notes is CH3COOH + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + H2O, so 4 reducing hydrogen atoms are required per molecule.

mcqs.q: Methyl ethanoate reduction, CH3COOCH3 + 4[H], gives which two alcohols?
mcqs.why: Working: CH3COOCH3 + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + CH3OH, so one ester molecule gives one ethanol and one methanol molecule.

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are prepared by addition to alkenes, substitution of halogenoalkanes, reduction of carbonyl compounds, acids and esters, and hydrolysis of esters.

Key Reactions

MethodReagents / ConditionsReaction
Electrophilic addition of steam to an alkeneH3PO4 catalyst, steamR—CH=CH2 + HOH → R—CH(OH)—CH3
Alkene to a diolCold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4/H2SO45CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 3H2SO4 + 2H2O → 5HOCH2—CH2OH (ethane-1,2-diol) + 2MnSO4 + K2SO4
Substitution of a halogenoalkaneAqueous NaOH or KOH, heatCH3CH2Br + KOH → CH3CH2OH + KBr
Reduction of an aldehyde or ketoneNaBH4 or LiAlH4; NaBH4 needs a polar solvent (water, ethanol)CH3CHO → CH3CH2OH (1° alcohol); CH3COCH3 → propan-2-ol (2° alcohol)
Reduction of carboxylic acids and estersLiAlH4 in ether (strong reducing agent)CH3COOH + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + H2O; CH3COOCH3 + 4[H] → CH3CH2OH + CH3OH

LiAlH4 is a strong reducing agent: it reduces carboxylic acids and esters to alcohols, unlike NaBH4, which reduces only aldehydes and ketones under mild conditions in polar protic solvents.

Key Points

  • Steam adds to alkenes with an H3PO4 catalyst to give alcohols.
  • Cold dilute acidified KMnO4 converts an alkene into a diol.
  • Aqueous NaOH/KOH and heat replace the halogen of a halogenoalkane by —OH.
  • NaBH4 or LiAlH4: aldehydes → primary alcohols; ketones → secondary alcohols.
  • Only LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acids and esters to alcohols.
  • Ester hydrolysis (dilute acid or alkali, heat) gives an alcohol plus an acid or its salt.
lessons.title: Preparations of Alcohols

mcqs.q: Complete combustion of an alcohol in excess oxygen produces what?
options: Carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat
mcqs.why: Complete combustion in excess oxygen gives CO2 + H2O + heat: ROH + O2 → CO2 + H2O + Heat, making alcohols fuels.

mcqs.q: What is the balanced equation for methanol combustion given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Working: 2 CH3OH needs 3 O2: C: 2→2 CO2, H: 8→4 H2O, O check 2+6=8 and 4+4=8, so the equation balances as given.

mcqs.q: How many moles of O2 are needed to burn 2 moles of methanol completely?
mcqs.why: Working: from 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O, the ratio is 2 methanol : 3 oxygen, so 2 mol methanol needs 3 mol O2.

mcqs.q: Ethanol combustion CH3CH2OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O: how many moles of water form from 1 mole of ethanol?
mcqs.why: Working: H in ethanol = 6 atoms, water contains 2 H per molecule, 6/2 = 3, so the balanced equation gives 3 H2O per ethanol.

mcqs.q: Methanol burns with what kind of flame?
options: A clean, nearly smokeless flame, nearly invisible in daylight
mcqs.why: Methanol burns with a clean, nearly smokeless flame that is nearly invisible in daylight, used in racing engines.

mcqs.q: Ethanol is described as ideal for which uses as a fuel?
options: Spirit burners and as a renewable biofuel blended with petrol
mcqs.why: Ethanol burns cleanly and is ideal for spirit burners and as a renewable biofuel blended with petrol.

mcqs.q: Methanol is used as a fuel in which application in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state methanol is used as a fuel in high-performance racing engines because of its clean combustion.

mcqs.q: Why is alcohol combustion described as a clean energy source?
options: It releases no gases at all
It releases only CO2 and water, reducing harmful emissions
mcqs.why: Combustion of hydroxy compounds releases only carbon dioxide and water while reducing harmful emissions.

mcqs.q: Complete combustion requires which condition regarding oxygen?
mcqs.why: Complete combustion needs excess oxygen and gives CO2 + H2O + heat, as stated in the key points.

mcqs.q: From 2 moles of methanol burned, how many moles of CO2 are produced?
mcqs.why: Working: carbon atoms: 2 methanol contain 2 C atoms, each forms one CO2, so 2 mol methanol → 2 mol CO2 in the equation.

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols undergo complete combustion in excess oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water and releasing heat, which makes them potential fuels: ROH + O2 → CO2 + H2O + Heat.

Examples

  • Methanol burns with a clean, nearly smokeless flame: 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O + Heat. It is used as a fuel in high-performance racing engines; its flame is nearly invisible in daylight.
  • Ethanol also burns cleanly: CH3CH2OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O + Heat. It is ideal for spirit burners and as a renewable biofuel blended with petrol.

Combustion of hydroxy compounds is a clean energy source, releasing only carbon dioxide and water while reducing harmful emissions.

Key Points

  • Complete combustion needs excess oxygen and gives CO2 + H2O + heat.
  • Methanol: 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O; clean, nearly smokeless flame.
  • Ethanol: CH3CH2OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O; used in spirit burners and as a biofuel.
  • Alcohol combustion is a clean energy source with reduced harmful emissions.
lessons.title: Combustion of Organic Hydroxy Compounds (Alcohols)

mcqs.q: SOCl2, PCl3 and PCl5 all convert alcohols into what?
mcqs.why: In substitution with phosphorus halides or thionyl chloride, the hydroxyl group is replaced by chlorine, giving alkyl chlorides.

mcqs.q: The reaction of ethanol with SOCl2 also produces which gases/products besides chloroethane?
mcqs.why: R—OH + SOCl2 → R—Cl + SO2 + HCl, with pyridine as catalyst, so ethanol gives chloroethane plus SO2 and HCl.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst is used with SOCl2 in this conversion?
mcqs.why: Thionyl chloride conversion of alcohols uses a pyridine catalyst, as shown in the reactions table.

mcqs.q: 3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 gives 3CH3CH2Cl plus what other product?
mcqs.why: Working: 3 ethanol + PCl3 → 3 chloroethane + H3PO3; the phosphorus ends in H3PO3, balancing 3 Cl to 3 products.

mcqs.q: Ethanol with PCl5 gives chloroethane plus which products?
mcqs.why: CH3CH2OH + PCl5 → CH3CH2Cl + POCl3 + HCl; PCl5 reacts readily with alcohols to give these products.

mcqs.q: Ethanol reacts with sodium metal to produce what?
mcqs.why: 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2ONa + H2, producing sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas from ethanol and sodium.

mcqs.q: In the general reaction R—OH + Na → R—ONa + 1/2 H2, the product R—ONa is called what?
mcqs.why: Sodium reacts with alcohols to give an alkoxide, for example sodium ethoxide, plus hydrogen gas.

mcqs.q: How many moles of H2 form when 2 moles of ethanol react fully with sodium?
mcqs.why: Working: 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2ONa + H2, ratio 2 ethanol : 1 H2, so 2 mol ethanol gives 1 mol H2.

mcqs.q: The reaction of alcohols with sodium shows which character of the —OH group?
mcqs.why: The reaction with sodium, evolving hydrogen, shows the acidic character of the hydroxyl group in alcohols.

mcqs.q: How many ethanol molecules react with one PCl3 molecule in the given equation?
mcqs.why: Working: the equation is 3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3, so the stoichiometric ratio is 3 ethanol to 1 PCl3.

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols undergo many conversions. In substitution with phosphorus halides or thionyl chloride, the hydroxyl group is replaced by a chlorine atom, giving alkyl chlorides.

Reaction with SOCl2, PCl3, and PCl5

ReagentConditionsReaction
SOCl2 (thionyl chloride)Pyridine catalystR—OH + SOCl2 → R—Cl + SO2 + HCl; CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 → CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl
PCl3—3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3
PCl5Reacts readilyCH3CH2OH + PCl5 → CH3CH2Cl + POCl3 + HCl

Reaction of Hydroxy Organic Compound with Sodium

Ethanol reacts with sodium metal to produce sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas: 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2ONa + H2. In general: R—OH + Na → R—ONa + 1/2 H2.

Key Points

  • SOCl2 (pyridine), PCl3 and PCl5 all convert alcohols into alkyl chlorides.
  • SOCl2 also gives SO2 + HCl; PCl5 also gives POCl3 + HCl; PCl3 gives H3PO3.
  • Sodium reacts with alcohols to give an alkoxide (e.g. sodium ethoxide) + H2.
  • The reaction with Na shows the acidic character of the —OH group.
lessons.title: Reactions of Alcohols

mcqs.q: Which oxidising agents are used for oxidation of alcohols in the notes?
mcqs.why: Oxidation uses acidified potassium dichromate in aqueous H2SO4 or acidified KMnO4, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Methanol is oxidised first to formaldehyde, then to what?
mcqs.why: Methanol oxidises CH3OH → HCHO (formaldehyde) → HCOOH (formic acid) in two successive oxidation steps.

mcqs.q: How can oxidation of a primary alcohol be stopped at the aldehyde stage?
options: By removing the aldehyde from the oxidising medium by distillation
mcqs.why: The reaction can be stopped at the aldehyde by removing the aldehyde from the oxidising medium using distillation.

mcqs.q: Primary alcohols are oxidised in sequence to what products?
mcqs.why: Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes then to carboxylic acids: ethanol → CH3CHO → CH3COOH with [O] each step.

mcqs.q: Secondary alcohols on oxidation give what, which resists further easy oxidation?
mcqs.why: Secondary alcohols give ketones, which are not oxidised further easily because that needs breaking a C—C bond.

mcqs.q: Propan-2-ol oxidation gives acetone; drastic oxidation of acetone gives what products?
mcqs.why: CH3COCH3 + 4[O] → CH3COOH + CO2 + H2O under drastic conditions, as shown for secondary alcohol oxidation.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary alcohols not oxidise under acidic conditions?
options: The —OH carbon is attached to three carbons and cannot form a C=O double bond
They contain no hydrogen at all in the molecule
mcqs.why: The carbon bearing —OH in a tertiary alcohol is attached to three carbons and cannot form C=O, so no oxidation occurs.

mcqs.q: Under reflux, primary alcohols oxidise fully to what?
mcqs.why: Under reflux, primary alcohols oxidise fully to carboxylic acids, while tertiary alcohols still do not oxidise.

mcqs.q: Methylpropan-2-ol with acidified oxidising agent shows what?
mcqs.why: Methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol and shows no oxidation reaction under acidic conditions in the notes.

mcqs.q: Oxidation can differentiate primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols because what?
options: The product depends on the type of alcohol and the conditions
mcqs.why: The product depends on alcohol type and conditions, so oxidation differentiates 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.

lessons.notes_html:
Oxidation uses acidified potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4) or acidified KMnO4. The product depends on the type of alcohol and the conditions, so oxidation differentiates primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

Oxidation of Methyl Alcohol and Primary Alcohols

Methanol is oxidised first to formaldehyde, then to formic acid: CH3OH + [O] → HCHO + H2O; HCHO + [O] → HCOOH. The reaction can be stopped at the aldehyde stage by removing the aldehyde from the oxidising medium (distillation). Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes, then to carboxylic acids: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O; CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH.

Oxidation of Secondary Alcohols

Secondary alcohols give ketones, which are not oxidised further easily because that needs breaking a C—C bond; only drastic conditions give acids: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O; CH3COCH3 + 4[O] → CH3COOH + CO2 + H2O.

Oxidation of Tertiary Alcohols

Tertiary alcohols are not oxidised under acidic conditions: the carbon bearing —OH is attached to three carbons and cannot form a C=O double bond, so methylpropan-2-ol shows no oxidation reaction. Under reflux, primary alcohols oxidise fully to carboxylic acids and secondary alcohols also give carboxylic acids, but tertiary alcohols still do not oxidise.

Key Points

  • Oxidising agent: acidified K2Cr2O7 or acidified KMnO4.
  • 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; distil off the aldehyde to stop at stage one.
  • Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid.
  • 2° alcohol → ketone; further oxidation only under drastic conditions.
  • 3° alcohol: no oxidation, even under reflux.
  • Reflux gives more extensive oxidation than distillation.
lessons.title: Oxidation of Alcohols

mcqs.q: Dehydration of an alcohol with conc. H2SO4 or H3PO4 gives what type of product?
mcqs.why: Dehydration in the presence of an acid catalyst gives alkenes, removing —OH and a hydrogen as water.

mcqs.q: In dehydration, —OH is removed from the α-carbon and hydrogen from where?
mcqs.why: The —OH group is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon, forming the double bond of the alkene.

mcqs.q: The ease of dehydration follows which order?
mcqs.why: Ease of dehydration follows 3° > 2° > 1°, which is the order of carbocation stability given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Ethanol dehydration to ethene requires which conditions?
mcqs.why: Primary ethanol is most difficult to dehydrate, needing concentrated H2SO4 at 170–180°C to give ethene + water.

mcqs.q: Butan-2-ol dehydrates to but-2-ene under which conditions?
mcqs.why: Secondary butan-2-ol dehydrates with 60% H2SO4 at 100°C, in the 100–140°C range, to but-2-ene + water.

mcqs.q: Methylpropan-2-ol dehydrates under which mild conditions?
options: 20% H2SO4 at 85°C, range 25–80°C just above room temperature
mcqs.why: Tertiary methylpropan-2-ol dehydrates with 20% H2SO4 at 85°C, in the 25–80°C range just above room temperature.

mcqs.q: Besides conc. H2SO4 or H3PO4, dehydration can use which heated catalyst?
mcqs.why: The key points note a heated catalyst such as Al2O3 also works for dehydration of alcohols to alkenes.

mcqs.q: The product of dehydrating methylpropan-2-ol is what?
mcqs.why: Methylpropan-2-ol loses water to give 2-methylpropene, the alkene from its four-carbon tertiary structure.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary alcohols dehydrate easiest?
options: Their carbocations are the most stable
mcqs.why: The dehydration order follows carbocation stability, so tertiary carbocations being most stable dehydrate easiest.

mcqs.q: Primary alcohols need which conditions compared with tertiary?
options: The highest temperature and strong acid
mcqs.why: Primary alcohols are most difficult, needing high temperature and strong acid, unlike tertiary near room temperature.

lessons.notes_html:
Dehydration of alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst (conc. H2SO4 or H3PO4) gives alkenes. The —OH group is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon. The ease of dehydration follows the order 3° > 2° > 1°, the order of carbocation stability.

Key Reactions

AlcoholConditionsProduct
Primary (ethanol)Conc. H2SO4, 170–180°C (most difficult; high temperature, strong acid)CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O (ethene)
Secondary (butan-2-ol)60% H2SO4, 100°C (range 100–140°C)Butan-2-ol → but-2-ene + H2O
Tertiary (methylpropan-2-ol)20% H2SO4, 85°C (range 25–80°C, just above room temperature)2-methylpropene + H2O

Key Points

  • Dehydration removes —OH from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon, forming an alkene.
  • Catalyst: concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4; a heated catalyst such as Al2O3 also works.
  • Ease of dehydration: tertiary > secondary > primary (carbocation stability order).
  • Primary alcohols need the highest temperature; tertiary dehydrate near room temperature.
lessons.title: Dehydration of Alcohols

mcqs.q: Esterification is the reaction of an alcohol with what, using conc. H2SO4 catalyst?
options: A halogen acid, giving an alkene
A carboxylic acid, giving an ester + water
mcqs.why: Alcohols react with carboxylic acids with conc. H2SO4 or H3PO4 catalyst to form esters plus water.

mcqs.q: Ethanol + acetic acid in esterification gives which ester?
mcqs.why: CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O; the product CH3COOC2H5 is ethyl acetate, the standard example.

mcqs.q: The general esterification equation R—COOH + R—OH ⇌ R—COOR + H2O is what type of reaction?
mcqs.why: The ⇌ symbol shows esterification is reversible, with ester and water in equilibrium with acid and alcohol.

mcqs.q: Alcohols react with halogen acids HX to form what?
mcqs.why: R—OH + HX → R—X + H2O, so halogen acids convert alcohols to alkyl halides plus water.

mcqs.q: Reaction of ethanol with HCl requires which catalyst?
mcqs.why: With HCl a ZnCl2 catalyst is used: CH3CH2OH + HCl → CH3CH2Cl + H2O, unlike HBr and HI.

mcqs.q: How do HBr and HI differ from HCl in reaction with alcohols?
options: They do not react at all
They react in the same way but without a catalyst
mcqs.why: HBr and HI react in the same way as HCl to give alkyl halides, but without needing a catalyst.

mcqs.q: Ethanol + HBr gives which products?
mcqs.why: CH3CH2OH + HBr → CH3CH2Br + H2O, forming bromoethane as the alkyl halide product plus water.

mcqs.q: Which acid can also catalyse esterification besides conc. H2SO4?
mcqs.why: The notes state alcohols with carboxylic acids use concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4 as catalyst to form esters.

mcqs.q: In esterification, which atoms combine to form the water molecule lost?
options: Two H from the alcohol only
—OH from the acid and H from the alcohol in the overall RCOOH + ROH equation
mcqs.why: The overall equation R—COOH + R—OH ⇌ R—COOR + H2O shows water is the small molecule formed alongside the ester.

mcqs.q: Esterification is also called formation of esters from what pair?
mcqs.why: Formation of esters is from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, giving ester plus water under acid catalysis.

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 (or H3PO4) as catalyst to form esters. This process is called esterification: R—COOH + R—OH ⇌ R—COOR + H2O. Example: CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 (ethyl acetate) + H2O.

Reaction with Halogen Acids

Alcohols react with halogen acids to form alkyl halides: R—OH + HX → R—X + H2O.

  • With HCl, a ZnCl2 catalyst is used: CH3CH2OH + HCl → CH3CH2Cl + H2O.
  • HBr and HI react in the same way, but without a catalyst: CH3CH2OH + HBr → CH3CH2Br + H2O.

Key Points

  • Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water, conc. H2SO4 catalyst.
  • Ethanol + acetic acid gives ethyl acetate, the standard example.
  • Halogen acids convert alcohols to alkyl halides + water.
  • HCl needs ZnCl2 catalyst; HBr and HI do not.
lessons.title: Formation of Esters

mcqs.q: Lucas reagent consists of what?
options: Anhydrous zinc chloride in concentrated hydrochloric acid
mcqs.why: Lucas reagent is anhydrous zinc chloride dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid, used in the Lucas test.

mcqs.q: In the Lucas test, a tertiary alcohol shows what observation?
options: Immediately forms two layers, becoming cloudy at once
mcqs.why: Tertiary alcohols immediately form two separate layers and become cloudy at once in the Lucas test.

mcqs.q: A secondary alcohol in the Lucas test becomes cloudy after how long?
options: After a few minutes, 5 to 10 minutes
mcqs.why: Secondary alcohols become cloudy after a few minutes, specifically 5 to 10 minutes, in the Lucas test.

mcqs.q: A primary alcohol in the Lucas test shows what?
options: Very slow reaction; no turbidity except on prolonged heating
mcqs.why: Primary alcohols react very slowly with Lucas reagent, with no turbidity unless heated for a prolonged time.

mcqs.q: In the oxidation test, acidified K2Cr2O7 changes colour how for 1° and 2° alcohols?
options: From orange Cr(VI) to green Cr(III)
mcqs.why: Chromium is reduced from Cr(VI) orange to Cr(III) green when primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised.

mcqs.q: Tertiary alcohols in the oxidation test with acidified K2Cr2O7 show what?
options: No colour change, because they do not oxidise
mcqs.why: Tertiary alcohols do not oxidise, so there is no colour change with acidified K2Cr2O7 in the oxidation test.

mcqs.q: The Lucas test reaction is written as R—OH + HCl -> R—Cl + H2O with which catalyst above the arrow?
mcqs.why: The Lucas reaction uses ZnCl2: R—OH + HCl → R—Cl + H2O, converting the alcohol to an alkyl chloride.

mcqs.q: Which two tests are used together to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols?
mcqs.why: Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols are identified by the Lucas test and the oxidation test together.

mcqs.q: An unknown alcohol becomes cloudy immediately in Lucas reagent and shows no K2Cr2O7 colour change. It is what?
mcqs.why: Immediate cloudiness in Lucas test plus no oxidation colour change is the combined signature of a tertiary alcohol.

mcqs.q: An alcohol cloudy in 5–10 minutes in Lucas test and turning dichromate green is what?
mcqs.why: Cloudiness in 5–10 minutes indicates secondary, and dichromate turning green confirms it can be oxidised to a ketone.

lessons.notes_html:
Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols are identified by the Lucas test and the oxidation test.

Lucas Test

The unknown alcohol is added to Lucas reagent (anhydrous zinc chloride dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid), stoppered, shaken and left to stand at room temperature: R—OH + HCl → R—Cl + H2O (ZnCl2).

AlcoholObservation
PrimaryReacts very slowly; no turbidity (turbidity only on prolonged heating)
SecondaryBecomes cloudy after a few minutes (5 to 10 minutes)
TertiaryImmediately forms two separate layers, becoming cloudy at once

Oxidation Test

With acidified K2Cr2O7, the chromium ion is reduced from Cr(VI) (orange) to Cr(III) (green). Primary alcohols (oxidised to aldehydes or acids) and secondary alcohols (oxidised to ketones) give this colour change; tertiary alcohols do not oxidise, so there is no colour change.

Key Points

  • Lucas reagent = anhydrous ZnCl2 in conc. HCl.
  • Lucas test: 3° cloudy immediately, 2° cloudy in 5–10 minutes, 1° no turbidity.
  • Oxidation test: acidified K2Cr2O7 changes orange → green for 1° and 2° alcohols.
  • Tertiary alcohols give no colour change with acidified K2Cr2O7.
lessons.title: Distinction between Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Alcohols

mcqs.q: Methanol and ethanol are distinguished by which test?
mcqs.why: Methanol and ethanol are distinguished by the iodoform test: ethanol gives iodoform, methanol does not.

mcqs.q: Ethanol with iodine and NaOH forms what distinctive product?
options: A deep yellow precipitate of iodoform, CHI3
mcqs.why: Ethanol reacts with I2/NaOH to form a deep yellow precipitate of iodoform, tri-iodomethane, CHI3.

mcqs.q: Methanol with I2 and NaOH shows what result?
options: No reaction, no deep yellow precipitate
mcqs.why: The equation for methanol is given as no reaction: CH3OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH → no deep yellow precipitate.

mcqs.q: In the ethanol iodoform equation, besides CHI3, which sodium salt forms?
mcqs.why: CH3CH2OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H2O, so sodium formate is the salt formed.

mcqs.q: How many moles of NaI form per mole of ethanol in the iodoform equation given?
mcqs.why: Working: the balanced equation shows 5NaI on the product side per 1 ethanol, with 5H2O also formed, so the coefficient is 5.

mcqs.q: The iodoform test with alkaline I2 detects which group in an alcohol?
options: The CH3CO— group only in ketones
mcqs.why: Reaction with alkaline I2 detects the CH3CH(OH)— group; forming tri-iodomethane confirms this group is present.

mcqs.q: Methanol is dangerous in the body because in the liver it is metabolised to what?
options: Formaldehyde and formic acid, which can cause blindness or death
mcqs.why: Methanol is metabolised to formaldehyde and formic acid, which can cause blindness or death, unlike ethanol's products.

mcqs.q: Ethanol in the body gives which less harmful metabolites, per the notes?
mcqs.why: Ethanol gives the less harmful acetaldehyde and acetic acid, in contrast to methanol's toxic metabolites.

mcqs.q: The reagents for the iodoform test are what?
options: Iodine in the presence of NaOH (alkaline iodine)
mcqs.why: The iodoform test uses iodine with NaOH, i.e. alkaline iodine solution, to produce the yellow CHI3 precipitate.

mcqs.q: How many I2 molecules are used per ethanol in the given iodoform equation?
mcqs.why: Working: the equation is CH3CH2OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH → products, so the stoichiometric coefficient for iodine is 4 per ethanol.

lessons.notes_html:
Methanol and ethanol are distinguished by the iodoform test. Ethanol reacts with iodine in the presence of NaOH to form a deep yellow precipitate of iodoform (tri-iodomethane, CHI3); methanol does not give this test.

CH3OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH → No reaction (no deep yellow ppt)

CH3CH2OH + 4I2 + 6NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa (sodium formate) + 5NaI + 5H2O

The reaction with alkaline I2(aq) detects the CH3CH(OH)— group in an alcohol: formation of tri-iodomethane confirms this group in the original alcohol, which is then oxidised to a carboxylic acid. Methanol is dangerous: in the liver it is metabolised to formaldehyde and formic acid, which can cause blindness or death, while ethanol gives the less harmful acetaldehyde and acetic acid.

Key Points

  • Iodoform test: ethanol gives a deep yellow ppt of CHI3; methanol gives no reaction.
  • Reagents: I2 with NaOH (alkaline iodine).
  • The test detects the CH3CH(OH)— group in an alcohol.
  • Ethanol + 4I2 + 6NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H2O.
lessons.title: Distinction between Methanol and Ethanol

mcqs.q: The acidity of alcohols is due to what feature?
mcqs.why: Alcohols are acidic due to the polar O—H bond; greater polarity of —OH means higher acidity.

mcqs.q: The acidity order for alcohols given in the notes is what?
mcqs.why: Acidity order is methanol > primary > secondary > tertiary: CH3OH > RCH2OH > R2CHOH > R3COH.

mcqs.q: Why does acidity decrease as alkyl groups on the α-carbon increase?
options: Alkyl groups are electron-donating, lowering —OH polarity and destabilising the alkoxide ion
mcqs.why: Electron-donating alkyl groups lower —OH polarity and destabilise the alkoxide ion, making proton donation less likely.

mcqs.q: Tert-butyl alcohol compared with methanol is what?
options: Less acidic than methanol or ethanol
mcqs.why: Tert-butyl alcohol is less acidic than methanol or ethanol because its three alkyl groups donate electrons strongly.

mcqs.q: Compared with water, methanol's acidity is what?
options: Methanol is more acidic than water
Methanol is less acidic than water
Methanol is not acidic at all
mcqs.why: Generally alcohols are less acidic than water, except methanol, which is more acidic than water.

mcqs.q: Water has a pKa of 15.7 and lies in acidity between which alcohols?
mcqs.why: Water's pKa of 15.7 places it between methanol and ethanol in acidity, with ethanol nearly equal to water.

mcqs.q: The acidity of ethanol compared with water is described as what?
options: Nearly equal to that of water
mcqs.why: The acidity of ethanol is nearly equal to that of water, while longer-chain alcohols are weaker than water.

mcqs.q: Reaction with sodium, evolving H2, demonstrates what about alcohols?
mcqs.why: 2R—OH + 2Na → 2R—ONa + H2; evolving hydrogen with sodium demonstrates the acidity of alcohols.

mcqs.q: Longer chains and more branching have what effect on alcohol acidity?
mcqs.why: Longer chains and more branching lower acidity because electron-donating alkyl groups destabilise the alkoxide ion.

mcqs.q: Water dissociates as H2O(l) -> OH-(aq) + H+(aq). This is compared in the lesson to what?
options: Alcohol acidity via its polar O—H bond
mcqs.why: Water's dissociation is used to compare acidity: both water and alcohols ionise through a polar O—H bond.

lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are acidic in nature due to the polar O—H bond; the greater the polarity of the —OH group, the higher the acidity. Acidity order: CH3OH > RCH2OH > R2CHOH > R3COH — primary alcohols are more acidic than secondary, which are more acidic than tertiary. The polarity of —OH decreases as electron-donating alkyl groups on the α-carbon increase, so tert-butyl alcohol is less acidic than methanol or ethanol. Acidic character is shown by reaction with sodium metal, releasing hydrogen: 2R—OH + 2Na → 2R—ONa + H2; e.g. 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2ONa + H2.

Comparison of the Acidity of Alcohols and Water

Generally alcohols are less acidic than water, except methanol, which is more acidic than water; the acidity of ethanol is nearly equal to that of water. Water dissociates as H2O(l) → OH−(aq) + H+(aq) and has a pKa of 15.7, placing it between methanol and ethanol in acidity. Longer chains and more branching lower acidity, because electron-donating alkyl groups destabilise the alkoxide ion, making it less likely to donate a proton.

Key Points

  • Acidity comes from the polar O—H bond; more polar —OH means stronger acid.
  • Order: methanol > primary > secondary > tertiary alcohol.
  • Alkyl groups are electron-donating: they lower —OH polarity and destabilise the alkoxide ion.
  • Methanol is more acidic than water; ethanol is about equal; longer-chain alcohols are weaker than water.
  • Reaction with Na (H2 evolved) demonstrates the acidity of alcohols.
lessons.title: Acidity of Alcohols

mcqs.q: Carbonyl compounds contain which group?
options: A carbonyl group C=O, carbon double-bonded to oxygen
mcqs.why: Carbonyl compounds contain C=O, in which a carbon atom is double-bonded to an oxygen atom.

mcqs.q: In the carbonyl group, how is the charge distributed?
options: Carbon is δ− and oxygen is δ+
Carbon is δ+ and oxygen is δ−, highly polarised
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon is highly polarised: carbon carries δ+ and oxygen carries δ− partial charges.

mcqs.q: An aldehyde has what attached to its carbonyl carbon?
options: One alkyl/aryl group and one hydrogen atom
mcqs.why: An aldehyde has one alkyl or aryl group and one hydrogen attached to the carbonyl carbon, e.g. formaldehyde HCHO.

mcqs.q: A ketone has what attached to its carbonyl carbon?
mcqs.why: A ketone has two alkyl or aryl groups attached to the carbonyl carbon, for example acetone.

mcqs.q: Carboxylic acids contain which group, with general formula what?
mcqs.why: Carboxylic acids contain a carboxyl group —COOH with general formula R—COOH, where R is aliphatic or aromatic.

mcqs.q: The name 'carboxyl' comes from combining which two group names?
mcqs.why: The name carboxyl comes from carbonyl + hydroxyl, the two groups present in carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde in aqueous solution is called what and used as what?
options: Formalin, used as a preservative in medical laboratories
Acetone, used as nail polish remover
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde in aqueous solution is formalin, used as a preservative in medical labs and as a disinfectant.

mcqs.q: Acetone is given as used in which products?
options: Nail polish removers, paint thinners and cleaning products
mcqs.why: Acetone, the simplest ketone example, is used in nail polish removers, paint thinners and cleaning products.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde is also used in making what materials?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is used in resins, adhesives and plywood, but it is an irritant and a health risk on long exposure.

mcqs.q: Which are listed as carbonyl compounds in the notes?
mcqs.why: Carbonyl compounds include aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids, all containing the carbonyl group.

lessons.notes_html:
Carbonyl compounds contain a carbonyl group (C=O), in which a carbon atom is double-bonded to an oxygen atom. The carbonyl carbon is highly polarised: carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ+) and oxygen a partial negative charge (δ−). Carbonyl compounds include aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids.

  • An aldehyde has one alkyl (or aryl) group and one hydrogen atom attached to the carbonyl carbon, e.g. formaldehyde, HCHO.
  • A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups attached to the carbonyl carbon, e.g. acetone, used in nail polish removers, paint thinners and cleaning products.

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain a carboxyl group (—COOH); general formula R—COOH, where R is an aliphatic or aromatic group. The name carboxyl comes from carbonyl + hydroxyl, the two groups present in carboxylic acids. Formaldehyde (in aqueous solution, formalin) is used as a preservative in medical laboratories, as a disinfectant, and in resins, adhesives and plywood; it is an irritant and a health risk on long exposure.

Key Points

  • Carbonyl group C=O is polarised: C is δ+, O is δ−.
  • Aldehyde: carbonyl carbon carries one R group and one H.
  • Ketone: carbonyl carbon carries two R groups.
  • Carboxylic acids contain —COOH (carbonyl + hydroxyl), general formula R—COOH.
  • Formaldehyde and acetone are the simplest aldehyde and ketone.
lessons.title: Carbonyl Compounds

mcqs.q: Aldehydes and ketones are prepared by which process on alcohols?
options: Controlled oxidation with acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4
mcqs.why: Aldehydes and ketones are prepared by controlled oxidation of alcohols with acidified dichromate or permanganate.

mcqs.q: Controlled oxidation of a primary alcohol gives what?
mcqs.why: Primary alcohols give aldehydes on controlled oxidation: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O.

mcqs.q: Controlled oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives what?
mcqs.why: Secondary alcohols give ketones: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 (acetone) + H2O.

mcqs.q: Ethanol on controlled oxidation gives which aldehyde?
mcqs.why: Ethanol oxidises to acetaldehyde CH3CHO using K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, as shown in the preparations lesson.

mcqs.q: Propan-2-ol on oxidation gives which ketone?
mcqs.why: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, so oxidation gives the ketone acetone, CH3COCH3, plus water.

mcqs.q: Distillation in this preparation is used to do what?
options: Separate and collect the desired aldehyde or ketone product and purify it
Speed up full oxidation to acid
mcqs.why: Distillation separates and collects the desired product and isolates and purifies it from the reaction mixture.

mcqs.q: Distilling the aldehyde out as it forms also prevents what?
options: Its further oxidation to a carboxylic acid
mcqs.why: Distilling the aldehyde out as it forms prevents its further oxidation to a carboxylic acid, keeping the aldehyde.

mcqs.q: Which oxidising solution is specified for ethanol to acetaldehyde?
options: Cold dilute KMnO4 only for diols
mcqs.why: The equation for ethanol to acetaldehyde specifies K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 as the acidified oxidising agent.

mcqs.q: Why must the oxidation be 'controlled' to obtain an aldehyde?
options: So the alcohol does not burn
So the aldehyde is not oxidised further to a carboxylic acid
mcqs.why: Controlled oxidation and distillation stop the primary alcohol product at the aldehyde stage before it becomes an acid.

mcqs.q: A secondary alcohol and a primary alcohol differ in oxidation product because what?
options: Secondary gives a ketone, primary gives an aldehyde
mcqs.why: The type of alcohol determines the carbonyl product: primary → aldehyde and secondary → ketone on oxidation.

lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones are prepared by the controlled oxidation of alcohols with an acidified solution of potassium dichromate or potassium permanganate.

  • Primary alcohols give aldehydes: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO (acetaldehyde) + H2O, using K2Cr2O7/H2SO4.
  • Secondary alcohols give ketones: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 (acetone) + H2O.

Distillation is commonly used to separate and collect the desired product — the aldehyde from a primary alcohol or the ketone from a secondary alcohol — and so isolate and purify it from the reaction mixture. Distilling the aldehyde out as it forms also prevents its further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.

Key Points

  • Controlled oxidation: acidified K2Cr2O7 or acidified KMnO4.
  • Primary alcohol → aldehyde; secondary alcohol → ketone.
  • Ethanol → acetaldehyde; propan-2-ol → acetone.
  • Distillation isolates and purifies the carbonyl product.
lessons.title: Preparations of Aldehydes and Ketones

mcqs.q: NaBH4 and LiAlH4 reduce an aldehyde to what?
mcqs.why: Metal hydrides reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Reduction of a ketone with NaBH4 gives what type of alcohol?
mcqs.why: Ketones reduce to secondary alcohols: CH3COCH3 → propan-2-ol on reduction with NaBH4 or LiAlH4.

mcqs.q: Reduction with NaBH4 requires which solvents?
options: Polar solvents like water and ethyl alcohol
mcqs.why: Reduction with NaBH4 requires polar solvents like water and ethyl alcohol, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: HCN reacts with aldehydes and ketones to form what?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen cyanide adds to aldehydes and ketones to form hydroxynitriles, also called cyanohydrins.

mcqs.q: CH3CHO + HCN gives which hydroxynitrile?
mcqs.why: Acetaldehyde plus HCN gives CH3CH(OH)CN, named 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, a hydroxynitrile product.

mcqs.q: Acetone + HCN gives which product?
mcqs.why: CH3COCH3 + HCN → (CH3)2C(OH)CN, which is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, from acetone.

mcqs.q: In the HCN addition mechanism, KCN is added for what purpose?
options: To increase the supply of CN− ions, acting as catalyst
mcqs.why: KCN is added to increase the supply of CN− ions; a little dilute H2SO4 supplies H+ for the final step.

mcqs.q: Step 2 of the mechanism: CN− attacks what, breaking which bond?
options: The δ+ carbonyl carbon, breaking the π bond of C=O
mcqs.why: CN− attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon nucleophilically, breaking the π bond of C=O and forming an alkoxide intermediate.

mcqs.q: The final step of HCN addition mechanism is what?
options: Protonation: the negatively charged oxygen accepts H+ to give the hydroxynitrile
mcqs.why: In step 3 the negatively charged oxygen accepts H+ from the medium, giving the stable hydroxynitrile product.

mcqs.q: The carbonyl carbon is attacked by nucleophiles because it is what?
options: Electrophilic, carrying a δ+ partial positive charge
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (δ+), so it is attacked by nucleophiles such as CN− in this addition.

lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols and add hydrogen cyanide to form hydroxynitriles.

Reduction to Alcohols (Reduction with NaBH4)

Metal hydrides NaBH4 (sodium borohydride) and LiAlH4 (lithium aluminium hydride) reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. Reduction with NaBH4 requires polar solvents like water and ethyl alcohol: CH3CHO → CH3CH2OH; CH3COCH3 → propan-2-ol.

Reaction with HCN — Hydroxynitriles

Hydrogen cyanide (a weak acid) reacts with aldehydes and ketones, with KCN as catalyst and heat, to form hydroxynitriles (cyanohydrins): CH3CHO + HCN → CH3CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile); CH3COCH3 + HCN → (CH3)2C(OH)CN (2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile).

Mechanism of Nucleophilic Addition of HCN

  • Step 1 — Ionisation: HCN ⇌ H+ + CN−. KCN is added to increase the supply of CN− ions; a little dilute H2SO4 supplies H+.
  • Step 2 — Nucleophilic attack: CN− attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, breaking the π bond of C=O and forming an alkoxide intermediate.
  • Step 3 — Protonation: the negatively charged oxygen accepts H+ from the medium, giving the stable hydroxynitrile.

Key Points

  • NaBH4 or LiAlH4: aldehyde → 1° alcohol; ketone → 2° alcohol.
  • HCN adds across C=O to give a hydroxynitrile (cyanohydrin); KCN is the catalyst.
  • Mechanism: ionisation of HCN, nucleophilic attack by CN−, then protonation.
  • The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (δ+), so it is attacked by nucleophiles.
lessons.title: Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones

mcqs.q: 2,4-DNPH gives an orange-yellow precipitate with which compounds?
options: Both aldehydes and ketones (any carbonyl group)
mcqs.why: 2,4-DNPH forms an orange-yellow 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone precipitate with the carbonyl group in both types.

mcqs.q: Fehling's test gives a brick-red precipitate of what, and for which compounds?
options: Cu2O, for both aldehydes and ketones
Cu2O, for aldehydes only; ketones do not react
mcqs.why: Fehling's test: aldehydes give a red precipitate of Cu2O and are oxidised to acids; ketones do not react.

mcqs.q: Tollens' test positive result is what?
options: A grey-black precipitate or a silver mirror, for aldehydes only
mcqs.why: Tollens' test gives a silver mirror (or grey-black precipitate) with aldehydes only; ketones generally do not react.

mcqs.q: The iodoform test for carbonyl compounds detects which group?
options: The acetyl group CH3CO— (methyl ketones and ethanal)
mcqs.why: Alkaline I2 detects the CH3CO— group, in methyl ketones and ethanal, giving a yellow precipitate of CHI3.

mcqs.q: In Fehling's test, the aldehyde does what to Cu2+ ions?
options: Reduces Cu2+ ions, itself being oxidised to an acid (as its salt)
mcqs.why: RCHO + 2Cu(OH)2 + NaOH → RCOONa + Cu2O + 3H2O; the aldehyde reduces Cu2+ to Cu2O.

mcqs.q: Tollens' reagent must be prepared how, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes warn to always use freshly prepared Tollens' reagent for the silver mirror test with aldehydes.

mcqs.q: In the iodoform reaction for ethanal, CH3CHO + 3I2 + 4NaOH gives CHI3 plus what salt?
mcqs.why: Working: CH3CHO + 3I2 + 4NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa + 3NaI + 3H2O, so the salt from ethanal is sodium formate.

mcqs.q: Acetone iodoform reaction gives CHI3 plus which salt?
mcqs.why: Working: CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH → CHI3 + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O, so acetone gives sodium ethanoate.

mcqs.q: Which test confirms a carbonyl group but does NOT distinguish aldehyde from ketone?
mcqs.why: 2,4-DNPH gives the orange-yellow precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones, so it confirms C=O without distinguishing.

mcqs.q: Fehling's and Tollens' tests identify aldehydes because aldehydes have which property?
options: Ease of oxidation compared with ketones
mcqs.why: Fehling's and Tollens' identify aldehydes by their ease of oxidation; ketones fail both tests.

lessons.notes_html:
Different tests detect carbonyl compounds selectively: the choice of test depends on the information wanted.

Tests for Carbonyl Compounds

TestPositive resultDetects
2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH)Orange-yellow precipitate (a 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone)Carbonyl group in both aldehydes and ketones
Fehling's testRed (brick-red) precipitate of Cu2O; aldehyde oxidised to an acidAldehydes only; ketones do not react
Tollens' test (silver mirror test)Grey-black precipitate or a silver mirrorAldehydes only; ketones generally do not react
Iodoform test (alkaline I2)Yellow precipitate of CHI3The acetyl group CH3CO— (methyl ketones and ethanal)

Fehling's: RCHO + 2Cu(OH)2 + NaOH → RCOONa + Cu2O + 3H2O; the aldehyde reduces Cu2+ ions. Tollens': RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]OH + H2O → RCOOH + 4NH3 + 2Ag + 2H2O; the aldehyde reduces silver ions to a silver mirror — always use freshly prepared Tollens' reagent. Iodoform: CH3CHO + 3I2 + 4NaOH → CHI3 + HCOONa + 3NaI + 3H2O; CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH → CHI3 + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O.

Key Points

  • 2,4-DNPH confirms a carbonyl group: orange-yellow precipitate with aldehydes and ketones.
  • Fehling's and Tollens' tests identify aldehydes (ease of oxidation); ketones fail both.
  • Fehling's: brick-red Cu2O. Tollens': silver mirror; use freshly prepared reagent.
  • Iodoform test detects the CH3CO— group; it does not apply to all carbonyl compounds.

mcqs.q: Carboxylic acids are prepared by oxidation of which starting materials?
mcqs.why: Acids are prepared by oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes, and by hydrolysis of nitriles and esters.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid under reflux uses which reagents?
mcqs.why: Primary alcohols oxidise via aldehydes to acids using K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 under reflux; KMnO4 can be used instead.

mcqs.q: Acidic hydrolysis of CH3C≡N gives ethanoic acid plus what?
mcqs.why: Working: CH3C≡N + 2H2O + HCl → CH3COOH + NH4Cl, so acidic nitrile hydrolysis gives the acid plus NH4Cl.

mcqs.q: Alkaline hydrolysis of a nitrile first gives what, which is then acidified?

mcqs.why: CH3C≡N + H2O + NaOH → CH3COONa + NH3; the sodium ethanoate is then acidified to give CH3COOH.

mcqs.q: To convert CH3COONa from nitrile hydrolysis into CH3COOH, what is added?
mcqs.why: CH3COONa + HCl → CH3COOH + NaCl; dilute HCl or dilute H2SO4 acidifies the carboxylate salt to the acid.

mcqs.q: Ester hydrolysis with dilute acid differs from alkaline hydrolysis how?
options: Acid hydrolysis is reversible; alkaline is not, because alkali neutralises the acid formed
Acid gives the salt, alkali gives acid
mcqs.why: Acid hydrolysis is reversible, whereas alkaline hydrolysis is not, because alkali neutralises the acid and prevents reversal.

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis of nitriles requires which conditions?
options: A hot aqueous solution of an acid or an alkali
mcqs.why: Alkyl nitriles react with a hot aqueous solution of an acid or an alkali to produce carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: Esters react with aqueous NaOH to give what, which yields the acid with dilute HCl?
options: The sodium salt of the acid
mcqs.why: Esters with aqueous NaOH give the sodium salt of the acid, which with dilute HCl yields the carboxylic acid.

mcqs.q: The two-step oxidation CH3CH2OH -> CH3CHO -> CH3COOH uses what in each step?
options: [O] from the oxidising agent in each step
mcqs.why: Each arrow uses [O]: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O, then CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH, under reflux conditions.

mcqs.q: Alkaline hydrolysis of a nitrile releases which gas/product besides the salt?
mcqs.why: CH3C≡N + H2O + NaOH → CH3COONa + NH3, so ammonia is released during alkaline nitrile hydrolysis.

lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids are prepared by oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes, and by hydrolysis of nitriles and esters.

Oxidation of Primary Alcohols

Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes, which on further oxidation give carboxylic acids, using K2Cr2O7 and H2SO4 (KMnO4 can be used instead) under reflux: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O; CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH.

Hydrolysis of Nitriles

Alkyl nitriles (alkyl cyanides) react with a hot aqueous solution of an acid or an alkali to produce carboxylic acids.

  • Acidic hydrolysis: CH3C≡N + 2H2O + HCl → CH3COOH + NH4Cl.
  • Alkaline hydrolysis: CH3C≡N + H2O + NaOH → CH3COONa + NH3; the sodium ethanoate is then acidified with dilute HCl or dilute H2SO4: CH3COONa + HCl → CH3COOH + NaCl.

Hydrolysis of Esters

Esters react with aqueous NaOH to give the sodium salt of the acid, which with dilute HCl yields the carboxylic acid: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O →(Δ) CH3COONa + C2H5OH. With dilute acid the hydrolysis is reversible: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + C2H5OH. Acid hydrolysis is reversible, whereas alkaline hydrolysis is not, because the alkali neutralises the acid formed and prevents the reverse reaction.

Key Points

  • Oxidation: 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid (acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4, reflux).
  • Nitrile hydrolysis: hot aqueous acid gives the acid + NH4+ salt; alkali gives the carboxylate salt + NH3, then acidify.
  • Ester hydrolysis with dilute acid is reversible; with alkali it goes to completion.
  • Alkaline hydrolysis gives a carboxylate salt, converted to the acid by dilute acid.
lessons.title: Preparations of Carboxylic Acids

mcqs.q: Carboxylic acids with reactive metals such as sodium give what products?
options: A salt plus CO2 and water
mcqs.why: 2CH3COOH + 2Na → 2CH3COONa + H2; the metal is oxidised and H+ is reduced in this redox reaction.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid with NaOH gives what products?
mcqs.why: Neutralisation: CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COONa + H2O, giving a salt plus water with an alkali.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid with sodium carbonate gives what products?
mcqs.why: 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O, via carbonic acid which decomposes to CO2 and water.

mcqs.q: Esterification of acetic acid with methanol gives which ester?
mcqs.why: CH3COOH + CH3OH → CH3COOCH3 + H2O with H2SO4 catalyst, giving methyl ethanoate as the ester.

mcqs.q: LiAlH4 reduction of a carboxylic acid gives what type of product?
options: An aldehyde that can be isolated
mcqs.why: CH3COOH is reduced by LiAlH4 (ether, then H2O/H+) to CH3CH2OH, a primary alcohol, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Step 1 of the esterification mechanism is what?
options: Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen, increasing the carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity
Loss of H+ from the ester
mcqs.why: First the carbonyl oxygen is protonated by H+ from the catalyst, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: Step 2 of esterification mechanism involves what attack?
options: The lone pair on the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate
mcqs.why: In step 2 the alcohol oxygen's lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.

mcqs.q: Why can the aldehyde intermediate in LiAlH4 reduction of an acid not be isolated?
options: It is reduced more easily than the original carboxylic acid
It reacts with ether to vanish
mcqs.why: An aldehyde forms as an intermediate but cannot be isolated because it is reduced more easily than the acid itself.

mcqs.q: In step 3 of esterification, a proton transfer converts —OH into what?
mcqs.why: A proton transfer converts one —OH group into —OH2+, a good leaving group, before water is eliminated in step 4.

mcqs.q: In the final esterification step, what is regenerated?
options: The acid catalyst, as the protonated ester loses H+
mcqs.why: Water is eliminated and the protonated ester loses H+, regenerating the acid catalyst and giving the neutral ester.

lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids behave as acids — reacting with metals, alkalis and carbonates — form esters, and are reduced to primary alcohols.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation (acetic acid)Products
Redox reaction with reactive metals2CH3COOH + 2Na → 2CH3COONa + H2Salt + hydrogen (metal is oxidised; H+ is reduced)
Neutralisation with alkalisCH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COONa + H2OSalt + water
Acid–base reaction with carbonates2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + CO2 + H2OSalt + water + carbon dioxide (via carbonic acid, which decomposes)
Esterification with alcoholsCH3COOH + CH3OH → CH3COOCH3 + H2O (H2SO4 catalyst)Ester + water
Reduction by LiAlH4CH3COOH → CH3CH2OH (1. LiAlH4, ether; 2. H2O, H+)Primary alcohol

Esterification Mechanism

  • Step 1: the carbonyl oxygen of the acid is protonated by H+ from the catalyst, increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.
  • Step 2: the lone pair on the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.
  • Step 3: a proton transfer converts one —OH group into a good leaving group (—OH2+).
  • Step 4: water is eliminated and the protonated ester loses H+, regenerating the acid catalyst and giving the neutral ester.

In LiAlH4 reduction, an aldehyde forms as an intermediate but cannot be isolated, because it is reduced more easily than the original carboxylic acid.

Key Points

  • With reactive metals: salt + H2. With alkalis: salt + water. With carbonates: salt + water + CO2.
  • Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, acid catalyst (conc. H2SO4).
  • Esterification mechanism: protonation, nucleophilic attack, proton transfer, elimination of water.
  • LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols; the aldehyde intermediate cannot be isolated.
lessons.title: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis is defined as a reaction in which what happens?
options: Water breaks down a molecule into smaller parts
An acid protonates a molecule only
mcqs.why: Hydrolysis is a reaction in which water breaks down a molecule into smaller parts, here splitting an ester.

mcqs.q: Ester hydrolysis can be carried out by which two methods?
options: Dilute acid and heat, or dilute alkali and heat
mcqs.why: Esters are hydrolysed by dilute acid and heat or dilute alkali and heat; both methods require heat.

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis of an ester with dilute acid gives which products?
options: A carboxylate salt and an alcohol only
A carboxylic acid and an alcohol, reversibly
mcqs.why: Acid hydrolysis: R—COOR + H2O ⇌ R—COOH + ROH, forming a carboxylic acid and an alcohol reversibly.

mcqs.q: CH3COOCH3 hydrolysed with dilute acid gives what pair?
mcqs.why: CH3COOCH3 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + CH3OH, so methyl ethanoate gives ethanoic acid and methanol on acid hydrolysis.

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis of an ester with dilute alkali gives which products?
options: A free acid and an alcohol, reversibly
A carboxylate salt and an alcohol, in one direction only
mcqs.why: Alkaline hydrolysis: R—COOR + NaOH → R—COONa + ROH, proceeding in only one direction to the salt and alcohol.

mcqs.q: Why is alkaline hydrolysis preferred for complete conversion?
options: It proceeds in one direction, giving complete conversion and products easier to separate
It gives the free acid directly
mcqs.why: Alkaline hydrolysis proceeds in only one direction, so complete conversion is easier and products are easier to separate.

mcqs.q: In acid hydrolysis, what is the role of the dilute acid catalyst?
options: It makes the ester oxygen more reactive so water can attack it
mcqs.why: The acid makes the oxygen atom in the ester more reactive, so it can be attacked by water to form acid and alcohol.

mcqs.q: In alkaline hydrolysis, the alkali attacks what part of the ester?
options: The carbonyl carbon of the ester
mcqs.why: The alkali acts as a base and attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester, forming a carboxylate salt and an alcohol.

mcqs.q: Acid hydrolysis of esters can go in both directions, meaning the products can do what?
options: React to form the original ester again
mcqs.why: With dilute acid the reaction is reversible: the acid and alcohol products can react to form the original ester again.

mcqs.q: Both ester hydrolysis methods require which condition besides the reagent?
mcqs.why: Both methods require heat: dilute acid and heat, or dilute alkali and heat, as stated at the start of the lesson.

lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis is a reaction in which water breaks down a molecule into smaller parts. Esters are hydrolysed by two methods — dilute acid and heat, or dilute alkali and heat; both methods require heat.

Hydrolysis with Dilute Acid

A dilute acid (hydrochloric or sulfuric acid) acts as a catalyst: the acid makes the oxygen atom in the ester more reactive, so it can be attacked by water, forming a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. The reaction can go in both directions — the products can react to form the original ester again (reversible): R—COOR + H2O ⇌ R—COOH + ROH (HCl); e.g. CH3COOCH3 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + CH3OH.

Hydrolysis with Dilute Alkali

A dilute alkali (sodium hydroxide) is used instead of acid. The alkali acts as a base and attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester, forming a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. This reaction proceeds in only one direction, so complete conversion is easier and the products are easier to separate: R—COOR + NaOH(aq) → R—COONa(aq) + ROH.

Key Points

  • Ester hydrolysis needs water, heat, and dilute acid or dilute alkali.
  • Acid hydrolysis: ester ⇌ carboxylic acid + alcohol (reversible).
  • Alkaline hydrolysis: ester → carboxylate salt + alcohol (one direction only).
  • Alkaline hydrolysis gives complete conversion and products that are easier to separate.
lessons.title: Hydrolysis of Esters
Functional Group Interconversion (FGI)
lessons.notes_html:
Organic synthesis is the process of creating organic compounds from simpler starting materials through a series of chemical reactions, designing efficient pathways to produce molecules with specific structures or properties — crucial for pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, materials and other essential substances. More than 80% of modern pharmaceuticals are formed through synthetic methods designed by chemists.

Functional group interconversions (FGI) are a crucial part of organic synthesis: the transformation of one functional group into another through chemical reactions such as substitution, addition, elimination, oxidation or reduction. Functional groups are specific arrangements of atoms within a molecule that determine its chemical reactivity, so FGI lets chemists modify a molecule's structure and influence its chemical and physical properties.

Methods of Functional Group Interconversion

Reaction TypeWhat HappensBook Example
Addition reactionsAtoms or groups add across double or triple bondsAlkene + H2O —H2SO4→ alcohol (hydration)
Substitution reactionsOne functional group is replaced by anotherNH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI (halide to amine, nucleophilic substitution)
Elimination reactionsAtoms or groups are removed from a moleculeCH3CH2OH —conc. H2SO4, 170–180°C→ CH2=CH2 + H2O (dehydration of an alcohol to an alkene)
Oxidation–reduction reactionsTransfer of electrons converts one functional group into anotherSec. propyl alcohol (CH3–CHOH–CH3) + [O] —K2Cr2O7/H2SO4→ acetone (CH3–CO–CH3) + H2O
Functional group transformationA sequence of reactions changes one functional group into another; often needs multiple steps and strategic planningMulti-step routes linking the groups below

The FGI Web (Fig. 14.1)

  • Alkane ⇌ alkene: dehydrogenation / hydrogenation. Alkane ⇌ haloalkane: halogenation / reduction (Zn/HCl).
  • Alkene ⇌ haloalkane: addition of HX/X2 / dehydrohalogenation (alc. KOH, heat). Alkene ⇌ alcohol: hydration (acid catalysed) / dehydration.
  • Haloalkane → amine: substitution (conc. NH3). Haloalkane → nitrile: substitution (KCN, ethanolic). Haloalkane ⇌ alcohol: nucleophilic substitution (aq. KOH).
  • Alcohol ⇌ ketone: oxidation / reduction. Alcohol → aldehyde (oxidation); aldehyde → carboxylic acid (oxidation).
  • Carboxylic acid ⇌ ester: esterification / hydrolysis. Acid → acid halide (chlorination), acid anhydride (dehydration), amide (ammonia/amines via acid chloride); each returns by hydrolysis.

Key Points

  • FGI = converting one functional group into another by substitution, addition, elimination, oxidation or reduction.
  • Functional groups determine a molecule's reactivity and properties.
  • Hydration converts alkenes to alcohols; dehydration converts alcohols back to alkenes.
  • Oxidation links alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid, and secondary alcohols → ketones.
  • Haloalkanes are key intermediates: they lead to amines, nitriles and alcohols.

lessons.title: Functional Groups and Their Properties and Reactions in Organic Molecules (Part 1: Alkanes, Alkenes and Alkynes)
lessons.notes_html:
Functional groups are specific atoms or groups of atoms within organic molecules that determine the properties and reactivity of molecules. By identifying these groups, we can predict how organic molecules will react and what physical characteristics they will have.

Alkanes

Alkanes have low reactivity due to their saturated hydrocarbon structures — they lack reactive sites (reactive functional groups) and mainly participate in combustion reactions with oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water vapour and energy. Examples: methane, ethane and propane, found in natural gas, petrol and diesel.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), ΔH = −891 kJ/mol

Alkenes

Alkenes undergo addition reactions, such as hydrogenation and halogenation; the double bond provides their reactivity. They may also undergo polymerisation. Examples: ethene, propene and butene. Ethylene (ethene) polymerises in the presence of a catalyst at high temperature and pressure to form polyethene:

nCH2=CH2 (ethene) —400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2/peroxide→ –[CH2–CH2]n– (polythene)

Alkynes

Alkynes are hydrocarbons characterised by a triple bond and are less reactive than alkenes. They can form acetylide compounds; for example, ethyne (acetylene) reacts with sodium amide (a strong base) to produce sodium acetylide and ammonia:

HC≡CH + NaNH2 → HC≡C−Na+ + NH3

Key Points

  • Functional groups decide both the properties and the reactions of a molecule.
  • Alkanes are saturated and unreactive, but burn completely to CO2 and H2O.
  • Alkenes react by addition across the C=C bond and can polymerise.
  • Ethene polymerises to polythene at 400°C and 100 atm with a peroxide/O2 initiator.
  • Alkynes have a C≡C triple bond and form acetylides with strong bases like NaNH2.
